papers.title: Show Your Work: Can Small Open Models Read SEC Filings with Evidence a Machine Can Check?
papers.abstract: A fluent answer from a language model is not a verified one. We ask whether small open models that run on a single consumer GPU can extract numbers from SEC filings with evidence a machine can check: the page and a verbatim quote containing the number. We introduce Filing-Evidence, a benchmark of 1,000 questions over 90 recent 10-K and 10-Q filings of 45 US companies, with answer keys taken from the filers' inline XBRL tags. We evaluate ten instruct models from ten developers (7-21B parameters) on one RTX 4090 in three setups: plain, check-and-retry, and the model's own reasoning mode. Accuracy with checkable evidence ranges from 17.1% to 82.7% in the plain setup, and the best result is 84.5% (Qwen3.5-9B). An automatic checker rejects many wrong answers, but between 16 and 167 answers per 1,000 give a wrong value for an answerable question and still pass every check. In the plain setup, 57% of these are scale or unit errors and 30% take another period or column of the right line. Reasoning significantly reduces such errors for 4 of 5 models that offer it. Retrying after a failed check raises accuracy by up to 3.9 points but never reduces them. Questions, model outputs, code and protocol are public.
papers.summary: Small open models that fit on a single consumer GPU are tested on extracting numbers from SEC filings along with machine-checkable evidence: the page and a verbatim quote containing the number. The `Filing-Evidence` benchmark holds 1,000 questions over 90 recent 10-K and 10-Q filings, with answer keys taken from the filers' inline XBRL tags, and ten 7-21B-parameter models are run on one RTX 4090 in plain, check-and-retry, and reasoning setups. Accuracy with checkable evidence spans 17.1% to 82.7% in the plain setup and peaks at **84.5% with `Qwen3.5-9B`**, yet 16 to 167 answers per 1,000 give a wrong value and still pass every check, mostly through scale or unit errors (57%) or reading another period or column (30%). Reasoning mode significantly reduces these errors for 4 of 5 models that offer it, and retrying after a failed check adds up to 3.9 points of accuracy.

papers.title: How Much Dependency Can a Marginal Rule See? Total Correlation in Diffusion LM Parallel Decoding
papers.abstract: A masked diffusion language model is fast because it commits several tokens per step. Each token is sampled from its own marginal, so the dependency between the tokens is lost, and the size of that loss is the conditional total correlation C of the committed set. Most decoders choose the set from per-position marginals, which can bound C but cannot determine it. We ask how well they predict it. We estimate C for fixed candidate sets on four masked diffusion LMs from two families. On three of the four, the best marginal-only predictor is off by about one bit (0.74 to 1.17), 1.8 to 3.7 times less than a baseline that knows only the bound, and most of this accuracy comes from the bound itself. On a subset, our estimate ranks sets like the exact KL cost of a parallel commit, but sits a median 0.4 to 1.1 bits below it on prose and when the rest of the text is still masked. Dream-instruct is the exception, mainly on prose, where its conditionals are least self-consistent. Among six common marginal rules, pooling over the set beats gating on its weakest position in all 24 paired comparisons. The measurement needs a validated readout: Dream and LLaDA place a position's prediction at different logit indices, and the wrong index inflates an inconsistency diagnostic 14 to 41 times. We give three checks that measure the convention. Our results concern predicting C for a fixed set, not what a dependency-aware decoder gains.
papers.summary: Masked diffusion language models commit several tokens per step by sampling each from its own marginal, and the dependency lost is the conditional total correlation of the committed set, which decoders that look only at per-position marginals can bound but not determine. The authors estimate this quantity for fixed candidate sets on four masked diffusion models from two families and test how well marginal-only rules predict it. On three of the four models **the best marginal-only predictor is off by about one bit (0.74 to 1.17)**, 1.8 to 3.7 times better than a baseline that knows only the bound, with `Dream-instruct` on prose the exception; pooling over the set beats gating on its weakest position in all 24 paired comparisons. They also show that `Dream` and `LLaDA` place a position's prediction at different logit indices, and that using the wrong index inflates an inconsistency diagnostic 14 to 41 times.

papers.title: Context Scaling: A New Frontier of AI Scaling
papers.abstract: Many failures of deployed AI arise not from weak inference but from a mismatch between the state a task depends on and the context available when the system acts. Relevant user state, repository revisions, tool traces, sensor readings, or environment changes may be unavailable, distorted, or poorly selected. We call the effort to reduce this bottleneck context scaling. We frame a model as $P_\theta(d\mid c)$ within a system governed by three budgets: training $B_\theta$, decision-time $B_d$, and context-infrastructure $B_c$. Pretraining scaling invests in $\theta$; decision-time scaling searches, refines, or verifies decisions under supplied context; context scaling improves the system's capacity to acquire, represent, deliver, evaluate, and persist deployment state for model use. The three programs interact, but only $B_c$ targets what the system can make available before a decision. This view makes the model-infrastructure pair the unit of analysis. We define effective-context value as a task- and intervention-dependent attribution, separate deployment state from model-visible context, and identify availability, fidelity, selection, and utilization failures. We then organize current mechanisms through a five-operation context lifecycle and propose controlled budget interventions and utility-cost curves for evaluation. The resulting agenda centers on grounded reporting, interaction-data and full-cost infrastructure, and safety and governance for persistent, adaptive systems.
papers.summary: Many deployed AI failures are attributed here to a mismatch between the state a task depends on and the context the system actually has when it acts, such as user state, repository revisions, tool traces, or sensor readings. The authors frame a system as governed by three budgets, for training, decision-time computation, and context infrastructure, and argue that **only the context-infrastructure budget targets what the system can make available before a decision**. They separate deployment state from model-visible context, name four failure types (availability, fidelity, selection, and utilization), organize existing mechanisms into a five-operation context lifecycle, and propose controlled budget interventions and utility-cost curves for evaluation.

papers.title: Constraint-Aware Test-Time Scoring for LLM and VLM Candidate Selection
papers.abstract: When an LLM or VLM produces several candidate answers, picking the best one usually relies on the model's own confidence, a learned judge model, or a domain check. Each has a known weakness: an answer can be fluent but insecure, mathematically plausible but physically infeasible, or rated highly by a judge while quietly breaking a task requirement. We propose a scoring framework that combines a small set of hard checks every answer must pass with a wider set of softer checks whose scores are blended into one number per candidate. This adaptive scoring framework consists of three components: a drafting model that produces the candidates, a configuring model that selects and weights the checks for each task, and scoring models that rate properties no grounded tool can compute. We apply our proposed method to four tasks: writing code that is both correct and secure (CWEval), generating robot manipulation plans (LIBERO with added safety variants), passing competitive-programming hidden tests (LiveCodeBench), and answering questions from retrieved documents (HotpotQA). An ablation study isolates the contribution of each component and finds that the largest gains come from combining hard checks with candidate comparison: on tasks where the first sampled answer is often broken or unsafe, this pairing lifts joint correctness-and-safety by up to +0.21 (retrieval-augmented QA) and code-generation safety by up to +0.28 (CWEval), with the size of the gain tracking how weak the first sample is, falling to near zero or slightly negative where it is already strong. The per-task layer that selects and weights the softer checks adds no measurable value over simpler alternatives. This builds a unified scoring framework, together with an ablation that identifies the grounded hard checks, not the soft-factor configuration, as the source of the gain.
papers.summary: Choosing the best of several candidate answers from a language or vision-language model usually relies on model confidence, a learned judge, or a domain check, each of which can miss answers that are fluent but insecure or infeasible. The proposed framework combines a small set of hard checks every candidate must pass with softer checks blended into one score, using a drafting model, a configuring model that picks and weights checks per task, and scoring models. Across `CWEval`, `LIBERO` with safety variants, `LiveCodeBench`, and `HotpotQA`, an ablation finds that **the gains come from pairing hard checks with candidate comparison, up to +0.28 code-generation safety on `CWEval`** and +0.21 joint correctness-and-safety on retrieval-augmented question answering. The gain shrinks to near zero where the first sample is already strong, and the per-task layer that selects and weights soft checks adds no measurable value over simpler alternatives.

papers.title: Attributing Agentic Failure in Reasoning Vision-Language Models with Interactive 2D Environments
papers.abstract: Agentic benchmarks report a success rate that confounds distinct causes of failure: misreading the environment, never working out how components of the environment operates, operating the components in the wrong order, and failing to recover from a mistake, each of which calls for a different fix. We present an early preview of MultiNet v2.0-Gridworld - an interactive maze environment built for attribution rather than ranking. Four different types of mechanisms, namely key-door pairs, switch-gate pairs, distractors and decoys, and ordered combinations of these mechanisms, can be added, modified, or removed independently while the renderer, the action space, and the scoring function stay fixed. A breadth-first search over the joint state of position, facing direction, inventory, and mechanism state gives every instance an exact optimal action count, which sets its difficulty and grades unfinished episodes. We fix the evaluation protocol on 15 held-out mazes over 540 episodes, then evaluate three vision-language models on 50 mazes. They solve 6 of 150 episodes, 45 of the 50 mazes were not solved by any model, and no episode containing a switch-gate mechanism was solved.
papers.summary: Agentic benchmark success rates mix together distinct failure causes: misreading the environment, not working out how its components operate, operating them in the wrong order, and failing to recover from mistakes. An early preview of `MultiNet v2.0-Gridworld` offers an interactive maze environment where key-door pairs, switch-gate pairs, distractors and decoys, and ordered combinations can be added or removed independently while the renderer, action space, and scoring stay fixed, with breadth-first search giving each instance an exact optimal action count. Three vision-language models evaluated on 50 mazes **solve only 6 of 150 episodes**, 45 mazes are solved by no model, and no episode containing a switch-gate mechanism is solved.

papers.title: Quantum Machine Learning for Signature Forgery Detection
papers.abstract: Offline handwritten signatures remain a primary behavioural biometric in legal and financial documents. Detecting skilled forgeries from a static raster image is hard because pen pressure, timing and stroke order are missing. This work studies a family of quantum machine learning pipelines for offline signature forgery detection on a public Kaggle corpus of images split into two classes. We pair a ZZ feature map quantum kernel with three classical learners: K-Nearest Neighbours, Support Vector Machine and Random Forest. We then propose a deeper hybrid that uses EfficientNetB0 as a frozen feature extractor, reduces the resulting 1280 dimensional representation to a qubit register sized subspace through a quantum compatible principal component projection and decides class membership with a nearest neighbour rule. On a single held out test fold the proposed hybrid reaches 92.62 percent accuracy. On stratified five fold cross validation the same pipeline yields a mean accuracy of 91.26 percent with a standard deviation of 1.13 percent. The pipeline keeps a quantum embedding step that is portable to NISQ hardware. We report a controlled ablation across six quantum variants, confusion matrices, a t SNE projection and per class precision, recall and F1 score.
papers.summary: Detecting skilled forgeries from static signature images is hard because pen pressure, timing, and stroke order are missing. The authors pair a ZZ feature map quantum kernel with K-Nearest Neighbours, Support Vector Machine, and Random Forest classifiers, and propose a hybrid that uses a frozen `EfficientNetB0` feature extractor, projects its 1280-dimensional output to a qubit-register-sized subspace, and classifies with a nearest-neighbour rule. On a public Kaggle signature corpus the hybrid reaches 92.62 percent accuracy on a single held-out fold and **91.26 percent mean accuracy under stratified five-fold cross-validation**, alongside an ablation over six quantum variants.

papers.title: AutoformBench: A Lean Formalization Benchmark for Advanced Mathematics
papers.abstract: AI systems are increasingly capable of producing machine-checked Lean proofs of advanced mathematical results. Real mathematical formalization, however, is not isolated theorem proving: it requires building the definitions and intermediate lemmas that connect a result to a formal library. Existing evaluations often provide isolated theorem statements in settings where much of this supporting theory is already available in Mathlib. We introduce AutoformBench, a benchmark of 341 Lean 4 formalization tasks drawn from 24 advanced mathematical sources. Lean-experienced mathematicians formalized and audited each target statement, leaving the corresponding Lean proof to the evaluated agent. Each problem is embedded in a broader mathematical development: agents receive the informal proof but must translate it into Lean while constructing the missing definitions, intermediate lemmas, and supporting infrastructure. We compare the performance of frontier models on these problems. We find a largely shared difficulty frontier: success depends less on mathematical domain than on models' ability to construct missing formal infrastructure. Data and code at https://github.com/facebookresearch/autoformbench
papers.summary: Existing evaluations of machine-checked proving tend to give isolated theorem statements whose supporting theory already exists in `Mathlib`, whereas real formalization requires building definitions and intermediate lemmas. `AutoformBench` contains **341 `Lean 4` formalization tasks drawn from 24 advanced mathematical sources**, with target statements formalized and audited by Lean-experienced mathematicians and the proofs left to the evaluated agent, which receives the informal proof but must construct the missing infrastructure. Comparing frontier models reveals a largely shared difficulty frontier, where success depends less on mathematical domain than on the ability to build missing formal infrastructure.

papers.title: The Bundesrat corpus: A dataset of political discourse in the German Federal Council
papers.abstract: The Bundesrat is Germany's second legislative chamber and a constitutional veto player within its political system. The members of the Bundesrat are delegates of state governments. Tracing the political discourse in the Bundesrat is challenging as it has a limited machine-readable corpus available. To address this issue, we present a speaker-attributed corpus of 1,067 Bundesrat plenary sessions from the chamber's first session on 7 September 1949 to 10 July 2026. In this period, a total of 53,362 speeches by 2,473 individuals were delivered in the chamber, including written statements. Each speech includes a speech ID, the full German text, the speaker's name, the date and location of the session, the federal state that the speaker represents, the speaker's role (if applicable), the type of contribution, and the speaker's gender. The dataset provides interdisciplinary research opportunities across computational political science, legislative studies, and parliamentary discourse analysis, coupled with discourse from the Bundestag.
papers.summary: Germany's second legislative chamber, the Bundesrat, has had little machine-readable text available for studying its political discourse. The authors release a speaker-attributed corpus covering **1,067 plenary sessions from 7 September 1949 to 10 July 2026, with 53,362 speeches by 2,473 individuals**, including written statements. Each speech carries an ID, full German text, speaker name, session date and location, the federal state represented, speaker role, contribution type, and speaker gender.

papers.title: MGMem: An Efficient, Deterministic, and Provenance-Preserving Framework for Long-Horizon Agent Memory
papers.abstract: Long-horizon Large Language Model (LLM) agents need persistent memory that surfaces the right past interaction at the right time across thousands of turns. Many systems index by invoking generative LLMs to rewrite history into summaries, facts, or knowledge graphs--a step that is (a) costly (thousands of generative calls per build), (b) non-deterministic (undermining reproducibility and giving inconsistent answers across runs), and (c) provenance-erasing (the reader sees synthesized text, not the original turn). We propose MGMem, a framework with no generative indexing calls that replaces this step with a deterministic discriminative-parser pipeline: recurring mentions across sessions are organized into an incidence graph, question mentions are resolved by a subject-conditioned three-stage resolver, and raw dialogue episodes are returned to the reader. On English multi-session dialogue QA, MGMem outperforms matched-protocol baselines on LoCoMo without generative indexing calls; on the full LongMemEval-S, it remains competitive overall and leads or ties on single-session types among local retrieval comparisons. Code: https://github.com/junhong-h/MGMem
papers.summary: Memory systems for long-horizon large language model (LLM) agents often index history by having a generative model rewrite it into summaries, facts, or knowledge graphs, which is costly, non-deterministic, and hides the original turns from the reader. `MGMem` replaces that step with a deterministic discriminative-parser pipeline: recurring mentions across sessions form an incidence graph, question mentions are resolved by a subject-conditioned three-stage resolver, and raw dialogue episodes are returned. It **outperforms matched-protocol baselines on `LoCoMo` with no generative indexing calls**, and on the full `LongMemEval-S` it stays competitive overall while leading or tying on single-session question types among local retrieval comparisons.

papers.title: Feature-Based Explainability of Transformer Scoring Models: A Fidelity-First Framework for Automated Writing Assessment
papers.abstract: Transformer-based automated writing scoring models can achieve strong agreement with human scores while providing limited transparency into the response characteristics associated with their predictions. This study evaluated a feature-based post-hoc explanation approach in which explanatory fidelity was established before feature importance was interpreted. English Language Arts responses from three writing prompts in Grades 6 and 8 were analyzed, with about 12,700 responses per prompt and separate DeBERTa-v3-base research models for Expression and Conventions. Each response was represented by 61 interpretable linguistic and writing-quality features. Four approaches - theory-driven composites, hierarchical feature groupings, exploratory factor analysis, and Random Forest surrogates - were compared in their ability to reproduce DeBERTa predictions. Random Forest surrogates produced the largest observed R2 values across all six prompt-by-trait conditions, with held-out R2 values from .81 to .95. SHAP analyses showed substantial overlap in high-importance features across traits, with 75% to 90% of the top 20 features shared. Trait differentiation occurred mainly through relative feature weighting: Expression showed greater importance for lexical and conceptual indicators, whereas Conventions showed greater importance for sentence-level and syntactic-control indicators. Under researcher-defined mappings, rubric correspondence was 90%-95% for Expression and 12%-18% for Conventions. These percentages are descriptive and conditional on the mappings and available linguistic features. The findings support a fidelity-first framework for examining apparent scoring priorities while distinguishing post-hoc evidence about model behavior from direct explanation of transformer internals.
papers.summary: Transformer-based automated writing scorers agree well with human raters but reveal little about which response characteristics drive their predictions. Using about 12,700 Grade 6 and 8 English Language Arts responses per prompt and separate `DeBERTa-v3-base` models for Expression and Conventions, the study represents each response with 61 interpretable linguistic features and checks how faithfully four surrogate approaches reproduce the model's scores before interpreting feature importance. **Random Forest surrogates reproduce the predictions best, with held-out R2 from .81 to .95**, and `SHAP` analyses show 75% to 90% of the top 20 features shared across the two traits, which differ mainly in relative weighting. Under researcher-defined mappings, correspondence with the rubric is 90%-95% for Expression but only 12%-18% for Conventions.

papers.title: Psychophysics of Duration Perception in Multimodal Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Studies of time perception in language models focus mainly on text-based settings. Yet multimodal models are increasingly used for tasks that require perceiving the passage of time, making the limits of their temporal perception important to understand. We measure the limits of duration perception from audio against a human baseline to address this gap. Drawing from psychophysics, we operationalise duration perception as a melody recognition task, testing when a melody becomes unrecognisable as it is slowed down. Of 21 tested models, most cannot recognise well-known melodies without labelled in-context examples. With in-context examples, seven recognise melodies reliably, most peaking within the median human recognition band. Generalisation is limited: (i) recognition peaks shift with in-context example speed, (ii) melody titles induce prediction bias, and (iii) providing examples with scientific pitch notation does not prevent accuracy declining at long note durations for most models. In humans, the recognition window is a property of the perceiver; in current models, it is largely a property of the prompt.
papers.summary: Duration perception from audio in multimodal language models is measured against a human baseline using a psychophysics-style task: recognising a well-known melody as it is progressively slowed down. Of 21 models tested, most cannot recognise melodies without labelled in-context examples, and **only seven recognise them reliably once examples are given**, mostly peaking within the median human recognition band. Generalisation is limited, since recognition peaks shift with the speed of the in-context examples, melody titles bias predictions, and supplying scientific pitch notation does not stop accuracy falling at long note durations for most models. The recognition window therefore behaves largely as a property of the prompt, whereas in humans it is a property of the perceiver.

papers.title: Neighbor Crowding Predicts Feature Stability in Sparse Autoencoders
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) offer an approach to identify language model representations by breaking apart polysemantic features into more sparse, interpretable ones. Yet, it is challenging to identify which of the learned features are actually stable, rather than artifacts of initialization. One approach is to train multiple SAE seeds, and compare the learned features across seeds by cosine similarity, but this is notably costly. This raises the question of whether stable features can be identified without the computational expense of training multiple seeds. In this work, we examine cross-seed feature stability across differing levels of training tokens, and demonstrate that in TopK SAEs, it is highly predictable using six computationally cheap statistics derived from a single training run. Neighbor crowding, a geometric property of the dictionary, is the strongest single predictor, with features that sit in dense regions of the unit sphere more likely to be stable than isolated ones.
papers.summary: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) decompose language model representations into sparser features, but telling stable features from artifacts of initialization normally requires training several seeds and comparing them by cosine similarity. The authors examine cross-seed stability at different amounts of training tokens and find that in `TopK` SAEs it is highly predictable from six cheap statistics computed on a single training run. **Neighbor crowding, a geometric property of the dictionary, is the strongest single predictor**: features sitting in dense regions of the unit sphere are more likely to be stable than isolated ones.

papers.title: REI: Learning Ideation from Repository Evolution
papers.abstract: As AI systems become increasingly capable of executing and evaluating experiments, ideation is emerging as a bottleneck in automated scientific and engineering iteration. In many real-world domains, useful ideas are sparse and their validation is costly, making direct online exploration inefficient. We observe that repository evolution provides a scalable source of reusable technical experience: code changes record concrete technical hypotheses, while subsequent revisions, adoption, and reuse provide signals about their utility. Based on this observation, we propose REI, a Repository Evolution-driven Ideation framework that learns reusable ideation policies from repository evolution, injecting domain-specific technical experience into model parameters and reducing reliance on costly trial-and-error. We further identify a hidden failure mode in quality-driven ideation optimization: semantic diversity collapse. Although generated ideas can remain lexically diverse, they increasingly concentrate in a small number of dominant method families, limiting cross-task generalization and long-tail exploration. To address this problem, we introduce Semantic Prior Optimization and Debiasing (SPOD), a diversity-preserving alignment mechanism that makes method identity explicit, corrects category-level reward bias, and limits redundant accumulation within the same method family while retaining strong representatives. Experiments on public benchmarks and a real-world industrial setting demonstrate improvements in ideation quality, method diversity, cross-task generalization, and long-tail exploration.
papers.summary: Generating useful technical ideas is treated as a bottleneck for automated experimentation, since good ideas are sparse and validating them is expensive. `REI`, a Repository Evolution-driven Ideation framework, learns ideation policies from the history of code repositories, where code changes record concrete hypotheses and later revisions, adoption, and reuse signal their usefulness. The authors identify **semantic diversity collapse, in which quality-optimized ideas stay lexically varied but concentrate in a few dominant method families**, and counter it with Semantic Prior Optimization and Debiasing (`SPOD`), which makes method identity explicit, corrects category-level reward bias, and limits redundancy within a family. Experiments on public benchmarks and an industrial setting report gains in idea quality, method diversity, cross-task generalization, and long-tail exploration.

papers.title: Semantic Density Does Not Predict Agent-Memory Collapse
papers.abstract: Persistent textual memory can improve LLM agents, but repeated updates can erode task performance. We ask whether memory-store statistics warn before held-out accuracy declines. We registered mean pairwise cosine similarity ($\rho$) and 13 additional geometry, retrieval, and graph statistics on 805 snapshots from 13 memory methods across ALFWorld, AppWorld, ScienceWorld, WebShop, and two ARC-AGI settings. These methods store trajectories, rules, workflows, strategies, or linked records, using selective retrieval or whole-store prompting. No such statistic reliably predicted early signs of task accuracy decline, and $\rho$ had zero median lead. With the checkpoint after peak accuracy as a secondary decline point, measures of highly similar pairs and nearest-neighbor crowding changed earlier but did not consistently outperform stored-item count. We trained classifiers on this corpus and applied them unchanged to PropWorld runs of up to 5,000 crafting tasks. They falsely flagged 56.9% of checkpoints from size-limited stores with stable accuracy and detected only 18% of checkpoints after task success fell to zero. Thus, global semantic density did not provide a reliable warning, while local crowding did not transfer consistently across memory designs. In these long-horizon runs, size-limited stores remained stable, while the sole failure arose when unbounded whole-store prompting exceeded model input capacity, which token growth predicted directly.
papers.summary: Persistent textual memory can help LLM agents, but repeated updates can erode performance, so the authors test whether statistics of the memory store give advance warning of an accuracy decline. They track mean pairwise cosine similarity and 13 other geometry, retrieval, and graph statistics over 805 snapshots from 13 memory methods across `ALFWorld`, `AppWorld`, `ScienceWorld`, `WebShop`, and two `ARC-AGI` settings. **No statistic reliably predicted early accuracy decline**, and classifiers trained on this corpus and applied unchanged to `PropWorld` runs of up to 5,000 tasks falsely flagged 56.9% of checkpoints from stable size-limited stores while catching only 18% of checkpoints after success fell to zero. Size-limited stores stayed stable in the long runs, and the one failure came from unbounded whole-store prompting exceeding the model's input capacity, which token growth predicted directly.

papers.title: General-Purpose Decision Models for AI Configuration Tuning
papers.abstract: AI configuration tuning searches for settings that improve the performance of AI systems under a limited budget. Existing tuners use different sampling and search policies, making the choice of decision strategy central to both tuning quality and cost. We investigate whether general-purpose decision models can guide tuning, using Jev as a deployed representative that returns structured choices and numeric scores across diverse tasks. To assess where it helps, we compare its use as an optimizer, performance predictor, and region guider against conventional methods and a large language model (LLM) on eight AI tuning tasks. Conventional optimizers attain rank 1 in six of eight comparisons. Similarly, established predictors outperform Jev in seven. Through region guidance, however, it finds configurations with lower perplexity than those selected by the native tuner, offering a quality gain when additional decision time and API fees are acceptable. These findings yield actionable recommendations on selecting the decision role, retaining conventional predictors, and balancing tuning quality against cost.
papers.summary: Configuration tuning for AI systems searches for better settings under a limited budget, and the study asks whether a general-purpose decision model can guide that search. Using `Jev` as a deployed representative, the authors test it as an optimizer, a performance predictor, and a region guider against conventional methods and a large language model on eight tuning tasks. **Conventional optimizers rank first in six of eight comparisons** and established predictors beat `Jev` in seven, but when used for region guidance it finds lower-perplexity configurations than the native tuner at the cost of extra decision time and API fees.

papers.title: Dynamics of Collective Diversity in Human-AI Co-Creation for Creative Tasks
papers.abstract: Generative AI systems are increasingly deployed at scale to support human users in creative tasks across a variety of domains. However, as more users adopt the same AI agent, the resulting artifacts may become increasingly homogeneous, leading to a collapse in collective diversity. Prior work has documented this risk, but lacks a systematic framework for understanding how collective diversity changes as AI adoption scales across co-creation settings. In this work, we conduct a large-scale crowdsourcing study to understand and model the dynamics of collective diversity, quality, and effort in human-AI co-creation across two creative domains: Creative Hypothesis Generation and Creative Story Writing. We find that current AI agents used in co-creation can improve artifact quality and reduce effort, but at the cost of declining collective diversity as adoption increases. We further show that more fine-grained human-AI interaction, along with more diverse agent policies, can mitigate this collapse. Finally, we fit predictive models that quantify how collective diversity scales with adoption across co-creation settings, providing insights for designing AI agents that aim to preserve collective diversity.
papers.summary: When many people use the same generative AI assistant for creative work, their outputs may converge, reducing diversity across the population. A large-scale crowdsourcing study models how collective diversity, quality, and effort change with AI adoption in two domains, creative hypothesis generation and creative story writing. Current AI agents improve artifact quality and reduce effort, but **collective diversity declines as adoption increases**; finer-grained human-AI interaction and more diverse agent policies mitigate the collapse. The authors also fit predictive models of how collective diversity scales with adoption across co-creation settings.

papers.title: Formalization, Transparency, and Collusion in Open-Source Game Theory
papers.abstract: Cooperation among AI agents will undermine alignment protocols when it takes the form of collusion. Under these protocols, agents often have some information about one another, and how much they have may determine whether they collude. Open-source game theory studies the extreme case, in which each program reads its opponent's source code and acts based on what it can prove about it. We develop formal foundations for this theory: we specify a concrete proof system, resolve an open problem concerning DupocBot and CupodBot through a transposition argument, and mechanize the framework in Lean 4; to our knowledge, this is the first mechanization of resource-bounded open-source game theory. We then extend the framework to the more realistic setting of partial transparency, where each program receives only partial information about its opponent. In Prisoner's Dilemma experiments, where mutual cooperation models collusion, greater transparency increases both the cooperation sustainable in equilibrium and the cooperation selected by replicator dynamics. This suggests that controlling how much agents can know about one another matters for alignment protocols.
papers.summary: Collusion among AI agents could undermine alignment protocols, and whether agents collude may depend on how much they know about each other; open-source game theory studies the extreme case where each program reads its opponent's source code and acts on what it can prove. The authors specify a concrete proof system, resolve an open problem about `DupocBot` and `CupodBot` with a transposition argument, and mechanize resource-bounded open-source game theory in `Lean 4`. Extending the framework to partial transparency, their Prisoner's Dilemma experiments show that **greater transparency increases both the cooperation sustainable in equilibrium and the cooperation selected by replicator dynamics**.

papers.title: Verified experience improves materials prediction with large language models
papers.abstract: Materials discovery is an iterative loop: experiments and calculations verify predictions, and each outcome can inform the next. Yet most predictors are specialized single-task models fixed after training. Large language models have recently emerged as predictors across heterogeneous tasks but generally underperform specialized models, and retrieval-augmented variants discard their own outcomes. Benchmarks also score queries in isolation, leaving improvement from outcomes untested. Here we construct MatMemBench, a sequential benchmark of 22 materials tasks that reveals outcomes only after prediction and tests online adaptation, memory retention and cross-task transfer. We present MatRecall, a framework that lets large language models store verified predictions, with evidence, outcome and error, as episodes and recall them without retraining. MatRecall improved median performance by 62% over a memory-free model, exceeded specialized models on 11 tasks, remained useful after feedback stopped and transferred between related tasks. Verified experience could become a reusable resource for self-improving discovery loops.
papers.summary: Most materials-property predictors are single-task models fixed after training, and large language model predictors generally trail them while discarding the outcomes of their own predictions. `MatMemBench` is a sequential benchmark of 22 materials tasks that reveals outcomes only after each prediction, testing online adaptation, memory retention, and cross-task transfer. `MatRecall` lets a language model store verified predictions with their evidence, outcome, and error as episodes and recall them without retraining; it **improved median performance by 62% over a memory-free model** and exceeded specialized models on 11 tasks. The benefit persisted after feedback stopped and transferred between related tasks.

papers.title: Extraneous Cognitive Load in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Cognitive Load Theory (CLT) shows that human problem-solving is affected by both intrinsic load, arising from task difficulty, and extraneous load, arising from how task information is presented. Large language models (LLMs) show analogous effects: presentation alone can affect model performance, but these effects have not yet been systematically isolated from task difficulty. To address this gap, we introduce CogLoadBench, a controlled benchmark that varies five CLT-inspired presentation factors across three reasoning task families. Across models, we find that higher extraneous load conditions often reduce accuracy by either adding competition or complicating the reasoning path. To support diagnosis and mitigation of load-related effects, we propose the Extraneous Load Score (ELS), a prompt-time metric computed from activations that estimates a model's extraneous load, and show that it generalizes across reasoning task types and load levels. We further show that shifting model representations toward lower-load directions at inference time can improve average model performance without changing prompt content.
papers.summary: Cognitive Load Theory (CLT) separates intrinsic load from task difficulty and extraneous load from how information is presented, and large language models show analogous sensitivity to presentation that has not been isolated from difficulty. `CogLoadBench` varies five CLT-inspired presentation factors across three reasoning task families and finds that higher extraneous load often lowers accuracy by adding competing information or complicating the reasoning path. The authors propose the Extraneous Load Score (`ELS`), a prompt-time metric computed from activations that generalizes across task types and load levels. They further show that **shifting model representations toward lower-load directions at inference time can improve average performance without changing the prompt**.

papers.title: UniMoE-CP: Unified Conditional Waveform Prediction Across Measured Optical Wireless Links
papers.abstract: Shared prediction across measured optical wireless links requires a common model to accommodate link-dependent waveform dynamics. This paper studies unified learning for underwater optical, 100-m visible-light communication and 4.3-km free-space optical links. We formulate received-waveform forecasting from historical observations and known future transmitted excitation using one shared parameter set. UniMoE-CP combines a shared pool of temporal experts, window-dependent routing and spectral covariate fusion with an autoregressive decoder. The design permits conditional specialization while reusing expert parameters across the measured links. Pooled-training benchmarks evaluate each link separately and report an aggregated result using normalized mean square error (NMSE) and normalized mean absolute error (NMAE). The reported average NMSE reductions are 29.9% for 100-m VLC, 29.1% underwater and 21.4% for 4.3-km FSO. The aggregated average NMSE decreases from 0.1645 for the best baseline to 0.1178 for UniMoE-CP.
papers.summary: A single shared model is trained to forecast received waveforms on three measured optical wireless links: underwater optical, 100-m visible-light communication, and 4.3-km free-space optical. `UniMoE-CP` predicts from historical observations and the known future transmitted signal, combining a shared pool of temporal experts, window-dependent routing, and spectral covariate fusion with an autoregressive decoder. Under pooled training, **aggregated average normalized mean square error (NMSE) falls from 0.1645 for the best baseline to 0.1178**, with per-link reductions of 29.9% for visible-light, 29.1% for underwater, and 21.4% for free-space links.

papers.title: The AI Disclosure Paradox: Operational Disclosure and the Rise of Corporate AI Narratives
papers.abstract: AI-related corporate disclosure can expand while becoming less concentrated on current use. Across U.S. SEC filings from 2017 to 2025, AI-related passage intensity increased 6.3-fold between 2017-2022 and 2023-2025, whereas corrected operational-disclosure intensity increased 3.3-fold. The operational share fell from 25.76% to 13.45%; approximately 89% of the net increase in passage intensity fell outside the operational category. The decline persists within sectors and filing types and in 10-K-only analysis. These estimates combine frozen language-model predictions for 26,279 AI-related passages with an audit of 1,000 annotated passages. The findings distinguish growth in organizational attention from growth in implementation-specific claims: more operational disclosure can coexist with a substantially lower operational share. Operational disclosure was thus diluted, not displaced, by nonoperational disclosure. Reading corporate technology narratives therefore requires attention to both disclosure intensity and the organizational state described.
papers.summary: Corporate filings mention AI far more often than before, but it is unclear how much of that text describes AI actually in use. The authors classify 26,279 AI-related passages from U.S. SEC filings (2017-2025) with frozen language-model predictions, corrected against an audit of 1,000 annotated passages. AI passage intensity rose 6.3-fold between 2017-2022 and 2023-2025 while operational disclosure rose 3.3-fold, so **the operational share fell from 25.76% to 13.45%**, a decline that persists within sectors and filing types. They conclude that operational disclosure was diluted by nonoperational narrative, not displaced by it.

papers.title: How Many Samples Is RL Worth? Best-of-N versus RL Post-Training for Text-to-Image Models
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) on a reward that can be checked automatically has become a common last step in the training of text-to-image models. A simpler way to get more correct images is best-of-N: draw N images from the base model and keep the one that a picker prefers. We ask how many base model samples one RL sample is worth, and call this number the exchange rate. We measure it for Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium and its public Flow-GRPO checkpoint on 398 new prompts in the style of GenEval, the benchmark behind the RL reward, with human labels on every prompt and two automatic judges other than the reward. The answer depends on the prompt. Four fifths of the prompts do not ask for a position (for example, one object left of another). On these, the base model catches up: best-of-16 with an off-the-shelf vision-language model (VLM) as the picker is about as good as one RL image. A person who looks through up to 3 base images finds a correct one as often as one RL image is correct. On the prompts that ask for a position, RL is far ahead: a person finds a correct image among 8 base images for only 52% of the prompts, against 92% for one RL image. Over all prompts, our primary test, which we fixed in advance, finds best-of-16 with the VLM picker 9.3 points behind one RL image when both automatic judges must pass an image. People see a smaller gap, 5.5 and 6.5 points in two checks. FLUX.1-dev shows a similar gap in the same test. RL also solves 20 prompts that the base model misses in 128 tries, and 1,024 tries recover half of them. The automatic judges are wrong in opposite directions: a detector-based judge like the reward, as used in our primary test, reports a larger gap than people see, and VLM judges report little or none. Comparisons of RL with best-of-N should therefore check the selected images by hand.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training of text-to-image models is compared against the simpler alternative of drawing N samples from the base model and keeping the best one, to estimate how many base samples one RL sample is worth. Using `Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium` and its `Flow-GRPO` checkpoint on 398 new `GenEval`-style prompts with human labels, the authors find that on the four fifths of prompts without a positional requirement, best-of-16 with a vision-language model (VLM) picker roughly matches one RL image. On positional prompts RL is far ahead: **a person finds a correct image among 8 base samples for only 52% of prompts, versus 92% for a single RL image**. Automatic judges err in opposite directions, with detector-based judges overstating the gap and VLM judges understating it, so the authors recommend checking selected images by hand.

papers.title: Diagnostically Meaningful, Privacy-aware Synthetic Chest CT via Class-Conditional Latent Sampling in Diffusion Autoencoders
papers.abstract:
Large, well-annotated datasets are essential for developing medical artificial intelligence models, yet data sharing is often restricted by privacy regulations. Synthetic images may help address this limitation if they preserve diagnostic information while reducing the risk of reproducing patient data. We developed a diffusion autoencoder-based framework for class-conditional synthetic chest CT generation that incorporates latent-space distance filtering to reduce the likelihood of regenerating training samples.
  A diffusion autoencoder was trained on the public RSNA 2020 Pulmonary Embolism (PE) dataset. PE-positive and PE-negative images were synthesized by sampling latent representations from class-specific kernel density estimates. Samples with a nearest-neighbor latent-space distance below a predefined threshold were rejected. To assess diagnostic utility, ResNet-50 classifiers were trained across 10 independent runs using real, synthetic, or mixed real-synthetic datasets. Performance was evaluated on a held-out real test set using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), with DeLong 95% confidence intervals (CIs).
  Models trained on synthetic data achieved an AUC of 0.862 (95% CI, 0.851-0.874), only slightly lower than models trained on real data (AUC = 0.872, 95% CI, 0.861-0.883) and mixed real-synthetic data (AUC = 0.865, 95% CI, 0.855-0.876). These differences were statistically significant (p < 0.05) but small in absolute terms. A nearest-neighbor copy-detection analysis of 38,000 synthetic slices found no direct copies of real training images.
  These findings indicate that the synthetic CT images preserve diagnostically meaningful information for image-level PE classification while incorporating measures intended to enhance privacy awareness and reduce similarity to real patient data.
papers.summary: Privacy rules limit sharing of medical images, so the authors generate synthetic chest CT slices with a diffusion autoencoder trained on the `RSNA 2020 Pulmonary Embolism` dataset. Latents are sampled from class-specific kernel density estimates, and samples too close to a training latent are rejected to avoid reproducing patient data. `ResNet-50` classifiers trained only on synthetic data reach **an area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.862 versus 0.872 for real data** on a held-out real test set, and a nearest-neighbor check of 38,000 synthetic slices found no direct copies of training images.

papers.title: KiRA: Kronecker Input-Gated Rank Adaptation for Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning of Pretrained Models
papers.abstract: Full fine-tuning of large pretrained models is expensive, and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) is the standard alternative. Most PEFT methods use low-rank updates, whose rank lies far below that of full fine-tuning and is the same for every input. Input-adaptive variants vary the capacity per input but remain within the low-rank bottleneck, and whether a task benefits from input conditioning is not known before training. This paper introduces Kronecker input-gated rank adaptation (KiRA). Instead of the conventional low-rank product, the update $\Delta W$ is the Kronecker product of a frozen random $p\times p$ matrix $A$ and a trainable factor $M(x)$, which overcomes the rank ceiling: because rank is multiplicative under this product, $A$ multiplies the rank of $M(x)$ by $p$ without adding trainable parameters. The factor $M(x)$ is further decomposed as $B_1\,\mathrm{diag}(g(x))\,B_2$, where the input gate $g(x)$, computed once per sample by a network shared across all adapted layers, adjusts the rank of the update to each input in steps of $p$. Where input conditioning is unnecessary, the gate is folded into $B_1$ at deployment. Because the gate changes the rank only in discrete steps, the benefit of input conditioning can be predicted before training from a few hundred labeled inputs. Across six medical imaging and language benchmarks, KiRA attains the highest mean score against five published baselines with 8.7--9.7 times fewer trainable parameters than low-rank adaptation, and the pre-training criterion agrees with the measured benefit of input conditioning on all six tasks.
papers.summary: Low-rank parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods cap the rank of the weight update and use the same rank for every input. `KiRA` instead forms the update as a Kronecker product of a frozen random matrix and a trainable factor, which multiplies the rank without adding trainable parameters, and a shared input gate adjusts the rank per sample in discrete steps. Because the gate acts in discrete steps, the authors say the benefit of input conditioning can be predicted before training from a few hundred labeled inputs. Across six medical imaging and language benchmarks, it attains the highest mean score against five baselines with **8.7 to 9.7 times fewer trainable parameters than low-rank adaptation**.

papers.title: Sequential Testing on Complex and High Dimensional Data Streams Leveraging Unsupervised Model Errors
papers.abstract: We propose two general, distribution-free test statistics for binary Sequential Hypothesis Testing (SHT) and Sequential Change Point Detection (SCPD) respectively, in streaming environments where the data (e.g., network traffic metadata) are too complicated for the exact probabilistic modeling required by conventional likelihood ratio-driven tests. Our framework also addresses the challenge of information asymmetry, where data is available only from the null/pre-change regime and not from the alternative/post-change one such as zero-day attacks or emerging disease related regimes. The proposed statistics monitor the errors of a predictive or reconstructive machine learning model trained solely on null/pre-change data, relying on imperfect generalization (the model's performance will degrade when deployed on data from the alternative/post-change class). Under mild assumptions on the model's errors, we establish rigorous analytical guarantees: strict non-asymptotic error control for SHT, and explicit bounds on the Average Run Length (ARL) and the Expected Detection Delay (EDD) for SCPD. Extensive evaluations in target tracking, chaotic dynamical systems, and real-world network security datasets, demonstrate that our framework consistently satisfies prescribed constraints where existing algorithms succumb to inflated missed detections and/or false alarms. Finally, because our methods operate on scalar errors without requiring online retraining or kernel evaluations, they are highly scalable.
papers.summary: Sequential Hypothesis Testing (SHT) and Sequential Change Point Detection (SCPD) usually need exact probabilistic models of the data, which are unavailable for complex streams such as network traffic, and data from the alternative regime (for example zero-day attacks) is often missing altogether. The authors propose distribution-free test statistics that monitor the errors of a predictive or reconstructive model trained only on null or pre-change data, relying on its performance degrading under the alternative. They prove **non-asymptotic error control for SHT and explicit bounds on Average Run Length and Expected Detection Delay for SCPD** under mild assumptions on the errors. Experiments on target tracking, chaotic dynamical systems, and network security datasets show the prescribed constraints holding where existing algorithms produce inflated missed detections or false alarms.

papers.title: CypherMAS: Benchmarking Routing Reliability in LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems
papers.abstract: Multi-agent systems (MAS) built on large language models (LLMs) distribute reasoning across specialized agents that must exchange messages and invoke tools reliably. Existing evaluations typically couple communication with open domain tasks, making it difficult to determine whether a failure arises from reasoning, malformed tool use, lost messages, or forgotten requests. Prior benchmarks do not isolate communication execution or measure routing redundancy against a known optimal path. We introduce CypherMAS, a synthetic benchmark that isolates communication and routing in fixed multi-agent graphs. Agents in chain, star, bipartite, or ring graphs route cyphered messages to remote peers holding the matching decoders; since the optimal route is known, redundant LLM calls can be measured and routing failures may be easily tracked. Across eleven open-weight models from 4B to 753B, small models fail at routing and tool use, dense models above 27B degrade with diameter, and successful runs exceed minimum LLM calls. These findings identify communication reliability as a distinct scaling bottleneck for multi-agent systems and provide a controlled diagnostic for complex multi-agent systems. The source code is freely available: https://github.com/Andoree/CypherMAS.
papers.summary: Failures in LLM-based multi-agent systems are hard to attribute, because existing benchmarks mix communication with open-domain reasoning. `CypherMAS` is a synthetic benchmark in which agents arranged in chain, star, bipartite, or ring graphs must route cyphered messages to remote peers holding the matching decoders, so the optimal route is known and redundant LLM calls can be counted. Across eleven open-weight models from 4B to 753B parameters, **small models fail at routing and tool use, dense models above 27B degrade as graph diameter grows**, and even successful runs use more than the minimum number of LLM calls. The authors conclude that communication reliability is a scaling bottleneck distinct from reasoning ability.

papers.title: Beyond the Efficiency-Efficacy Dilemma: A Critical Analysis of Transferability in Adversarial Malware Detection
papers.abstract: Machine Learning (ML) models are already being deployed at scale for malware detection. Therefore there is a pressing need to rigorously study adversarial robustness. To that end, we introduce the Adversarial AI Engine (AAIE): a platform for automated security stress-testing. We performed transfer attacks, via EMBER2018, against a Random Forest target. Counterintuitively, we found single-step FGSM to have the highest attack success rate (ASR) of 52.9% compared to iterative PGD with 45.2% (p < 0.002). Compared to iterative attacks which tend to overfit surrogate networks creating brittle perturbations, FGSM created more transferable examples. We benchmarked our attacks using ASR, transferability score, evasion rate, and resilience index. Through these metrics, proposed in concordance with emerging standards in AI governance, we expose shortcomings as our transferability scores peak at ~0.8 with constrained perturbations. We highlight the practical security implications of these findings and demonstrate AAIE for automated adversarial auditing.
papers.summary: Machine-learning malware detectors are tested for robustness to transfer attacks using the Adversarial AI Engine (`AAIE`), a platform for automated security stress-testing. With adversarial examples crafted on surrogate networks from `EMBER2018` and transferred to a Random Forest target, **single-step `FGSM` reached a 52.9% attack success rate versus 45.2% for iterative `PGD`**. The authors attribute this to iterative attacks overfitting the surrogate and producing brittle perturbations. Attacks are also scored by transferability, evasion rate, and a resilience index, with transferability peaking at about 0.8 under constrained perturbations.

papers.title: Focus On Facts: Stylistically Invariant and Factually Sensitive Text Embeddings
papers.abstract: Text embedding models can conflate surface-form similarity with factual identity. Given an altered near-copy with one corrupted fact and a differently worded fact-preserving rewrite, the base model prefers the altered near-copy. We test whether hard-negative contrastive supervision can reduce this surface-similarity shortcut. We construct FOF-Bench, an 83,263-triplet benchmark spanning five domains. Each anchor is paired with an LLM-generated, fact-preserving stylistic rewrite and a matched fact-altered near-copy. We fine-tune FOF-80M (Focus On Facts), an 80M-parameter embedding model, with a triplet contrastive objective that ranks the rewrite above the factual alteration. On 8,327 held-out test triplets, the base model chooses the factually altered text in 99.58% of cases (0.42% factual preference rate; mean separation -0.1650). After fine-tuning, mean positive--negative separation is +0.0329, 98.5% of individual margins move in the intended direction, and the preference rate reaches 29.37%. On DiSC, an external style-transfer corpus, mean cross-style similarity increases from 0.7905 to 0.9559. The model also penalizes omission and transfers poorly to directional tasks such as NLI and summarization. We characterize FOF-80M as a soft factual fingerprint for studying factual retention under stylistic variation, not as a general-purpose factuality metric.
papers.summary: Text embedding models tend to rate a near-copy with one corrupted fact as closer to the original than a reworded version that preserves every fact. The authors build `FOF-Bench`, 83,263 triplets across five domains pairing each anchor with a fact-preserving stylistic rewrite and a fact-altered near-copy, and fine-tune an 80M-parameter embedding model, `FOF-80M`, with a triplet contrastive objective. On held-out triplets, **the rate at which the model prefers the faithful rewrite rises from 0.42% to 29.37%**, and cross-style similarity on the external `DiSC` corpus increases from 0.7905 to 0.9559. The model also penalizes omissions and transfers poorly to natural language inference and summarization, so the authors describe it as a soft factual fingerprint and not a general factuality metric.

papers.title: Anti-AI in the Wild: From Toxic Discourse to Action
papers.abstract: Online discussion of generative AI has become increasingly contentious, and communities devoted to supporting, opposing, or debating AI have emerged on social media. Some of these communities take anti-AI actions, such as deploying crawler tarpits and data-poisoning services to interfere with data collection and model training. Yet, the scope of these actions and their relationship to online discourse remain poorly understood. In this paper, we present the first measurement study of online conflict over generative AI, from toxic discourse to anti-AI actions. We collect 931,640 posts from 25 Reddit communities, label them with a large language model detector validated against human labels, identify 3,312 anti-AI actions, and trace the output of three deployed anti-AI tools. Our analysis reveals that 30.0% of posts in communities devoted to this conflict are toxic, compared to 4.4% in general AI communities. Anti-AI actions in these communities mainly target AI crawling or model training data, such as image cloaking and data poisoning. We further examine the implications of these anti-AI actions for AI training, by analyzing the text and code generated from deployed tools. Notably, 66.5% of the code samples generated by a data-poisoning service contain fabricated facts, misused APIs, or broken logic, yet 93.6% passes a public code-curation pipeline, close to the rate for real source code (95.0%). For crawler tarpit output, adding a period to the end of each paragraph increases the curation survival rate from 16.4% to 91.9%. We also find that crawler tarpit and data-poisoning output has already entered Common Crawl, a widely used public web archive, and that crawler tarpit output has also entered FineWeb, a released pretraining dataset. We hope our study can facilitate a better understanding of online conflict over generative AI and its implications for content moderation and AI training.
papers.summary: Online conflict over generative AI is measured from discourse through to action, using 931,640 posts from 25 Reddit communities labeled by an LLM detector validated against human labels. In communities devoted to the conflict 30.0% of posts are toxic, against 4.4% in general AI communities, and the 3,312 identified anti-AI actions mostly target crawling and training data through image cloaking, data poisoning, and crawler tarpits. Examining output from deployed tools, the authors find **66.5% of code samples from a data-poisoning service contain fabricated facts, misused APIs, or broken logic, yet 93.6% pass a public code-curation pipeline**, close to the 95.0% rate for real code. Tarpit and poisoning output has already entered `Common Crawl`, and tarpit output has also entered the `FineWeb` pretraining dataset.

papers.title: One Token, Many Lessons: Sliding-Window Attention within Gated Delta Networks
papers.abstract: Linear attention compresses historical context into a fixed-size recurrent state, reducing the computational and memory costs of long-sequence modeling. From the perspective of test-time regression (TTR), the state matrix can be viewed as an online-learned regression model, where keys and values serve as inputs and targets respectively, and queries are used to read from the model. From this perspective, the effectiveness of state learning depends not only on the update rule but also on how the key-value learning pairs used for state updates are constructed. While existing work has largely focused on how the state is updated and organized, we investigate how the learning pairs used for state updates are constructed. To this end, we propose Sliding-Window Gated DeltaNet (SWGDN), which replaces short convolutions in Delta-Rule linear attention with sliding-window attention to perform content-dependent local aggregation of projected queries, keys, and values. Our experiments show that SWGDN makes the key-value pairs used in consecutive updates more similar in both GDN2 and KDA. In SWGDN, carrying information from the same token across updates can help the recurrent state reinforce a previously learned association. The local mixing strategy can be incorporated into any Delta-Rule-based linear attention architecture without changing its state update equations or chunkwise parallel algorithms. We apply this strategy to two Delta-Rule variants, GDN2 and KDA, and experimental results demonstrate that SWGDN outperforms the original Delta-Rule baseline across multiple benchmarks.
papers.summary: Linear attention compresses history into a fixed-size recurrent state, which can be viewed as a regression model learned online from key-value pairs. The authors study how those pairs are constructed, where prior work concentrates on the update rule, and propose Sliding-Window Gated DeltaNet (`SWGDN`), which replaces the short convolutions in Delta-Rule linear attention with sliding-window attention over projected queries, keys, and values. This makes the pairs used in consecutive updates more similar, which they argue lets the state reinforce associations it has already learned. Applied to the `GDN2` and `KDA` variants without changing their state update equations or chunkwise parallel algorithms, **it outperforms the original Delta-Rule baselines across multiple benchmarks**.

papers.title: Fast and Scalable Abstract Interpretation for Deep Neural Networks
papers.abstract:
Abstract interpretation can certify properties of Deep Neural Networks (DNNs), but precise analyses remain expensive. General implementations repeat work when analyzing the same architecture under different inputs and properties. Interleaving this work with numerical operations limits GPU utilization and restricts how much of the analysis a tensor compiler can process together.
  We present Scepter, a framework for specializing DNN abstract interpreters through structural semantics. The semantics determine the structure of intermediate abstract values while deferring their numerical evaluation. Structural computations from successive operations can therefore be performed together before certification, generating an executable tensor program. With the abstract interpreter and DNN architecture fixed, the program can be reused with different weights and input regions. We prove that it computes the same bounds as the general interpreter in exact arithmetic. The generated program also exposes operations and their dependencies for tensor compilation and memory planning. We implement Scepter for the tensor programs that Neuton generates from ConstraintFlow specifications.
  We evaluate Scepter on eight abstract interpreters and 44 DNNs against six baseline systems on GPUs and CPUs. Scepter handles networks with up to 153x as many neurons as the largest completed by the corresponding baselines. It completes DeepPoly on ResNet50 and VGG-16, whereas none of the evaluated DeepPoly baselines completes either network. On configurations completed by both systems, GPU geometric-mean speedups over Neuton range from 11.9x to 44.4x across eight analyses, with a 2.60x geometric-mean reduction in peak memory. In an input-splitting case study, Scepter proves 68 properties for which the baselines time out.
  Code: https://github.com/uiuc-focal-lab/constraintflow.git
papers.summary: Certifying deep neural network properties by abstract interpretation is expensive, partly because general implementations redo structural work for each input and property and interleave it with numerical operations. `Scepter` specializes an abstract interpreter to a fixed architecture by resolving the structure of intermediate abstract values ahead of time, producing a reusable tensor program that provably computes the same bounds in exact arithmetic. Evaluated on eight abstract interpreters and 44 networks against six baselines, it handles networks with up to 153x as many neurons and completes `DeepPoly` on `ResNet50` and `VGG-16`, which no evaluated `DeepPoly` baseline does. **GPU geometric-mean speedups over `Neuton` range from 11.9x to 44.4x**, with a 2.60x reduction in peak memory.

papers.title: Onnx2TEE: Automated Graph-Aware Model Partitioning for TEE-based Edge AI Protection
papers.abstract: AI models are increasingly being deployed at the edge. Since these models often require significant research and development to produce, are often deployed in potentially hostile environments, and downstream systems often rely on accurate data; protecting them from theft or manipulation is worthy of serious consideration. Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs), which provide hardware-enforced separation of software execution, can protect model weights but impose strict resource constraints, making full-model execution impractical for large neural networks. We present Onnx2TEE, an automated, model-independent pipeline that partitions ONNX models across rich, trusted execution environments for non-sequential feed-forward networks using graph-aware segmentation to preserve computational dependencies while minimizing boundary communication and reducing TEE-induced inference latency. Evaluation on an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin using an Arm TrustZone TEE demonstrates that model parameters can be highly concentrated in individual segments, supporting selective protection of parameter-dense model components. The evaluation further shows that the generated trusted app's memory requirements depend on both computation and intermediate tensor sizes.
papers.summary: Models deployed on edge devices can be stolen or tampered with, and Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) can protect weights but are too resource-constrained to run large networks whole. `Onnx2TEE` is an automated, model-independent pipeline that partitions non-sequential feed-forward ONNX models between the normal and trusted environments, using graph-aware segmentation to preserve dependencies and limit boundary communication. On an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin with Arm TrustZone, the evaluation shows that **model parameters can be highly concentrated in individual segments**, which supports protecting only the parameter-dense parts. The trusted application's memory needs depend on both the computation and the size of intermediate tensors.

papers.title: What, Who, and When: Structured Harm Assessment for Mental Health Safety via Short Reasoning
papers.abstract: The growing use of large language models (LLMs) for mental health support raises important safety concerns. Existing guard models primarily identify categories of harmful content, often overlooking the context needed to determine an appropriate response. We introduce a clinically grounded taxonomy that characterizes harm along three dimensions: what the harm is, who is involved, and when it occurs. It further separates harm characterization from intervention decisions, thus enabling safety policies to be specified outside the model weights through explicit, clinician-curated instructions that can be updated and audited. We validate the taxonomy with expert clinicians and validate a panel of LLM judges to scale annotation. Relabeling public benchmarks in this taxonomy shows that they rarely contain harm directed at the user, which accounts for nearly half of the harm in real conversations. We then train MindGuard2, a 35B-A3B reasoning-based guard model using supervised fine-tuning on short reasoning traces followed by reinforcement learning with a reasoning-length penalty, to minimize inference overhead while preserving the benefits of reasoning. On two public benchmarks and real-world conversations, MindGuard2 achieves balanced accuracy comparable to the substantially larger GLM-5.3 at approximately 10x lower median latency, advancing the accuracy-latency Pareto frontier. Furthermore, it achieves low false-positive rates at high recall, helping balance the need to detect unsafe situations against the risk of unnecessary interventions that may disrupt support and undermine user trust. We release a safety guardrail model with SOTA performance trained on synthetic data, together with synthetic conversations and annotations of public benchmarks in our taxonomy.
papers.summary: Guard models for mental health conversations usually classify categories of harmful content without the context needed to choose a response. The authors define a clinically grounded taxonomy describing what the harm is, who is involved, and when it occurs, and keep intervention policy outside the model weights in clinician-curated instructions. Relabeling public benchmarks shows they rarely contain harm directed at the user, which makes up nearly half of harm in real conversations. Their guard model `MindGuard2`, trained with supervised fine-tuning on short reasoning traces and then reinforcement learning with a reasoning-length penalty, reaches **balanced accuracy comparable to the much larger `GLM-5.3` at roughly 10x lower median latency**.

papers.title: FrId\'eo: French News Outlet Ideology Scoring via Multi-Source Evidence Fusion and Distancing-Aware Lexical Scoring
papers.abstract: Outlet ideology is a standard explanatory variable in media framing, media effects, and political communication research, but continuous, ecosystem-wide coverage lets it enter as graded exposure rather than a coarse bin. For France, existing references are either broad but non-analytic or analytic but sparse and source-specific, and none we are aware of offers ecosystem-wide coverage on a unified continuous scale. We contribute FrId\'eo: to our knowledge the first ecosystem-wide continuous ideology scores for the French press, a transparent composite score for 30 French news outlets, fusing nine independent families of evidence with empirical-Bayes-style shrinkage toward a structural prior. For the text-based family we introduce symmetric plain/qualified scoring, which separates the plain use of ideologically loaded vocabulary from its qualified (distanced) use on both sides, a distinction bag-of-words methods miss. The resulting scale runs from L'Humanit\'e on the far left to Valeurs actuelles on the far right; the far-right pole is near-indistinguishable and CNews ties Le Figaro. Because the text family reads current articles, it also captures editorial change that static sources miss, such as the Journal du Dimanche's sharp rightward shift after its 2023 ownership change. The ordering is robust to perturbation and to dropping any single family, and agrees with held-out Media Bias Fact Check labels. We release the scores, confidence intervals, and replication code.
papers.summary: Research on French media has lacked a continuous ideology scale covering the whole press ecosystem. `FrIdéo` provides composite scores for 30 French news outlets by fusing nine independent families of evidence with empirical-Bayes-style shrinkage toward a structural prior. Its text-based component separates plain use of ideologically loaded vocabulary from qualified, distanced use, which bag-of-words methods miss. The scale runs from L'Humanité on the far left to Valeurs actuelles on the far right, and **the ordering is robust to dropping any single evidence family and agrees with held-out `Media Bias Fact Check` labels**.

papers.title: Two Timescales of Forgetting in Fine-tuning of Language Models: Fast Behavioral Suppression and Slow Representational Drift
papers.abstract: Today, a core pipeline of artificial intelligence systems is pretraining on a broad range of text corpora and then fine-tuning on specific tasks or desired behaviors. Yet we still have limited understanding of how fine-tuning on a restricted data distribution modifies representations acquired during pretraining. In particular, it remains unclear whether surface behavioral suppression happens together with the erasure of latent representations that support it. In this work, we study supervised fine-tuning (SFT) by pretraining transformers on a controlled context-free grammar with hierarchical latent structure, the Random Hierarchy Model (RHM), and fine-tuning with a restricted subset of its generative rules. While during pretraining the model's ability to generate with the correct grammar rules coincides with building the internal representations of the corresponding latent, we find that SFT exhibits a very different dynamics: (i) the generation of deleted rules changes on a fast timescale inversely proportional to the magnitude of the token-latent correlation; meanwhile, their corresponding representations stay intact; (ii) the hidden representations of the deleted rules become forgotten on a much longer timescale, associated with a slow drift of the network parameters. Finally, we observe analogous results in a realistic setup with natural language, suggesting that this timescale separation in forgetting is a more general phenomenon of fine-tuning language models.
papers.summary: Whether fine-tuning erases a pretrained model's internal representations or only suppresses the behavior they support is studied in a controlled setting. Transformers are pretrained on a context-free grammar with hierarchical latent structure, the Random Hierarchy Model (`RHM`), and then fine-tuned on a restricted subset of its rules. **Generation of the deleted rules disappears quickly while their hidden representations stay intact, and those representations are forgotten only on a much longer timescale** tied to slow parameter drift. The authors report analogous results in a natural-language setup.

papers.title: Certify What You Plant: Shortcut-Free Proof Depth in Logical Reasoning Data
papers.abstract: Procedurally generated logic problems are used to both evaluate and train reasoning in language models. Their difficulty is usually set by planting a proof, that is, by sampling a proof of the desired depth and stating its premises as the problem. However, a planted proof is only one possible proof.
