A problem can also have shorter proofs, or several unrelated ones, and its stated depth then overstates what solving it requires. We measure what a problem actually requires, relative to a stated set of inference rules. For each problem, we compute the steps every proof must make, the shortest proof, the number of minimal proofs and the indispensable premises, and export certificates that an independent checker verifies. Audits of eight datasets find depth that is forced (ProofWriter, Blocksworld), problems labelled depth 5 that require about two specific rule applications (FLDx2), and answers that need no particular step (ZebraLogic). We then construct problems whose every proof has a requested structure, using a catalog of shortcuts proved once per rule set. Every constructed problem is checked in full and comes with its own certificate. In training, the best data mixes depths and problem types. At equal size, such mixtures of certified problem types, including model-checking problems that forward generation does not produce, transfer better than FLDx2-style derivation data for Qwen3 models from 0.6B to 8B.
papers.summary: Procedurally generated logic problems set difficulty by planting a proof of a chosen depth, but a problem may also admit shorter or unrelated proofs, so its stated depth can overstate what solving it requires. The authors compute, for each problem, the steps every proof must make, the shortest proof, the number of minimal proofs, and the indispensable premises, and export certificates that an independent checker verifies. Audits of eight datasets find forced depth in `ProofWriter` and `Blocksworld`, but **problems labelled depth 5 in `FLDx2` that require only about two specific rule applications**, and `ZebraLogic` answers that need no particular step. They then construct certified shortcut-free problems, and mixtures of these transfer better than `FLDx2`-style data when training `Qwen3` models from 0.6B to 8B parameters.

papers.title: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis in Jacobian-Space: Language and Vision Models Agree Approximately Up to a Rotation
papers.abstract: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) posits that AI models converge toward a shared representation of the world, even when trained on different data modalities. Previous work has found evidence for the PRH in the activations of vision and language models. In this work, we ask whether vision and language models also converge in how they act on these representations: precisely, in how these internal representations affect the models' output. At a chosen layer of a transformer, the Jacobian lens gives every word in the vocabulary (or class in an image classifier) a vector in the hidden state: the vector that most increases the model's tendency to generate that word, at that position or later, or to predict that class. Collectively, these vectors make up what is referred to as the model's J-space. We find evidence of the PRH in J-space across vision and language models, and furthermore, we find that J-spaces mostly converge up to a rotation. That is, a single rotation, fitted on a subset of words, approximately maps one model's J-space onto another's, and so applies to words and classes it was not fitted on. A word's vector, rotated from a text-only language model's J-space into the visual patch tokens of a vision-language model, changes the object the vision-language model says is in the image (and only in the image region where it is added). Rotated into an image generator's text conditioning, a word's vector changes the object in the generated image. Rotated into an ImageNet classifier (trained without text), it raises that object's class score above almost all others, and vice versa. This suggests that models converge not only in how they represent the world, but also in how they act on it.
papers.summary: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) holds that models trained on different modalities converge toward a shared representation. The authors test whether models also converge in how representations affect outputs, using the Jacobian lens to assign each word or class the hidden-state vector that most increases the model's tendency to produce it, which together form the model's J-space. They find that **a single rotation fitted on a subset of words approximately maps one model's J-space onto another's**, including for words it was not fitted on. Word vectors rotated from a text-only language model change the object a vision-language model reports in an image region, the object an image generator draws, and the class score of an `ImageNet` classifier trained without text.
papers.highlight_summary:
Prior evidence for the Platonic Representation Hypothesis compares static activations, leaving open whether models also converge in how hidden states drive their outputs. Here each word or class gets a `J-lens` vector (its unembedding row pulled back through a context-averaged Jacobian), and the test is whether a single orthogonal Procrustes rotation fitted on a subset of words maps one model's "J-space" onto another's, across 45 language, vision, and multimodal models.

- Across 23 language models from five families, debiased `CKA` between J-space cosine kernels rises from 0.50 at the first block to **0.78** in late layers, above static unembeddings (0.64) and a shuffled null (0.002) but below clipped activation alignment (0.88), and it plateaus beyond roughly 1B parameters.
- A rotation fitted on 6,000 words and tested on 300 held-out words over 56 cross-family pairs reproduces the receiver's own steering side-effect profile at Spearman 0.72–0.78, recovering **92% of the best linear (ridge) map**, with the remaining gap attributed to per-axis rescaling rather than shear.
- Rotated language-model vectors also steer models with paired image–text training: in `Qwen3-VL` they change the reported object in only the steered half of an image on **92%** of tests (87% on full images), and in `SDXL`'s text conditioning they make the generator draw the new object in **55%** of images versus 89% for its own vector and 66% for ridge.
- Supervised `ImageNet` ViTs that never saw text and language models steer each other through one class-agnostic rotation per direction, raising the target's relative logit by about **3.1 nats** (~20× odds) on held-out classes, with positive transfer in all 437 model pairs and 84–85% of ridge.
- Transfer is partial, since ViT–LM rotation reaches only **20–23%** of the receiver's own vector with two-thirds of the gain shared across WordNet siblings, self-supervised `DINOv2` and contrastive `CLIP`/`SigLIP2` backbones without an end-to-end semantic head do not align in J-space, and the explanation for why a rotation suffices remains an untested conjecture.

papers.title: Lost in Translation, Not in Confidence: Benchmarking and Calibrating Multilingual Decision Models
papers.abstract: Decision models are language models fine-tuned to return a probability for each option of a typed query, which routers and guardrails threshold directly. They are built on multilingual bases but ranked almost entirely in English. We evaluate 25 top-ranked open-weight decision models on 17 tasks in 14 languages, comparing each language with English on parallel items. Every model loses accuracy in every language, from about 2 points in high-resource languages to 8 in Tamil, while confidence falls only half as much: a threshold set for 95\% accuracy in English yields 90% in Tamil. The size of the loss is set by the language and the base model rather than by leaderboard rank. In 81 controlled fine-tuning runs, task skill learned in English transfers to other languages and a few thousand target-language items narrow large losses, but neither more data nor full-parameter tuning closes them. Finally, the same test items are answered more accurately in all 23 benchmark--language pairs we compare when an LLM rather than a person translated them, so LLM-translated test sets understate the gap.
papers.summary: Decision models are language models fine-tuned to return a probability per option, which routers and guardrails threshold directly, and they are ranked almost entirely in English. Evaluating 25 open-weight decision models on 17 tasks in 14 languages with parallel items, the authors find every model loses accuracy in every language, from about 2 points in high-resource languages to 8 in Tamil, while confidence falls only half as much. As a result, **a threshold set for 95% accuracy in English yields 90% in Tamil**. In 81 fine-tuning runs, a few thousand target-language items narrow large losses without closing them, and LLM-translated test sets are answered more accurately than human-translated ones in all 23 benchmark-language pairs compared, so they understate the gap.

papers.title: Building a Unified Inline Code Editing Model for GitHub Copilot
papers.abstract: AI-assisted coding ranges from fully agentic coding to inline code suggestions in the editor. Inline suggestions require predicting a developer's most likely next edit from an editing session. The next edit may lie at the cursor, in nearby lines, or farther away, and one editing intent can span several of these. The preceding system queries separate completion, nearby edit, and long-distance edit models, each with its own output format, in a fixed sequence; it thus cannot express intents spanning distant locations in one response, can require several sequential model calls per suggestion, and prioritizes completion even when a correction would serve better. We present a unified model that predicts all three edit types in one output space: a sequence of anchored diff patches specifying locations, deleted lines, and added lines. This representation permits multiple edits per response, so the client can serve later edits from a cache without further model calls. We train this model in two phases, first unifying next edit and long-distance edit prediction, then adding code completion. We synthesize multi-edit supervision from single-edit data via model pseudolabeling and edit history playback. We use a binary LLM-graded reward, a patch validity taxonomy shared by data filtering, reward, and evaluation, and grader boosting for targeted failure modes. Phase 2 also adapts how the client processes and presents model outputs. In controlled online A/B experiments in GitHub Copilot, Phase 1 significantly reduces time to display by 6.77% and output tokens by 58.93% relative to the three-model baseline. In Phase 2, the 3-in-1 model and client adaptations reduce dismissed suggestions per user by 10.06% relative to the 2-in-1 model paired with the completion model. Throughout this report, we also share our methodology and learnings in evaluation, training, and end-to-end model and system design.
papers.summary: Inline suggestions in `GitHub Copilot` previously came from separate completion, nearby-edit, and long-distance-edit models queried in a fixed sequence, which could not express one intent spanning distant locations and could need several model calls per suggestion. The authors replace them with a single model that emits a sequence of anchored diff patches, allowing multiple edits per response that the client can serve from a cache. Training uses multi-edit supervision synthesized from single-edit data and a binary LLM-graded reward. In online A/B experiments, the first phase **cut output tokens by 58.93% and time to display by 6.77%** relative to the three-model baseline, and the full three-in-one model reduced dismissed suggestions per user by 10.06%.

papers.title: Brand Recall and Category Accuracy in Language Models: An Audit of 1,000 B2B SaaS Brands
papers.abstract: A language model can name a brand without classifying it correctly. This study measures these outcomes separately for 1,000 B2B SaaS brands across 333 product categories. On Gemma 4 12B, with no external retrieval, category prompts elicit 510 brands (51.0%). A separate five-candidate category probe ranks the reference label first for 787 brands, a distractor first for 194, and yields little separation for 19. Among the 981 separated rankings, the error rate is 19.8%. It falls to 3.5% for the 547 brands with a winner-to-runner-up log-probability margin above 0.6. These are within-cohort measurements, not calibrated confidence estimates. Exploratory regressions associate technical coverage with recall and an owned-properties composite with category accuracy, but the composites use different adjustment sets and do not establish causal effects. Across four Gemma generations, measured recall is 39.8%, 44.3%, 51.1% and 51.0%. A separate representation-based sentiment measure has little linear association with customer ratings (r=0.03, n=921). The findings support reporting recall and category accuracy separately. Failure to elicit a brand does not establish its absence from model parameters or training data.
papers.summary: Whether a language model can name a brand is measured separately from whether it classifies that brand correctly, for 1,000 B2B SaaS brands across 333 product categories. On `Gemma 4 12B` without retrieval, category prompts elicit 51.0% of the brands, and a five-candidate category probe ranks the reference label first for 787 of them. **Among the 981 brands with separated rankings the category error rate is 19.8%**, falling to 3.5% for brands with a larger log-probability margin. Recall across four `Gemma` generations is 39.8%, 44.3%, 51.1%, and 51.0%, and a representation-based sentiment measure shows almost no linear association with customer ratings.

papers.title: Who Attributes a Mind to Whom? Mutual Theory of Mind in Simulated User-Assistant Conversation
papers.abstract: When users assume that an AI chatbot has mental states, they are more likely to develop over-reliance, emotional dependence, and in extreme cases, psychological harm or self-harm. However, how these mind attributions arise in conversations and how human or AI factors influence this is still unknown. We study how users attribute minds using a minimal framework: a simulated user with different characteristics chats with assistants that differ in social style and memory. We also introduce a message-level measure of who attributes a mind to whom in four directions, checked with trained coders and applied by a fine-tuned encoder that reproduces an LLM judge. Our results show that, on average, nine out of thirteen characteristics raised simulated users' attribution to the assistant. We found that relational needs such as attachment anxiety raised it as theory predicts, some general personality traits raised it as well, and AI-specific characteristics the least. By contrast, the assistant's social style barely changed simulated users' mind attribution. Instead, sycophantic instructions raised the assistant's attribution to itself. Memory raised users' attribution only with some user models. The model playing the user changed overall attribution and the effects of characteristics, style, and memory. Our framework measures how persona descriptions affect mind attribution in simulation. It gives concrete hypotheses for human studies and shows the need for more consistent user simulators.
papers.summary: Users who attribute mental states to chatbots are more prone to over-reliance and emotional dependence, yet how such attributions arise in conversation is unclear. A simulated user with varying characteristics chats with assistants that differ in social style and memory, and a message-level measure, applied by a fine-tuned encoder that reproduces an LLM judge, tracks who attributes a mind to whom in four directions. On average, **nine of thirteen user characteristics raised the simulated user's mind attribution to the assistant**, with relational needs such as attachment anxiety among them, while the assistant's social style barely mattered and sycophantic instructions instead raised the assistant's attribution to itself. Results shifted with the model playing the user, which the authors take as showing the need for more consistent user simulators.

papers.title: A Hierarchy of Risk Certificates for Representation-Based Prediction
papers.abstract: Representation-based prediction underlies many machine-learning systems. Yet a fitted predictor's failure to meet an accuracy requirement does not establish that its representation-decoder class cannot meet it. We study optimal population mean squared error (MSE) over Lipschitz decoders acting on a fixed representation. For blocks of $b\geq2$ independent and identically distributed (iid) observations, we minimize total squared error (normalized by $b-1$) under pairwise Lipschitz constraints. We prove that expected block scores form nondecreasing lower bounds on optimal class risk and converge to that risk on compact metric feature spaces, although no fixed block size provides a uniform relative guarantee. Verified dual lower bounds and iid calibration observations independent of model development, with bounded targets and predictions, yield simultaneous lower confidence bounds on optimal class risk and upper confidence bounds on fitted-predictor risk. These bounds can establish that every admissible decoder exceeds a prescribed MSE threshold or that an admissible fitted predictor meets it. Controlled experiments illustrate population-risk certification; fixed PTB-XL and Bike Sharing experiments provide deterministic empirical-risk conclusions. The results support principled assessment and selection of representation-decoder configurations. Efficient certification at scale and extensions to dependent observations remain open problems.
papers.summary: A fitted predictor missing an accuracy target does not prove that its representation-decoder class cannot meet it, so the authors study the optimal population mean squared error (MSE) achievable by Lipschitz decoders on a fixed representation. They score blocks of independent observations by minimizing total squared error under pairwise Lipschitz constraints and prove that **expected block scores form nondecreasing lower bounds that converge to the optimal class risk** on compact metric feature spaces, though no fixed block size gives a uniform relative guarantee. Combined with independent calibration data, this yields simultaneous confidence bounds that can certify either that every admissible decoder exceeds an MSE threshold or that a fitted predictor meets it. Experiments on controlled data, `PTB-XL`, and `Bike Sharing` illustrate the certificates, with efficient certification at scale left open.

papers.title: Temporal Weight Surgery: Repairing Video Grounding with LLM Editors
papers.abstract: A surgeon first finds what is wrong, then fixes only that part. We use this idea for video grounding, where video-language models often find the right moment in a long video but write its time wrong. In Temporal Weight Surgery (TWS), a general-purpose LLM reads the model's weights and activations, finds where the error arises and repairs it there, without gradients. Separate sessions find the same cause, and this diagnosis of where and why the model fails is our main contribution. Three GPT-6 Astra sessions trace a dropped digit in TimeLens-8B to one MLP layer, and the largest edit gains 7.9 mIoU on 1,215 unseen questions and 18.3 on videos of 30 minutes or more. Two Claude Opus 5.5 sessions trace minutes written as seconds in Qwen3-VL-8B to the separator and gain 2.9 and 1.3. Before any edit, its answers often have the right minute and the wrong separator, and fixing only the separator lifts their mIoU from 13.1 to 19.2. Every improving edit beats a random edit of its size, and the edited models run as fast as before.
papers.summary: Video-language models often locate the right moment in a long video but write its timestamp incorrectly. In `Temporal Weight Surgery` (TWS), a general-purpose LLM inspects the target model's weights and activations, locates where the error arises, and edits the weights there without gradients, with separate sessions converging on the same diagnosis. `GPT-6 Astra` sessions trace a dropped digit in `TimeLens-8B` to one MLP layer, where the largest edit **gains 7.9 mIoU on 1,215 unseen questions** and 18.3 on videos of 30 minutes or more, while `Claude Opus 5.5` sessions trace minutes written as seconds in `Qwen3-VL-8B` to the separator token and gain 2.9 and 1.3. Every improving edit beats a random edit of the same size, and the edited models run at unchanged speed.

papers.title: Benchmarking Segmentation Models for Scalable Mangrove Mapping with Sentinel-1/2 Imagery
papers.abstract: Mangroves are dynamic coastal ecosystems that contribute to carbon storage, coastal protection and biodiversity conservation, but are vulnerable to climate change. Very-high-resolution imagery such as Pl\'eiades enables detailed mangrove mapping but it is costly and have a low revisit rate. Large-scale monitoring requires free and regularly available data such as Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 but their spatial resolution poses challenges for detailed mangrove mapping. In this work, we benchmark deep learning approaches for mangrove mapping from Sentinel-1 radar and Sentinel-2 optical imagery using reference maps derived from very-high-resolution Pl\'eiades imagery. We compare four segmentation configurations based on CROMA and BigEarthNet-pretrained ResNet50 representations with different segmentation decoders. We construct a mangrove mapping dataset covering French Guiana, Suriname, and Amap\'a. CROMA + UPerNet achieves the best performance, with an F1-score of 0.9218 and an IoU of 0.8549. These results highlight the potential of pretrained multimodal Earth observation representations and open Sentinel data to support mangrove resilience through scalable monitoring.
papers.summary: Mapping mangroves at scale requires free, frequently revisited satellite data, but `Sentinel-1` radar and `Sentinel-2` optical imagery are much coarser than costly very-high-resolution `Pléiades` imagery. Using reference maps derived from `Pléiades`, the authors build a dataset covering French Guiana, Suriname, and Amapá and benchmark four segmentation configurations built on `CROMA` and BigEarthNet-pretrained `ResNet50` representations with different decoders. `CROMA` with a `UPerNet` decoder performs best, reaching **an F1-score of 0.9218 and an IoU of 0.8549**.

papers.title: Poisoning Self-Evolving Security Policies in LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Self-evolving defenses improve LLM-agent security by learning reusable policies from observed attacks. However, we demonstrate that this learning process itself can become an attack surface. Using SED (Self-Evolving Defense) in the AgentDojo benchmark, we construct a single prompt-injection episode that causes the defense to learn an over-broad policy and subsequently refuse legitimate requests. Across 10 Nemotron runs, every poisoned run over-refuses at least one legitimate task, while unrelated-task performance remains unchanged and the original prompt-injection defense remains effective. The attack also transfers to gpt-oss-120b; however, its poisoning mechanism depends on a successful initial prompt injection and therefore fails to activate when the target agent resists the underlying injection. In contrast, integrity-oriented attacks targeting SED's judge, policy synthesis, retrieval, and organization mechanisms fail in our evaluated settings, identifying over-refusal as the primary exploitable failure mode observed in our experiments. We further identify self-poisoning from false-positive harm judgments without an attacker. Finally, contrastive policy synthesis and an automatic broadness-check gate substantially reduce, but do not eliminate over-refusal, without compromising security in our evaluated settings.
papers.summary: Self-evolving defenses that learn reusable security policies from observed attacks can themselves be attacked through that learning process. Using `SED` (Self-Evolving Defense) on the `AgentDojo` benchmark, the authors craft a single prompt-injection episode that makes the defense learn an over-broad policy, and **in all 10 `Nemotron` runs the poisoned defense over-refuses at least one legitimate task** while unrelated-task performance and the original injection defense stay intact. The attack transfers to `gpt-oss-120b` but only activates when the initial injection succeeds, and integrity-oriented attacks on the judge, policy synthesis, retrieval, and organization mechanisms fail in the evaluated settings. Self-poisoning also occurs without an attacker through false-positive harm judgments, and contrastive policy synthesis plus a broadness-check gate reduce but do not eliminate over-refusal.

papers.title: Measuring and Predicting Image-Token Repair Boundaries in Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Degraded images make vision-language models answer wrongly. Using synthetic paired blur, noise, and low light, we trace which clean image states can still repair those answers from the vision encoder through the language model. In four encoder models, 12 to 23 ranked tokens recover half of the full-patch effect, whereas random orders require four to fifteen times as many; encoder-free Gemma needs 22.2 versus 53.1. Full-block repair expires at a model-specific language-model crossing. The matched reverse-direction intervention is algebraically identical to text-token restoration, so its gap from image restoration measures a redundancy band rather than an independent predictor. A clean-image gray-ablation crossing independently predicts held-out repair with 1.53-layer error, against 3.65 for shared depth. Gemma MMBench has the only large attention-to-repair point gap; Gemma GQA does not. Restormer provides a non-oracle consistency check on two models.
papers.summary: Degraded images cause vision-language models to answer incorrectly, and this study traces which clean image states can still repair those answers as they flow from the vision encoder through the language model, using synthetic paired blur, noise, and low light. In four encoder-based models, **12 to 23 ranked image tokens recover half of the full-patch repair effect**, whereas random orderings need four to fifteen times as many, and full-block repair stops working at a model-specific layer of the language model. A crossing point measured by gray-ablating clean images predicts held-out repair depth with 1.53-layer error, compared with 3.65 for a shared-depth baseline. Encoder-free `Gemma` shows a smaller ranked-versus-random gap, and `Restormer` serves as a non-oracle consistency check on two models.

papers.title: RoboARC: Physical Puzzles for Robotic Manipulation under Spatial Constraints
papers.abstract: Many hard manipulation tasks come down to a spatial constraint that only a few motions satisfy, such as passing a part through a gap barely wider than itself or separating two interlocked parts. These motions depend on the exact geometry of each scene, so demonstrations and skills recorded elsewhere rarely transfer. We therefore ask: when manipulation hinges on spatial constraints, can robots reason out the right motions? We introduce RoboARC, a benchmark of 90 tasks in six constraint types over rigid and soft materials, on three robots in MuJoCo. Every task is a frozen scene with a physics-based grader and a verified reference solution that replays bit-identically. Each task comes in a Privileged regime, with the full simulator state and resets, and a Standard regime with real-sensor inputs (camera images and proprioception) and a single attempt without resets. We evaluate seven coding agents and four VLA policies, none trained on these tasks. The strongest agent, GPT-6 Astra in Codex, solves 86% of the tasks in the Privileged regime and 43% in the Standard regime, and the four VLA policies, run zero-shot, solve none of their 18 one-arm puzzles. On 15 puzzles that GPT-6 Astra solved in the Privileged regime and failed in the Standard regime, object poses add 4 points and part geometry 13, but both together add 36, from 24% to 60%. Only 7% of the coding agents' failed runs pass more than half of a task, and 53% of the failed runs in the Standard regime are stuck on a single step. Frontier coding agents already reason out the right motions for many of these tasks once they know where the parts are and what shape they have. From their own sensors, in a single attempt, the strongest solves fewer than half of the tasks. The website can be found at https://roboarc.embodied-first-exam.ai
papers.summary: Many hard manipulation tasks hinge on a spatial constraint that only a few motions satisfy, such as threading a part through a tight gap or separating interlocked pieces. `RoboARC` is a benchmark of 90 such tasks across six constraint types on three robots in `MuJoCo`, each with a physics-based grader and a verified reference solution, offered in a Privileged regime with full simulator state and resets and a Standard regime with camera images, proprioception, and a single attempt. Among seven coding agents and four vision-language-action (VLA) policies, none trained on the tasks, **the strongest agent, `GPT-6 Astra` in `Codex`, solves 86% of tasks in the Privileged regime but only 43% in the Standard regime**, and the VLA policies solve none of their 18 one-arm puzzles zero-shot. On 15 puzzles failed only in the Standard regime, supplying both object poses and part geometry raises success from 24% to 60%, far more than either alone.

papers.title: Confidence scores for gated automation of large language models
papers.abstract: AI agents built on large language models (LLMs) demonstrate strong capabilities in automated decision-making. However, LLMs may produce incorrect answers with high confidence, limiting their applicability in decisions that affect individuals and organizations. Reliable confidence scores are necessary to gate such decisions, and existing estimates are frequently unavailable or too coarse to support effective gating. This work uses supervised learning to train models to predict the correctness of LLM-generated answers, enabling automated confident responses and routing uncertain ones for human review. A linear confidence score head is fitted to the final-layer hidden state of the frozen LLM backbone, and text-only metamodels are trained as an alternative for closed models. All results come from a single 2B-parameter backbone, on graded answers that are about 98% SQuAD and the remainder TruthfulQA. Against multiple baselines, the confidence score head outperforms all baselines and metamodels, automating the largest fraction of the workload at high accuracy targets. Prompted confidence scores can appear well calibrated yet lack the resolution needed for thresholding. Although transferability to unseen datasets is modest, the confidence score head remains the most robust approach. The proposed confidence scoring framework enhances the safety of automating LLM-based agents and can be adapted to gate other properties, including safety or compliance.
papers.summary: LLMs can give wrong answers with high confidence, which makes it hard to decide which outputs can be automated and which need human review. The authors train supervised predictors of answer correctness: a linear confidence head on the final-layer hidden state of a frozen LLM, and text-only metamodels as an alternative for closed models, evaluated on a single 2B-parameter backbone with graded answers that are about 98% `SQuAD` and the rest `TruthfulQA`. **The linear confidence head outperforms all baselines and metamodels, automating the largest share of the workload at high accuracy targets**, while prompted confidence scores can look well calibrated yet lack the resolution needed for thresholding. Transfer to unseen datasets is modest, though the head remains the most robust option.

papers.title: Best-of-$N$ Test-Time Steering Can Lead to Reward Hacking in Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have shown promise for general-purpose robotic manipulation, but adapting to changing environmental conditions still remains challenging. Recent test-time steering methods have shown promise in enabling adaptive VLA policies by utilizing additional computation during deployment. In this paper, we consider best-of-$N$ test-time steering for VLA models, where multiple action candidates are sampled from a fixed policy and a verifier is used to select the best one during deployment. We show that increasing $N$ does not always improve performance when the verifier is inaccurate, and can favor candidates whose scores exploit prediction errors, a form of reward hacking. We study this effect on 60 LIBERO-Safety task-level cases using a $\pi_{0.5}$ policy, with ten repetitions per case. We introduce controlled errors in a MuJoCo trajectory verifier and show that as $N$ increases, selected candidate rewards diverge from the accurate verifier rewards, leading to reward hacking. We also show that verifier calibration and softmax-based candidate selection can mitigate reward hacking in some settings.
papers.summary: Best-of-N test-time steering for vision-language-action (VLA) robot policies samples several action candidates from a fixed policy and lets a verifier pick the best one. Using a `π0.5` policy on 60 `LIBERO-Safety` task-level cases with controlled errors injected into a `MuJoCo` trajectory verifier, the authors show that **increasing N does not always help when the verifier is inaccurate, because selection increasingly favors candidates that exploit the verifier's prediction errors**, a form of reward hacking. As N grows, the rewards of selected candidates diverge from those given by the accurate verifier. Verifier calibration and softmax-based candidate selection mitigate the effect in some settings.

papers.title: Sequentially Acquiring Concept Knowledge to Guide Continual Learning
papers.abstract: The goal of continual learning (CL) is to adapt to new data (plasticity) while retaining the knowledge acquired from old data (stability). Existing methods are explicitly designed to focus on balancing stability and plasticity to mitigate the challenge of catastrophic forgetting while promoting learning. However, the impact of order and nature of samples from the new data that the network is trained on remains an under explored factor. We argue that a CL algorithm should have the ability to rank incoming samples in terms of their relationship with prior data and their effect on the learning process. In this work, we investigate if scoring and prioritizing incoming data based on their semantic relationships with the model's current knowledge can benefit CL. We propose SACK, short for Sequentially Acquiring Concept Knowledge, a plug and play technique for continual learning methods. SACK dissects categorical knowledge of the model into fine-grained concepts, computes the relationships between previously learned concepts and new concepts in each experience, and uses this relationship knowledge for prioritizing new samples. Experiments across several types of CL methods (regularization, replay, and prompt based) in class incremental and task incremental settings demonstrate that integration of SACK not only improves accuracy and reduces forgetting but also handles long tail distribution, helps focus on semantically interpretable regions, and yields better calibrated and robust models compared to prior approaches.
papers.summary: Continual learning (CL) methods focus on balancing plasticity and stability, but the order and nature of the new samples a network trains on is rarely considered. `SACK` (Sequentially Acquiring Concept Knowledge) is a plug-in technique that breaks the model's class knowledge into fine-grained concepts, computes relationships between previously learned and incoming concepts, and uses them to prioritize new samples. Across regularization, replay, and prompt-based CL methods in class-incremental and task-incremental settings, **adding `SACK` improves accuracy and reduces forgetting**, and is also reported to handle long-tailed distributions and yield better calibrated, more robust models.

papers.title: Partial Routing: Trace-Tuned Delegation for Resource-Efficient Agentic Workflows
papers.abstract: AI models vary enormously in capability and price. Model routing exploits this by sending easier tasks to cheaper models. However, a single agentic task often combines easy and difficult subtasks, making one model choice for the entire task inefficient. We introduce partial routing, which guides a frontier lead model to delegate suitable subtasks to a cheaper worker model. From both models' past runs, we identify recurring subtasks and measure each model's quality and cost on them. These measurements produce delegation guidance, with a parameter, $\delta$, controlling how much is delegated. The lead decides when and what to delegate during execution, without training either model. On held-out tasks from ViBench and Terminal-Bench 4.0, partial routing achieves higher mean task performance than the lead alone and task-level routing. With $\delta = 0.75$, it raises the lead's ViBench score from 70.2 to 78.5 at 19% lower cost, and its Terminal-Bench pass rate from 54% to 61% at similar cost. Giving the lead only the subtask breakdown, without a worker, also reduces cost on both benchmarks and raises the Terminal-Bench pass rate. These results show that analysis of past runs can support more efficient planning and more effective delegation, with little cost and implementation overhead.
papers.summary: Model routing sends whole tasks to cheaper models, but a single agentic task usually mixes easy and hard subtasks. Partial routing mines past runs of a frontier lead model and a cheaper worker to identify recurring subtasks and measure each model's quality and cost on them, then turns this into delegation guidance with a parameter δ controlling how much the lead hands off, without training either model. On held-out tasks, with δ = 0.75 it **raises the lead's `ViBench` score from 70.2 to 78.5 at 19% lower cost** and its `Terminal-Bench 4.0` pass rate from 54% to 61% at similar cost, beating both the lead alone and task-level routing. Giving the lead only the subtask breakdown, with no worker, also cuts cost on both benchmarks and raises the Terminal-Bench pass rate.

papers.title: A Semantics-First Approach to Multimodal Video Captioning with Frozen Encoders and Stabilized Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: We propose the Audio-Visual Query Transformer (AVQFormer), a highly efficient architecture built upon a 2.7B parameter LLM featuring a fixed-length $K=16$ semantic alignment module, stabilized via Adaptive Self-Critical Sequence Training (ASCST) with Entropy Regularization. Multimodal Large Language Models (LLMs) often rely on global audio representations to compensate for inefficient, frame-based visual encoders. While our Phase 1 prompted evaluations demonstrate that the Multimodal Base Model achieves strong deep semantic alignment (scoring 0.889 on BERTScore F1), optimizing this architecture for legacy metrics reveals a performance gap. We explore this gap as a hypothesis we term temporal alignment friction: a conflict where global audio representations disrupt the chronological sequence of visual frames, leading to penalties under visually-focused evaluation metrics. Consequently, by stripping away the audio, our Video-Only ablation conforms more closely to this rigid syntax, achieving 63.0 CIDEr. While trailing larger models such as Qwen2.5-VL (67.4 CIDEr), this establishes a strong baseline for sub-3B parameter LLM-based models. This indicates that CIDEr, as applied to datasets such as MSR-VTT, may exhibit a bias toward visually grounded syntax, limiting its ability to fully capture multimodal semantic richness.
papers.summary: `AVQFormer` (Audio-Visual Query Transformer) is a video captioning architecture built on a 2.7B-parameter LLM with a fixed-length K=16 semantic alignment module, trained with Adaptive Self-Critical Sequence Training and entropy regularization. The full audio-visual model scores 0.889 BERTScore F1 in prompted evaluation but underperforms on legacy metrics, which the authors hypothesize is due to temporal alignment friction, where global audio representations disrupt the chronological ordering of visual frames. Removing audio, the **video-only ablation reaches 63.0 CIDEr**, trailing `Qwen2.5-VL` at 67.4, and the authors suggest that CIDEr on datasets such as `MSR-VTT` may be biased toward visually grounded syntax.

papers.title: Collaborative Language Models for Semantic IoT Data Processing: Validation through Zero-Shot Human Activity Recognition
papers.abstract: Internet of Things (IoT) systems generate low-level sensor observations that are not directly suitable for process analysis and must first be transformed into semantically meaningful events. This paper investigates collaborative language models as a zero-shot semantic abstraction layer for converting such observations into higher-level event and activity labels. We propose a five-stage workflow comprising semantic mapping, semantic aggregation, temporal and contextual aggregation, specialized reasoning, and final event abstraction. The resulting labels and contextual information can subsequently be represented as event records for downstream Process Mining (PM) tasks. The approach is evaluated through Human Activity Recognition on the CASAS Aruba smart home dataset using eleven workflow configurations. The experiments show that collaboration alone does not guarantee improved performance: general-purpose auxiliary SLMs can degrade recognition, whereas assigning complementary specialist roles leads to better results and allows a smaller final classifier to retain much of the performance of a larger model. The selected workflow achieves a macro F1 of 0.643 in the 1.5-day comparison and 0.567 (weighted F1 0.680) in a one-week evaluation. Although trained ML approaches remain more accurate on this dataset, the results demonstrate a different design point: modular semantic event abstraction using off-the-shelf models without task-specific parameter fine-tuning. The findings indicate that the structure of LM collaboration and task decomposition is more important than simply increasing the number of participating models.
papers.summary: Raw Internet of Things sensor readings must be turned into meaningful events before process analysis, and this work tests collaborating language models as a zero-shot abstraction layer for that step. A five-stage workflow of semantic mapping, semantic aggregation, temporal and contextual aggregation, specialized reasoning, and final event abstraction is evaluated on human activity recognition with the `CASAS Aruba` smart home dataset across eleven configurations. **Collaboration alone does not guarantee gains: general-purpose auxiliary small models can degrade recognition, whereas complementary specialist roles improve it** and let a smaller final classifier retain much of a larger model's performance. The selected workflow reaches a macro F1 of 0.643 on a 1.5-day comparison and 0.567 over one week, still below trained machine-learning approaches on this dataset.

papers.title: Temporal Selective Exploration for Reinforcement Learning-Guided Continuous-Discrete Flow Matching in 3D Molecular Design
papers.abstract: Flow matching has shown strong potential in generative tasks, while its optimization via Reinforcement Learning (RL) remains underexplored, especially in continuous-discrete mixed settings. Moreover, flow matching is formulated as an Ordinary Differential Equation (ODE), whose deterministic trajectories do not naturally support RL optimization. Introducing stochasticity by converting the entire trajectory into a Stochastic Differential Equation (SDE) is a common practice. Nevertheless, not all timesteps contribute to the final outcomes, and redundant exploration introduces additional noise. Furthermore, in multi-objective settings, some objectives may dominate the optimization while others receive insufficient updates. In this study, we propose an RL-guided continuous-discrete flow matching framework with temporal selective exploration for 3D de novo molecular design. Specifically, our method jointly optimizes continuous and discrete flow matching for atomic coordinates and molecular identities, respectively, while restricting exploration to timesteps that primarily contribute to target properties, reducing ineffective exploration. We also introduce a reward-based advantage calibration mechanism to mitigate objective dominance in multi-objective optimization. The framework is applied to design inhibitors for both the well-studied target protein EGFR and the challenging Pin1 protein. We identify some novel candidate inhibitors, supported by in silico validation.
papers.summary: Optimizing flow matching models with reinforcement learning (RL) is hard because their ordinary differential equation trajectories are deterministic, and converting the whole trajectory to a stochastic one adds exploration noise at timesteps that do not affect the outcome. The proposed framework jointly optimizes continuous flow matching for atomic coordinates and discrete flow matching for atom identities in 3D de novo molecular design, while **restricting exploration to the timesteps that mainly contribute to target properties**. A reward-based advantage calibration mechanism keeps individual objectives from dominating multi-objective optimization. Applied to inhibitor design for the proteins EGFR and Pin1, the method yields novel candidate inhibitors supported by in silico validation.

papers.title: When the Knowledge Runs Out: A Part-Level Pilot Evaluation of How Language Models Handle Partially Covered Questions
papers.abstract: Assistants that answer from supplied reference material often receive material that covers some parts of a user's question and not others. Existing evaluations of insufficient context mostly score one answer per question, and often treat partially sufficient context as simply insufficient. We describe a small, open evaluation that scores each part of a three-part question separately, with a verdict for parts that are answered correctly from the material but carry an added unsupported claim. On 30 cases (five scenarios, six coverage patterns, five samples each) we test claude-haiku-4-5 and llama3.1:8b. Without an explicit instruction to stay within the material, both models fill most gaps from their own knowledge (unsupported-claim rates of 0.71 and 0.90). One added sentence instructing them to answer only from the material brings these rates to 0.00 and 0.06, consistent with prior work. What remains is less visible: answers that strengthen the material, for example turning "many job sites prohibit bots" into a flat "no". We also report on the judge. Three rounds of blind hand labelling show that this added-claim verdict is the hardest to apply, for the judge and the author alike; RAGAS faithfulness is unsuitable for this task because it penalises correct withholding; and a difference between the two models that is clear under one judge disappears when the judge model is replaced. The dataset, code, hand labels and per-run figures are public.
papers.summary: Assistants answering from supplied reference material often get material that covers only some parts of a question, yet most evaluations score one answer per question. This small open pilot scores each part of a three-part question separately across 30 cases, testing `claude-haiku-4-5` and `llama3.1:8b`, with a dedicated verdict for correct answers that carry an added unsupported claim. Without an instruction to stay within the material both models fill most gaps from their own knowledge, and **one added sentence telling them to answer only from the material cuts unsupported-claim rates from 0.71 and 0.90 to 0.00 and 0.06**; what remains are answers that subtly strengthen what the material says. The added-claim verdict proved hardest to label for both judge and author, `RAGAS` faithfulness penalizes correct withholding, and a between-model difference seen under one judge disappears when the judge model is swapped.

papers.title: Open-Source FUTO Keyboard Layouts and Predictive Text for a Few Endangered Languages
papers.abstract: We present open-source FUTO Keyboard layouts and predictive text dictionaries for five endangered Uralic languages: Erzya, Moksha, Komi-Zyrian, Livonian, and Skolt Sami. Existing Divvun Android keyboard layouts are converted automatically into the YAML format used by FUTO Keyboard. For predictive text, we construct weighted AOSP dictionaries using translated Finnish lemma frequencies together with morphological frequencies extracted from small target-language corpora using finite-state transducers. This combination provides a practical way to rank inflected word forms when large monolingual corpora are unavailable. The resulting resources offer reusable mobile keyboard support for endangered Uralic languages.
papers.summary: Open-source `FUTO Keyboard` layouts and predictive text dictionaries are released for five endangered Uralic languages: Erzya, Moksha, Komi-Zyrian, Livonian, and Skolt Sami. Existing `Divvun` Android layouts are converted automatically into the keyboard's YAML format. For prediction, weighted AOSP dictionaries are built by **combining translated Finnish lemma frequencies with morphological frequencies extracted from small target-language corpora using finite-state transducers**, which gives a way to rank inflected word forms when large monolingual corpora are unavailable.

papers.title: HumblePRM: Improving VLM Abstention in Ambiguous Situations through Process Reward Modeling
papers.abstract: Reliable deployment of Vision Language Models (VLMs) requires that a model's expressed confidence remain grounded in what it can actually see, and that it recognize when the visual evidence is too ambiguous to commit to a confident response. Standard post-training uses outcome reward models (ORMs) that supervise only the final decision, rewarding a confident answer regardless of whether the image supports one, while existing methods either tend to detect uncertainty post-hoc or assume an objective verdict always exists. We instead split multimodal reasoning into two stages: perception, where the model must factually describe the scene, and calibration, where it must judge whether that evidence is sufficient to commit to a conclusion. We introduce HumblePRM, a lightweight process reward model (PRM) that scores each stage independently, rewarding agreement between evidence and expressed confidence rather than outcome correctness alone. Training with HumblePRM increases abstention due to uncertainty on ambiguous inputs considerably while leaving accuracy on clear images roughly unchanged. We also find that the improvement transfers to Gemma 4 E4B, a larger, popular edge model. Our findings show that process reward supervision is a promising route to VLMs with better calibrated abstention, ensuring more reliability rather than unpredictable behavior.
papers.summary: Vision Language Models (VLMs) trained with outcome reward models are rewarded for confident answers even when the image does not support one. `HumblePRM` is a lightweight process reward model (PRM) that splits multimodal reasoning into a perception stage, where the model describes the scene factually, and a calibration stage, where it judges whether that evidence is sufficient to commit, scoring each stage on agreement between evidence and expressed confidence. Training with it **considerably increases abstention on ambiguous inputs while leaving accuracy on clear images roughly unchanged**, and the improvement transfers to the larger edge model `Gemma 4 E4B`.

papers.title: SecID: An LLM-Guided Framework for Threat-Aware Secondary Asset Identification with Quantitative RTL Analysis
papers.abstract: The growing complexity of modern hardware designs is making security assurance increasingly difficult. One of the foundational steps in pre-silicon security verification is identifying security assets. While primary assets are often evident from design functionality, the internal signals that can facilitate their compromise are much less apparent. Complex data- and control-flow dependencies create many such internal security-critical locations, whose exploitation depends on the threat-specific attack mechanism---these are the secondary assets. To precisely identify these, we propose SecID, a multi-agent framework that combines deterministic RTL analysis with bounded dynamic evaluation and LLM reasoning to identify threat-specific secondary assets. Each asset decision is supported by functional influence, threat features, and explicit attack mechanisms. We demonstrate SecID on seven open-source SoC and IP designs, including openMSP430, NEORV32, and CV32E40P. The experimental results are corroborated through comparison with prior work, fault simulation, and formal analysis, and further evaluated through pipeline- and final-stage ablation, threshold-sensitivity studies, and final-stage repeatability analysis. Together, these evaluations show that SecID can identify highly threat-relevant secondary assets with respect to a given primary asset, providing a scalable path toward hardware-security verification.
papers.summary: Pre-silicon hardware security verification requires identifying secondary assets, the internal signals whose compromise can expose a primary asset under a specific threat, and these are hard to spot amid complex data- and control-flow dependencies. `SecID` is a multi-agent framework that combines deterministic RTL analysis, bounded dynamic evaluation, and LLM reasoning, backing each asset decision with functional influence, threat features, and an explicit attack mechanism. Demonstrated on seven open-source SoC and IP designs including `openMSP430`, `NEORV32`, and `CV32E40P`, it is reported to **identify highly threat-relevant secondary assets for a given primary asset**, with results corroborated by comparison with prior work, fault simulation, and formal analysis, plus ablation, threshold-sensitivity, and repeatability studies.

papers.title: AI-human hybrid conversations: Can AI Agents Improve Discourse Quality?
papers.abstract: Conversations are central to how people exchange information, share experiences, and develop collective understanding. Yet, across conversational settings, discussions often suffer from uneven participation, unanswered contributions, and a narrow range of perspectives. As generative AI agents increasingly participate alongside humans, hybrid human-AI conversations present a new opportunity to address these challenges. We investigate whether AI agents can serve as catalysts for human interaction, improving conversational engagement and broadening collective discourse. We develop a framework for introducing generic and persona-conditioned AI agents into evolving discussions and evaluate it through two complementary studies. First, using agent-based simulations grounded in Reddit discussions across four domains, we find that AI-generated conversations are more positive and less toxic than human conversations, but substantially less semantically diverse. Persona conditioning produces more human-like contributions and narrows this diversity gap, while increasing the representation of underrepresented personas can shift which perspectives emerge without necessarily increasing overall diversity. Second, we conduct a pre-registered experiment with 221 participants across nine discussion threads, comparing human-only conversations with those involving generic or persona-conditioned AI agents. We find that AI participation increases responsiveness, reduces unanswered contributions, and broadens the range of ideas expressed by human participants, even though the AI agents themselves do not fully reproduce human conversational diversity. These findings suggest that the value of hybrid human-AI conversations lies not simply in the content AI agents generate, but also in their potential to stimulate more responsive and diverse interactions among humans.
papers.summary: Group discussions often suffer from uneven participation, unanswered contributions, and a narrow range of perspectives, and this work asks whether adding generic or persona-conditioned AI agents can help. In agent-based simulations grounded in Reddit discussions across four domains, AI-generated conversations are more positive and less toxic than human ones but substantially less semantically diverse, with persona conditioning narrowing the gap. In a pre-registered experiment with 221 participants across nine threads, **AI participation increases responsiveness, reduces unanswered contributions, and broadens the range of ideas expressed by the human participants**, even though the agents themselves do not match human conversational diversity.

papers.title: PAC Learning to Sample: On Computational Aspects of Language Generation
papers.abstract:
The success of language models has motivated theoretical work on learning to sample from distributions on discrete domains. A prominent abstraction is the model of language generation in the limit, introduced by Kleinberg and Mullainathan (NeurIPS 2024), in which the algorithm must generate from the target language after some finite but unspecified number of positive examples. While its positive results are surprisingly general, most guarantees are qualitative. In this work, we seek quantitative guarantees on sample and time complexity, inspired by statistical and computational learning theory.
  To this end, we study a PAC model of language generation, proposed (in a different context) by De, Diakonikolas, and Servedio (SODA 2015), in which a Boolean concept class $C$ over $\{-1,1\}^n$ defines the target languages: given uniformly random positive examples of an unknown concept $f \in C$, the learner must output a sampler whose output distribution (conditioned on the training data) is close in total variation to the uniform distribution over $f^{-1}(1)$. Their work implicitly gives an efficient algorithm for PAC learning to sample $C$, given three primitives for $C$: an online learner, approximate sampling and counting oracles, and an SQ learner.
  We ask whether these ingredients, in particular online learnability, are necessary. First, we construct a Boolean concept class $C$ for which online learning is cryptographically hard, yet PAC learning to sample is computationally efficient. Then, we develop new algorithms that use offline ERM oracles instead of online learners, together with approximate sampling/counting oracles for intersections of concepts in $C$ and an SQ learner for $C$. We view our results, together with the work of De, Diakonikolas, and Servedio, as a first step towards understanding the computational complexity of language generation.
papers.summary: Theoretical work on language generation in the limit gives general but mostly qualitative guarantees, so this work seeks quantitative sample and time complexity bounds in a PAC model where a learner sees uniformly random positive examples of an unknown Boolean concept and must output a sampler close in total variation to uniform over that concept's positive set. Prior work implicitly gives an efficient algorithm from three primitives: an online learner, approximate sampling and counting oracles, and an SQ learner. The authors show online learnability is not necessary by **constructing a concept class for which online learning is cryptographically hard yet PAC learning to sample is computationally efficient**. They also give new algorithms that replace the online learner with offline ERM oracles, together with sampling and counting oracles for intersections of concepts and an SQ learner.

papers.title: Learning from Recurrence: Internalizing Depth-Induced Preferences in Looped Language Models
papers.abstract: A looped language model repeatedly applies the same block to its hidden state before predicting each token. The number of passes is its recurrent depth. Increasing this depth gives the model more computation per token with the same parameters. Can the shared block learn from the predictions it makes at greater depth? Following prior work, we retrofit pretrained OLMo-2-1B with a shared recurrent block and continue mid-training over varying recurrent depths. In the four-pass model, additional passes mainly redistribute probability among tokens that already rank highly after one pass. We use the continuations generated at greater depth to train only the shared block through a single pass, without reference answers or correctness filtering. We call this transfer preference write-back. Write-back further improves one-pass and multi-pass accuracy on most tasks. At their target depths, the updated models outperform a non-recurrent control matched for mid-training data and token budget on all six mathematical reasoning benchmarks, with a mean relative gain in accuracy of up to 46.2% across tasks. At four-pass inference, one-pass training outperforms full-depth training on the same targets in the model with input injection. This advantage disappears in the matched model without injection. On GSM8K, using the updated block only on passes two through four recovers nearly the entire four-pass gain, showing that an update learned in one pass can improve later applications of the same block.
papers.summary: A looped language model applies one shared block repeatedly to its hidden state, and the authors ask whether that block can learn from the predictions it makes at greater recurrent depth. They retrofit `OLMo-2-1B` with a shared recurrent block, then use continuations generated at greater depth to train the block through a single pass, with no reference answers or correctness filtering, a transfer they call `preference write-back`. Write-back improves one-pass and multi-pass accuracy on most tasks, and at their target depths the updated models beat a data- and token-matched non-recurrent control on all six mathematical reasoning benchmarks, with **a mean relative accuracy gain of up to 46.2%**. On `GSM8K`, using the updated block only on passes two through four recovers nearly the whole four-pass gain.

papers.title: Dynamic Reasoning in Next-Gen Detection and Response: An Empirical Study of LLM Triage, Reinforcement Tuning, and Adversarial Evasion
papers.abstract: We present an end-to-end empirical study of dynamic reasoning in next-generation detection and response pipelines, evaluating how static classifiers, graph-based signal fusion, and large language model (LLM) triage agents perform under strict human-analyst attention budgets (Recall at B alerts/day). Across 56 reproducible experiments spanning a multi-layer enterprise-and-cloud simulator and four public datasets (SOREL-20M, BODMAS, LANL, and DARPA Transparent Computing), we test twelve architectural claims governing modern fleet-scale defense. First, we show that fleet growth halves recall at a fixed analyst budget even at negligible compute cost (<$0.0003 per million events), and that rarity-weighted graph risk propagation outperforms GraphSAGE without neural training. Second, evaluating frontier reasoning models (Gemini) and fine-tuned open-weight models (Qwen3-4B) for alert triage reveals that unconstrained LLM auto-closure eliminates 90% of false positives while silently discarding 31-44% of true attack cases. Third, post-training with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) causes severe reward hacking on unseen attack classes, suppressing up to 86% of novel attacks compared to two-epoch supervised fine-tuning. Finally, against an adaptive adversary generating plausible cover stories in benign telemetry fields, LLM triage evasion rises sharply unless gated by a deterministic policy harness prior to model invocation.
papers.summary: Static classifiers, graph-based signal fusion, and large language model (LLM) triage agents are compared for security detection and response under a fixed human-analyst attention budget, across 56 experiments on an enterprise-and-cloud simulator and four public datasets (`SOREL-20M`, `BODMAS`, `LANL`, `DARPA Transparent Computing`). Fleet growth halves recall at a fixed analyst budget, and rarity-weighted graph risk propagation beats `GraphSAGE` without any neural training. Unconstrained LLM auto-closure with `Gemini` and fine-tuned `Qwen3-4B` removes 90% of false positives but **silently discards 31-44% of true attack cases**. Post-training with Group Relative Policy Optimization (`GRPO`) causes reward hacking that suppresses up to 86% of novel attacks compared with supervised fine-tuning, and evasion through plausible cover stories in benign telemetry fields rises sharply unless a deterministic policy harness gates the model.

papers.title: Benchmarking Open-Ended Vulnerability Discovery in Windows Kernel Binaries
papers.abstract: Frontier models are increasingly used to discover real-world security vulnerabilities, making it critical to systematically evaluate their cybersecurity capabilities. However, existing security benchmarks primarily focus on known vulnerabilities in open-source projects, largely overlooking closed-source binaries, which underpin much of the software industry. In this paper, we ask: how effective are frontier models at uncovering deep vulnerabilities in production binaries? To answer this question, we present DeepBinary, the first comprehensive benchmark for open-ended vulnerability discovery in Windows kernel binaries. Given a target binary, an agent analyzes it using a disassembler and kernel debugger in network-isolated VMs and reports each vulnerability with a crashing proof of concept (PoC). Unlike existing benchmarks, DeepBinary replays every report on fresh VMs and employs an LLM-based judge to assess its validity, uniqueness, and impact (estimated by bug bounty values). Beyond known vulnerabilities, DeepBinary also enables the discovery and validation of previously unknown (0-day) vulnerabilities. We conduct a comprehensive evaluation of representative open- and closed-weight models (including GPT-6 Sol, Claude Opus 5, and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash) across diverse coding agents (including Codex and Claude Code) on 12 target binaries. In total, they discover over 200 vulnerabilities with an estimated aggregate bounty of $661,000, including 146 distinct previously unknown vulnerabilities across all experiments. Our results further reveal substantial differences in models' ability to analyze binaries, conduct experiments, and sustain vulnerability discovery over long horizons. Overall, DeepBinary makes long-horizon, open-ended vulnerability discovery in complex binaries measurable, revealing fundamental differences in how frontier models analyze and explore such systems.
papers.summary: Existing security benchmarks mostly cover known vulnerabilities in open-source projects, so `DeepBinary` instead measures open-ended vulnerability discovery in closed-source Windows kernel binaries. An agent analyzes a target binary with a disassembler and kernel debugger in network-isolated virtual machines and must report each bug with a crashing proof of concept, which is replayed on fresh machines and scored by an LLM-based judge for validity, uniqueness, and estimated bug-bounty value. Across 12 target binaries, models including `GPT-6 Sol`, `Claude Opus 5`, and `DeepSeek V4.1 Flash`, run through coding agents such as `Codex` and `Claude Code`, found over 200 vulnerabilities with an estimated aggregate bounty of $661,000, **146 of them distinct and previously unknown**. The models differ substantially in how well they analyze binaries, run experiments, and sustain discovery over long horizons.

papers.title: The Geometry Is the Memory: Task-Density Routing for Continual LoRA
papers.abstract: Freezing older adapters does not ensure that a continual learner will select and use them properly at inference time. When multiple adapters exist, routing among them and identifying the adapter whose representation space matches the query's answer can be difficult. We propose CONTLORA, which replaces stored examples with compact class statistics for adapter selection and classification. Gaussian class models in a frozen representation select LoRA adapters, while accumulated feature moments exactly recover a class-balanced ridge classifier for fixed training features. Trained without retaining images or feature vectors, CONTLORA reaches 88.55% accuracy on 20-task CIFAR-100 and 86.99% on CUB-200. Across three benchmarks in the matched component study, its mean final accuracy differs from an independently trained stored-feature counterpart by at most 0.07 percentage points. Ablations show that improved task coverage need not improve classification and adapter composition also matters. On held-out classes, competitor-centered likelihood scores improve novelty AUROC over raw likelihood without altering routing ranks. These results support statistical memory as an alternative to example-retention approaches in the evaluated settings, while identifying task ambiguity as an ongoing limitation.
papers.summary: Freezing old low-rank adapters (LoRA) in continual learning does not guarantee that the right adapter is selected at inference time. `CONTLORA` replaces stored examples with compact class statistics: Gaussian class models in a frozen representation route queries to adapters, and accumulated feature moments exactly recover a class-balanced ridge classifier for fixed training features. Without retaining images or feature vectors it reaches **88.55% accuracy on 20-task `CIFAR-100`** and 86.99% on `CUB-200`, and its mean final accuracy stays within 0.07 percentage points of a stored-feature counterpart across three benchmarks. Ablations show that better task coverage does not necessarily improve classification, and task ambiguity remains a limitation.

papers.title: Joint Estimation of Abilities and Item Parameters for Large Language Models Using Probability and Binary Responses: A Fractional-Response IRT Framework
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) evaluations provide two response types: probabilities assigned to correct answers and binary indicators of correctness. Restricting evaluation to one type narrows the range of available models or discards probability information. We propose a method to integrate both types through a common two-parameter logistic item response model and fractional-response quasi-maximum likelihood estimation. The framework includes binary-only models in common-scale evaluation without discarding available probabilityinformation; broader measurement coverage does not by itself ensure greater precision or measurement equivalence. Simulations evaluate statistical efficiency when both response types have the same expected value. Moreover, adding probability respondents improves item calibration more efficiently than adding binary respondents. However, adding noisier binary responses to an already precise probability sample can increase estimation error under equal observation weights. An application to Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU) combines probability response data from the Open LLM Leaderboard with binary response data from Holistic Evaluation of Language Models (HELM) and reveals model-family response patterns, differences in item characteristics, and systematic ability shifts between evaluation protocols. The proposed framework extends common-scale IRT evaluation to models with different response formats while highlighting the roles of observation variability and evaluation-protocol comparability in statistical efficiency and interpretation.
papers.summary: Large language model (LLM) evaluations report either probabilities assigned to correct answers or binary correctness, and using only one type either excludes models or throws away probability information. The authors combine both through a two-parameter logistic item response theory (IRT) model fitted with fractional-response quasi-maximum likelihood, placing all models on a common scale. In simulations, **adding probability respondents improves item calibration more efficiently than adding binary respondents**, while adding noisier binary responses to an already precise probability sample can increase estimation error. Applied to `MMLU` with probability data from the `Open LLM Leaderboard` and binary data from `HELM`, the method shows model-family response patterns and systematic ability shifts between evaluation protocols.

papers.title: CA-RAG: Constraint-Aligned Retrieval for Structurally Faithful Long-Form Generation
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) typically optimises evidence selection for semantic relevance, whereas compliance-sensitive long-form generation also requires evidence supporting explicit structural obligations. Semantically relevant retrieval may therefore omit information needed for mandatory downstream clauses. We propose Constraint-Aligned RAG (CA-RAG), a retrieval-conditioning framework that augments section-specific queries with ontology-derived structural constraints and policy-grounded knowledge-graph relations before evidence selection. Retrieval-only evaluation with manually annotated evidence shows consistent improvements across retrieval budgets. At $k=6$, CA-RAG increases Precision@$k$ from $0.5268$ to $0.5692$, pooled Recall@$k$ from $0.5402$ to $0.5950$, and F1@$k$ from $0.5389$ to $0.5672$ over standard RAG. Generation experiments further show improvements in compliance and reliability in several model--domain settings, while generation-only constraints achieve higher clause coverage but lower overall compliance and reliability. These results indicate that structurally aligned retrieval can improve evidence sufficiency in compliance-sensitive long-form generation.
papers.summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) usually selects evidence by semantic relevance, which can miss information needed for mandatory clauses in compliance-sensitive long documents. Constraint-Aligned RAG (`CA-RAG`) augments section-specific queries with ontology-derived structural constraints and policy-grounded knowledge-graph relations before evidence is selected. With six retrieved passages and manually annotated evidence, it raises **pooled recall from 0.5402 to 0.5950** and precision from 0.5268 to 0.5692 over standard RAG. Generation experiments show compliance and reliability gains in several model and domain settings, whereas applying constraints only at generation time gives higher clause coverage but lower overall compliance.

papers.title: Evaluating Large Language Models on conversational African American English: Feature classification and next-turn generation
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are known to misinterpret and misrepresent regional and social varieties of English other than Mainstream American English (MAE), such as African American English (AAE), yet most evaluations of these biases have relied on synthetic, stylized or decontextualized data. This paper instead evaluates LLMs on authentic, conversational AAE to more closely reflect how such models may encounter AAE when deployed as chatbots. Concretely, we perform two complementary evaluation tasks on 100 six-turn segments randomly sampled from the Corpus of Regional African American Language (CORAAL; Kendall and Farrington, 2024), comparing three closed-weight LLM configurations: Gemini 2.5 Flash with and without reasoning, and GPT-4.1 mini. The first task compares the models against gold-standard manual annotations for five AAE morphosyntactic features, while the second assesses their ability to generate contextually appropriate next turns, evaluating outputs for AAE feature frequency, diversity (Self-BLEU), and pragmatic quality. Reasoning-enabled Gemini is the strongest feature detector by a clear margin (macro F1 of 0.91), outperforming both other LLMs as well as a finetuned BERT-based baseline (Masis et al., 2022). In generation, however, all LLMs underproduce AAE relative to the human speakers and produce relatively uniform continuations, with reasoning-enabled Gemini producing the least AAE and the least diverse output. We conclude that a model's ability to detect AAE does not straightforwardly translate into its spontaneous use of AAE in generation, and argue that addressing this gap requires changes upstream, in how pretraining and alignment data represent dialectal variation.
papers.summary: Most evaluations of large language model (LLM) bias against African American English (AAE) use synthetic or decontextualized data, so this study uses 100 six-turn segments of authentic conversation from the Corpus of Regional African American Language (`CORAAL`). `Gemini 2.5 Flash` with and without reasoning and `GPT-4.1 mini` are tested on detecting five AAE morphosyntactic features and on generating appropriate next turns. Reasoning-enabled `Gemini` is the strongest detector with **a macro F1 of 0.91**, ahead of a fine-tuned `BERT`-based baseline, yet all models underproduce AAE relative to human speakers and give relatively uniform continuations, with reasoning-enabled `Gemini` producing the least AAE. The authors conclude that detecting AAE does not translate into using it in generation.

papers.title: Using AI to Simulate the Behaviour of European Populations
papers.abstract: Language models can stand in for survey respondents, but leading approaches build their simulated people from interviews or individual records. We show that a model can learn how European population groups respond from published statistics, without interviews and without training on individual records. We fine-tune an open-weight language model on more than 12 million published group-level answer distributions from about 40 European countries, setting it up to predict each group's departure from a reference distribution. On opinion surveys from its training families it calls the direction of group differences right 84% of the time, ahead of a demographic statistical model (77%, paired test) and level with Claude Opus 5 and 5.5, which it also ties on accuracy; the frontier models are more accurate on new questions. On 278 held-out questions, almost all from the survey families seen in training, its error is 12% lower than that statistical model. It runs on a single 32 GB GPU or a high-memory laptop, and in a test with an earlier model, an evidence gate calibrated on half of a survey's questions fell back to the reference where the model's adjustments did not help. Coupled to a transport simulation of a planned metro closure, with a conventional elasticity as the reference, it adds a testable age gradient to the response, which we freeze for later scoring.
papers.summary: Simulated survey respondents are usually built from interviews or individual records; here an open-weight language model is instead fine-tuned on more than 12 million published group-level answer distributions from about 40 European countries, predicting each group's departure from a reference distribution. On opinion surveys from its training families it **gets the direction of group differences right 84% of the time**, ahead of a demographic statistical model at 77% and level with `Claude Opus 5` and `5.5`, although the frontier models are more accurate on new questions. On 278 held-out questions its error is 12% lower than the statistical model, and it runs on a single 32 GB GPU. Coupled to a transport simulation of a planned metro closure, it adds an age gradient to the predicted response that the authors freeze for later scoring.
