papers.title: LogToPersona: New Benchmark and Efficient Persona Prediction through Semantic Log Filtering
papers.abstract: Detailed knowledge of a user's persona is valuable for personalizing generative AI models and agents, yet such details are difficult to obtain and change over time. We address the task of inferring persona attributes from a single day of mobile activity logs. No suitable publicly available benchmark exists for this task, so we introduce a synthetic benchmark of 1,600 persona-log pairs. We target on-device inference so that raw logs never leave the phone, which makes memory rather than speed the limiting constraint: a day of activity yields roughly 30K tokens, whose key-value cache alone exceeds the INT4 weights of a 4B-parameter model. We therefore propose a log filtering method that retains only behaviorally distinct entries. Filtering reduces the memory footprint by up to 39% across nine models from four families and more than halves prefill time, while maintaining or improving prediction quality. For Qwen3-4B it removes 2.5GB, bringing the model from well beyond a realistic per-process budget to a manageable one. Within our benchmark, these results indicate that preserving diverse behavioral events matters more for persona prediction than retaining every semantically similar log entry.
papers.summary: Inferring a user's persona attributes from one day of mobile activity logs is studied as an on-device task, where memory is the limiting constraint because roughly 30K tokens of logs produce a key-value cache larger than the 4-bit weights of a 4B-parameter model. The authors introduce a synthetic benchmark of 1,600 persona-log pairs, `LogToPersona`, and a log filtering method that keeps only behaviorally distinct entries. Filtering **cuts the memory footprint by up to 39%** across nine models from four families and more than halves prefill time while maintaining or improving prediction quality. For `Qwen3-4B` it removes 2.5 GB, bringing the model within a realistic per-process budget.

papers.title: Learning to Reason in Real-Time
papers.abstract: AI agents that operate in the real world must reason correctly and on-time, yet they currently do not account for how time should alter their reasoning. Modern agents learn to do tasks in environments that are entirely synchronous: where the world waits for the agent to act before changing. A real-time environment, by contrast, changes independent of the agent. Existing approaches try to bridge this gap by imposing a ratio of thinking to acting. However, for an agent to succeed in real-time it must learn to act quickly when delay is costly and to reason longer when the benefit outweighs the missed opportunities. To this end, we introduce real-time reasoning training (RRT) as the class of training techniques for real-time reasoning agents. We develop three standard RRT techniques: (1) using real-time data, (2) decoupling acting and observing, and (3) curriculum learning in time. Together, these simple techniques substantially outperform strong baselines. Across time pressures, we outperform the strongest non-RRT baseline by an average of 33% reward on in-distribution and 55% reward on out-of-distribution tasks in two real-time environments: Frogger and Snake. These results demonstrate that we can teach agents to balance reasoning and responsiveness under real-time constraints, and that RRT opens a broad, new set of capabilities for real-time agents.
papers.summary: Agents are normally trained in synchronous environments that wait for them to act, whereas real-time environments change regardless of how long the agent reasons. Real-time reasoning training (`RRT`) is introduced as a class of techniques for this setting, with three components: training on real-time data, decoupling acting from observing, and a curriculum over time pressure. Across time pressures in real-time versions of `Frogger` and `Snake`, the approach beats the strongest non-`RRT` baseline by an average of 33% reward on in-distribution tasks and **55% reward on out-of-distribution tasks**. The trained agents learn to act quickly when delay is costly and to reason longer when it pays off.

papers.title: PRECEPT: Security Self-Improvement of Coding Agents via Evolving Principles
papers.abstract: AI coding agents increasingly write and submit code with limited human review, and much of it passes functional tests while remaining insecure. We show that these failures persist. Across 14 task sequences, Codex, Claude Code, and Qwen Code fixed a vulnerability 85.7% of the time when shown the failing security test, then reintroduced the same vulnerability class in a new session 26.7% of the time, about as often as agents that had never seen it (27.5%). The capability is present; the retention is not. Neither recording the repair in the agent's persistent context nor supplying published secure coding principles closed the gap: the recorded fix stayed tied to the family of the task it came from, and the principles, written for human developers, remained too general to apply to the code at hand. The knowledge exists; it is not activated. We call the missing ability security self-improvement: an agent learns from its own security failures so that each lesson persists across sessions, applies to new code, and does not break what works. We present PRECEPT, which equips coding agents with this ability through an evolving library that starts from authoritative secure coding principles and revises them against the agent's own failures, so that each principle comes to fire on the code where that agent actually goes wrong. A revision is kept only if fresh executions show it makes code more secure while keeping functional success within a small tolerance of the agent without the library. Improvement continues across evolution steps rather than saturating after the first. On task families never seen during evolution, PRECEPT's weakest agent reaches 97.1% secure working code, above the strongest unaided agent at 81.9% and the strongest baseline at 87.7%.
papers.summary: Coding agents often produce code that passes functional tests but is insecure, and the authors show the failures persist across sessions: `Codex`, `Claude Code`, and `Qwen Code` fixed a vulnerability 85.7% of the time when shown the failing security test, then reintroduced the same vulnerability class in a new session 26.7% of the time, about as often as agents that had never seen it. Recording the repair in persistent context or supplying published secure coding principles did not close the gap. `PRECEPT` maintains an evolving library that starts from authoritative principles and revises them against the agent's own failures, keeping a revision only if fresh executions show more secure code with functional success within a small tolerance. On task families unseen during evolution, **its weakest agent reaches 97.1% secure working code**, against 81.9% for the strongest unaided agent and 87.7% for the strongest baseline.

papers.title: RankCast: Phase-Aware Rank Balancing in MoE Serving
papers.abstract: Modern large language model (LLM) inference increasingly adopts disaggregated architectures that separate Prefill (P) and Decode (D) phases. Meanwhile, Expert Parallelism (EP) has been widely adopted in large Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model serving. However, load imbalance still slows down MoE inference because each layer must wait for the busiest EP rank. The main source of latency differs between prefill and decode. Prefill is compute-bound, and its MoE layers' latency is determined by the maximum token count of the busiest rank. At the same time, under moderate batch sizes, Decode is memory-bound, so the latency is dominated by the maximum active-expert count across ranks. To solve both problems under a unified framework, we present RankCast, a system that reduces rank-level maximum token counts during prefill and active-expert counts during decode. For every token, RankCast preserves the predicted Top-p experts and chooses the remaining k-p from its Top-L candidates (L > k). In prefill, RankCast yields a price per rank that steers flexible assignments to less loaded ranks. In decode, RankCast closes experts on the busiest ranks while preserving the constraints for each token. Both paths are implemented and tested in the state-of-the-art inference frameworks SGLang and DeepEP. We overlap RankCast's kernels with model execution and reuse the existing DeepEP communication channel for metadata transmission. On Qwen3-235B-A22B with EP=8 and Qwen3.5-397B-A17B with EP=16, RankCast removes over 75% of the busiest rank's excess prefill load, improves prefill input throughput by up to 19%, and reduces decode time per output token by up to 10%. The quality cost is below one percentage point.
papers.summary: Serving large Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models with Expert Parallelism (EP) is slowed by load imbalance, because each layer waits for the busiest rank; in the compute-bound prefill phase the bottleneck is the maximum token count per rank, and in the memory-bound decode phase it is the maximum number of active experts. `RankCast` keeps each token's top predicted experts and picks the rest from a wider candidate set, steering flexible assignments to less loaded ranks during prefill and closing experts on the busiest ranks during decode. Implemented in `SGLang` and `DeepEP` and tested on `Qwen3-235B-A22B` and `Qwen3.5-397B-A17B`, it removes over 75% of the busiest rank's excess prefill load, **improves prefill input throughput by up to 19%**, and cuts decode time per output token by up to 10%. The reported quality cost is below one percentage point.

papers.title: PeerReveal: Learning to Generalize in AI Peer Review Detection
papers.abstract: Can we distinguish fully AI-generated reviews from those using AI only to rewrite human judgement? Furthermore, can we do so reliably when reviews are generated from diverse AI models and workflows across scientific domains? To this end, we introduce PeerReveal, a new detector that grounds its decisions in learned relationships between a review's claims and reference claims drawn from AI-generated reviews of the same paper, complemented by review-level textual signals. We evaluate PeerReveal on PeerShift, a new, challenging test set of 5,430 reviews spanning multiple domains, including machine learning, life sciences, and social sciences, combining variation in disciplinary review conventions with diverse AI review-production mechanisms. With regular training, PeerReveal achieves 70.52% pooled Macro-F1 on this benchmark, improving over the strongest baseline by 11.48 points. We develop an effective and practical adversarial training framework that further improves the detector's generalization using a small local generator optimized to produce challenging reviews, raising pooled Macro-F1 from 70.52% to 82.40%. These results show that robust AI-review detection benefits from richer review-level evidence and adversarial training on more challenging generation processes.
papers.summary: The task is to separate fully AI-generated peer reviews from reviews where AI only rewrote human judgement, across many models, workflows, and scientific fields. `PeerReveal` bases its decision on learned relationships between a review's claims and reference claims from AI-generated reviews of the same paper, combined with review-level textual signals. On `PeerShift`, a new test set of 5,430 reviews spanning machine learning, life sciences, and social sciences, it reaches 70.52% pooled Macro-F1 with regular training, 11.48 points above the strongest baseline. Adversarial training against a small local generator optimized to produce hard reviews **raises pooled Macro-F1 to 82.40%**.

papers.title: FIG-MAC: A Fine-grained Inspiration Graph Empowered Multi-Agent Collaboration for Automated Scientific Hypothesis Generation
papers.abstract: Automated Scientific Hypothesis Generation (ASHG) leveraging large language models (LLMs) aims to harness their strengths in knowledge integration, logical reasoning, and text generation for efficiently producing innovative, verifiable scientific hypotheses. However, existing approaches face three critical limitations: (i) insufficient fine-grained knowledge representation, as unstructured context impairs LLM comprehension and reasoning; (ii) lack of knowledge evolution traceability, constraining the generation of innovative cross-domain conjectures; (iii) absence of human-inspired and role-specialized multi-agent collaboration, failing to leverage the efficient innovation mechanisms arising from cognitive diversity and division of labor among expert roles to complete the full ASHG-evaluation loop. To address these limitations, we propose the Fine-grained Inspiration Graph-empowered Multi-Agent Collaboration framework (FIG-MAC) including: (i) Fine-grained Inspiration Graph module (FIG), to obtain fine-grained structured knowledge representations, where nodes represent academic semantic units and edges encode heuristic relationships among them; (ii) ontology-guided hybrid reasoning module, which follows the FIG ontology to construct structured reasoning paths and uses vector search to enrich them with semantic evidence, to obtain the traceable scientific conjecture paths; (iii) role-specialized Multi-Agent framework, inspired by real scientific teamwork, enabling a closed-loop process of scientific conjecture generation, screening, and validation. Experimental results demonstrate that FIG-MAC significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods on source diversity, provenance-adjusted novelty, and raw novelty.
papers.summary: Automated scientific hypothesis generation with large language models (LLMs) is limited by unstructured context, poor traceability of how knowledge evolves, and a lack of role-specialized collaboration. `FIG-MAC` builds a fine-grained inspiration graph whose nodes are academic semantic units and whose edges encode heuristic relationships, uses an ontology-guided hybrid reasoning module with vector search to construct traceable conjecture paths, and runs role-specialized agents that generate, screen, and validate hypotheses in a closed loop. Experiments report that it **outperforms state-of-the-art methods on source diversity, provenance-adjusted novelty, and raw novelty**.

papers.title: DexEngine: Scaling Human Demonstrations into Physically Executable Whole-Robot Data
papers.abstract: A growing body of recent work addresses the retargeting of human hand-object demonstrations to robotic hands. To train whole-robot policies, however, the retargeted motions must be kinematically feasible and physically executable, and be produced efficiently at scale. We present DexEngine, a simulation pipeline that turns human manipulation data into train-ready, physically executable arm-hand trajectories. DexEngine first places each clip's hand-object motion where the arms can reach it, finds an arm motion that follows the human hands, and then corrects the motion in physics simulation with residual reinforcement learning. From nine human hand-object datasets, we generate about 5,200 clips for each of four dexterous hands, augmented into 65,000 trajectories (116 h) and 325,000 episodes (578 h) in total. Even with arms attached, DexEngine tracks objects more accurately than prior floating-hand methods and runs over 10x faster than RL-based ones. Policies trained on our data far outperform those trained on the same clips without physics correction or with the arms attached after a floating-hand correction, showing that fine-tuning data need physics correction. Mid-training on our data further improves them at equal fine-tuning budget, in simulation and on a real robot.
papers.summary: Retargeted human hand-object demonstrations must be kinematically feasible and physically executable on a full arm-hand robot before they can train whole-robot policies. `DexEngine` places each clip where the arms can reach it, finds an arm motion that follows the human hands, and corrects the motion in physics simulation with residual reinforcement learning. From nine human datasets it produces about 5,200 clips for each of four dexterous hands, augmented into 65,000 trajectories and 325,000 episodes, tracking objects more accurately than prior floating-hand methods and running **over 10x faster than RL-based ones**. Policies trained on the physics-corrected data far outperform those trained on uncorrected clips, in simulation and on a real robot.

papers.title: SEEL: Towards End-to-End 3D Sign Generation with Language Models
papers.abstract: 3D sign language generation aims to produce signing motion from written text. Motivated by the linguistic nature of sign language, recent methods combine a motion tokenizer with a language model to predict motion tokens from text. However, both components are optimized through a two-stage pipeline with mismatched objectives: the tokenizer minimizes reconstruction error in isolation, while the generator learns from rigid one-hot reference tokens. A straightforward end-to-end extension bridges discrete token selection with straight-through estimators (STE), suffering from biased gradients and codebook collapse. To address these limitations, we propose SEEL, an end-to-end framework that aligns tokenization and generation with motion quality through two complementary mechanisms. First, to overcome rigid one-hot supervision, reconstruction-aware generation decodes candidate tokens in context and converts their 3D motion errors into soft targets, guiding the generator with physical motion quality. Second, to propagate generation feedback without STE, generation-aware tokenization passes continuous codebook expectations through the frozen generator, routing generated-motion gradients to the tokenizer to prevent codebook collapse. Combining both mechanisms enables the tokenizer and generator to co-evolve, achieving state-of-the-art performance on CSL-Daily, How2Sign, and Phoenix-2014T. Code and models will be released to facilitate future research.
papers.summary: Text-to-3D sign language generation typically trains a motion tokenizer and a language-model generator in two stages with mismatched objectives, and naive end-to-end training with straight-through estimators (STE) suffers from biased gradients and codebook collapse. `SEEL` couples the two: reconstruction-aware generation decodes candidate tokens and turns their 3D motion errors into soft targets for the generator, while generation-aware tokenization passes continuous codebook expectations through the frozen generator so that gradients from generated motion reach the tokenizer without STE. With both mechanisms the tokenizer and generator co-evolve, giving **state-of-the-art results on `CSL-Daily`, `How2Sign`, and `Phoenix-2014T`**.

papers.title: Aligned Machine: A Benchmark for Evaluating Multimodal Embedding Similarity via Human Comparative Judgements
papers.abstract: Embedding models increasingly inform how people search, recommend, and retrieve information, yet we lack credible ways to test whether these similarity judgments reflect how humans understand meaning. Existing benchmarks typically rely on static, expert-labeled pairs with coarse Likert-style annotations, limiting scalability and making it difficult to obtain consistent, high-confidence annotations. We introduce Aligned Machine, an interactive, public-facing platform that transforms broad participation into a continuously growing Human-Aligned Similarity Benchmark (HASB) for evaluating semantic alignment in embedding-based systems. Participants complete a cognitively-natural, forced-choice task, comparing two pairs of items (text or images) and selecting which pair is more similar. This comparative design is accessible to non-experts, yields clean preference data, and supports robust aggregation. We report results from an initial deployment with 115 participants contributing 2,875 total labeled pairs and 872 unique pairs. Using HASB, we evaluated 12 widely used embedding models and found only partial alignment between embedding similarity and human judgments. Text-only models consistently achieve higher overall agreement than multimodal models, while multimodal performance varies systematically by task type: alignment is strongest for image-image comparisons, weaker for image-text comparisons, and lowest for text-text comparisons. Aligned Machine is designed to evolve over time as participation grows, supporting longitudinal analysis, domain-specific studies, bias detection, and measurement of concept drift across model versions. By combining accessible public participation with rigorous comparative evaluation, HASB provides a scalable and accountable framework for auditing semantic alignment in embedding models.
papers.summary: Benchmarks for whether embedding similarity matches human judgement usually rely on static expert-labeled pairs with coarse rating scales. `Aligned Machine` is a public platform where participants see two pairs of items (text or images) and choose which pair is more similar, feeding a growing Human-Aligned Similarity Benchmark (`HASB`). An initial deployment with 115 participants yielded 2,875 labeled pairs, 872 of them unique, and an evaluation of 12 widely used embedding models found **only partial alignment between embedding similarity and human judgments**. Text-only models agree with humans more than multimodal models overall, and multimodal alignment is strongest for image-image comparisons, weaker for image-text, and lowest for text-text.

papers.title: The Detour Is the Danger: Preserving Security During LLM Agent Recovery
papers.abstract: LLM agents increasingly rely on external tools and reusable Skills to execute complex workflows, autonomously replanning when operations fail. However, such recovery may preserve task functionality while silently discarding the security protections required by the original workflow. In this paper, we investigate workflow security downgrade, a failure-induced security threat in which agents execute sensitive operations without satisfying their original protection requirements. Unlike prompt injection, this threat exploits autonomous recovery decisions triggered by execution failures, without modifying instructions or tool definitions. We systematically evaluate this behavior through fault injection in an executable MCP/Skill environment spanning seven LLMs, twelve task templates, and three security-sensitive domains. To address this threat, we propose ARGUS, an obligation-preserving recovery framework that combines resource-bound security evidence, isolated recovery-plan validation, and execution-time enforcement. In a separate 864-run evaluation, ARGUS prevents all observed protection-loss events under enforcement, while recovery assistance yields model-dependent improvements in protected task completion over blocking alone. Our findings demonstrate that secure agent recovery requires preserving security obligations across workflow changes, rather than merely restoring task functionality.
papers.summary: When a tool call fails, a large language model (LLM) agent may replan in a way that completes the task while dropping the security protections the original workflow required, a threat the authors call workflow security downgrade. Unlike prompt injection, it needs no change to instructions or tool definitions, and it is measured through fault injection in an executable Model Context Protocol (MCP) and Skill environment covering seven LLMs, twelve task templates, and three security-sensitive domains. The proposed `ARGUS` framework combines resource-bound security evidence, isolated validation of recovery plans, and execution-time enforcement. In a separate 864-run evaluation it **prevents all observed protection-loss events under enforcement**, while recovery assistance gives model-dependent gains in protected task completion over blocking alone.

papers.title: Failure Broadens, Success Sharpens: Continual Adaptation of Tool-Use Agents Across Diverse Tasks with Dual-Polarity Memory
papers.abstract: Large language model agents can self-improve over time by utilizing procedural memory derived from prior task trajectories, yet the distinct utilities of memories derived from local successes and failures remain underexplored. This work studies this question in a realistic setting with heterogeneous streams of multi-domain tool-use tasks and various environment constraints common in real-world scenarios. We develop \emph{Dual-Polarity Memory with Periodic Maintenance} (DualPM), a simple, retrieval-free memory workflow characterized by (1) customizable reflection and procedural memory generation from both local successes and failures within each trajectory, and (2) periodic memory consolidation over long task streams under a given memory capacity, preventing memory explosion. Online prequential evaluation with fine-grained metrics reveals that failure memory more strongly broadens coverage, success memory better streamlines execution, while combining both polarities effectively integrates both benefits. Further studies demonstrate that DualPM enables cross-domain memory generalization and continual memory adaptation, while external evaluation on EvoMemBench reveals the portability and effectiveness of DualPM as a general long-term procedural memory method.
papers.summary: Procedural memory built from past trajectories lets large language model agents improve over time, but the separate value of memories drawn from successes and from failures has been little studied. `DualPM` (Dual-Polarity Memory with Periodic Maintenance) is a retrieval-free workflow that generates reflections and procedural memories from both local successes and failures within each trajectory, and periodically consolidates them under a fixed memory capacity. Online evaluation on heterogeneous multi-domain streams of tool-use tasks shows that **failure memory mainly broadens task coverage while success memory streamlines execution**, and combining the two gives both benefits. The method also generalizes across domains and transfers to the external `EvoMemBench` benchmark.

papers.title: Learning from Natural Images Untangles Number Sense
papers.abstract: Numerical cognition is a simple yet fundamental ability that remains challenging for modern vision-language models. Meanwhile, number sense is already present in numerically na\"ive animals, suggesting that it can emerge without explicit numerical learning. Deep neural networks provide a related observation, with numerosity-selective units appearing after training on unrelated natural-image tasks and even before any training. However, these findings leave unresolved whether visual learning contributes beyond the spontaneous emergence of numerical selectivity. Human development provides a clue, as children become better at making judgments in which numerosity and proportion conflict. Here, we introduce a geometric framework to trace how representations of these two quantities change across learning. Although untrained and pretrained networks exhibited similar unit-level numerosity selectivity and basic comparison performance, natural-image pretraining increased the angle between numerosity and proportion subspaces while reducing their overlap, supporting more robust readout under conflict. Direct manipulation of these geometric properties further demonstrated their functional contributions to decoding accuracy and functional independence. Importantly, conventional supervised pretraining was not essential for quantity separation, which also emerged through self-supervised learning without category labels and synthetic-image training without natural-image exposure. Together, our findings suggest that structured visual learning can refine spontaneously emerging number sense into robust and functionally independent quantity representations without explicit numerical training.
papers.summary: Numerosity-selective units appear in neural networks even before training, leaving open what visual learning adds to number sense. Using a geometric framework that tracks representations of numerosity and proportion, the authors find that untrained and pretrained networks show similar unit-level selectivity and basic comparison performance, but **natural-image pretraining increases the angle between the numerosity and proportion subspaces and reduces their overlap**, supporting more robust readout when the two quantities conflict. Directly manipulating these geometric properties changes decoding accuracy and functional independence. The same separation emerges with self-supervised learning without category labels and with training on synthetic images, so supervised pretraining on natural images is not essential.

papers.title: Controllable CAD Generation and Interactive Editing of Fluid Rotors
papers.abstract: Computer-aided design (CAD) provides the geometric foundation for rotors in fluid rotating machinery. However, creating models for different rotors requires different modeling processes, making it difficult to control geometry through design intent and reuse existing models. We introduce VaneCraft, an agent-driven framework for rotor generation, inverse recovery, and editing through a unified analytical representation. The agent interprets design requests and invokes geometric modeling operations. The representation defines geometric controls through meridional geometry and independent boundary angle laws. An anisotropic partial differential equation (PDE) maps these controls to the blade surfaces. Geometric parameter correction (GPC) uses a joint geometric encoder and a parameter decoder to refine controls initialized from rotor category and dimensions. Inverse recovery maps existing CAD to the same geometric controls for reconstruction and continued editing. Experiments demonstrate that VaneCraft supports anisotropy control and parameter editing and outperforms representative baselines in rotor CAD generation tasks. Project page is available on \href{https://github.com/shenchen333/vanecraft}{GitHub}.
papers.summary: Building computer-aided design (CAD) models of rotors for fluid machinery normally needs a different modeling process per rotor type, which makes geometry hard to control by design intent and existing models hard to reuse. `VaneCraft` has an agent interpret design requests and call geometric modeling operations over one analytical representation, in which meridional geometry and boundary angle laws are mapped to blade surfaces by an anisotropic partial differential equation, with a geometric parameter correction module refining the initial controls. Existing CAD can be mapped back to the same controls for further editing, and the authors report that the system **outperforms representative baselines on rotor CAD generation tasks**.

papers.title: State Space Attention: Learning Context-Dependent Memory Retention
papers.abstract: Standard attention's key-value cache grows linearly with context length. Bounding it raises the question of what a sequence model should retain for long-context reasoning. We argue this choice should be learned, and introduce State Space Attention (SSA), which learns to keep a bounded set of past representations and reads them with standard attention. A learned scorer rescores every chunk against newly arriving context and the rest of memory. A fixed-context Transformer is then the special case that always keeps the most recent tokens. We train the scorer and reader jointly, either moving gradually from a differentiable soft weighting of memories to hard retention, or with hard retention from the start. To produce signal for the scorer, we generate supervised samples during training, a technique we call recovery. We compare SSA with recurrent models, bounded-memory attention methods, and full-attention Transformers across retrieval, variable tracking, multi-hop reasoning, and language modeling. On our retrieval and reasoning benchmarks, SSA matches or comes within a few points of full attention on most tasks, far outperforms a Transformer with the same readable budget on every long-context retrieval task we evaluate, and matches or outperforms one with about 4 times that budget, while using constant inference memory. The largest remaining gap to full attention at small language model scale is on RULER. SSA makes a fixed number of tokens useful over a longer context, and since it reads memory with standard attention, we propose that it can be stacked with KV cache eviction methods. We also pretrain and post-train 400M-parameter models and measure how SSA's training and inference costs scale with context length and model size. Together, these experiments examine the capabilities and limitations of learned memory retention for long-context sequence modeling.
papers.summary: Standard attention's key-value cache grows linearly with context length, so bounding it requires deciding what to keep. State Space Attention (`SSA`) learns that choice: a scorer rescores every stored chunk against newly arriving context and the rest of memory, a bounded set is retained and read with ordinary attention, and supervised samples generated during training (a technique called recovery) provide signal for the scorer. On retrieval and reasoning benchmarks, `SSA` matches or comes within a few points of full attention on most tasks and **matches or outperforms a Transformer with about 4 times its readable budget while using constant inference memory**. The largest remaining gap to full attention at small language-model scale is on `RULER`.

papers.title: What Is Redundant at High Resolution? Efficient Attention and Feed-Forward Design for All-in-One Image Restoration
papers.abstract: Multi-scale architectures are widely adopted in all-in-one image restoration (AIO-IR) to capture larger-scale context at low-resolution stages and refine details at high-resolution (HR) stages. However, processing spatially large feature maps at HR stages incurs substantial computational costs and memory traffic, making efficient HR processing challenging. To address this challenge, we propose High-resolution Global-Local Restoration (HiGLR), an efficient multi-scale AIO-IR network grounded in an analysis of spatial redundancy in self-attention and convolutional feed-forward networks (ConvFFNs). Specifically, this analysis identifies three key redundancies: per-query readout at the finest-scale stage, key routing across neighboring queries at intermediate stages, and spatial mixing in the expanded feature spaces of ConvFFNs. Accordingly, HiGLR replaces costly self-attention at the finest-scale stage with a learned input-independent kernel. At intermediate stages, we propose a Block-Routed Hybrid Attention, which combines coarse-scale dense attention with fine-scale block-sparse attention over value residuals relative to coarse summaries, and shares routing indices across neighboring queries. We further introduce a Dual-Space FFN that performs spatial mixing in a compact space and pointwise nonlinear transformation in an expanded space, enabling efficient kernel fusion. Combining these designs, HiGLR achieves state-of-the-art performance while delivering up to a $4.24\times$ inference speedup over existing methods.
papers.summary: Multi-scale networks for all-in-one image restoration (AIO-IR) spend much of their compute and memory on large high-resolution feature maps. An analysis of spatial redundancy in self-attention and convolutional feed-forward networks motivates `HiGLR`, which replaces finest-scale self-attention with a learned input-independent kernel, uses a `Block-Routed Hybrid Attention` that shares routing indices across neighboring queries at intermediate stages, and adds a `Dual-Space FFN` that mixes spatially in a compact space. The authors report state-of-the-art restoration quality with **up to a 4.24x inference speedup** over existing methods.

papers.title: How Much Effort Does an AI Code Reviewer Need? Evidence from Claude 5.5 Models on Plausible-but-Wrong Patches
papers.abstract: AI coding agents write code faster than people can review it, so teams add AI reviewers. Reasoning models let such a reviewer trade cost for diligence through an effort setting. We asked how much effort a reviewer needs to catch plausible-but-wrong patches, which pass a benchmark's tests but fail stronger ones. Claude Opus 5.5 (preregistered), Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5 (exploratory) each reviewed the same 90 agent-written Django patches from SWE-bench Verified at low, medium and high effort. By strengthened SWE-ABS tests, 55 patches were wrong and 35 correct. In every model, high effort accepted fewer wrong patches than low (false success .45 against .67 for Opus, .49 against .65 for Sonnet, .51 against .78 for Haiku), a supported difference for Opus and Haiku. For Opus, medium was non-inferior to high within 15 percentage points (difference .018, 95% CI [-.065, .108]) and cost 20% less, short of the preregistered 30%. For Sonnet and Haiku, medium cost 39% and 51% less than high but was not shown non-inferior. Opus at medium or high agreed best with the labels; Haiku at high cost about 8% as much per review as Opus at medium, accuracy difference unresolved. Exploratory coding showed that most rejections named the tested defect and that effort added such rejections. No setting is a strong gate: each accepted at least 45% of wrong patches. For 32 of the 55 wrong patches the issue may not require what the failing test checks; without them, neither accuracy hypothesis holds for any model.
papers.summary: The study measures how much reasoning effort an AI code reviewer needs to catch plausible-but-wrong patches, meaning patches that pass a benchmark's tests but fail stronger ones. `Claude Opus 5.5`, `Sonnet 5.5`, and `Haiku 5.5` each reviewed the same 90 agent-written Django patches from `SWE-bench Verified` at low, medium, and high effort, with 55 labeled wrong by strengthened `SWE-ABS` tests. High effort accepted fewer wrong patches than low in every model, and for Opus medium effort was non-inferior to high while costing 20% less, but **no setting was a strong gate: each accepted at least 45% of the wrong patches**. The authors caveat that for 32 of the 55 wrong patches the issue may not require what the failing test checks, and without those neither accuracy hypothesis holds for any model.

papers.title: Sparse-to-Sparse Feature Learning for Cross-Layer Analysis and Steering
papers.abstract: Understanding how models internally represent information is a central challenge in interpretation and control. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose dense hidden representations into sparse features, and cross-layer methods capture structure spanning multiple layers. However, existing objectives do not explicitly train the sparse code at one layer to predict the sparse code at the next layer. We propose sparse-to-sparse feature learning (S2S), where sparse features at each intermediate layer are trained to predict those of the immediately following layer, with the final layer anchored by an output-distribution loss and optimization proceeding sequentially from output to input. Experiments across eight language models show stronger adjacent-layer correspondence than matched sparse-feature baselines. We evaluate feature-based interventions at matched output-distribution shift, separating steering-induced effects from sparse-pathway reconstruction effects. Causal ablation provides complementary evidence beyond correspondence metrics.
papers.summary: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose a model's hidden states into sparse features, but existing cross-layer objectives do not explicitly train one layer's sparse code to predict the next layer's. Sparse-to-sparse feature learning (`S2S`) does this, anchoring the final layer with an output-distribution loss and optimizing sequentially from output back to input. Across eight language models, the authors report **stronger adjacent-layer feature correspondence than matched sparse-feature baselines**, and they evaluate feature-based steering at matched output-distribution shift alongside causal ablations.
papers.highlight_summary:
Sparse autoencoders and transcoders decompose hidden states into sparse features, but none of their objectives train one layer's sparse code to predict the next layer's, which makes features hard to follow through the network. `S2S` trains each layer's sparse features to predict the following layer's sparse code, anchoring the final layer with an output-distribution loss and optimizing backward from output to input.

- Training has two phases over the same 1B `OpenWebText` tokens: TopK transcoders with a `16d` dictionary are first pretrained to predict next-layer hidden states at `K=64`, then fine-tuned layer by layer at `K=32` so that each decoded prediction, re-encoded by the frozen next-layer encoder, matches that layer's sparse code.
- Across eight models from `GPT-2 Small` to `Gemma-2-2B`, adjacent-layer coupling is far more concentrated than in any of seven baselines, with a Top-5 ratio of **0.49–0.59** against 0.33–0.39 for the strongest baseline, `Crosscoders`, and a column-wise effective rank of **11–17** against 20–26.
- With steering calibrated to the same output-KL budget of 0.05 nats/token, `S2S` gives the largest sentiment shift on `SST-2` prompts and the largest `TruthfulQA` MC1 improvement in **15 of 16** model-task settings, significantly so in 12, the exception being sentiment on `Pythia-160M`, where `e2e-SAE` is slightly stronger.
- Output preservation also improves on average, with output KL of **0.048** against 0.052 for `e2e-SAE` and causal importance under top-feature ablation of **0.216** against 0.185, though `e2e-SAE` wins one model on each metric, and training costs about 1.5 times as much as a standard SAE.
- The authors caution that the correspondence metrics partly overlap with the training objective, that there are no blinded human studies of the features, that steering is tested only on English sentiment and truthfulness, and that a uniform TopK budget may underallocate capacity at later layers.

papers.title: SlicePlanner: Logic-Guided Agentic AI for Online QoS-Aware Network Slicing in Open RAN
papers.abstract: Adaptive network slicing in Open Radio Access Network (O-RAN) demands reconfiguration decisions that respond to live traffic conditions while remaining safe with respect to Service Level Agreement (SLA) constraints, a combination that purely data-driven controllers cannot reliably guarantee without continuous retraining. We present SlicePlanner, a logic-guided closed-loop framework that treats each RAN reconfiguration as a controlled hypothesis: proposed from live and historical KeyPerformance Indicator (KPI) evidence, filtered through explicit SLA constraints and mined RAN control rules, and committed only when post-action measurements confirm improvement. SlicePlanner comprises two cooperating agents: SliceSense, which monitors live KPIs, retrieves context-conditioned evidence, and ranks candidate RAN actions through a surrogate-guided admissibility filter; and SliceGuard, which validates post-action KPI responses, rolls back harmful configurations, and refreshes rules under distribution drift. Validated over the air using OpenAirInterface, FlexRIC, and commercial Sierra Wireless 5G devices, SlicePlanner reduces SLA latency violations by up to 86% over static slicing and 50% over Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL)-based slicing, while maintaining comparable cell throughput and auditable decisions without online retraining.
papers.summary: Network slicing in Open Radio Access Networks (O-RAN) must adapt to live traffic without violating Service Level Agreement (SLA) constraints, which purely data-driven controllers cannot reliably guarantee without continuous retraining. `SlicePlanner` treats each reconfiguration as a hypothesis proposed from Key Performance Indicator (KPI) evidence, filtered through explicit SLA constraints and mined control rules, and committed only if post-action measurements confirm improvement; a `SliceSense` agent ranks candidate actions and a `SliceGuard` agent validates them, rolls back harmful ones, and refreshes rules under drift. In over-the-air tests with `OpenAirInterface`, `FlexRIC`, and commercial 5G devices, it **reduces SLA latency violations by up to 86% versus static slicing and 50% versus Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL)-based slicing** at comparable cell throughput.

papers.title: Verifiable but Not Predictable: What Sentence Embeddings Know About Propositional Decomposition
papers.abstract: Quality control for proposition decomposition by large language models (LLMs) raises two asymmetric questions. After decomposition, one can verify: given a sentence and a candidate proposition, does the proposition belong to that sentence? Before decomposition, one would like to predict: how many propositions should the sentence yield? On PropSegmEnt, a corpus of English Wikipedia sentences each segmented by three human annotators, we find that the two questions live in different representational spaces. A natural language inference (NLI) judge verifies membership with 92.8% accuracy and an area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.977, and its residual errors turn out to be mostly propositions that are true in document context rather than genuine entailment mistakes. Vector geometry cannot verify: cosine similarity saturates, and a sentence embedding is not a linear combination of its propositions' embeddings. For prediction, every symbolic anchor we test, namely token count, the CPIDR idea-density counter, and a Neo-Davidsonian predicate count, reduces to a length proxy once token count is controlled. A linear ridge probe on sentence embeddings is the only predictor that keeps genuine count signal: its length-partialled correlation with human counts is 0.40-0.49 with bootstrap confidence intervals (CIs) excluding zero, and it orders length-matched sentence pairs correctly 67-71% of the time against a 50% chance level, statistically matching the inter-annotator agreement ceiling. This signal survives INT8 quantization without loss, INT4 at a small cost, and Matryoshka truncation to 256 dimensions, and it works as well in a 2021 encoder as in a 2025 one. Its structured weakness is a systematic under-splitting of long sentences. We distill the protocol lessons, including a retracted pilot study, into a checklist for probing length-confounded quantities.
papers.summary: Checking the quality of large language model (LLM) proposition decomposition involves two questions: verifying that a candidate proposition belongs to a sentence, and predicting in advance how many propositions a sentence should yield. On `PropSegmEnt`, a natural language inference (NLI) judge verifies membership with 92.8% accuracy, whereas embedding geometry cannot, because cosine similarity saturates and a sentence embedding is not a linear combination of its propositions' embeddings. For count prediction, token count, the `CPIDR` idea-density counter, and a predicate count all reduce to length proxies, while **a linear ridge probe on sentence embeddings is the only predictor that keeps real count signal, ordering length-matched sentence pairs correctly 67-71% of the time**, which statistically matches inter-annotator agreement. That signal survives INT8 quantization and truncation to 256 dimensions, and the authors distill a checklist for probing length-confounded quantities.

papers.title: Rethinking Knowledge Distillation for Diffusion Language Models
papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation has recently proven highly effective for improving autoregressive models, but its applicability to DLMs remains poorly understood. We present the first systematic study of KD for DLMs and uncover two non-intuitive failures of classical forward-KL (FKL) distillation: (i) student perplexity does not improve monotonically with more teacher-generated data, and (ii) on the same teacher-generated corpus, FKL distillation underperforms simply training the student with the original DLM denoising objective. To address them, we propose a unified, data-free distillation framework for masked DLMs. First, the framework runs an off-policy distillation phase that absorbs general knowledge from a static set of teacher-generated data. Then, the framework employs on-policy distillation which consists of three techniques: a trajectory loss along the student's own reverse process, confidence reweighting that down-weights tokens where the teacher is unsure, and a trust-region anchor that stabilizes the moving target. On MDLM, the resulting student attains a GPT-2 perplexity of $24.75$, surpassing the teacher's $27.04$; on Dream-7B distillation to a 93M student model, the framework reduces Qwen-2.5 perplexity from the FKL-distilled baseline of $25.23$ to $19.83$ while preserving performance on zero-shot general capability benchmarks.
papers.summary: A systematic study of knowledge distillation for diffusion language models finds two failures of classical forward-KL distillation: student perplexity does not improve monotonically with more teacher-generated data, and it underperforms simply training the student with the original denoising objective on the same data. The proposed data-free framework for masked diffusion models starts with an off-policy phase on static teacher-generated data, then distills on-policy using a trajectory loss along the student's own reverse process, confidence reweighting, and a trust-region anchor. On `MDLM`, **the student reaches a `GPT-2` perplexity of 24.75, better than the teacher's 27.04**, and distilling `Dream-7B` into a 93M student lowers `Qwen-2.5` perplexity from 25.23 to 19.83 while preserving zero-shot benchmark performance.

papers.title: Interactive Proofs as a Unified Framework for Evaluating and Leveraging Verifiable Proof Generation by LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Recent advances in LLM-assisted theorem proving and program verification have attracted widespread attention. Beyond determining whether a proposition is true, LLM agents must produce evidence that can be independently checked by humans or formal verification tools. To evaluate the underlying, protocol-agnostic ability of LLM agents to construct verifiable proofs-rather than their proficiency with any particular proof language or verification tool, we introduce Merlin-Bench. Drawing on interactive proof systems from computational complexity theory, we cast an LLM agent as the prover: under a designated protocol, the agent interacts with a formal verifier to substantiate its claimed answer to a problem instance. We develop an automated framework for constructing test cases and use it to create 100 cases across 15 problem families, each formulated within this prover-verifier framework. Experiments with 10 frontier LLMs across multiple agent harnesses show that reliably producing verifiable proofs in accordance with specified protocols remains a substantial challenge. Our case studies further provide actionable insights into improving agents' ability to generate verifier-accepted proofs: tool use is essential for completing practical proof tasks; different forms of guidance, ranging from engineering instructions to problem-specific knowledge, substantially affect success rates on interactive-proof tasks; and proof-solving experience distilled from abstract tasks can transfer to concrete, real-world verification tasks.
papers.summary: `Merlin-Bench` evaluates whether large language model (LLM) agents can produce independently checkable proofs, separately from their skill with any particular proof language or verification tool. Borrowing interactive proof systems from complexity theory, it casts the agent as a prover that must convince a formal verifier of its claimed answer under a designated protocol, with 100 automatically constructed cases across 15 problem families. Tests of 10 frontier models across several agent harnesses show that **reliably producing verifier-accepted proofs under specified protocols remains a substantial challenge**. Case studies indicate that tool use is essential, that the form of guidance strongly affects success, and that experience distilled from abstract tasks transfers to concrete verification tasks.

papers.title: Faster and Better Query (FBQ): Learning Future-Position Probes from the First Generated Token
papers.abstract: When a large language model (LLM) evicts prompt keys and values at the end of prefill, it must decide what to keep before it sees the queries from subsequent decoding steps. Generating a draft continuation can approximate those queries at the cost of extra autoregressive steps. Can we use the embedding of the first output token, already available from the final prefill logits, to construct low-cost pseudo queries that approximate future decoding queries? We start with FTQ-8, which places eight copies of the first token ID at consecutive future positions and reads their attention to the prompt in one causal forward pass. Each copy sees a different prefix, but a generic opening such as the offers a poor literal guess for seven successive tokens. Faster and Better Query (FBQ) preserves the first embedding and learns an additive offset at each of the seven remaining positions. We train these offsets to predict the average prompt attention of a full-cache continuation. On LongBench, FBQ performs comparably to eight-step Lookahead Q-Cache at the same cache budget, using a single forward pass to compute all probe queries.
papers.summary: When a large language model (LLM) evicts prompt keys and values at the end of prefill, it has to choose what to keep before seeing the queries of later decoding steps, and generating a draft continuation to approximate them costs extra autoregressive steps. Faster and Better Query (`FBQ`) keeps the embedding of the first output token, already available from the final prefill logits, and adds a learned offset at each of seven further positions, with the offsets trained to predict the average prompt attention of a full-cache continuation. On `LongBench`, it **performs comparably to eight-step `Lookahead Q-Cache` at the same cache budget while computing all probe queries in a single forward pass**.

papers.title: Read Before You Use: Improving Visual Memory Utilization in Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Multimodal memory enables long-horizon vision-language agents to preserve and retrieve past experiences. While prior research has focused on memory construction and retrieval, effectively using the provided memory remains a challenge for vision-language models (VLMs). We find that VLMs often fail to answer downstream questions even when sufficient multimodal evidence is provided. To investigate why VLMs struggle, we replace memory images with reference captions and observe substantial performance gains, suggesting difficulties in reading visual evidence directly. However, model-generated captions may omit critical information, limiting this approach in practice. These limitations motivate a closer examination of memory utilization, revealing failures in both evidence reading and downstream question answering. Building on this distinction, we propose \textbf{MemRU}, a two-stage training framework that improves evidence reading through supervised fine-tuning (Read SFT) and downstream evidence utilization through Group Relative Policy Optimization (Use GRPO). Experimental results demonstrate that our 8B model generalizes across three unseen multimodal memory systems, outperforming Qwen3-VL-32B and approaching GPT-5-mini.
papers.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) often fail to answer questions even when the retrieved multimodal memory contains sufficient evidence, and replacing memory images with reference captions substantially improves results, which points to difficulty reading visual evidence directly. `MemRU` is a two-stage training framework that improves evidence reading through supervised fine-tuning (`Read SFT`) and downstream use of that evidence through Group Relative Policy Optimization (`Use GRPO`). The resulting **8B model generalizes across three unseen multimodal memory systems, outperforming `Qwen3-VL-32B` and approaching `GPT-5-mini`**.

papers.title: Refusal Is Not Scored: A Coverage Limit in Content-Based Bias Evaluation
papers.abstract: Bias audits of conversational models often discard refusals (responses such as "I can't assist with that request") before scoring, a filtering step which is rarely examined as a measurement decision even though it determines which responses an audit is capable of evaluating. This work examines what the step removes, applying seven bias-evaluation instruments spanning both deployed paradigms, three dictionary-based and four LLM-as-judge, to two intersectional datasets of 360 generated responses each. In both datasets, the filter removed a demographically skewed subset produced entirely by one of the three responder models, which refused North Korean prompts at 2.15 times the rate of American prompts on declarative content and 1.76 times on operational content. We then remove the filter and pass every refusal to all seven instruments. Bias-Lexicon scores refusals as clean, and including them shrinks the nationality disparity it reports. HurtLex appears to register the disparity, but we trace this entirely to a single lexicon entry matching the token "can" in "I can't". The LLM judges either flag most responses or rate refusals as unbiased. For the two judges that discriminate, including refusals lowers the nationality disparity they report, and no instrument identifies the refusal disparity. The failure is therefore a coverage limit upstream of scoring rather than a calibration gap that a better lexicon or judge prompt would be expected to close, which makes the behavioral channel an instrument is sensitive to a question of construct validity rather than one of method selection.
papers.summary: Bias audits of conversational models commonly discard refusals before scoring, and this study examines what that filtering step removes. Applying seven bias-evaluation instruments (three dictionary-based, four LLM-as-judge) to two intersectional datasets of 360 responses each, the authors find the filter removed a demographically skewed subset from one responder model, which **refused North Korean prompts at 2.15 times the rate of American prompts** on declarative content and 1.76 times on operational content. When refusals are scored instead, no instrument identifies the refusal disparity; the one apparent detection by `HurtLex` traces to a single lexicon entry matching the token can inside a contraction. The authors conclude this is a coverage limit upstream of scoring, a construct-validity issue rather than something a better lexicon or judge prompt would be expected to fix.

papers.title: Rethinking Sequential Locate-Then-Edit: Optimality and Stability
papers.abstract: The Locate-Then-Edit framework enables efficient knowledge updates in large language models without requiring full retraining. Recent research has increasingly focused on sequential editing, where knowledge arrives continuously and the model is updated incrementally. However, existing sequential methods commonly suffer from catastrophic forgetting and model collapse after only a few hundred edits. In contrast, batch editing - which jointly optimizes all edits and yields the optimal solution under a specified editing objective - can support tens of thousands of edits with high edit efficacy while preserving the model's general capabilities, resulting in a substantial performance gap between the two editing paradigms. In this paper, we demonstrate that this gap can be closed via a batch-equivalent sequential editing approach. Moreover, we investigate the underlying mechanism of model degradation in existing sequential methods by analyzing the convergence behavior of weight perturbations as edits accumulate. Our analysis reveals that current methods typically exhibit linear or logarithmic growth in perturbation, whereas the proposed batch-equivalent method achieves time-invariant growth, thereby theoretically guaranteeing long-term stability and preserving the integrity of pretrained knowledge throughout massive-scale sequential editing.
papers.summary: Sequential Locate-Then-Edit methods for updating knowledge in large language models tend to suffer catastrophic forgetting and model collapse after a few hundred edits, whereas batch editing, which jointly optimizes all edits, supports tens of thousands. The authors show the gap can be closed with a batch-equivalent sequential editing approach and analyze how weight perturbations grow as edits accumulate. Their analysis finds that existing methods show linear or logarithmic perturbation growth, while **the batch-equivalent method achieves time-invariant growth**, which they present as a theoretical guarantee of long-term stability.

papers.title: Sports Agent: A Self-Evolving System for Conversational Data Analytics
papers.abstract:
Conversational sports analytics requires accurate, evidence-based responses with low latency. Changes in query distributions, data resources, and model behavior can degrade static agent configurations, motivating controlled evolution guided by runtime evidence.
  We present Sports Agent, a self-evolving framework integrating an Agentic SQL Model for structured-data reasoning, a harness for planning and tool orchestration, and a unified Feedback Engine connecting online execution with offline evolution. The engine assesses responses and execution trajectories, verifies factual claims, diagnoses failures, and generates evolution signals. Model evolution combines SQL-to-Question Scaling for coverage expansion with Graph-Guided Scaling for error-targeted synthesis. Generated questions undergo trajectory distillation and quality filtering for iterative supervised fine-tuning, followed by a separate Post-RL stage. Harness evolution translates recurrent failures into bounded prompt and skill updates, validated through independent audits, execution replay, and regression testing. Performance-tolerance checks guard against unacceptable degradation during simplification.
  The resulting Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-based model outperforms Qwen3.8-Max on sports question answering and analysis while achieving approximately three times the inference efficiency. Across 30 harness-evolution rounds, the aggregate performance score improves by 10.8 points. In a live sports analytics product, the evolved system improves factual correctness by 10.5 points and average response length, a proxy for answer richness, by 158.1%, while reducing average latency by 41.3% relative to the baseline.
papers.summary: `Sports Agent` is a self-evolving conversational analytics system that combines an agentic SQL model, a harness for planning and tool orchestration, and a feedback engine that assesses responses and execution trajectories, verifies factual claims, and diagnoses failures. Model evolution synthesizes new training questions for iterative supervised fine-tuning followed by a reinforcement learning stage, while harness evolution turns recurrent failures into bounded prompt and skill updates validated by audits, execution replay, and regression tests. The `Qwen3.6-35B-A3B`-based model outperforms `Qwen3.8-Max` on sports question answering at about three times the inference efficiency, and in the live product **factual correctness improves by 10.5 points while average latency falls 41.3%**.

papers.title: EVA: Evidence-seeking Visual Agent for Hallucination-Resistant Multimodal Reasoning
papers.abstract: Hallucinations in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) often arise from visual assumptions that go unchecked. Self-reflection, multi-agent debate, and counterfactual verification can reinforce erroneous conclusions when they rely on the same unverified visual assumptions. External visual tools can provide verifiable evidence, but models may select the wrong tools, supply incorrect parameters, or ignore or contradict the evidence they obtain. In this work, we propose EVA, an Evidence-seeking Visual Agent that reframes multimodal reasoning as an explicit process of evidence acquisition and verification. At the core of EVA is a unified evidence-grounded execution pipeline designed to address the above challenges through two tightly coupled mechanisms. First, we introduce Iterative Tool Replanning, which dynamically refines tool selection and parameters based on intermediate observations, improving the reliability of tool usage. Second, we develop Evidence Consistency Verification, an answer validation mechanism that improves alignment between the final prediction and the collected evidence, mitigating evidence--reasoning inconsistencies. In addition, to balance robustness and efficiency, EVA incorporates Selective Evidence Routing, an adaptive fast--slow reasoning strategy that determines when external evidence is necessary. Visually straightforward queries are handled via direct reasoning, while complex or high-risk cases trigger tool-based evidence acquisition. By jointly addressing how to reliably acquire evidence and how to use it consistently, EVA transforms multimodal reasoning from passive answer validation into explicit evidence-backed decision making. Experimental results demonstrate that EVA achieves significantly improved reasoning reliability over direct VLM inference and multi-agent methods, while maintaining efficiency through selective tool invocation.
papers.summary: Hallucinations in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) often come from unchecked visual assumptions, and external visual tools only help if the model picks the right tool, supplies correct parameters, and respects the evidence it gets back. `EVA` structures reasoning as evidence acquisition and verification through `Iterative Tool Replanning`, which refines tool choice and parameters from intermediate observations, and `Evidence Consistency Verification`, which checks the final answer against collected evidence. A `Selective Evidence Routing` step answers visually simple queries directly and invokes tools only for complex or high-risk ones, and the authors report **improved reasoning reliability over direct inference and multi-agent methods while keeping efficiency through selective tool use**.

papers.title: P-FedSkill: A Personalized Federated Skill Learning Framework under Task Heterogeneity
papers.abstract: Skill learning has become an important way to improve agent performance. However, agent trajectories often contain sensitive information and cannot be shared across clients, hindering collaborative skill learning. To tackle this issue, federated skill learning (FSL) has emerged as a solution by distilling trajectories into compact skill representations and uploading them to a central server for sharing. However, existing FSL methods typically share skills based on skill similarity without considering their contributions to heterogeneous tasks across clients, thereby degrading agent performance. To address this challenge, we propose P-FedSkill, a personalized FSL framework that comprises three key components: local skill extraction (LSE), personalized skill selection (PSS), and task-aware skill routing (TASR). Specifically, LSE first extracts skill patches (i.e., task applicability conditions and execution strategies) and task execution outcomes from trajectories. PSS then uses these outcomes to evaluate each skill patch's performance on client tasks and incorporates its task applicability condition to construct a personalized skill set for each client. Finally, TASR adaptively selects a task-relevant subset of skill patches based on their applicability conditions to guide agent execution. We further provide a theoretical guarantee for personalized skill selection in P-FedSkill, and extensive experiments also demonstrate its effectiveness.
papers.summary: Federated skill learning (FSL) lets agents on different clients share distilled skills rather than sensitive trajectories, but existing methods share by skill similarity without regard to how much a skill helps each client's differing tasks. `P-FedSkill` extracts skill patches (applicability conditions plus execution strategies) and task outcomes locally, uses those outcomes to **build a personalized skill set for each client**, and at run time routes a task-relevant subset of patches to guide the agent. The authors provide a theoretical guarantee for the personalized selection step and report experiments supporting its effectiveness.

papers.title: PowerFix: Physics-Guided Iterative Repair for LLM-Assisted Power Converter Design
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly being explored for automated engineering design. However, repairing power-converter designs that fail engineering validation remains challenging: the system must identify physical causes, locate responsible design variables, and resolve violations without compromising other constraints. We introduce PowerFix, a physics-guided iterative repair framework that converts validation failures into structured diagnoses and executable patches while preserving topology and design requirements. PowerDiagGraph links failed checks to possible physical causes and constrains repair routes. An LLM prioritizes these routes, while a deterministic compiler translates selected repairs into authorized field-level edits. Candidates are validated on isolated design copies and committed only after all required engineering checks pass; failed validation can guide replanning. On our constructed 96-task flyback repair benchmark, comprising injected single faults, coupled faults, and held-out natural failures from our design generator, PowerFix achieves 78.7% verified repair success rate (VRSR), compared with 30.1% for the strongest of three LLM baselines. Three additional replanning rounds increase VRSR to 88.4%. These offline results provide pilot-stage evidence within a simulation-based design workflow, with hardware prototype validation and transfer to a second converter topology as the next steps toward deployment.
papers.summary: Repairing power-converter designs that fail engineering validation requires identifying physical causes and fixing the responsible design variables without breaking other constraints. `PowerFix` links failed checks to possible physical causes through a `PowerDiagGraph`, has a large language model (LLM) prioritize the permitted repair routes, and uses a deterministic compiler to turn chosen repairs into authorized field-level edits that are committed only after all checks pass on an isolated design copy. On a constructed 96-task flyback repair benchmark it reaches a **78.7% verified repair success rate, against 30.1% for the strongest of three LLM baselines**, rising to 88.4% with three additional replanning rounds. The results are offline and simulation-based, with hardware validation and a second converter topology left as next steps.

papers.title: KeyDeck: Multi-Paper-to-Slide Generation via Cross-Paper Synthesis and Reference-Guided Personalization
papers.abstract: Multi-paper-to-slide generation (multi-PTSG) is the task of constructing a unified presentation from multiple research papers by selecting, organizing, and synthesizing information across sources. This task introduces two main challenges: (i) combining multiple sources into a coherent narrative requires identifying cross-paper relationships and synthesizing their content, and (ii) the desired organization and emphasis varies substantially across presenters, making personalization essential for user satisfaction. Motivated by these challenges, we propose KeyDeck, the first multi-PTSG framework that integrates per-paper and cross-paper analysis to identify relationships among sources and synthesize their contributions into a coherent narrative, and reference-guided personalization to infer presenters' narrative, content, textual, and visual preferences and adapt slide generation accordingly. To evaluate generation quality, personalization adherence, and conversational goal satisfaction, we introduce KeyBench, a benchmark of 100 expert-authored multi-paper presentations, together with a comprehensive evaluation framework. Our results demonstrate that KeyDeck outperforms existing approaches in multi-PTSG quality, personalization adherence, and conversational goal satisfaction.
papers.summary: Multi-paper-to-slide generation (multi-PTSG) builds a single presentation from several research papers, which requires synthesizing content across sources and adapting to presenters' differing preferences. `KeyDeck` combines per-paper and cross-paper analysis to identify relationships among sources, and uses reference-guided personalization to infer a presenter's narrative, content, textual, and visual preferences. The authors also introduce `KeyBench`, a benchmark of 100 expert-authored multi-paper presentations, on which `KeyDeck` **outperforms existing approaches on generation quality, personalization adherence, and conversational goal satisfaction**.

papers.title: Practice Makes Fluent: Learning to Use Earlier Predictions in Looped Models
papers.abstract: People become faster at a task through practice, but models that improve with experience do not necessarily learn to use less computation. We train looped models, whose intermediate predictions allow earlier exits, to perform tasks with fewer iterations through practice. This is difficult because shared-weight updates can degrade the final-loop prediction while improving early ones, and the exit gate must track early predictions as their quality changes. We propose FLUENT, which requires no additional task labels or rewards: it distills the initial model's final-loop prediction into early predictions, anchors the current final-loop prediction to the same frozen teacher, and trains the exit gate to balance disagreement with the current final-loop prediction against computation cost. FLUENT improves performance at shallower depth in new Crafter worlds, raises LIBERO success with fewer action-head iterations, and maintains language-model accuracy at lower selected depth. On a real robot, success rises from 62.3\% to 74.6\% while mean time over successful episodes falls from 69\,s to 31\,s. The project page is available at https://msseok96-cpu.github.io/FLUENT/.
papers.summary: Looped models produce intermediate predictions that allow early exits, but training them to use fewer iterations is hard because shared-weight updates can degrade the final-loop prediction and the exit gate must track changing early predictions. `FLUENT` needs no extra task labels or rewards: it distills the initial model's final-loop prediction into early predictions, anchors the current final-loop prediction to the same frozen teacher, and trains the exit gate to trade off disagreement against computation cost. It improves performance at shallower depth in new `Crafter` worlds, raises `LIBERO` success with fewer action-head iterations, and maintains language-model accuracy at lower depth. On a real robot, **success rises from 62.3% to 74.6% while mean time over successful episodes drops from 69 s to 31 s**.

papers.title: NORMCRAFT: Cultural Norm Generation for Context-Aware Language Model Alignment
papers.abstract: Cultural alignment requires large language models (LLMs) to infer often-implicit social norms from a scenario and its cultural context. Existing approaches typically adapt individual models or supply external cultural knowledge, while learning norm inference independently of downstream response generation remains underexplored. We introduce NORMCRAFT, a modular framework that decouples norm inference from response generation. Through norm-centric multi-view supervision, we train an LLM as a norm generator to recover shared norms from prospective, adherence, and violation scenarios without downstream response labels. The generated norms guide a separate, frozen LLM (the responder). With Qwen3.5-4B as the responder, NORMCRAFT outperforms prompting and supervised fine-tuning (SFT) baselines on four of five downstream metrics. On SafeWorld, its responses reflect the reference norms more often (Coverage) and more precisely (Faithfulness), exceeding Responder SFT by 18.0 and 14.1 percentage points, respectively. Direct norm evaluation also shows higher norm quality than the base and few-shot generators. The same trained generator improves cultural alignment on SafeWorld across fourteen frozen LLMs spanning five families and 0.8B to 27B parameters, with the largest gains for the smallest models.
papers.summary: Cultural alignment requires large language models (LLMs) to infer often-implicit social norms from a scenario and its cultural context. `NORMCRAFT` separates the two steps: one LLM is trained as a norm generator with multi-view supervision over prospective, adherence, and violation scenarios, without downstream response labels, and its norms then guide a separate frozen responder model. With `Qwen3.5-4B` as responder, it beats prompting and supervised fine-tuning (SFT) baselines on four of five downstream metrics, and on `SafeWorld` **exceeds responder SFT by 18.0 points on Coverage and 14.1 on Faithfulness**. The same generator improves cultural alignment across fourteen frozen LLMs from 0.8B to 27B parameters, with the largest gains for the smallest models.

papers.title: Asset4D-Bench: Benchmarking Coding Agents for Editable 3D and 4D Reconstruction
papers.abstract: A cart can follow its reference trajectory while its cargo floats above the deck. Asset4D-Bench tests whether coding agents recover objects, motion and interactions from visual references as editable Blender scenes. Its 114 conditions span image editing, video reconstruction with matched full or partial starter assets, and independently selected from-scratch tasks. We independently reopen projects and measure them against native reference states. The 228 archived scores include original delivery outcomes and versioned measures of scene quality. On 24 from-scratch tasks, each model earns full dynamics credit on 14. Of these, three GPT-6.1-Sol and eight GPT-6-Astra reconstructions earn zero relation points. Under the fixed scoring weights, relations contribute 5.15 points to the 6.50-point Sol-minus-Astra difference in mean recovered fidelity. Differences in execution and recovery policy across archived runs preclude a causal estimate of starter-asset effects.
papers.summary: `Asset4D-Bench` tests whether coding agents can turn images and videos into editable `Blender` scenes that recover objects, motion, and the interactions between them. Its 114 conditions cover image editing, video reconstruction with full or partial starter assets, and from-scratch tasks, with each project independently reopened and scored against native reference states. On 24 from-scratch tasks both models earn full dynamics credit on 14, yet three of the `GPT-6.1-Sol` and eight of the `GPT-6-Astra` reconstructions among those score zero on relations, and **relations account for 5.15 of the 6.50-point gap in mean recovered fidelity between the two models**. The authors note that differences in execution and recovery policy across runs prevent a causal estimate of how starter assets affect results.

papers.title: JOVE ICE: Intent Guided Cloud Edge Device Collaboration for AI Glasses
papers.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) and LLM based agents have expanded the capabilities of AI glasses, enabling egocentric visual question answering, memory retrieval, and proactive assistance.
