These applications involve diverse inputs, including speech, images, and video, and range from simple device control to complex visual reasoning, posing challenges for efficient computation and communication. While video centric capabilities have received considerable attention, simple text based and device executable tasks remain underexplored despite their prevalence in daily interactions. Efficiently supporting diverse workloads within a unified assistant remains an open challenge. We propose JOVE ICE, an intent guided cloud, edge, and device collaborative framework that routes requests among AI glasses, a paired smartphone, and cloud servers according to user intent. JOVE ICE integrates hierarchical intent classification with dynamic subagent orchestration to select efficient execution paths and flexibly incorporate new applications through specialized subagents. Analysis of real world AI glasses requests reveals that simple device control tasks account for over 30% of interactions, which JOVE ICE handles directly on device to avoid unnecessary cloud computation and costs. Evaluations on three public benchmarks demonstrate that JOVE ICE reduces time to first token by approximately 13% and token usage by over 11% compared with conventional device and cloud architectures, while maintaining task quality. These results demonstrate the potential of intent guided collaboration to improve the efficiency and scalability of AI glasses.
papers.summary: AI glasses handle requests ranging from simple device control to complex visual reasoning, and sending everything to the cloud wastes computation and adds latency. `JOVE ICE` routes each request among the glasses, a paired smartphone, and cloud servers using hierarchical intent classification combined with dynamic subagent orchestration, which also lets new applications be added as specialized subagents. Analysis of real-world requests shows simple device control makes up over 30% of interactions, which the system handles on device. On three public benchmarks it **cuts time to first token by about 13% and token usage by over 11%** versus conventional device-and-cloud architectures while maintaining task quality.

papers.title: FlashProve-Next: Verifiable Inference for Production LLM APIs
papers.abstract:
Clients of closed-weight LLM APIs cannot verify whether a provider ran the advertised model, precision, hidden prompt, and reasoning budget. Existing approaches either trust hardware or third parties, or re-prove every layer of an integer surrogate at high cost while diverging from native floating-point serving.
  FlashProve-Next produces verifiable, zero-knowledge-masked proofs for individual LLM API responses without modifying native serving (bf16/fp8/mxfp4, random sampling, FlashAttention, CUDA graphs, batching, prefix caching) and without disclosing weights, hidden prompts, hidden reasoning, or activations (dense profiles fix coarse geometry; cross-architecture hiding is deferred). A non-depleting Reed-Solomon weight commitment model_id opens inside proofs via hidden column openings, while local per-operator rounding contracts remove integer surrogates and the refusal-bit leak. Cost-weighted spot-checking supports non-interactive public verification (NI-315, $\varepsilon \le 2^{-40}$, $Q \le 2^{64}$) and external-seed C_pre mode (ExtSeed-153, $\varepsilon \le 2^{-20}$, $Q_{\rm samp} \le 2^{30}$).
  Twenty-eight Lean 4 modules (696 declarations, zero sorry, standard axioms only) mechanize round-by-round soundness, bucketed sampling, $\mathbb{F}_{p^3}$ constrained-mask binding, causal masking, six IR gadgets, and executable FPN2 verifiers. Five-model Blackwell calibration gives zero false rejections across 1.85M GEMM/MoE blocks and 1.96M non-GEMM rows. Our zero-Phase-2 folded backend (folded ZK simulator open) proves Qwen3-0.6B ExtSeed-153 (1.47B cells, 8 MiB) in 450.2 s GPU (10.76 s CPU) at unique-decoding $Q=128$, passes a 14/14 cheating matrix, and scales to 36-layer Qwen3-4B (dev $4+2$) and live vLLM Qwen3-30B-A3B-FP8 Relation 6 (1.49 s prove, 23.4 ms Rust verify, public weight tiles). Rust fpn-verify checks 8 MiB FPN2 Relation 2 proofs in 10.1 ms on CPU.
papers.summary: Clients of closed-weight large language model (LLM) APIs cannot check that a provider actually ran the advertised model, precision, hidden prompt, and reasoning budget. `FlashProve-Next` produces zero-knowledge-masked proofs for individual API responses without changing native floating-point serving and without revealing weights, hidden prompts, or activations, using a Reed-Solomon weight commitment, per-operator rounding contracts, and cost-weighted spot-checking. Its soundness arguments are mechanized in 28 `Lean 4` modules, and calibration across five models produced zero false rejections over millions of checked blocks. A proof for `Qwen3-0.6B` takes 450.2 s on GPU, while on a live `vLLM` deployment of `Qwen3-30B-A3B-FP8` one relation is **proved in 1.49 s and verified in 23.4 ms in Rust**.

papers.title: WhatIf: Counterfactual World Models over Action-Grounded Causal Graphs for Robotic Manipulation
papers.abstract: World models predict what happens under an action, but choosing between actions requires comparing their outcomes in the same physical situation. Factual transitions alone determine action-wise marginal futures and average effects, but not individual effects or the probability that switching actions causes harm. We introduce WhatIf, a counterfactual world model for manipulation that couples candidate futures through shared latent physics and transition noise inferred from factual history. Each candidate action induces a sparse object-factor causal graph describing the physical pathways it activates. Rolling out these graphs under the shared situation anchors predictions to observed outcomes and confines action contrasts to the objects each action reaches. Shared type-conditioned functions support varying numbers of objects, while a round-trip loss enforces action-invariant abduction without counterfactual labels. We show that replacing an individual effect with its conditional mean incurs mean-squared error equal to its conditional variance, motivating comparisons between coupled futures. Building on these comparisons, Counterfactual Advantage Planning (CAP) ranks plans by their advantage over an incumbent within shared situations and constrains the probability of harm. Paired advantages reduce estimator variance by a factor of $1-\rho$, where $\rho$ is the correlation between branch outcomes, and cancel model errors shared by both branches. Each executed transition provides hindsight advantages to update the physics posterior, the next plan, and an amortized policy without a learned critic. We further establish when observational transitions identify interventional dynamics. Paired simulator interventions evaluate counterfactual accuracy, graph recovery, compositional generalization, and decision quality.
papers.summary: Choosing between robot actions requires comparing their outcomes in the same physical situation, which ordinary world models trained on factual transitions cannot do at the level of individual effects or probability of harm. `WhatIf` is a counterfactual world model for manipulation that couples candidate futures through shared latent physics and transition noise inferred from history, with each action inducing a sparse object-factor causal graph of the physical pathways it activates. On top of it, Counterfactual Advantage Planning (`CAP`) ranks plans by their advantage over an incumbent and constrains the probability of harm. The authors show that **paired advantages reduce estimator variance by a factor of 1−ρ**, where ρ is the correlation between branch outcomes, and evaluate counterfactual accuracy, graph recovery, and decision quality with paired simulator interventions.

papers.title: Tells of a Lying Machine: Analyzing LLM-Generated Strategic Dialogue in Chinese Werewolf
papers.abstract: Social-deduction games give models opposing objectives, but they also give roles different information and speaking obligations. We analyze 5,404 public utterances from 150 Chinese Werewolf games played by 12 models, comparing ordinary wolves with ordinary villagers so that special roles are excluded. Private knowledge and goals still differ, and no utterance is verified as true or false. After model and length adjustment, wolf utterances score higher on both certainty and uncertainty (coefficients +0.074 and +0.072). Emotional intensification has the largest rank-biserial effect (r = .145), but it depends on a single degree marker and correlates weakly with human-rated affect. Three annotators' ratings of 392 utterances show higher wolf scores on four behavioral dimensions, and five LLM judges reach 60.8%-70.2% accuracy on a shared evaluation set. In a generation probe that prompts six models with a wolf identity but a villager speaking goal under fixed public context, certainty (+0.164) and emotional intensification (+0.095) increase. These findings describe role-associated language rather than verified lying, and they argue for explicit comparison groups and lexicon sensitivity checks in game-based deception evaluation. Data and code are available at https://github.com/justinchoi929/Tells-of-a-Lying-Machine
papers.summary: Social-deduction games are used to study machine deception, but roles differ in information and speaking obligations, which confounds comparisons. This analysis covers 5,404 public utterances from 150 Chinese `Werewolf` games played by 12 models, comparing only ordinary wolves against ordinary villagers. After adjusting for model and length, wolf utterances score higher on both certainty and uncertainty, human annotators rate wolves higher on four behavioral dimensions, and **five LLM judges identify roles with only 60.8% to 70.2% accuracy**. The authors stress that these are role-associated language patterns rather than verified lies, and recommend explicit comparison groups and lexicon sensitivity checks in game-based deception evaluation.

papers.title: REFORGE: LLM-Assisted RTL Bug Repair with Structured Context and Verification Feedback
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can write and repair RTL, but successful compilation or testbench execution does not establish defect removal, behavioral preservation, security, or implementation feasibility. Existing LLM-based RTL repair methods often report a single repair rate without retaining separate evidence for these properties, limiting reproducible comparison and integration into hardware design flows. We present REFORGE, which, to our knowledge, is the first LLM-assisted RTL repair framework that maintains and accumulates structured repair evidence across iterations, allowing it to generate fixes that satisfy multiple objectives simultaneously, including functionality, behavioral equivalence, security, and cost efficiency. REFORGE profiles buggy RTL, identifies structural and security-relevant features, localizes failing behavior, and uses verification-guided diagnosis to generate complete RTL repair variants. Each variant undergoes syntax checking, simulation, formal analysis, off-trigger preservation, security re-scan, and synthesis-based power, performance, and area analysis. We implement REFORGE as a backend-independent repair-and-verification flow and evaluate it in 288 runs across three LLM backends and three benchmark suites. On CirFix, the proposed context and diagnosis increase runs delivering a checked repair from 32/63 to 51/63, while every configuration repairs the Hack@DAC OpenTitan defect. Evidence records also show that a testbench-only criterion reports 3.9 times more repairs than the full set of applicable checks, security-clean outputs may lack functional verification, and different RTL repairs can implement equivalent hardware. These results show that LLM-generated RTL repairs require explicit multi-stage verification evidence rather than a single pass/fail outcome.
papers.summary: Large language models can repair RTL hardware code, but a design that compiles or passes a testbench has not been shown to be defect-free, behavior-preserving, secure, or implementable. `REFORGE` profiles the buggy RTL, localizes failing behavior, generates full repair variants through verification-guided diagnosis, and runs each through syntax checking, simulation, formal analysis, security re-scan, and synthesis-based power, performance, and area analysis, keeping structured evidence across iterations. Across 288 runs with three LLM backends, its context and diagnosis raise checked repairs on `CirFix` from 32/63 to 51/63, and every configuration repairs the `Hack@DAC` `OpenTitan` defect. The evidence records show that **a testbench-only criterion reports 3.9 times more repairs than the full set of applicable checks**.

papers.title: Teaching Students to Stand on Their Own: Distilling Vision Foundation Models for Fine-Grained Few-Shot Class-Incremental Learning
papers.abstract: Fine-grained few-shot class-incremental learning (FG-FSCIL) aims to incrementally learn visually similar new classes from limited images without catastrophic forgetting. Prior work typically learns strong representations on base classes or leverages vision foundation models (VFMs) directly as backbones or via knowledge distillation. However, VFM backbones incur high computational costs and do not guarantee fine-grained recognition. Although knowledge distillation reduces inference cost, our preliminary experiments reveal that distilled students still lag substantially behind their VFM teachers, particularly on new classes. To address this limitation, we propose STAND, a systematic VFM-to-student distillation design tailored for FG-FSCIL. Specifically, STAND connects the teacher and student by equipping the student with a fixed copy of the teacher's classifier, aligning their outputs via projectors, and feeding both models composite images that combine different training images. On these composite images, relation distillation matches how the teacher and the student relate each image to other images, while difference distillation matches how this relation changes between two composite images. Finally, we freeze the student and classify new classes using length-calibrated prototypes, which restore the reduced similarity of few-shot prototypes. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that STAND achieves state-of-the-art performance across FG-FSCIL datasets at low computational cost, while generalizing across student backbones and broader datasets.
papers.summary: Fine-grained few-shot class-incremental learning (FG-FSCIL) requires learning visually similar new classes from a handful of images without forgetting old ones, and students distilled from vision foundation models (VFMs) lag well behind their teachers on new classes. `STAND` gives the student a fixed copy of the teacher's classifier, aligns outputs through projectors, and feeds both models composite images on which it matches how each image relates to others and how that relation changes between composites. The frozen student then classifies new classes with length-calibrated prototypes. The authors report **state-of-the-art accuracy across FG-FSCIL datasets at low computational cost**, with gains that carry over to other student backbones and broader datasets.

papers.title: TransHarness: From Benchmark Overfitting to Transferable Harness Evolution
papers.abstract: Harness evolution offers a path to improving coding agents without updating model weights. However, existing methods can overfit their evolution benchmarks, producing gains that fail to carry over to new tasks. To address this challenge, we introduce Transferable Harness Evolution (TransHarness), which evolves harness intervention policies from same-task success-failure contrasts. These policies couple execution-context triggers with diagnostic guidance, enabling task-dependent checks and corrections beyond the source executions. Cross-task replay and independent semantic selection retain policies that intervene selectively and ground corrections in current-task evidence rather than source-specific solutions. We further curate an independent evolution set for cross-distribution transfer and conduct a cross-benchmark evaluation covering multiple strong models and a range of lightweight and mature harnesses. Experiments show that, with only 300 source trajectories from outside the test distribution, TransHarness further improves strong agents across distinct target benchmarks, demonstrating transferable harness evolution beyond benchmark overfitting. Specifically, TransHarness achieves state-of-the-art scores of 76.4% on DeepSWE v1.1 and 95.5% on Terminal-Bench 2.1, surpassing the strongest baseline model, GPT-6 Astra, by 2.4 and 5.6 percentage points, respectively.
papers.summary: Harness evolution improves coding agents without changing model weights, but evolved harnesses tend to overfit the benchmark they were tuned on. `TransHarness` learns intervention policies from contrasts between successful and failed attempts at the same task, pairing execution-context triggers with diagnostic guidance, then keeps only policies that survive cross-task replay and an independent semantic selection step. Using just 300 source trajectories from outside the test distribution, it improves strong agents across several models and harnesses on separate target benchmarks. It reports **76.4% on `DeepSWE v1.1` and 95.5% on `Terminal-Bench 2.1`**, exceeding the strongest baseline model, `GPT-6 Astra`, by 2.4 and 5.6 percentage points.

papers.title: ScanAR: Parallel Row-Scan Decoding for Efficient Image Generation in Unified Autoregressive Models
papers.abstract: Unified multimodal autoregressive (AR) models represent text and images in one token sequence and generate all modalities with a shared next-token prediction head. Their image generation, however, decodes an $H\times W$ visual grid token by token in raster order, which takes $HW$ sequential steps and dominates inference time. Existing acceleration methods for visual AR generation either change the tokenizer, the prediction head, or the model interface, or keep the model but cannot reach high parallelism without losing quality, so they do not carry over to unified AR models. We propose ScanAR, a row-scan parallel decoding method that only redefines the predecessors of visual tokens. The first visual row is generated from left to right as usual, and each later row is generated in a single parallel step, with every token predicted from the vertically aligned token of the previous row. Nonvisual tokens keep the standard autoregressive rule. ScanAR reduces the visual decoding depth from $HW$ to $H+W$ without changing the backbone, vocabulary, or output head and without adding parameters, and it supports both training from scratch and lightweight post-training. On Emu3.5-Image-34B, ScanAR post-training reaches a GenEval score of 82.36, the best among post-training acceleration methods trained on the same data, and generates $512\times512$ images $13.8\times$ faster than raster decoding under the same inference setting. On ImageNet, ScanAR trained from scratch has the highest throughput at every model size with FID comparable to raster LlamaGen. On the 34B Xiaomi-Robotics-U0 model, ScanAR preserves the overall quality of embodied scene generation, interleaved image-text generation, and video generation.
papers.summary: Unified autoregressive models that generate text and images in one token sequence decode an H×W image grid one token at a time, which dominates inference time. `ScanAR` generates the first row left to right and then produces each later row in a single parallel step, predicting every token from the one directly above it, which cuts decoding depth from HW to H+W without changing the backbone, vocabulary, or output head. Post-trained on `Emu3.5-Image-34B`, it reaches a `GenEval` score of 82.36 and **generates 512×512 images 13.8× faster than raster decoding**. Trained from scratch on `ImageNet` it has the highest throughput at every model size with FID comparable to raster `LlamaGen`, and it preserves quality on the 34B `Xiaomi-Robotics-U0` model.

papers.title: Improving Building Energy Efficiency with an Indoor Environmental World Model and Counterfactual Adaptive Learning
papers.abstract: Optimizing indoor climate systems plays a critical role in achieving the United Nations' Sustainable Development Goals 11 and 13. However, indoor delayed thermodynamic responses and partial observability severely hinder existing reinforcement learning (RL) methods, which are primarily limited by implicit thermal inertia, occupancy dynamic prediction, and cumulative prediction errors during long-horizon rollouts. Thus, we propose a novel occupant-centric indoor climate control framework. It develops indoor environmental world models to predict future physical thermal baselines and dynamic occupancy, explicitly capturing latent thermal inertia. By formulating adaptive regulation as counterfactual advantage learning against future environments via a Branching Dueling Q-Network, and integrating a Held-Action TD-{\lambda} target, it effectively mitigates delayed credit assignment. Additionally, a proposed physics-aligned smoothness regularization suppresses high-frequency actuator fluctuations, potentially extending equipment service life. Experiments on SemiBuildingSim and Sinergym demonstrate that our method achieves a superior multi-objective trade-off. Compared to the best-performing methods, it further reduces energy consumption by 11.2%, occupant discomfort by 44.2%, and action fluctuation by 47.3%, achieving better sample efficiency and cross-region effectiveness. This interdisciplinary study offers an energy-efficient, occupant-centric AI solution for control science, building science, and energy sustainability.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning for indoor climate control struggles with delayed thermal responses, partial observability, and prediction errors that accumulate over long rollouts. The proposed framework builds indoor world models that forecast the thermal baseline and occupancy, then learns control as counterfactual advantage against those predicted futures using a `Branching Dueling Q-Network` with a held-action TD-lambda target and a smoothness regularizer on actuator commands. On `SemiBuildingSim` and `Sinergym`, it **reduces energy consumption by 11.2%, occupant discomfort by 44.2%, and action fluctuation by 47.3%** relative to the best competing methods, with better sample efficiency.

papers.title: Triage Before Fine-Tuning: Feasibility-Gated Selection and Monitored Adaptation of Embodied Foundation Models for a Fixed Physical Platform
papers.abstract: Embodied foundation models are increasingly deployed by selection: a practitioner picks a public checkpoint by benchmark rank and fine-tunes it on local data. The platform is fixed before the model is chosen, with little or no local data. We ask what such a checkpoint loses on a fixed platform and which part of the loss local data can buy back. We split the gap by what can repair it. A sensing gap, information the sensors do not capture, cannot be closed with their data; a latency gap, output arriving after the control loop needs it, belongs to the loop, not the weights; only a distribution gap is fine-tuning's to repair. TRIAGE turns this into feasibility-gated selection and monitored adaptation in five stages: gates on the sensor contract and on end-to-end latency that no score can override, probes on ten minutes of local logs, a ranking by target-relevant score among the candidates that pass, and fine-tuning that is monitored and checked in closed loop before release. On driving benchmarks, a deadline below a leading closed-loop model's latency makes it collide on 80 to 90% of routes, and losing field of view moves plans 2.2 to 5.7 times more than losing resolution at equal pixels. Local frames close 75% of a stability gap but raise perturbation sensitivity at small budgets, and picking by score violates a gate in two of four deployment profiles. On a full-scale vehicle, the factory camera failed the sensing gate and an added camera repaired it. The latency gate removed the two highest-scoring candidates, neither of which completed a closed-loop trip. The selected model passed acceptance in 4 of 5 closed-loop trips, and the closed-loop check withheld a fine-tuned model that had improved offline. TRIAGE lets organizations that cannot train foundation models from scratch find out whether a public checkpoint can run on the robot or vehicle they own, and what to fix if not.
papers.summary: Practitioners often pick a public embodied foundation model by benchmark rank and fine-tune it for a robot or vehicle whose sensors and compute are already fixed. `TRIAGE` separates the resulting performance loss into a sensing gap, a latency gap, and a distribution gap, of which only the last can be repaired by fine-tuning, and turns this into five stages: hard gates on sensors and end-to-end latency, probes on ten minutes of local logs, ranking among passing candidates, and monitored fine-tuning with a closed-loop check. On driving benchmarks, **a deadline below a leading model's latency makes it collide on 80 to 90% of routes**, and choosing by score alone violates a gate in two of four deployment profiles. On a full-scale vehicle the latency gate removed the two highest-scoring candidates, and the selected model passed acceptance in 4 of 5 closed-loop trips.

papers.title: CHD-Bench: Diagnosing Congenital Heart Disease through Interactive Examination
papers.abstract: Diagnosis of congenital heart disease (CHD) requires understanding the spatial relationships between cardiac structures, which clinicians assess by scrolling through CT or cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) slices and rotating 3D reconstructions. Although automated methods have advanced cardiac segmentation, identifying congenital heart defects from volumetric scans remains an open challenge. The two existing approaches rely on handcrafted diagnostic rules limited to static anatomical abnormalities. We introduce CHD-Bench, the first benchmark for interactive CHD diagnosis, defining a multi-label task and evaluation protocol over 247 CT and MRI scans from three cohorts covering 38 CHD types. We also present CHD-Harness, open-source software that runs a VLM in a 3D Slicer environment through 22 tools, manages each examination, and records the resulting diagnosis and supporting views. We evaluate off-the-shelf medical, open weight, and closed weight VLMs and compare them with a 3D CNN classifier and published rule-based results. Gemini 4 Argon with CHD-Harness achieves the highest macro F1 across all three cohorts (0.63, 0.63, and 0.43). Allowing for interactive examination raises its macro F1 by up to 20 points over static views. These results establish CHD-Bench and CHD-Harness as a foundation for developing and evaluating VLMs for interactive CHD diagnosis.
papers.summary: Diagnosing congenital heart disease (CHD) depends on spatial relationships between cardiac structures that clinicians inspect by scrolling through CT or MRI slices and rotating 3D reconstructions. `CHD-Bench` defines a multi-label diagnosis task over 247 scans from three cohorts covering 38 CHD types, and `CHD-Harness` lets a vision-language model (VLM) operate a `3D Slicer` environment through 22 tools while recording its diagnosis and supporting views. Among medical, open-weight, and closed-weight VLMs, a 3D CNN classifier, and rule-based results, `Gemini 4 Argon` with the harness scores the highest macro F1 on all three cohorts (0.63, 0.63, and 0.43). **Interactive examination raises its macro F1 by up to 20 points over static views**.

papers.title: InterGenEHR$^+$: An Interactive Framework for Natural Language-Conditioned Generation of Longitudinal Patient Trajectories
papers.abstract:
Objective: To develop and validate InterGenEHR$^+$, an interactive framework for natural language-conditioned generation of synthetic tabular electronic health records (EHRs) and longitudinal trajectories for scenario-based evaluation of machine learning models.
  Methods: An optional large language model (LLM) parser converts clinical requests into structured constraints. Conditional variational autoencoders and diffusion models generate single-time-point records, while diffusion models generate longitudinal trajectories. We evaluate parsing, distributional fidelity, imputation, clinical-constraint adherence, mortality prediction, and clinical plausibility using a multi-institutional cohort of 874 patients receiving venovenous extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VV-ECMO).
  Results: Gemma 3 4B with few-shot prompting achieves the highest parsing performance with a low spurious slot rate. IGE-TabDDPM and IGE-PMVAE perform well in single-time-point generation; IGE-CSDI, IGE-FGTI, and IGE-MTSCI lead on different longitudinal fidelity metrics. Across five random seeds and three classifiers, synthetic cohorts retain predictive utility for mortality prediction on real test data. Clinician ratings support trajectory plausibility and alignment with requested scenarios.
  Conclusion: InterGenEHR$^+$ supports clinician-specified generation of EHR trajectories with statistical fidelity and downstream predictive utility in the evaluated VV-ECMO cohort. Extension to other clinical settings requires further validation.
  Significance: The framework supports scenario-based evaluation of machine learning models in data-sparse critical care settings.
papers.summary: `InterGenEHR+` generates synthetic tabular electronic health records (EHRs) and longitudinal patient trajectories from natural-language clinical requests, for scenario-based testing of machine learning models. An optional large language model parser converts a request into structured constraints, conditional variational autoencoders and diffusion models produce single-time-point records, and diffusion models produce trajectories. Evaluated on a multi-institutional cohort of 874 patients on venovenous extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VV-ECMO), `Gemma 3 4B` with few-shot prompting was the best parser, and **synthetic cohorts retained predictive utility for mortality prediction on real test data** across five seeds and three classifiers. Clinician ratings supported the plausibility of the trajectories, and the authors note that other clinical settings need further validation.

papers.title: Multimodal Safety Evaluation of Vision-Language Models in Japanese
papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are increasingly deployed in Japanese-language settings, yet multimodal safety evaluation has been largely English-centric. We extend the Multimodal Safety Test Suite (MSTS) of R\"ottger et al. (2025) to Japanese as the 12th language, contributing 320 machine-translated and post-edited cases with reference answers plus 82 culturally localized Japanese images. We introduce an evaluation framework that (i) extends MSTS's 3-class safety grouping with a 5-point scale that also rewards useful (not just safe) responses, and (ii) separates image recognition from safety judgment to isolate recognition errors. Using this framework, we evaluate five modern Japanese VLMs (Gemini-3-Flash, GPT-5, InternVL3, LLM-JP-4-VL, Qwen3-VL) against human evaluation, and find substantial variance in the safety readiness across the models. Finally, we evaluate two LLM-as-a-Judge models and find that providing a reference answer improves agreement with human safety judgments, though recall for detecting unsafe responses remains limited, underscoring the difficulty of automating multimodal safety evaluation. The dataset created for our study will be released upon publication.
papers.summary: Safety evaluation of vision-language models (VLMs) has been largely English-centric despite growing Japanese deployment. This work extends the Multimodal Safety Test Suite (`MSTS`) to Japanese with 320 machine-translated and post-edited cases with reference answers plus 82 culturally localized images, and adds a 5-point scale that rewards useful as well as safe responses while separating image recognition errors from safety judgment. Human evaluation of `Gemini-3-Flash`, `GPT-5`, `InternVL3`, `LLM-JP-4-VL`, and `Qwen3-VL` shows substantial variance in safety readiness. For automated judging, **giving the judge model a reference answer improves agreement with humans, but recall on unsafe responses remains limited**.

papers.title: ExtractBench Pro: The Long Tail of Document Extraction
papers.abstract: We present ExtractBench Pro, a schema-guided document extraction benchmark that tests six challenging modes of extraction underrepresented in existing datasets. It is created following a framework for synthetic document generation, in which deterministic document generators assemble challenging components into documents that are designed to be difficult at a level calibrated for frontier systems. We synthesize 100 realistic documents spanning a diverse range of styles. On this data, we evaluate ten coding agents and eight extraction API configurations for accuracy, grounding, and their ability to perfectly extract documents. No extraction system extracts more than 61% of documents error-free. The strongest general-purpose coding agents, Claude Code Opus 5.5 and Codex GPT-6 Astra, outperform specialized extraction APIs on both perfect-document rate and Value F1, but at a higher cost per page. Among specialized extraction APIs, LlamaExtract spans the lower-cost frontier, with Agentic Plus Max Effort approaching the strongest coding agent on both perfect-document rate and Value F1 at lower cost per page. Our analysis of coding agent traces identifies intelligent image processing and programmatic reasoning, but also failures in applying document-specific definitions and recovering relationships from diagrams. We release ExtractBench Pro and these evaluation results as resources for the future development of improved frontier extraction systems.
papers.summary: `ExtractBench Pro` is a schema-guided document extraction benchmark of 100 synthetic documents, built by deterministic generators that assemble components targeting six difficult extraction modes underrepresented in existing datasets. Ten coding agents and eight extraction API configurations are scored on accuracy, grounding, and perfect-document rate, and **no system extracts more than 61% of documents error-free**. General-purpose coding agents `Claude Code Opus 5.5` and `Codex GPT-6 Astra` beat specialized extraction APIs on perfect-document rate and Value F1 but cost more per page, while `LlamaExtract` covers the lower-cost frontier. Trace analysis shows agents using image processing and programmatic reasoning well but failing to apply document-specific definitions and to recover relationships from diagrams.

papers.title: LSRP*-LA: Scalable and Anytime Multi-Agent Path Finding for Large Agents with Asynchronous Actions
papers.abstract: Multi-Agent Path Finding (MAPF) seeks collision-free paths for multiple agents from their start locations to their goal locations while minimizing path costs. Most MAPF algorithms assume that each agent occupies a single vertex and that the actions of all agents are synchronized. These assumptions may limit the use of MAPF planners in practice. Existing planners that get rid of both assumptions either handle only a few agents or cannot improve their solutions. Recently, a planner called LSRP* was proposed, which is scalable and anytime with asynchronous actions, but still limited by that each agent occupies a single vertex. This paper develops a new planner called LSRP*-LA for MAPF for large agents with asynchronous actions (LA-MAPF-AA), where an agent can occupy several cells. LSRP*-LA is scalable and complete, and it keeps improving solution quality after the initial solution is obtained until the runtime budget depletes. We analyze the properties of LSRP*-LA and test it against several baselines with up to 800 agents on various maps. LSRP*-LA can handle twice as many agents as baseline methods and its solution cost is about half that of recent synchronous planners for large agents.
papers.summary: Multi-Agent Path Finding (MAPF) planners usually assume each agent occupies a single vertex and that all agents act in sync, which limits practical use. `LSRP*-LA` extends the scalable, anytime planner `LSRP*` to large agents that occupy several cells and act asynchronously, and it is complete and keeps improving its solution until the runtime budget runs out. In tests with up to 800 agents on various maps, it **handles twice as many agents as baseline methods**, and its solution cost is about half that of recent synchronous planners for large agents.

papers.title: Keep or Roll Back? Out-of-Loop Judges for Self-Improving VLA and End-to-End Embodied Policies
papers.abstract: Self-improvement is now a practical recipe for embodied policies: a policy collects experience, is retrained, and is kept when a judge rates it higher. However, the judge is usually trained or chosen inside the same loop, so its evidence is not independent of the policy. We introduce SealedLoop, an evaluation framework that adds a sealed judge: an evaluator outside the loop that the improver cannot see or optimize against. A new policy is kept only when a sequential test on the sealed judge confirms the gain, with a bounded probability of keeping a worse one. Running the same loop under each judge, we separate two sources of a false gain, which we call judge error (the loop's judge is wrong on its own data) and transfer gap (a real gain there does not carry over to unseen conditions). We evaluate on LIBERO manipulation, NAVSIM driving, and a full-scale real vehicle. In manipulation, a success classifier accepted 65 of 196 failures in one generation. In driving, policies that gain on the loop's own frames lose in an unseen city, so even an exact in-loop judge would keep 8/15 of them. When the sealed test decides, a driving loop built to improve ends with a better policy than under its own critic (0.674 against 0.649 PDMS, from 0.638), and on driving pairs with known sealed gain the test accepted 11 of 12 real gains and none of 59 losses. In a real-world field experiment on a published improvement step, the reinforced version drove further into a curve than the version it started from in all 6 blind pairs, though neither completed it. These results show that evidence from inside the loop, however accurate, is not enough to decide whether a policy has improved. SealedLoop offers a foundation for trustworthy self-improvement of embodied policies, in which progress is judged by evidence the improving system cannot influence.
papers.summary: Self-improving embodied policies are typically kept or discarded by a judge trained or chosen inside the same improvement loop, so its evidence is not independent of the policy. `SealedLoop` adds a sealed judge the improver cannot see or optimize against, and keeps a new policy only when a sequential test on that judge confirms the gain with a bounded probability of accepting a worse one. This separates false gains into judge error and transfer gap: on `LIBERO` a success classifier accepted 65 of 196 failures, and on `NAVSIM` even an exact in-loop judge would keep 8 of 15 policies that lose in an unseen city. On driving pairs with known sealed gain, **the sealed test accepted 11 of 12 real gains and none of 59 losses**, and a loop governed by it ended with a better policy than one governed by its own critic.

papers.title: QPAT: A Universal Quantum Machine Learning Framework for Quantum-Assisted Training and Classical Inference
papers.abstract: Deep learning models often struggle with sharp local optima and overfitting in limited-data regimes, and exhibit limited capacity for capturing high-order, complex probability distributions. Quantum Machine Learning (QML) models, by operating in exponentially large Hilbert spaces, can efficiently represent such distributions and provide favorable inductive biases for learning, offering a promising pathway to overcome these limitations. However, their practical deployment in the Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) era is severely hindered by gradient coupling, barren plateaus, data-loading bottlenecks, and high inference latency. To bridge classical AI and QML, we propose QPAT (QCBM-Prior-Assisted Training), a universal framework that employs a Quantum Circuit Born Machine (QCBM) as a learnable generative prior to provide a task-aligned structured inductive bias during classical model training. The framework can be seamlessly integrated into any classical backbone, including LSTMs, CNNs, and Transformers. We introduce a decoupled fitness-based scoring mechanism and a stochastic "Drop-Prior" mechanism to implicitly distill quantum structural knowledge into the classical weights during training. Evaluated extensively on six benchmarks spanning time-series forecasting, computer vision, and natural language processing, our framework consistently outperforms purely classical backbones in both predictive performance and stability across random seeds; ablation studies further show that these gains are not reproduced by unstructured random priors or a classically learned generative prior. Remarkably, our approach enables completely classical inference, bypassing quantum latency while preserving quantum-enhanced accuracy, paving a highly practical path for QML deployment.
papers.summary: Quantum machine learning models are hard to deploy on Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) hardware because of barren plateaus, data-loading bottlenecks, and inference latency. `QPAT` uses a Quantum Circuit Born Machine (QCBM) as a learnable generative prior while training a classical model such as an LSTM, CNN, or Transformer, with a decoupled fitness-based scoring mechanism and a stochastic Drop-Prior step that distills the prior's structure into the classical weights. Across six benchmarks in time-series forecasting, vision, and language, it **outperforms purely classical backbones in accuracy and seed stability while running inference entirely classically**. Ablations indicate the gains are not reproduced by random priors or a classically learned generative prior.

papers.title: KnitNet: Learning to Search at Inference Time for Exact RNA Inverse Design
papers.abstract: RNA inverse design seeks nucleotide sequences that fold into specified target structures. Existing methods rely on learned generators that can miss exact structural matches, especially beyond their training distributions, or on costly search over a vast, multimodal sequence space. Search is further complicated by globally coupled nucleotide interactions, as correcting one pairing error can create new errors beyond a fixed repair scope. To address this, we introduce KnitNet, an inference-time scaling framework that learns from verifier feedback to refine sequences for exact fold-back matching. Starting from candidates generated for a target secondary structure, KnitNet uses mismatched folds to infer nucleotide dependencies and adapt its joint repair strategy, while an online surrogate learns to predict which edits are promising. This makes search progressively more informed and compute-efficient. Crucially, KnitNet generalizes across RNA structural regimes by changing only the optimization signal to match the verifier required by each setting. Across five secondary-structure benchmarks, KnitNet increases exact solve rates by an average of 21 percentage points over continued sampling with 70% less time-to-solve. On OpenKnot57 specifically, KnitNet is the first method to achieve exact computational matches for all complex, pseudoknotted structures. Beyond 2D, KnitNet improves 3D structural self-consistency over per-target RL by 7.8% while being 39.3% faster, demonstrating generalization and effective inference-time scaling across RNA design regimes.
papers.summary: RNA inverse design looks for nucleotide sequences that fold into a given target structure, where learned generators often miss exact matches and search is costly because fixing one pairing error can create others elsewhere. `KnitNet` refines candidate sequences at inference time using verifier feedback: it infers nucleotide dependencies from mismatched folds to adapt a joint repair strategy, while an online surrogate learns which edits are promising. Across five secondary-structure benchmarks it **raises exact solve rates by an average of 21 percentage points over continued sampling with 70% less time-to-solve**, and it finds exact computational matches for all pseudoknotted structures in `OpenKnot57`. In 3D design it improves structural self-consistency over per-target reinforcement learning by 7.8% while running 39.3% faster.

papers.title: Ensuring Deployment-Time Safety of Neural Network Controlled Systems via Localized Certificate Repair
papers.abstract: Barrier certificates provide formal safety guarantees for neural network controlled systems by ensuring that system trajectories avoid unsafe regions over time. However, after deployment, previously unseen obstacles or constraint changes may introduce new unsafe regions, invalidating the original certificate and potentially leading to unsafe behavior. We address this setting with adaptive piecewise barrier certificates, which preserve the original certificate and policy in unchanged regions while introducing localized updates around newly emerged unsafe regions. The central question is how to perform such updates efficiently during system execution without retraining from scratch. Our key idea is to cast deployment-time adaptation as a localized certificate repair problem and reduce it to an optimization task that leverages the learned structure of previous barrier certificates, enabling fast updates without global retraining. We further design a staged repair framework that progressively transitions from localized repair to joint policy-certificate updates and, when necessary, localized retraining. Empirical results on four benchmarks with five new obstacles show that our method succeeds in all cases and completes within tens of seconds on average, whereas retraining from scratch fails in most cases. On instances where retraining succeeds, our method is 17.3$\times$ faster on average. It incurs only 16.2% performance degradation relative to the original policy.
papers.summary: Barrier certificates give formal safety guarantees for systems controlled by neural networks, but new obstacles or constraints appearing after deployment can invalidate them. The proposed adaptive piecewise barrier certificates keep the original certificate and policy in unchanged regions and repair them locally around new unsafe regions, framed as an optimization that reuses the learned structure, with a staged fallback from local repair to joint policy-certificate updates to localized retraining. On four benchmarks with five new obstacles the method succeeds in every case within tens of seconds on average, whereas retraining from scratch fails in most cases. Where retraining does succeed, the repair is **17.3× faster on average**, with 16.2% performance degradation relative to the original policy.

papers.title: Spectral Optimal Transport for Dynamics-Aware Sign Language Generation
papers.abstract: Sign language generation (SLG) translates spoken-language text into pose sequences that convey its meaning. Recently, flow-based models with optimal transport (OT) have become a strong SLG baseline by handling the one-to-many nature of text-to-sign. While classifier-free guidance (CFG) could be applied to further strengthen the semantic alignment theoretically, its training involves conditional and unconditional training, which may contradict the pose-space OT, thus reducing the generation quality. Under the condition dropout, one noise sample can be paired with target motions exhibiting incompatible motion dynamics, interfering with the semantic guidance when the text condition is present. To address this issue, we propose Spectral Optimal Transport (SOT), which augments the pose-space cost with a spectral feature distance, reweighting the coupling toward the temporal-frequency structure of the target motions, thereby improving the performance when using CFG. The quantitative and qualitative experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.
papers.summary: Sign language generation (SLG) turns spoken-language text into pose sequences, and flow-based models trained with optimal transport (OT) are a strong baseline, but adding classifier-free guidance (CFG) can clash with the pose-space coupling: under condition dropout, a noise sample may be paired with target motions whose dynamics are incompatible. `Spectral Optimal Transport` (`SOT`) adds a spectral feature distance to the pose-space cost, so that **the coupling is reweighted toward the temporal-frequency structure of the target motions**. The authors report quantitative and qualitative improvements when CFG is used, without giving headline numbers in the abstract.

papers.title: RadOncGym: An Agent-Based Framework for Radiotherapy Dose-Mimicking Optimization
papers.abstract: AI dose-prediction models generate patient-specific 3D dose distributions from patient anatomy, providing an important intermediate representation for automated radiotherapy planning. However, an AI-predicted dose must undergo downstream optimization to produce a physically constrained treatment plan, a process that requires balancing competing planning objectives. We present RadOncGym, an agent-based framework that enables an LLM agent to iteratively tune 12 planning-objective weights for dose-mimicking optimization. To reduce iterative evaluation cost, RadOncGym incorporates a surrogate verifier that provides rapid feedback while allowing the agent to decide when to request a full planning solve within a fixed solve budget. We evaluate RadOncGym on 60 OpenKBP head-and-neck patients, each paired with 10 predictions from OpenKBP-Opt dose-prediction sets, yielding 600 patient-prediction contexts per experimental configuration. Under RadOncGym's 16-turn setting with a three-solve budget, a GPT-5.6 Sol agent reduces mean clinical-criterion violation by 0.6131 Gy and improves DVH and dose scores by 0.5986 and 0.2204 Gy relative to leaving all 12 weights fixed at 1, outperforming all evaluated non-agent weight-tuning methods under the same solve budget. It remains competitive with the 16-solve variants of these methods while requiring 75.0-77.6% less normalized runtime. RadOncGym demonstrates the potential of LLM agents as optimization planners in downstream radiotherapy plan optimization and provides a public testbed for their systematic evaluation. Code and configurations are available at https://github.com/miaot-usc/RadOncGym.
papers.summary: AI-predicted radiotherapy dose distributions must still be converted into physically feasible treatment plans through an optimization that balances competing objectives. `RadOncGym` lets an LLM agent iteratively tune 12 planning-objective weights for this dose-mimicking step, using a fast surrogate verifier for feedback and letting the agent decide when to spend one of a limited number of full planning solves. On 600 patient-prediction contexts built from 60 `OpenKBP` head-and-neck patients, a `GPT-5.6 Sol` agent with a three-solve budget cut mean clinical-criterion violation by 0.6131 Gy relative to uniform weights and beat all non-agent tuning methods at the same budget. It stayed competitive with 16-solve versions of those methods while using **75.0-77.6% less normalized runtime**.

papers.title: MetaDecomp: Adaptive Task Decomposition via Meta-Learned Procedural Memory
papers.abstract: Reusing past experience in long-horizon tasks requires more than storing successful procedures: Language agents must distinguish which procedures apply and what work remains as execution progresses. We introduce MetaDecomp, an in-context meta-learning framework for adaptive task decomposition that jointly learns a task-relative state space and reusable procedures. Its outer loop builds procedural memory from successful training executions, representing task progress as abstract states and procedures between states as directed acyclic graphs of operations and dependencies. As new progress distinctions are learned, MetaDecomp revisits historical execution evidence to reassess state assignments and reorganize the procedures they support. With memory fixed at test time, the inner loop refines an initial decomposition and revises it from environmental feedback, combining applicable procedure fragments with task-specific steps missing from memory. Evaluated on ALFWorld and ScienceWorld over three seeds, MetaDecomp achieves the highest mean performance among the compared methods in four of five settings, for example, an 86.3% success rate on ALFWorld with Qwen3-4B. Fixing the initial schema or omitting historical reprojection reduces performance in component ablations. MetaDecomp also uses fewer inference tokens than ReAct and AutoRefine in all five settings. Cross-benchmark analysis identifies a low-performance area where partial coverage degrades success relative to hidden memory; high coverage improves success, while low coverage changes little. Code will be released upon acceptance.
papers.summary: Language agents that reuse past experience on long-horizon tasks need to know which stored procedures apply and what work remains as execution proceeds. `MetaDecomp` is an in-context meta-learning framework whose outer loop builds procedural memory from successful runs, representing progress as abstract states and procedures as directed acyclic graphs of operations, and re-assigns historical evidence as new state distinctions are learned; at test time an inner loop refines a decomposition from environment feedback. On `ALFWorld` and `ScienceWorld` it has the best mean performance among compared methods in four of five settings, including **an 86.3% success rate on `ALFWorld` with `Qwen3-4B`**, while using fewer inference tokens than `ReAct` and `AutoRefine`. A cross-benchmark analysis finds that partial memory coverage can hurt success compared with hiding the memory altogether.

papers.title: Pitfalls of Dependency-Ready Decoding for Masked Diffusion Language Models
papers.abstract: Masked diffusion models (MDMs) have shown strong performance on structured reasoning tasks such as Sudoku, Trip Planning, and Countdown. MDMs introduce a freedom in the order in which tokens may be unmasked, and to exercise this freedom for good accuracy, early decoding strategies relied on signals of confidence or the downstream impact of decoding a token. However, simple examples seem to illustrate that resolving a token's dependencies before unmasking it should be important. Therefore, we examine whether this principle, which we call dependency-ready decoding, would contribute to better accuracy, from a practical and a theoretical perspective. We examine a recent decoder that implements dependency-readiness through attention, and generally find that when it performs better than confidence-based or future utility baselines, its decoding order collapses to left-to-right decoding. For theoretical analysis, we establish a definition of dependency without resorting to attention, measured by an information-theoretic score of how much revealing a single masked token (or a set) would shift the model's prediction for another. We prove that when the margin is large relative to this score, no such revelation can change the top prediction, so in this regime Maximum-Margin decoding already commits dependency-ready tokens. These findings leave only a narrow scope for future dependency-ready decoders: their potential benefit is limited to positions with margins smaller than the information-theoretic sensitivity, and reliance on attention should be questioned.
papers.summary: Masked diffusion models (MDMs) can unmask tokens in any order, and an intuitive principle, here called dependency-ready decoding, says a token's dependencies should be resolved before it is unmasked. Testing a recent attention-based decoder built on that principle, the authors find that **when it beats confidence-based or future-utility baselines, its decoding order collapses to plain left-to-right**. They then define dependency information-theoretically, as how much revealing one masked token shifts the prediction for another, and prove that when the prediction margin is large relative to this score no revelation can change the top prediction, so `Maximum-Margin` decoding already commits dependency-ready tokens. Any benefit from dedicated dependency-ready decoders is therefore confined to low-margin positions.

papers.title: FEAST: Fair and Efficient Adaptive Sampling for Task-Free On-Policy Learning
papers.abstract: Language agents trained from self-generated experience must allocate a limited rollout budget across heterogeneous capabilities. A common strategy is to prioritize capabilities with strong current learning signals, but in on-policy learning these signals are endogenous: past allocation changes the policy and therefore the evidence available for future allocation. This can create a feedback loop in which under-trained capabilities receive increasingly fewer opportunities to improve. We formalize this effect through the Quota-Efficiency Law (QEL), which shows that allocation history can change learning efficiency even under matched capability-specific exposure. Motivated by this, we introduce FEAST, a task-free adaptive sampling framework that separates opportunity allocation from compute allocation. FEAST dynamically discovers capability clusters while preserving their learning histories, maintains continued sampling opportunities across clusters, and reserves a rollout budget for each selected cluster. Within each budget, it progressively concentrates computation on prompts with informative reward variation. Across GURU-18K and SMC, FEAST improves average performance over competitive adaptive sampling baselines under matched rollout budgets, while better preserving learning progress on weaker capabilities. Ablation studies further support the complementary roles of cross-cluster opportunity protection and within-cluster selective allocation. Code will be released upon acceptance.
papers.summary: Language agents trained on self-generated experience must split a limited rollout budget across different capabilities, and prioritizing those with strong current learning signals can starve under-trained capabilities because past allocation shapes the evidence used for future allocation. The authors formalize this feedback effect as the Quota-Efficiency Law (QEL) and propose `FEAST`, a task-free sampling framework that discovers capability clusters, guarantees each continued sampling opportunities, and concentrates compute within a cluster on prompts with informative reward variation. On `GURU-18K` and `SMC`, `FEAST` **improves average performance over adaptive sampling baselines at matched rollout budgets while better preserving progress on weaker capabilities**.

papers.title: Teaching a Multilingual Translation Model Regional Varieties: Castilian and Latin American Spanish, Asturian, Aragonese and Aranese with MADLAD-400-3B-MT
papers.abstract: Massively multilingual translation models usually have one tag per language and no control over regional varieties, and they cover a region's smaller languages poorly or not at all. We report three fine-tunes of MADLAD-400-3B-MT, each adding target tags with low-rank adaptation (LoRA), back-translation of monolingual text and replay of the base model's own translations: <2es_ES> for Spanish as written in Spain, <2es_419> for Latin American Spanish, and one model for three Romance languages of the Iberian Peninsula, Asturian (<2ast>), Aragonese (<2an>) and Aranese (<2oc_aranes>). For the Spanish varieties we annotate the 250.9M documents of MADLAD-400's Spanish split with a domain-supervised Spain vs. Latin America classifier and select variety text with a rule that admitted no Latin American document in a 340-document reference set. The Castilian model chooses Spain's everyday vocabulary in 97% of a targeted test (base model 62%) and vosotros for informal plural address in 70% (10%), while improving chrF++ on human references. A first finding is tag collapse: with a new tag initialised from <2es>, the parent tag drifts to the new variety (84-87% identical outputs). In the Iberian model, contrastive pairs and a separate learning rate for the tag embeddings keep each tag in its own language. Trained only on publicly available data, mostly the TAN-IBE Wikipedia corpora, the Iberian model matches or beats the TAN-IBE Marian systems in four of six Spanish directions on FLORES+, is 1.9 BLEU behind in Spanish->Aranese, and is second only to SalamandraTA-7B in most directions. The exception, Spanish->Aragonese, reflects a difference of written variety between Aragonese Wikipedia and the FLORES+ reference, not model quality. All three fine-tunes lose 0.6-0.7 chrF++ on average in thirteen other FLORES-200 directions. We release the models, data and variety classifier under open licences
papers.summary: Massively multilingual translation models typically offer one tag per language, with no control over regional varieties and weak coverage of smaller regional languages. Three fine-tunes of `MADLAD-400-3B-MT` add new target tags using low-rank adaptation (`LoRA`), back-translation, and replay of the base model's own outputs: Spain Spanish, Latin American Spanish, and a single model for Asturian, Aragonese and Aranese. The Castilian model picks Spain's everyday vocabulary in **97% of a targeted test versus 62% for the base model**, and the Iberian model matches or beats the `TAN-IBE` Marian systems in four of six Spanish directions on `FLORES+`. The authors also document a tag-collapse failure in which the parent Spanish tag drifts to the new variety, mitigated with contrastive pairs and a separate learning rate for tag embeddings, and note an average loss of 0.6-0.7 chrF++ in thirteen other directions.

papers.title: Can Its Own Misses Teach an MLLM to Find Small Brain Metastases?
papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are becoming general readers of medical images, yet they remain weak at locating small abnormalities. Brain metastases expose this gap: at 384 px a 0.1 mL lesion covers less than a quarter of one visual token, and at one false positive per scan frontier MLLMs find fewer than 30% of lesions of 0.1-1 mL. Fine-tuning on one dataset helps but transfers poorly, and improving it further is slow trial and error steered by a single score. We introduce LANTERN (Lesion-finding AgeNt Through Error-driven Recursive learNing), a framework in which an MLLM improves recursively from its own misses. LANTERN recasts model development as an error-driven loop: a failure census attributes every missed lesion to one of four causes, an LLM mentor revises one of four levels (evidence acquisition, visual representation, learning policy, decision aggregation) per round, and a rule frozen before the first round decides what is kept, without test data and with every tool call audited. Over 15 unattended rounds, LANTERN raises a fine-tuned 4B MLLM from finding 75% to 94% of lesions at one false positive per scan on BraTS-MET, and 91% of those of 0.1-1 mL, compared with at most 51% and 29% for five frontier MLLMs read under the starting protocol; the gains hold on an external cohort (89%) and on unseen meningiomas (77%). These results show that an MLLM's own misses, attributed to their causes, can drive its reliable recursive self-improvement.
papers.summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) struggle to locate small abnormalities in medical images; for brain metastases, frontier models find fewer than 30% of 0.1-1 mL lesions at one false positive per scan. `LANTERN` turns model development into an automated error-driven loop: each missed lesion is attributed to one of four causes, an LLM mentor revises one level of the pipeline per round, and a rule fixed in advance decides which changes are kept without touching test data. Over 15 unattended rounds, a fine-tuned 4B MLLM improves from **finding 75% to 94% of lesions at one false positive per scan on `BraTS-MET`**, including 91% of the 0.1-1 mL lesions. The gains carry over to an external cohort (89%) and to unseen meningiomas (77%).

papers.title: The Missing Root: Geometric Imagination Without Images in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: This paper proposes a new paradigm and method for giving large language models spatial understanding. Standard language models operate exclusively over discrete words (secondary representations of things rather than continuous space itself), forcing them to guess geometry verbally. Whereas most multimodal approaches equate spatial grounding with camera images or video frames, spatial structure itself is not a picture: it consists of coordinate frames, solid boundaries, and how objects move and relate to each other in continuous space. Motivated by this distinction, we place continuous object tokens combining pose (position, orientation, and scale) and signed-distance shape embeddings alongside word tokens inside a single uninterrupted transformer sequence, allowing language and geometry to attend to each other as object scenes are built and updated step by step. Control tokens switch output automatically between natural-language words and continuous object state updates to a persistent object workspace, while an attention mask blocks earlier prose when generating the answer, so responses must be read directly from settled geometry. To prove this method works, we attach a narrow parallel spatial stream (+4.4% weights) alongside unfrozen Qwen3-1.7B layers. In our two-dimensional tests, the model spawns and transforms multi-object scenes from English descriptions, transfers shapes to held-out nouns, and relies causally on the workspace to answer spatial questions.
papers.summary: Language models handle spatial questions through words alone, and most multimodal approaches ground space in images rather than in geometry itself. The proposed method interleaves continuous object tokens, encoding pose and signed-distance shape embeddings, with word tokens in one transformer sequence, with control tokens switching between text output and updates to a persistent object workspace, and an attention mask that forces answers to be read from the settled geometry rather than earlier prose. It is implemented as a narrow parallel spatial stream adding 4.4% more weights to an unfrozen `Qwen3-1.7B`. In two-dimensional tests only, **the model builds and transforms multi-object scenes from English descriptions and causally relies on the workspace to answer spatial questions**, and transfers shapes to held-out nouns.

papers.title: When Rerankers Work Together: Better and Faster Reranking without Joint Training
papers.abstract: Standalone reranker quality does not determine its value in a multistage RAG pipeline. We systematically study heterogeneous rerankers composed without joint training, spanning lexical, single-vector, late-interaction, and joint query-context scoring. Two lightweight semantic coarse scorers, Cache-Pointwise and Cache-Shapley, learn from passage relevance labels and share cacheable representations and linear-time singleton inference. Under matched candidates and budgets, we compare cascades with stage-removal references to measure evidence retention, repair and breakage, reader accuracy, and online pruning cost. On NoLiMa 32K with Gemma, inserting these scorers before CrossEncoder or Provence improves answer accuracy by 4.02-9.43 percentage points while accelerating online pruning by 1.57-1.88x relative to the corresponding reranker alone. Cache-Pointwise composed with ColBERTv2 through reciprocal rank fusion improves accuracy by 4.60 points at 1.36x speedup over direct ColBERTv2. The stage-removal comparisons reveal an asymmetry: a cascade can outperform its final reranker alone while underperforming its coarse selector alone. Two readers, a second multi-hop dataset, and three-stage extensions show that the gains depend on the reader, reranker pairing, and stage configuration. These findings demonstrate a practical route to better and faster reranking without joint training and motivate studying stage order, candidate budgets, and rank fusion as determinants of composition quality.
papers.summary: How well a reranker scores on its own does not determine how much it helps inside a multistage retrieval-augmented generation pipeline. This study composes heterogeneous rerankers (lexical, single-vector, late-interaction, and joint query-context) without joint training, and introduces two lightweight cacheable coarse scorers, `Cache-Pointwise` and `Cache-Shapley`. On `NoLiMa` 32K with `Gemma`, placing these scorers before `CrossEncoder` or `Provence` **raises answer accuracy by 4.02-9.43 percentage points while speeding up online pruning by 1.57-1.88x** compared with the reranker alone. Stage-removal comparisons show an asymmetry in which a cascade can beat its final reranker alone yet lose to its coarse selector alone, and gains vary with the reader, reranker pairing, and stage configuration.

papers.title: ChemDeduce: Benchmarking LLMs for Unknown Chemical Identification through Interactive Simulated Experiments
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong performance in chemical knowledge and reasoning, yet it remains unclear whether they can solve problems whose answers must be discovered through experimentation. We investigate this question through Unknown Chemical Identification, where a model must actively design experiments, interpret observations, update hypotheses, and ultimately identify a hidden substance. We introduce ChemDeduce, an interactive evaluation framework for assessing LLMs through simulated experiments. ChemDeduce formulates chemical identification as a sequential decision process and provides a stateful simulated laboratory with explicit instrument and operational constraints, enabling scalable and reproducible evaluation of iterative experimental reasoning. We benchmark eight frontier LLMs on 200 chemicals, yielding 1600 model--target pairs and 4800 episodes over three independent repetitions, and evaluate identification accuracy, operational compliance, interaction efficiency, and trajectory-level reasoning quality. Despite generating seemingly plausible experimental plans, current models achieve an average identification accuracy ranging from 23.83% to 67.33%, revealing substantial limitations in experiment selection, evidence interpretation, and sequential hypothesis refinement.
papers.summary: Whether large language models can solve chemistry problems that require discovering the answer through experiments, rather than recalling knowledge, is tested here through unknown chemical identification. `ChemDeduce` is an interactive benchmark with a stateful simulated laboratory, including instrument and operational constraints, in which a model must design experiments, interpret observations, and refine hypotheses to name a hidden substance. Across eight frontier LLMs, 200 chemicals, and 4,800 episodes, **average identification accuracy ranges from only 23.83% to 67.33%**. The failures are traced to weak experiment selection, evidence interpretation, and sequential hypothesis refinement despite plausible-looking plans.

papers.title: Mitigating Overgeneralization in RND via Spectral Target Design
papers.abstract: Random Network Distillation (RND) is a scalable novelty signal for RL based on a fixed random target network and a trained predictor. However, it can overgeneralize: the predictor extrapolates the random target off the data manifold, causing novelty scores to collapse on unfamiliar inputs. This paper analyzes this failure through a kernel-theoretic lens. Under a GP target model and an NTK-regime predictor, we show that the RND novelty score is a cross-kernel residual variance: it is governed jointly by the target covariance kernel and the predictor NTK, rather than by either one alone. This identifies overgeneralization as spectral under-excitation. Motivated by this view, we formulate spectral target design as a principle for shaping RND novelty geometry. As a concrete instance, we replace the implicit random-network target with a bandwidth-controlled Random Fourier Feature (RFF) target, redistributing residual signal toward modes less attenuated by the predictor. Experiments on offline D4RL, online Atari, and Fetch manipulation benchmarks show improved novelty discrimination and downstream RL performance. The code for the RL implementation is available at https://github.com/tuuktuc86/RFF-RND.
papers.summary: Random Network Distillation (RND) gives reinforcement learning agents a novelty signal by training a predictor to match a fixed random target network, but the predictor can extrapolate the target off the data manifold, so novelty scores collapse on unfamiliar inputs. A kernel-theoretic analysis shows that **the RND novelty score is a cross-kernel residual variance governed jointly by the target's covariance kernel and the predictor's NTK**, which frames overgeneralization as spectral under-excitation. Based on this, the authors replace the random-network target with a bandwidth-controlled Random Fourier Feature (RFF) target that shifts residual signal toward modes the predictor attenuates less. Experiments on offline `D4RL`, online `Atari`, and `Fetch` manipulation show better novelty discrimination and downstream performance.

papers.title: Contextual language representations link narrative processing to language and literacy in children
papers.abstract: Spoken narratives extensively connect moment-to-moment language processing with knowledge accumulated through language and literacy experience. This study examined that relationship using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) during Cantonese story listening and contextual representations from large language model (LLM). The imaging cohort comprised 23 school-age children; 16 contributed complete standardized literacy and language assessments and served as held-out participants in a nested cross-subject encoding analysis of the same story. Contextual embeddings predicted distributed narrative responses, with prominent correspondence in temporoparietal and default-network parcels. Regional summaries of the top 25% of voxels ranked by held-out correlation yielded atlas-wide means of r=0.174 and partial R2=0.0165. A joint feature model identified negative surprisal and positive predictive-entropy coefficients across cortical and subcortical parcels, including control, salience, hippocampal and amygdalar regions. Higher word-dictation and overall literacy scores were associated with lower regional encoding performance. Higher Cantonese grammar scores were associated with more negative semantic-update coefficients in parietal control, somatomotor and dorsal-attention parcels. Together, these findings connect language and literacy skills to the regional strength and direction of neural coupling with narrative context. They position naturalistic context processing as a possibly measurable link between oral comprehension and literacy in childhood.
papers.summary: The link between children's moment-to-moment story comprehension and their language and literacy skills is examined using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) of 23 school-age children listening to a Cantonese story, modeled with contextual embeddings from a large language model. The embeddings predicted distributed brain responses, most strongly in temporoparietal and default-network regions, with an atlas-wide mean correlation of r=0.174 among top voxels. Among the 16 children with full assessments, **higher word-dictation and overall literacy scores were associated with lower regional encoding performance**, and higher grammar scores with more negative semantic-update coefficients in parietal control, somatomotor and dorsal-attention regions.

papers.title: Random Voronoi Networks
papers.abstract: Nearest-neighbor methods are local, simple, and interpretable, but their non-parametric form makes them memory-intensive, expensive at inference, and difficult to integrate into differentiable neural architectures. We introduce Random Voronoi Networks (RVNs), a family of structured three-layer MLPs that express nearest-neighbor geometry through sampled Voronoi comparisons. The first layer computes Random Voronoi Features (RVF) from affine pairwise separators between selected training samples, the second layer aggregates these comparisons into Voronoi cells or top-k neighborhood scores, and the readout layer produces classification or regression predictions. We show that, when all samples and pairwise comparisons are included, step RVNs recover exact Euclidean k-NN, while ReLU RVNs provide a violation-score realization for 1-NN that can be relaxed into a differentiable soft weighting. Subsampling yields approximate RVNs with explicit control over the number of cells and features. We study several unsupervised sampling methods that trade off random coverage, directional diversity, coordinate sparsity, and empirical feature variance. Empirically, RVFs produce a highly effective data encoding strategy, providing performance boosts to downstream methods ranging from linear to modern tabular deep learning models. Finally, we showcase that RVF provides an interpretable feature map due to its k-NN based construction and ties to pairwise local directions. These results position our Random Voronoi formulation as a bridge between nearest-neighbor rules, random features, and modern tabular models.
papers.summary: Nearest-neighbor methods are simple and interpretable but memory-hungry, slow at inference, and hard to embed in differentiable architectures. Random Voronoi Networks (RVNs) are structured three-layer multilayer perceptrons whose first layer computes Random Voronoi Features (RVF) from pairwise separators between training samples, whose second layer aggregates them into Voronoi cells or top-k neighborhood scores, and whose readout produces predictions. With all samples and comparisons included, step-activation RVNs recover exact Euclidean k-NN, and subsampling gives approximate versions with controllable size. Empirically, **RVF used as a data encoding boosts downstream models ranging from linear methods to modern tabular deep learning models**, while remaining interpretable.

papers.title: FORK: Co-Evolving Safe Disclosure and Decision Skills Against Attackers Who Read Every Refusal
papers.abstract: When a guardrail rejects an LLM agent's action, its message reaches any attacker observing the trajectory: a fixed refusal leaves benign users unable to recover, whereas an explanation can tell the attacker what to try next. We study this as safe disclosure: explaining rejections so that authorized tasks recover without increasing adaptive attack success. Safe disclosure depends on both the decision and the message: what the guardrail blocks and what it reveals to the agent and the attacker. Because hand-written rules alone cannot anticipate how adaptive attackers probe decisions or use messages, we introduce FORK, which co-evolves a guardrail's natural-language decision and disclosure skills with an attacker that reads every public message.
