Each exploited message and permissive decision gives FORK evidence for a gradient-free revision of its natural-language skill library. We evaluate FORK on four benchmarks. Averaged over three agents on FORK-World, FORK cuts attack success rate (ASR) under adaptive attack from 78.4% to 14.1% and keeps utility above 85%, outperforming baselines on both ASR and utility. Notably, on MT-AgentRisk, whose environments and tasks are unseen in training, FORK lowers ASR from 70.6% to 9.1% with 93.1% benign utility.
papers.summary: When a guardrail blocks an LLM agent's action, its rejection message is visible to any attacker watching the trajectory: a fixed refusal leaves legitimate users stuck, while an explanation can tell the attacker what to try next. `FORK` treats this as a safe-disclosure problem and co-evolves a guardrail's natural-language decision and disclosure skills against an attacker that reads every public message, revising its skill library without gradients after each exploited message or overly permissive decision. Averaged over three agents on `FORK-World`, it **cuts attack success rate (ASR) under adaptive attack from 78.4% to 14.1% while keeping utility above 85%**. On `MT-AgentRisk`, whose environments and tasks were unseen in training, ASR falls from 70.6% to 9.1% with 93.1% benign utility.

papers.title: When Are Parallel Subagents Effective for Coding? An Empirical Study on Repository Construction
papers.abstract: LLM-based coding agents are increasingly used for long-horizon tasks such as building an entire program from a specification. Products like Codex and Claude Code let an agent delegate work to parallel subagents, multiplying run cost, yet it remains unclear whether and when delegation produces a better program. We compare a single agent with a main agent delegating to subagents on repository-construction tasks from NL2Repo and ProgramBench (which also provides an executable reference program). We compare scores at equal time and equal cost, run intervention experiments, and analyze fine-grained behavior. On randomly drawn tasks, parallel subagents raise hidden-test pass rates by only about 1 to 5 percentage points at up to 3.8x the cost of a single agent. Their gain is larger on hard tasks, where we find evidence of three mechanisms. Self-checking: with GPT-5.6 Sol, one sentence telling a single agent to probe the reference program first recovers most of this gain at a fraction of the cost; from GPT-5.6 Sol to GPT-6.1 Sol, the gain shrinks as single agents check their own work more. Fresh context: in extended runs, a single agent that periodically starts a new session with an empty conversation makes faster early progress in every comparison than one that resumes its conversation. Modularity: multi-agent runs produce more modular code (more files and shorter functions), closer to the upstream source. We observe similar patterns in a smaller replication with Opus 5.5 on Claude Code. Overall, subagents help when (i) a single agent stops checking too early, (ii) a long session keeps editing with little improvement, or (iii) modular code helps on the task; otherwise, they mainly add cost.
papers.summary: Coding agents such as `Codex` and `Claude Code` can delegate to parallel subagents at multiplied cost, and this empirical study measures whether that yields better programs on repository-construction tasks from `NL2Repo` and `ProgramBench`. On randomly drawn tasks, **parallel subagents raise hidden-test pass rates by only about 1 to 5 percentage points at up to 3.8x the cost of a single agent**, with larger gains on hard tasks. Three mechanisms explain the gains: more self-checking (largely recovered for `GPT-5.6 Sol` by one sentence telling a single agent to probe the reference program first), fresh context (a single agent that periodically restarts with an empty conversation progresses faster early on), and more modular code. Subagents help when a single agent stops checking too early, stalls in a long session, or the task rewards modularity; otherwise they mainly add cost.

papers.title: Looped Models are Fast Multi-Token Predictors
papers.abstract: Looped language models can adapt computation for predicting a token without a proportional rescaling in unique model parameters by adjusting the number of loops. This property has been used for self-speculative decoding, taking shallow loops as fast drafters and deep loops as verifiers, which is effective since drafting still uses full parameters. In this paper, we show that shallow loops can be also predictive of several future tokens and leverage this to drastically accelerate the inference of looped language models. To that end, we present Floodgates, a simple self-speculative decoding method that appends a block of mask tokens as a suffix and learns via low-rank adaptation to draft these tokens in parallel. Across seven models, five benchmarks, a range of batch sizes, and both greedy and sampled decoding, Floodgates is the fastest lossless decoding method in most cases, attaining up to 7.5x acceleration. Through analysis, we show that this speedup is enabled by all-depth training of looped models, with the shallow drafter's ability to leverage full-depth computation by conditioning on deep prefix cache evaluated during verification.
papers.summary: Looped language models reuse the same parameters across a variable number of loops, which has enabled self-speculative decoding with shallow loops as drafters and deep loops as verifiers. `Floodgates` extends this by showing shallow loops can predict several future tokens at once: it appends a block of mask tokens as a suffix and trains a low-rank adapter to draft them in parallel. Across seven models, five benchmarks, various batch sizes, and both greedy and sampled decoding, it is the fastest lossless decoding method in most cases, reaching **up to 7.5x acceleration**. The analysis attributes the speedup to all-depth training of looped models and to the drafter conditioning on the deep prefix cache computed during verification.

papers.title: EATS: Scaling Tool-Use Experience for Medical Reasoning Agents
papers.abstract: Medical reasoning agents combine large language model (LLM) reasoning with clinical workflows and specialized neural tools. However, general-purpose LLMs receive limited training exposure to domain-specific medical tools, and the uncertainty and distributional shifts of neural tool outputs make selecting tools from simple descriptions significantly more challenging than in deterministic settings such as calculators or dictionary lookups. In this paper, we propose EATS, an experience-augmented tool selection strategy that leverages accumulated tool-use trajectories to improve tool selection in medical reasoning agents. EATS constructs a memory of past interactions, including queries, tool choices, arguments, and self-evaluated feedback, and retrieves relevant experiences to guide tool selection for new queries. As memory construction does not require ground-truth supervision, EATS scales naturally with test-time experience. We evaluate EATS on tool-augmented medical reasoning tasks, including closed-ended visual question answering and free-form report generation. Experiments on four public datasets, ChestAgentBench, CheXbench, MIMIC-CXR, and SLAKE-VQA, across three multimodal LLMs, Qwen3-VL 2B, Qwen3-VL 32B, and GPT-5.5, show consistent gains in tool selection behavior and downstream medical reasoning performance. Code is available at https://github.com/Limingyuan001/EATS.
papers.summary: Medical reasoning agents pair an LLM with specialized neural tools, but general-purpose models have little exposure to these tools, and the tools' uncertain outputs make selection from short descriptions harder than with deterministic tools. `EATS` builds a memory of past tool-use interactions, including queries, tool choices, arguments, and self-evaluated feedback, and retrieves relevant experiences to guide tool selection for new queries; since no ground-truth labels are needed, the memory grows with test-time use. Across `ChestAgentBench`, `CheXbench`, `MIMIC-CXR`, and `SLAKE-VQA` with `Qwen3-VL 2B`, `Qwen3-VL 32B`, and `GPT-5.5`, the authors report **consistent gains in tool selection behavior and downstream medical reasoning performance**.

papers.title: Correlation-Aware Evidential Fusion for Trusted Multi-View Classification
papers.abstract: Trusted multi-view classification aims to make accurate and reliable predictions by integrating information from multiple views. Existing methods typically estimate class evidence and uncertainty for each view and combine the resulting opinions through aggregation rules. However, they generally treat different views as independent information sources, overlooking the correlations among them. Highly correlated views tend to produce similar evidence, and treating them as independent sources may repeatedly count consistent information and give it disproportionate influence, while weakening complementary evidence that provides additional information. Consequently, such correlation-unaware fusion may not only limit classification performance but also produce miscalibrated uncertainty estimates. To address this issue, we propose Correlation-Aware Fusion of Evidence (CAFE), a framework for trusted multi-view classification. CAFE applies complementarity-based trust discounting to the evidence produced by view-private experts and introduces a correlation-aware constraint to reduce the repeated contribution of similar evidence. It then learns sample-specific weights from the global multi-view context to adaptively combine the correlation-adjusted private evidence with cross-view collaborative evidence. Extensive experiments on six real-world datasets demonstrate that CAFE consistently improves classification and calibration performance in general settings, with particularly significant gains when strong correlations exist among views.
papers.summary: Trusted multi-view classification combines per-view class evidence and uncertainty, but existing fusion rules treat views as independent, so highly correlated views get their shared evidence counted repeatedly, which can skew predictions and miscalibrate uncertainty. Correlation-Aware Fusion of Evidence (`CAFE`) discounts evidence from view-private experts according to complementarity, adds a constraint that reduces the repeated contribution of similar evidence, and learns sample-specific weights to combine the adjusted private evidence with cross-view collaborative evidence. On six real-world datasets it **improves both classification and calibration, with the largest gains when views are strongly correlated**.

papers.title: EGSE: Evidence-Grounded Skill Evolution for Medical Reasoning Agents
papers.abstract: Medical reasoning agents combine foundation models with specialized tools to interpret medical images, yet reusing their historical experience remains challenging. A correct final answer can conceal flawed reasoning or tool use, synthesized advice may lack source support, and superficially similar cases may require different diagnostic procedures. In this paper, we propose EGSE, an evidence-grounded skill evolution framework that distills historical dialogues from similar cases into reusable conditional workflows and progressively refines a multi-faceted skill library through supported and validated updates to improve medical agents. EGSE evaluates intermediate reasoning and tool use and contrasts repeated successful and failed rollouts to extract useful practices and evidence-supported avoidance guidance. These experiences are synthesized into workflows with applicability conditions and checks traceable to source dialogues. Library additions and merges require source-grounded review and execution validation. At inference time, EGSE routes queries to skill nodes organized by imaging modality, question task type, and disease category, then retrieves and selects applicable workflows based on their conditions, the current images, and the question to guide evidence acquisition and interpretation. Experiments across four chest X-ray benchmarks show that EGSE outperforms representative medical agents and skill evolution methods in reasoning accuracy while reducing tool calls. It also delivers consistent accuracy gains across seven foundation models and supports skill transfer across datasets.
papers.summary: Reusing the past experience of medical image-reasoning agents is difficult because correct answers can hide flawed reasoning, synthesized advice may lack source support, and similar-looking cases can need different diagnostic procedures. `EGSE` distills historical dialogues into conditional workflows in a skill library, evaluating intermediate reasoning and tool use, contrasting successful and failed rollouts, and admitting additions or merges only after source-grounded review and execution validation. At inference, queries are routed by imaging modality, question type, and disease category to retrieve applicable workflows. Across four chest X-ray benchmarks, `EGSE` **outperforms representative medical agents and skill-evolution methods in reasoning accuracy while reducing tool calls**, with gains across seven foundation models and skill transfer across datasets.

papers.title: DiCALM: Converting Autoregressive Convolution-Attention Language Models into Discrete Diffusion Language Models
papers.abstract: Existing methods for adapting autoregressive (AR) language models to diffusion generation focus mainly on full-attention architectures. More efficient hybrid architectures remain underexplored. We introduce DiCALM, a recipe for converting the hybrid convolution-attention models of the LFM2 family (LFM2 and LFM2.5) from AR to masked-diffusion generation. DiCALM progressively extends LFM2's causal gated convolution so that it captures local context in both directions. It combines this extension with a masking warm-up and joint AR--diffusion training. In controlled experiments, DiCALM performs comparably to the corresponding fine-tuned LFM2.5-based AR models and delivers consistent speedups over them at both the 350M and 1.2B scales: over 1.4x on average and up to 1.79x.
papers.summary: Methods for converting autoregressive (AR) language models into diffusion generators have focused on full-attention architectures, leaving efficient hybrid designs unexplored. `DiCALM` is a recipe for converting the hybrid convolution-attention `LFM2` and `LFM2.5` models to masked-diffusion generation by progressively extending the causal gated convolution to capture local context in both directions, combined with a masking warm-up and joint AR-diffusion training. In controlled experiments it performs comparably to the corresponding fine-tuned `LFM2.5` AR models while delivering **speedups of over 1.4x on average and up to 1.79x** at the 350M and 1.2B scales.

papers.title: Beyond the Happy Path: Generalizing Robot World Models from Simulated Failures
papers.abstract: Robot world models are increasingly used to evaluate and plan policies, yet robot training data are dominated by successful demonstrations. Off the happy path, when a grasp is misaligned or mistimed and the object is pushed, tilted, or slips, their predictions break down. Across five pretrained action-conditioned models, object-motion error is at most 10.4% lower than that of a static baseline that copies the first frame, and two models are worse than this baseline. We present WorldReforge, which teaches world models what happens when manipulation goes wrong. We construct the Reforge dataset of 62k simulated trajectories by perturbing reference grasps in position, orientation, and closure timing, recording each resulting push, slip, or failed pickup with ground-truth object pose, contact, and surface points. WorldReforge turns this ground truth into two training signals without additional inference cost. Interaction Alignment focuses reconstruction on the small object and contact regions that a global loss underweights, and Surface Correspondence trains backbone features to follow the same physical surface points across frames. On Cosmos3 Nano, WorldReforge reduces object trajectory error by 28.2% overall and by 35.0% on unseen objects, and it lowers the error in predicting how two actions' outcomes diverge by 43.3%. Although trained only in simulation, it also improves reconstruction on DROID and on real failure videos. Controlled data studies show that failed contact and successful holding teach complementary physics: failed contact teaches how objects respond, and holding teaches how a grasped state persists. Our code, data, and models are available at aim-uofa.github.io/WorldReforge/.
papers.summary: Robot world models are trained mostly on successful demonstrations, so their predictions break down when a grasp is misaligned or mistimed; across five pretrained action-conditioned models, object-motion error is at most 10.4% lower than a baseline that simply copies the first frame. `WorldReforge` addresses this with the `Reforge` dataset of 62k simulated trajectories built by perturbing reference grasps, plus two training signals that focus reconstruction on object and contact regions and train features to track the same surface points across frames. On `Cosmos3 Nano` it **reduces object trajectory error by 28.2% overall and 35.0% on unseen objects**, and it also improves reconstruction on `DROID` and real failure videos despite being trained only in simulation.

papers.title: Connecting AI Agents to Live Discrete Element Simulations via the Model Context Protocol
papers.abstract: This paper describes a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server through which a general-purpose AI agent operates a discrete element engine, commercial or open-source, while the simulation runs. The agent submits a long simulation to the engine and, while it computes, reads the running model, changes it, or stops it. The human modeler stays at the engine's console and graphical interface throughout, and the agent sees what the modeler does there. The tools are derived from what the agent needs to do at the engine and are held to four principles: correctness, coverage, orthogonality and simplicity. Two documentation tools let the agent search the engine's manual and browse it level by level. Five execution tools let the agent run code in the engine, submit long simulations in the background, check on them, read the running model, and stop them. A bridge inside the engine serves these tools in a commercial DEM engine, PFC, and an open-source one, YADE. In a case study, a general-purpose agent calibrated a drained triaxial model of dense Toyoura sand against laboratory data in both engines, while the modeler worked at the same engine; the agent noticed the modeler's actions at the console and acted on them. The same calibration on YADE was then given to seven language models, three sessions each and without human intervention. Twenty of the twenty-one sessions reached the targets, and nineteen of the parameter sets lie in one small region of the admissible ranges. The server and the bridge are released as two open-source packages, itasca-mcp, which also serves FLAC, 3DEC, MPoint and MassFlow, and yade-mcp.
papers.summary: A Model Context Protocol (MCP) server lets a general-purpose AI agent operate a discrete element method simulation engine while it runs, submitting long simulations, reading or changing the running model, and stopping it, while a human modeler keeps working at the same console. The design uses two documentation tools and five execution tools, served by a bridge inside the commercial engine `PFC` and the open-source engine `YADE`. In a calibration of a drained triaxial model of dense Toyoura sand given to seven language models without human intervention, **20 of 21 sessions reached the targets**, with nineteen parameter sets falling in one small region of the admissible ranges. The server and bridge are released as `itasca-mcp` and `yade-mcp`.

papers.title: Towards 360$^\circ$ Embodied UAV Tracking Without Turning
papers.abstract: Conventional embodied UAV tracking couples target observability with heading control because targets may leave the field of view of forward-facing cameras. We investigate a complementary paradigm that uses full-spherical perception to follow designated targets without active heading adjustment. To support this setting, we introduce 360UAV-ETrack, a simulation benchmark comprising 2,652 sequences, over 1.73 million synchronized observations, eight tracking tasks, and 150 held-out closed-loop scenarios. We propose 360UAV-TVLA, a panoramic vision--language--action (VLA) framework integrating persistent visual referring (PVR), compressed temporal memory (CTM), and geometry-aligned trajectory supervision (GTS) for instance identification, motion reasoning, and three-dimensional control. Experiments across two VLA backbones show consistent gains over standard fine-tuning, with normalized average tracking frames increasing from 22.56\% to 35.28\% for $\pi_0$ and from 25.68\% to 33.64\% for $\pi_{0.5}$. Our benchmark further reveals a substantial gap between offline imitation accuracy and closed-loop tracking reliability, establishing a challenging testbed for future research https://libingyu01.github.io/360UAV-ETrack_360UAV-TVLA/
papers.summary: Drone target tracking normally ties keeping the target in view to steering the heading, because forward-facing cameras lose targets that move out of frame; this work instead uses full-spherical perception so the drone can follow a target without turning. The authors introduce `360UAV-ETrack`, a simulation benchmark with 2,652 sequences and 150 held-out closed-loop scenarios, and `360UAV-TVLA`, a panoramic vision-language-action (VLA) framework combining persistent visual referring, compressed temporal memory, and geometry-aligned trajectory supervision. Compared with standard fine-tuning, normalized average tracking frames rise **from 22.56% to 35.28% for `pi_0`** and from 25.68% to 33.64% for `pi_0.5`. The benchmark also shows a large gap between offline imitation accuracy and closed-loop tracking reliability.

papers.title: InstructTTS-OPD: On-Policy Distillation for Multi-Objective Instruction-Following TTS
papers.abstract: Instruction-following text-to-speech (Instruct-TTS) renders a target transcript in the manner described by a free-form natural-language instruction, and a good rendition must succeed on three fronts at once: following the instruction, pronouncing the transcript correctly, and sounding natural. Reinforcement learning has become the standard way to post-train such generative models toward human preferences, and TTS systems increasingly adopt it. When the three objectives are optimized together under a single scalar reward, typically with group relative policy optimization (GRPO), training tends to be unstable: the objectives compete, and the shared update drifts toward whichever one is easiest to improve, producing a seesaw among them. We instead adapt on-policy distillation (OPD), which fuses several single-objective teachers by matching their velocity fields on the student's own rollouts. Realizing this for Instruct-TTS first calls for a sound reward on each axis, which we analyze carefully: a distilled Qwen-Omni proxy for the costly Gemini judge, dialect-free data for the WER reward, and DNSMOS in place of the language-biased UTMOS. We then train three single-objective teachers with GRPO and fuse them with OPD, routing each rollout to the instruction-following or WER teacher by its data domain and letting every rollout additionally follow the MOS teacher for quality. This lets instruction following and intelligibility improve together without a trade-off, but the quality target conflicts with instruction following, so following it additively reintroduces the seesaw. We therefore propose conflict-aware velocity fusion, which projects the quality target off the direction that opposes the primary objective before fusing, and show that it markedly reduces the instruction-following/quality trade-off. The fused model improves over scalar-reward GRPO on all three objectives at once.
papers.summary: Instruction-following text-to-speech must follow a free-form style instruction, pronounce the transcript correctly, and sound natural, and optimizing all three under one scalar reward with group relative policy optimization (`GRPO`) tends to seesaw between objectives. The authors instead train three single-objective teachers and fuse them with on-policy distillation (`OPD`), which matches the teachers' velocity fields on the student's own rollouts, after building a reward for each axis using a distilled `Qwen-Omni` judge, dialect-free data for word error rate, and `DNSMOS` for quality. Because the quality target conflicts with instruction following, they add conflict-aware velocity fusion, which projects the quality target off the direction opposing the primary objective. The fused model **improves over scalar-reward `GRPO` on all three objectives at once**.

papers.title: What Does Skill Lift Actually Measure? A Source-Code-Level Audit and Noise-Aware Reanalysis of SkillsBench
papers.abstract: Agent skills are directories of instructions, reference materials, and scripts loaded on demand by coding agents. According to SkillsBench, although human-curated skills can raise the passing rate by about 16.6 percentage points (pp) on average, they have actually reduced the results for some tasks. Later research has started to gate or eliminate skills according to the above per-task gains. We have audited the above benchmark at the source-code level and analysed 7,554 public trials to form 1,421 paired "(configuration, task) cells". Source-code audit identified two controlled-verified cases of grader dependence and one operational definition gap; the average lift on these three tasks was 74.6 pp, and the overall average lift for the full set was 18.7 pp. The audit also found that four tasks contained placeholder skill directories, and a certain execution harness additionally added 48 built-in skills in most runs. No task-level reduction achieved statistical significance in the pooled reanalysis with multiple-testing correction. As there were at most three runs per condition for each cell, the observed negative differences are very susceptible to run-sampling noise, and arithmetically, 58% of the cells could not have shown a decrease. Therefore, the raw numbers of negative cells cannot show that skills cause harm. A gating strategy based on the skill-free score seems to improve by 2-3 pp in the logs; however, even after shuffling condition labels to remove any skill effect, it still achieves an increase of 4-7 pp. On the held-out runs not used for fitting and decision-making, there was no statistically significant improvement. The audit ledger and analysis scripts have been published by us.
papers.summary: `SkillsBench` reported that human-curated agent skills, meaning directories of instructions and scripts loaded on demand by coding agents, raise pass rates by about 16.6 percentage points on average but hurt some tasks, and later work began gating skills on those per-task results. A source-code audit and reanalysis of 7,554 public trials found grader dependence in two tasks, a definition gap in a third, placeholder skill directories in four tasks, and a harness that added 48 built-in skills in most runs. With at most three runs per condition, **no task-level reduction was statistically significant after multiple-testing correction**, and 58% of cells could not arithmetically have shown a decrease. A gating strategy that appeared to gain 2-3 points still gained 4-7 points after condition labels were shuffled, and showed no significant improvement on held-out runs.
papers.highlight_summary:
A source-level audit and noise-aware reanalysis of `SkillsBench` asks whether the per-task gains and drops from mounting agent skills — which follow-up work already uses to gate or retire skills — reflect real skill effects. Across **7,554** public trials forming **1,421** paired (configuration, task) cells, the largest gains partly reflect grading rules stated only in the skill, and the apparent harms are indistinguishable from run-sampling noise.

- Comparing prompts, reference solutions, graders and skill packages turned up three tasks whose grading requirements appear only in the skill (for example the `EPSG:4087` projection in `earthquake-plate-calculation`, where the grader tolerates 0.01 km), and these average **74.6 pp** lift, make up 4% of cells but about 18% of cumulative lift, and pull the cell-weighted mean from **18.7 pp** to 16.1 pp when removed.
- The audit also found placeholder skill directories in four tasks and an `OpenHands` harness that listed 48 built-in skills in 155 of 184 sampled with-skill prompts and in 4 of 6 no-skill ones, so skill lift is not a like-for-like comparison across harnesses.
- Within-cell label permutation tests at 10% FDR find **26 of 83 tasks** with significant gains and **none with a significant loss**, while the 169 observed negative cells fall well below the roughly 328 that a zero-effect null would produce and 58% of cells have a zero no-skill baseline that makes a loss arithmetically impossible.
- Gating skills on the no-skill score looks **2-3 pp** better than always loading in log replay, yet the same policies gain **4.5-6.5 pp** on label-shuffled data with no skill effect and show no significant improvement on held-out trials, because the noisy baseline serves at once as gate input, training target and fallback score.
- With at most three runs per condition the tests can only detect a true loss above roughly 24 pp, apparent-loss cells still average −9.9 pp on held-out trials, and no agents were re-run with patched prompts, so the results neither show skills are harmless nor quantify how much lift the undeclared grading rules explain.

papers.title: Should Service Requirements Be Scalarized or Constrained When Minimizing Costs? A Case Study on HVAC Control
papers.abstract: Automated decision systems, from learned policies to model-based optimizers, often minimize costs such as energy or resource use while meeting a service requirement, for example the quality of service (QoS) specified in a service level agreement (SLA), a comfort band, or a safety margin. The requirement can be scalarized with the costs into a single objective, with a fixed or an adaptively tuned (Lagrangian) weight, or it can be imposed as a constraint. We study this choice in the Smart Buildings Challenge, in which a single policy controls the heating, ventilation and air conditioning (HVAC) of previously unseen buildings and is evaluated by a weighted sum of comfort, energy cost and carbon emissions. With all other components fixed, we compare the two treatments in model-based optimization, represented by model predictive control (MPC) with the requirement as a hard or a soft (l1-penalized) constraint, and in learned policies, represented by proximal policy optimization (PPO) with a fixed or a Lagrangian penalty in the reward or a projection layer on the action. In MPC, the soft constraint reproduces the hard one once its weight exceeds the requirement's shadow price, which the challenge's comfort weight exceeds approximately fourfold; below this weight, comfort is sacrificed, and under a metric that values comfort below its shadow price the soft constraint outperforms the hard one by up to 28%. A weight tuned on the training buildings is 3.9% worse than the hard constraint on 48 unseen buildings, because the shadow price varies across buildings. In PPO, the projected policy satisfies the requirement from the outset and leads early in training; with longer training, the Lagrangian policy overtakes it while the projected policy deteriorates, and the fixed penalty does not learn to satisfy the requirement.
papers.summary: Control systems that minimize cost while meeting a service requirement can either fold the requirement into the objective with a weight or impose it as a constraint, and this study compares the two on heating, ventilation and air conditioning control of unseen buildings in the `Smart Buildings Challenge`. In model predictive control, a soft constraint reproduces the hard one once its weight exceeds the requirement's shadow price, but a weight tuned on training buildings is **3.9% worse than the hard constraint on 48 unseen buildings** because the shadow price varies across buildings. With proximal policy optimization (`PPO`), an action-projection layer satisfies the requirement from the start and leads early, a Lagrangian penalty overtakes it with longer training, and a fixed penalty never learns to satisfy the requirement.

papers.title: DuoMI: Dual Mutual Information Regularization for Expert Reuse in Looped Transformers
papers.abstract: We introduce Dual Mutual Information Regularization (DuoMI), a method for regulating expert routing across rounds in looped mixture-of-experts (MoE) Transformers. When two rounds of computation share an expert pool, their routers may favor different expert subsets, limiting the reuse of individual expert parameters across rounds. Even when aggregate expert usage is identical across rounds, we would still prefer each token to retain some experts while switching to others. DuoMI addresses both aspects of routing: it uses round-level marginal mutual information to limit the dependence of aggregate expert usage on the round, and token-level conditional mutual information to penalize average cross-round routing changes that fall outside a target interval. During training, DuoMI computes differentiable penalties from soft routing distributions over all experts. It adds no model parameters and leaves sparse Top-$k$ routing strategy unchanged at inference. On a looped OLMoE backbone in which paired adjacent layers share experts, DuoMI improves the average score across $15$ downstream tasks from $50.08\%$ to $51.82\%$, a gain of $1.74$ percentage points over the looped baseline.
papers.summary: In looped mixture-of-experts Transformers, where two rounds of computation share one pool of experts, the routers in each round may favor different expert subsets, which limits reuse of expert parameters. `DuoMI` adds two differentiable training penalties: a round-level mutual information term that limits how much aggregate expert usage depends on the round, and a token-level conditional term that keeps each token's cross-round routing changes within a target interval. It adds no parameters and leaves sparse Top-k routing unchanged at inference. On a looped `OLMoE` backbone, the average score across 15 downstream tasks rises from 50.08% to 51.82%, **a gain of 1.74 percentage points**.

papers.title: PINN-Slicer: Exploiting Rotational Symmetry to Solve the Photon Orbit Equation Around a Black Hole
papers.abstract: Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) typically struggle with long-horizon domains, often requiring the network to be retrained as the domain grows. We present PINN-Slicer, a method for second-order autonomous ordinary differential equations, $\ddot{u} = G(u, \dot{u})$, which exploits the invariance of this class of equations under translations of the independent variable. A single PINN, embedded within a solution ansatz that enforces the initial conditions explicitly, is trained on a thin slice of the independent variable using Sobol-sampled initial conditions. The PINN is then deployed recursively, slice-by-slice, across the full domain. We demonstrate PINN-Slicer on the nonlinear equation that describes photon orbits around a black hole, and reach a point-by-point root-mean-square error (RMSE) below $10^{-3}$ in $u = r_s/r$ (the inverse radial coordinate in units of the Schwarzschild radius) relative to a finite-difference reference solution. A key advantage of PINN-Slicer is that a single trained network generalizes to any orbital initial condition within the training range, without retraining. In addition, PINN-Slicer can cope with solution domains that may not be known a priori.
papers.summary: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) struggle on long domains and often need retraining as the domain grows. `PINN-Slicer` targets second-order autonomous ordinary differential equations, which are invariant under shifts of the independent variable: a single network is trained on a thin slice with Sobol-sampled initial conditions and then applied recursively, slice by slice, across the full domain. On the nonlinear equation for photon orbits around a black hole, it reaches a **point-by-point root-mean-square error below 10^-3** against a finite-difference reference. One trained network covers any initial condition within the training range without retraining and handles domains whose extent is not known in advance.

papers.title: RefMix: Expanding Endpoint Proposals for Diversity-Preserving Reward Fine-Tuning
papers.abstract: Online forward matching aligns flow-based generative models by repeatedly generating, rewarding, and fitting model-produced endpoints. However, this behavior creates an on-policy feedback loop: as high-reward modes become increasingly favored, alternative modes become less likely to appear in subsequent training pools, progressively reducing visual diversity. We introduce RefMix, a reference-assisted endpoint proposal strategy that addresses this limitation by injecting alternative candidates into the training pool while retaining the original task reward and forward matching objective. In particular, RefMix uses a reference model during early high-noise steps to expose alternative visual modes, followed by the current reward-tuned model for endpoint completion. Across state-of-the-art online forward matching methods, RefMix consistently improves visual diversity while preserving task reward performance. Controlled inference experiments further demonstrate that training-time endpoint exposure is critical to improve reward--diversity trade-offs, beyond the impact of reference-assisted inference. By rethinking how training endpoints are proposed, RefMix achieves up to 44% higher diversity over forward matching baselines at comparable reward levels.
papers.summary: Reward fine-tuning of flow-based image generators through online forward matching creates a feedback loop in which high-reward modes increasingly dominate the training pool and visual diversity shrinks. `RefMix` changes how training endpoints are proposed: a reference model handles the early high-noise steps to expose alternative visual modes, and the current reward-tuned model completes the sample, with the reward and objective left unchanged. Across several online forward matching methods, the authors report **up to 44% higher diversity at comparable reward levels**. Controlled experiments indicate the gain comes from exposing these endpoints during training, not merely from using the reference model at inference.

papers.title: AI Buckingham: Agentic Discovery of Dimensionless Scaling Laws Across Physical Regimes
papers.abstract: Classical dimensional analysis defines admissible dimensionless representations but does not determine which combinations capture the dominant physical dependence, whether it changes across physical regimes, or when dependent-variable rescaling is required. We present AI Buckingham, an agentic framework for autonomous dimensionless discovery from natural-language descriptions of physical problems and observational data. It couples reasoning and planning by a large language model (LLM) with predefined symbolic and numerical tools. Literature-based knowledge retrieval supports dimensional checking, gradient-based clustering identifies physical regimes, and mutual information provides an objective, reparameterization-invariant criterion for identifying dominant dimensionless groups. Explicit numerical criteria determine the group count and assess simplification. Across ten physical systems spanning fluid dynamics, magnetohydrodynamics, thermal convection and additive manufacturing, AI Buckingham recovers established similarity representations and resolves regime-dependent scalings. For the longstanding challenge of predicting turbulent drag on rough surfaces, it identifies informative reparameterizations of surface statistics that improve equivalent sand-grain roughness estimates for engineering-oriented drag modelling.
papers.summary: Classical dimensional analysis lists the admissible dimensionless groups for a physical problem but does not say which ones dominate, whether that changes across regimes, or when the dependent variable must be rescaled. `AI Buckingham` is an agentic framework in which a large language model plans over symbolic and numerical tools, using literature retrieval for dimensional checks, gradient-based clustering to find regimes, and mutual information to rank candidate groups. Across ten physical systems spanning fluid dynamics, magnetohydrodynamics, thermal convection and additive manufacturing, it **recovers established similarity representations and resolves regime-dependent scalings**. For turbulent drag on rough surfaces, it finds reparameterizations of surface statistics that improve equivalent sand-grain roughness estimates.

papers.title: DLaR: Dynamic Stochasticity Control for Latent Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Latent reasoning enables LLMs to operate in continuous embedding space, yet existing methods suffer from deterministic inference that precludes exploration of diverse reasoning paths. While recent approaches inject stochasticity to restore exploration, we identify two fundamental limitations: \textit{uniform stochasticity} across all steps is suboptimal, and unconstrained perturbations disrupt reasoning coherence. We propose Dynamic Stochasticity Control for Latent Reasoning (DLaR), a framework with two complementary mechanisms that operate at different temporal granularities within the GRPO reinforcement learning framework. At the token level, Adaptive Stochasticity Modulation (ASM) dynamically adjusts perturbation intensity at each latent step based on a confidence-entropy fusion signal, increasing exploration when the model is uncertain and preserving stability when confident. At the training level, Training-Aware Stochasticity Tuning (TAST) progressively decays the base stochasticity level following a curriculum schedule. Through this dual-level design, DLaR establishes a hierarchical exploration-exploitation strategy that operates at both token and training levels. Extensive experiments on four in-distribution and three out-of-distribution mathematical reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that DLaR achieves the highest average performance across model scales, reaching 27.9%/50.6% Pass@1/Pass@8 on Llama-3.2-1B and 46.8%/68.2% on Qwen2.5-1.5B. Code: \href{https://github.com/xiaocen-luo/DLaR}{https://github.com/xiaocen-luo/DLaR}.
papers.summary: Latent reasoning lets language models reason in continuous embedding space, but inference is deterministic, and injecting uniform noise to restore exploration is suboptimal and can break reasoning coherence. `DLaR` controls the noise at two levels within `GRPO` reinforcement learning training: one mechanism scales the perturbation at each latent step using a combined confidence and entropy signal, and another decays the base noise level over training on a curriculum schedule. On four in-distribution and three out-of-distribution mathematical reasoning benchmarks it achieves the highest average performance across model scales, reaching 27.9% Pass@1 and 50.6% Pass@8 on `Llama-3.2-1B` and **46.8% Pass@1 and 68.2% Pass@8 on `Qwen2.5-1.5B`**.

papers.title: Embodied-VGGT: Preserving Reliable Local Geometry for Long-Sequence Reconstruction
papers.abstract: Long sequence reconstruction must correct accumulated drift while preserving locally consistent geometry. In robotics and autonomous driving, embodied acquisition provides recurring platform- environment geometry and repeated observations of scene structure and platform motion. We present Embodied-VGGT, which exploits these cues to establish reliable local relationships and selectively preserve them during global refinement. Memory-Augmented Grounded Chunks (MAGC) builds on Scal3R's global context memory and uses relative scale references derived from predicted ground geometry to regularize test-time memory updates, encouraging cross-chunk consistency while limiting changes to reliable local geometry. Superpoint Alignment (SA) and Cross-Loop Optimization (CL) jointly address the robust establishment and preservation of geometric relationships. SA balances ground and non-ground evidence across spatial regions to estimate inter-chunk translation. CL uses geometric and motion consistency across interleaved windows to select coherent chunk groups, each receiving a shared Sim(3) correction that preserves its internal relative transformations during global optimization. Experiments on five public driving benchmarks demonstrate consistent and substantial improvements in long sequence reconstruction. On KITTI Odometry, Embodied-VGGT achieves a mean absolute trajectory error of 7.30 m and a Chamfer distance of 2.67 m, reducing these errors by 46.8% and 23.3% compared with the state-of-the-art baseline under same evaluation protocol. To facilitate reproducibility, we released our code: https://github.com/Ang-Sheep/Embodied-VGGT.
papers.summary: Reconstructing 3D scenes from long driving or robot sequences requires correcting accumulated drift without damaging geometry that is already locally consistent. `Embodied-VGGT` builds on the global context memory of `Scal3R`, using scale references from predicted ground geometry to regularize test-time memory updates, balancing ground and non-ground evidence to estimate translation between chunks, and applying a shared correction to groups of coherent chunks during global optimization. On `KITTI Odometry` it reaches a mean absolute trajectory error of 7.30 m and a Chamfer distance of 2.67 m, **reducing these errors by 46.8% and 23.3%** relative to the strongest baseline under the same protocol. Gains are reported across five public driving benchmarks.

papers.title: PatternMiner: Automated Mathematical Discovery Through LLM-Guided Training and Interpretation of Small Models
papers.abstract: There are several approaches to AI-driven mathematical discovery. One of these involves the use of large language models (LLMs) to resolve well-specified conjectures via text-based reasoning, while another uses narrow models and interpretability for more open-ended, human-in-the-loop exploration using object-based mathematical data. The latter is limited in its ability to move beyond simple empirical pattern detection while the former is not well-designed for direct, open-ended exploration of large mathematical datasets. In this paper we introduce PatternMiner, a system that combines these two paradigms. In PatternMiner, an LLM agent generates mathematical datasets based on an initial broad question, trains narrow machine learning models on them, uses interpretability techniques to extract patterns from these trained models, and uses these patterns to formulate conjectures. Once an initial conjecture has been formulated, PatternMiner instructs the agent to search for counterexamples using calls to mathematical software. If a set of counterexamples can be found, these are used as feedback for conjecture refinement or another round of training and interpretability. The conjecture progressively evolves through this iterative sequence with the agent allowed to try to prove it at any point. We describe the results of applying PatternMiner to five well-known positivity problems in algebraic combinatorics. PatternMiner proves several new theorems related to Schubert positivity and projection, a character-row evaluation formula, a restricted version of the Kazhdan--Lusztig combinatorial invariance conjecture, and Schur positivity for a family of immanant coefficients. We end by analyzing the most common routes to conjecture generation that are used by PatternMiner in our case studies as well as documenting the most common failure modes.
papers.summary: Mathematical discovery with AI has split between large language models (LLMs) that attack well-specified conjectures through text reasoning and small models plus interpretability used for open-ended exploration of mathematical data. `PatternMiner` combines them: an LLM agent generates datasets from a broad question, trains narrow models, extracts patterns with interpretability techniques, forms conjectures, searches for counterexamples with mathematical software, and refines or attempts proofs in a loop. Applied to five positivity problems in algebraic combinatorics, the system **proves several new theorems**, covering Schubert positivity and projection, a character-row evaluation formula, a restricted case of the Kazhdan-Lusztig combinatorial invariance conjecture, and Schur positivity for a family of immanant coefficients. The authors also catalogue the most common routes to conjectures and the most common failure modes.

papers.title: Fine-Tuning Without Gradients? Closed-Form, LLM-Written Classifiers on a Frozen Encoder
papers.abstract: Can a classifier computed in closed form on a frozen encoder match gradient fine-tuning? We present closed-form weight-space programming (WSP): a large language model (LLM), used as a design assistant, writes programs that read a frozen masked language model through cloze-style prompt templates at several layers, fit closed-form heads (shrinkage discriminant analysis, kernel ridge regression and the encoder's label-word prior) on labelled data, and select among a pool of candidate heads by cross-fitting. No gradient is computed and no encoder weight changes. We instantiate the framework on RoBERTa-large. On 11 development datasets with 512 to 8,192 training labels, WSP is ahead of full fine-tuning (FT) and LoRA at every label budget (by 0.3 to 0.6 points on average; the registered non-inferiority tests pass) and within 0.5 points of prompt-based fine-tuning (PFT); these datasets also shaped the recipe. With fewer labels its lead over FT and LoRA grows: 1.2 to 3.5 points with 64 and 128 labels, and 3.8 to 5.3 points in the few-shot setting of 16 labels per class, where WSP is again within half a point of PFT on the development datasets. On six held-out datasets, WSP stays ahead of LoRA and within half a point of FT on average, although with six datasets no registered test passes, and PFT is ahead, by 1.30 points with 8,192 labels. WSP never collapses and is deterministic, but it needs one encoder pass per template (17 here). We report all eight recipe versions, every decision that saw test results, and 27 ideas that did not help.
papers.summary: Closed-form weight-space programming (`WSP`) asks whether a classifier computed without gradients on a frozen encoder can match fine-tuning: a large language model writes programs that read a frozen masked language model through cloze-style prompts at several layers, fit closed-form heads such as shrinkage discriminant analysis and kernel ridge regression, and choose among them by cross-fitting. On `RoBERTa-large` across 11 development datasets, it is **ahead of full fine-tuning and `LoRA` at every label budget from 512 to 8,192 labels** by 0.3 to 0.6 points on average, with the lead growing to 3.8 to 5.3 points at 16 labels per class. On six held-out datasets it stays ahead of `LoRA` and within half a point of full fine-tuning, though no registered test passes and prompt-based fine-tuning leads by 1.30 points at 8,192 labels. The method is deterministic but needs 17 encoder passes, and the authors report all eight recipe versions and 27 ideas that did not help.

papers.title: Kolpona: An Agentic Framework with Gradient-Free Neuron Programming for RTL Generation
papers.abstract: Open-weight large language models (LLMs) for register-transfer level (RTL) design are usually improved by fine-tuning on curated Verilog corpora, which needs large sets of verified designs and GPU training. We present Kolpona, an agentic framework that improves such models without gradient training. Its first component is neuron programming, a new form of weight-space programming (WSP) that writes single neurons in closed form into the weights to remove failure habits found on practice tasks, and keeps each edit only when testbench results on fresh tasks favour it. At inference time, tool-using agents propose designs, and a label-free selection stage delivers one design per task from the specification, the candidates and their simulations alone. On Qwen3.5-4B, edits to 16 neurons raise the VerilogEval v2 pass@1 of the model alone from 31.7% to 55.4%, and the full framework reaches 77.6%. On Qwen3.8-27B, Kolpona lifts pass@1 from 73.1% to 94.9% on VerilogEval v2 and from 66.0% to 92.0% on RTLLM v2.1 on a single 32 GB GPU, above every published system in our comparison. The RTL edits also carry over to Python and raise the pass@1 of the 4B model alone from 84.8% to 91.5% on HumanEval+ and from 67.7% to 77.5% on MBPP+.
papers.summary: Open-weight language models for register-transfer level (RTL) hardware design are usually improved by fine-tuning on curated Verilog, which needs verified designs and GPU training. `Kolpona` avoids gradient training with neuron programming, which writes single neurons in closed form into the weights to remove failure habits and keeps each edit only if testbench results on fresh tasks favour it, and then uses tool-using agents and a label-free selection stage at inference. On `Qwen3.5-4B`, edits to 16 neurons raise `VerilogEval v2` pass@1 from 31.7% to 55.4% and the full framework reaches 77.6%; on `Qwen3.8-27B` it **lifts pass@1 from 73.1% to 94.9% on `VerilogEval v2`** and from 66.0% to 92.0% on `RTLLM v2.1` on a single 32 GB GPU. The edits also transfer to Python, raising the 4B model's pass@1 on `HumanEval+` and `MBPP+`.

papers.title: Auto-Features: An LLM-Assisted Corpus for Contextual Recognition of Standard and Optional Car Features
papers.abstract: We present Auto-Features, a corpus for detecting a car's standard and optional features in advertisement text, given the feature catalogue of that exact vehicle. Sellers name the same feature in many ways. We therefore cast the task as feature-conditioned, or contextual, named entity recognition: extract the span that expresses one given catalogue feature. An entity-linking view follows from the same output. The corpus has a human-gold layer (430 adverts) from screened annotators and an LLM-silver layer (925 adverts) auto-annotated by a search-grounded LLM. We also contribute the way it was built. Every LLM output is validated, and each kind of failure has its own remedy. Malformed output is patched. Hallucinated content triggers a fresh attempt by a stronger model. Links to features outside the candidate list are dropped and counted (3 in 10,928 records). The LLM annotates alone only after its agreement with human annotators on link verification is comparable to human-human agreement. On advert-disjoint splits, a LoRA-tuned 4B LLM reaches 63.9% span F1 and 76.1% on the entity-linking view. A fine-tuned encoder reaches 59.0% and 74.1%. The margin is widest on catalogue features never seen in training (54.5% vs. 49.0%).
papers.summary: `Auto-Features` is a corpus for finding a car's standard and optional features in advertisement text given that exact vehicle's feature catalogue, framed as extracting the span that expresses one given catalogue feature. It has a human-annotated layer of 430 adverts and a 925-advert layer annotated by a search-grounded large language model, whose outputs are validated with a separate remedy for malformed output, hallucinated content, and out-of-list links. On advert-disjoint splits, a `LoRA`-tuned 4B language model reaches **63.9% span F1** and 76.1% on the entity-linking view, compared with 59.0% and 74.1% for a fine-tuned encoder. The gap is widest on catalogue features never seen in training, at 54.5% against 49.0%.

papers.title: MolGPAO: Molecular Generative Pre-trained Autoregressive Octree with Speculative Decoding and Sub-Millisecond Seam Healing for 3D Molecules
papers.abstract: Autoregressive generation over adaptive 3D octrees (Uni-3DAR) offers an intrinsic $O(N \log N)$ sparsity advantage over dense $O(N^2)$ equivariant diffusion and flow models on large drug-like molecules, yet lags in geometric equilibrium, closed-shell valence stability, and property fidelity due to Morton-seam coordinate jumps, leaf-heavy compute with root-count trapping, and target-shortcut collapse in internal critics. We introduce MolGPAO (Molecular Generative Pre-trained Autoregressive Octree), a standalone 3D octree architecture and single-output speculative tree-decoding engine using zero external surrogates, zero reinforcement learning, and zero inference-time MLIP relaxation. MolGPAO unifies: (1) non-trapping 6-D ScaleFreeBudgetEmbedding with L5-to-L1 covalent packing priors; (2) a FlashAttention-2 pause-and-gather speculative octree funnel ($m_{s1} \to m_{s2} \to 1$, $M_{\mathrm{out}} = 1$); (3) an anti-shortcut ground-truth TwoStageOctreeProcessCritic with 64-RBF covalent edge gating and $SO(3)$-invariant 12-channel multipole norms (blind QM9 $r = 0.9867$--$0.9989$); (4) a $<0.5$ ms 4-layer $SE(3)$ PostTreeGraphRefiner for Morton-seam healing, expected-XYZ bonded supervision, selective CFG, and zero-heavy-displacement valence reconciliation; and (5) bubble-free stride-2 GPU leaf decoding. Across GEOM-Drugs (0.49 GPU-h), disjoint 50k/50k QM9 (0.43 GPU-h), and PBE0/def2-TZVP-verified OE62 (0.56 GPU-h), MolGPAO lifts drug-scale valid-connected yield 6.78x (12.7% to 86.2%, 99.83% atom stability), runs 7.3x faster (or 1.65x faster at 2.0x yield) than 100-step FlowMol at $N=100$, beats 156 GPU-h PropMolFlow on QM9 HOMO (-12.7%) and dipole (-21.0%) at 362x lower compute, and doubles live DFT hit rate on OE62 (33.3% vs. 16.7%) at 92.8x lower compute.
papers.summary: Autoregressive generation of 3D molecules over adaptive octrees scales better than dense equivariant diffusion and flow models on large drug-like molecules, but trails them in geometric quality, valence stability, and property fidelity. `MolGPAO` is an octree architecture with a speculative tree-decoding engine, an internal critic designed to resist shortcut learning, and a sub-millisecond refinement network that repairs coordinate jumps at octree seams, using no external surrogates, reinforcement learning, or inference-time relaxation. The authors report that on `GEOM-Drugs` it **raises valid-connected yield from 12.7% to 86.2%**, and that it runs 7.3x faster than 100-step `FlowMol` at 100 atoms. They also claim better HOMO and dipole accuracy on `QM9` than `PropMolFlow` at 362x lower compute.

papers.title: Aegis-VLA: Reliability-Gated Action Refinement via a Trajectory World Model for Dynamic Object Manipulation
papers.abstract: Dynamic object manipulation requires maintaining spatial and temporal alignment with targets that continue to move during inference and execution. Although future prediction can inform action correction, an accurate forecast does not establish whether modifying an existing action would be beneficial. We present Aegis-VLA, a world-model-guided vision-language-action (VLA) framework that generates predictive action corrections and separately determines whether and how strongly to apply them. A Trajectory World Model combines kinematic extrapolation with learned residual dynamics to predict object motion and estimate positional uncertainty. Discrepancy-Guided Action Refinement uses differences between history-only and base-action-conditioned end-effector forecasts to propose bounded arm corrections. A Reliability Gate learns when to admit corrections based on demonstration-relative improvements over base actions, and regulates their application during inference using predictive uncertainty and anticipated object--end-effector proximity. Rejected corrections preserve the corresponding base actions. Aegis-VLA introduces only approximately 2.45M trainable parameters. On the simulated Dynamic Object Manipulation (DOM) benchmark, Aegis-VLA achieves 56.72\% success over 1,800 evaluation trials, exceeding our reproduced DynamicVLA baseline of 45.44\% by 11.28 percentage points.
papers.summary: Manipulating objects that keep moving during inference and execution requires correcting actions, yet an accurate forecast alone does not show that changing an action will help. `Aegis-VLA` adds to a vision-language-action (VLA) policy a trajectory world model that predicts object motion and its uncertainty, a refinement module that proposes bounded arm corrections, and a reliability gate that decides whether and how strongly to apply each correction, keeping the base action otherwise. The additions total about 2.45M trainable parameters. On the simulated `Dynamic Object Manipulation` benchmark it reaches **56.72% success over 1,800 trials, against 45.44% for a reproduced `DynamicVLA` baseline**.

papers.title: DosePET: An Open-Source Dataset with 2100 Radiation Dose Maps for PET/CT
papers.abstract: Large collections of three-dimensional radiation dose maps linked to patient anatomy are needed to develop artificial intelligence (AI) models for personalized internal dosimetry in nuclear medicine, but access to such data remains limited. Here we present DosePET, an open-source dataset of 2,100 patient-specific absorbed-dose maps generated by Monte Carlo simulation of publicly available PET/CT examinations: 1,503 [18F]FDG examinations from ENHANCE.PET and 369 [18F]PSMA-1007 and 228 [68Ga]Ga-PSMA-11 examinations from PSMA-PET-CT-Lesions, acquired at five institutions with seven scanner models. For each examination, the CT was resampled to the native PET grid to build a voxelized patient phantom, the quantitative PET image defined the radionuclide source, and radiation transport was simulated with GATE version 9.4. Organ and tissue masks were generated from the CT with TotalSegmentator. Each study folder contains a NIfTI dose map integrated from scan time to infinity, 117 binary organ/tissue masks, a report of regional dosimetric quantities, including mean absorbed doses, dose conversion factors and scan-time dose rates, and simulation metadata. The total processing time was 1,542.4 hours. Python tools support selective downloading and conversion to scan-time dose-rate or dose-per-decay maps, and an agent skill guides pairing with the source PET/CT images. DosePET is publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/eltzanis/DosePET.
papers.summary: Training AI models for personalized internal dosimetry in nuclear medicine requires large sets of 3D radiation dose maps linked to patient anatomy, which are hard to obtain. `DosePET` is an open dataset of **2,100 patient-specific absorbed-dose maps** produced by Monte Carlo simulation with `GATE` on public PET/CT examinations from `ENHANCE.PET` and `PSMA-PET-CT-Lesions`, covering three radiotracers, five institutions and seven scanner models. Each study includes a dose map, 117 organ and tissue masks generated with `TotalSegmentator`, a report of regional dosimetric quantities, and simulation metadata. Python tools support selective download and unit conversion.

papers.title: Honest but Wrong: Formalizing Retraction in the Ethics of Speech Acts
papers.abstract: A speaker who asserts honestly may later discover that its assertion was false. Such erroneous truths are not lies, yet they raise the question of whether, and on which moral grounds, the speaker must retract them. Using the FIPA-ACL performative disconfirm, we extend a belief-based framework that evaluates speech acts under deontologism and consequentialism to the case of retraction. We prove that the honesty duty of deontologism, which bears on utterances when they are made, never requires retracting an erroneous truth, and add a persistent one, which forbids letting the addressee believe what the speaker no longer believes. On a legal-advice case implemented in Answer Set Programming, we show that deontologism and consequentialism both require the retraction, but that consequentialism no longer does once it comes too late to prevent harm.
papers.summary: A speaker who asserts something honestly and later learns it was false has not lied, which raises the question of whether, and on what moral grounds, the assertion must be retracted. Using the `FIPA-ACL` disconfirm performative, the authors extend a belief-based framework that evaluates speech acts under deontologism and consequentialism to cover retraction. They prove that **the deontological honesty duty, which applies only when an utterance is made, never requires retracting an honest error**, and they add a persistent duty that forbids letting the addressee keep believing what the speaker no longer believes. In a legal-advice case implemented in Answer Set Programming, both ethical theories require the retraction, but consequentialism stops requiring it once it is too late to prevent harm.

papers.title: CARROT: Competitive Adaptive Graph Clustering via Semi-Relaxed Optimal Transport
papers.abstract: Deep graph clustering (DGC) has emerged as a prominent paradigm for unsupervised attributed graph clustering. However, existing methods often struggle with two practical challenges encountered in real-world applications: the number of clusters $K$ is unknown a priori, and cluster sizes are frequently highly imbalanced. Methods relying on a pre-specified $K$ may fail to recover the underlying clustering structure when $K$ is misspecified, while many approaches implicitly favor balanced partitions, hindering the discovery of minority clusters. We propose CARROT, a Competitive Adaptive gRaph clustering framework via semi-Relaxed Optimal Transport, which introduces semi-relaxed optimal transport into deep graph clustering to jointly address both challenges. CARROT first pre-trains node embeddings to establish a meaningful embedding space, and then jointly optimizes embeddings and cluster assignments through an Adaptive Clustering Mechanism. The mechanism combines semi-relaxed optimal transport to adapt cluster capacities to the underlying data, a competition loss to concentrate mass onto well-supported cluster prototypes, thereby starving degenerate ones, and hard pruning to progressively eliminate them. Extensive experiments on five public benchmarks demonstrate that CARROT achieves state-of-the-art NMI and ARI, accurately recovers the number of clusters without supervision, and faithfully preserves size-imbalanced community structures.
papers.summary: Deep graph clustering methods usually assume the number of clusters is known and tend to favor balanced partitions, which hides minority clusters. `CARROT` pre-trains node embeddings and then jointly optimizes embeddings and assignments using semi-relaxed optimal transport to adapt cluster capacities, a competition loss that starves poorly supported prototypes, and hard pruning to remove them. On five public benchmarks the authors report state-of-the-art normalized mutual information and adjusted Rand index while **recovering the number of clusters without supervision** and preserving size-imbalanced structure.

papers.title: Residual Cross-Model Narrative Convergence under Shared Prompts: Auditing Prompt Controls and Narrative Measurement
papers.abstract: Stories created by LLMs based on the same prompts can be narratively similar to one another. This similarity may reflect constraints imposed by the prompts as well as the models' writing tendencies. The current research analyzes 51,240 stories created by five models in the StoryScope corpus based on 10,248 common prompts. It uses 213 narrative features in seven dimensions to compare cross-model distances between stories generated from the same prompts with distances between stories generated from different but semantically matched prompts. To assess the relationship between narrative features and prompt content, a semantic relevance mask was evaluated against 420 author-annotated prompt-feature judgments (F1 = .813; near-threshold accuracy = .621). The equally weighted mean Residual Convergence Index (RCI) was .409 without masking and .406 with masking. These findings indicate measurable cross-model narrative convergence relative to a semantically matched-prompt baseline, with little change following semantic relevance masking.
papers.summary: Stories written by different LLMs from the same prompt can resemble each other, but it is unclear how much of that comes from the prompt versus shared model tendencies. Using 51,240 stories from five models in the `StoryScope` corpus and 213 narrative features, the study compares cross-model distances for same-prompt stories against stories from different but semantically matched prompts. The resulting mean Residual Convergence Index is **0.409 without masking and 0.406 with a semantic relevance mask**, indicating measurable cross-model convergence beyond what prompt content explains.

papers.title: Evaluating Ukrainian Grammatical Competence in Language Models: Probability Versus Prompting
papers.abstract: Organisations deploying large language models in Ukrainian-language information systems need to know whether a model produces normative Ukrainian. This paper establishes a protocol for measuring that reliably and applies it to 19 models. The instrument is a released set of 1,444 Ukrainian minimal pairs covering the vocative case, numeral-noun and adjective agreement, verb government and calques from russian, with subject-verb agreement as a control; a quarter of the set was checked against the answer key in two independent native-speaker ratings, which agreed at Cohen's $\kappa$ = 0.963. Every pair is scored twice: by comparing the probabilities a model assigns to the two sentences, and by asking the model directly, with the sentences presented in both orders so that answer-position effects are measured instead of being absorbed into the score. Three results follow. Order consistency (the share of pairs answered identically when the sentences are exchanged) falls below 0.05 for ten of the nineteen models, and what separates the usable models is instruction tuning, not scale. The vocative case is systematically inverted: 0.153 accuracy against 0.951 on the control, with models preferring the non-normative nominative form of address. Ukrainian adaptation substantially reduces this deficit, measured against the exact checkpoints two adapted models were trained from.
papers.summary: A released set of 1,444 Ukrainian minimal pairs (vocative case, numeral-noun and adjective agreement, verb government, calques from Russian, plus a subject-verb agreement control) is used to test whether 19 language models produce normative Ukrainian. Each pair is scored both by sentence probabilities and by direct prompting with the sentences shown in both orders. Order consistency falls below 0.05 for ten of the nineteen models, with instruction tuning rather than scale separating the usable ones, and the vocative case is systematically inverted at **0.153 accuracy versus 0.951 on the control**. Ukrainian-specific adaptation substantially reduces that deficit relative to the exact base checkpoints.

papers.title: Assessing the Physical Interpretability of AlphaEarth Foundation Embeddings Through Multi-Sensor Satellite Time-Series Benchmarking for Agricultural Mapping
papers.abstract: Accurate and dynamic maps of agricultural LULC are important for agricultural water resource management, particularly in areas where water scarcity is prevalent, such as Morocco. Here, we evaluate the utility of AlphaEarth Foundation Model (AEF) embeddings for agricultural LULC and irrigation-type mapping in Morocco. AEF embeddings were compared to single-date and time-series remote-sensing features using three machine-learning classifiers: XGBoost, CatBoost, and TabPFN. We also evaluated whether AEF embeddings can: (a) provide an efficient and transferable alternative to conventional direct use of Earth observation products and (b) reconstruct biophysical information. Results showed that multi-temporal feature time series achieved the highest performance, with accuracies of 0.93 for agricultural LULC and 0.87 for irrigation-type mapping when using TabPFN. However, AEF embeddings yielded comparable results, achieving accuracies of 0.91 for agricultural LULC and 0.85 for irrigation-type mapping, while reducing the need for extensive data processing and manual feature engineering typically required for satellite products. Spatial LULC mapping using TabPFN achieved comparable overall accuracies (0.85-0.86) across the three feature configurations, but revealed substantial differences in mapped tree cover, ranging from 14.57% for surface reflectance to 29.79% for AFE. Physical probing revealed that AEF embeddings strongly encode spectral indices (A30-SWIR: rho=0.58-0.67), (A38-NDMI: rho=-0.72), vegetation (A49-NDVI: rho = 0.72-0.73), and SAR structure (A25-VH: rho = 0.71). Future research should focus on enhancing the interpretability of embedding-based approaches by incorporating physical knowledge to develop more transparent and trustworthy AI systems for agricultural applications.
papers.summary: Embeddings from the `AlphaEarth Foundation` model are evaluated for mapping agricultural land use and land cover and irrigation type in Morocco, against single-date and time-series satellite features using `XGBoost`, `CatBoost`, and `TabPFN` classifiers. Hand-built multi-temporal features performed best (0.93 and 0.87 accuracy with `TabPFN`), but the embeddings came close at **0.91 for land cover and 0.85 for irrigation type** with far less data processing. Spatial maps had similar overall accuracy yet disagreed widely on tree cover (14.57% to 29.79%), and probing showed individual embedding dimensions correlate with spectral indices, vegetation indices, and radar structure.

papers.title: JHealthBench-L: Clinician-Reviewed Localization of HealthBench for Rubric-Based Medical LLM Evaluation in Japan
papers.abstract: Rubric-based benchmarks such as HealthBench evaluate large language models (LLMs) on open-ended health consultations using case-specific physician criteria, many of which presuppose the healthcare institutions, medications, and care pathways of their source region. Under machine translation alone, these regional assumptions remain in the rubric, leaving responses appropriate in Japan uncredited or falsely penalized under foreign clinical rules. To adapt established clinical evaluation perspectives to Japan without authoring rubrics from scratch, we construct JHealthBench-L (79 patient-facing consultations, 1,022 criteria) through source-cited LLM drafting, single-specialist selection and revision, independent dual-physician review, and meta-review. Specialists rewrote only 4.4% of criteria from scratch, and independent reviewers approved 93.6% of Stage-2 criteria without issue. Comparing JHealthBench-L with a machine-translated baseline across 18 LLMs reveals that translation-only evaluation preserves coarse model rankings ($\tau = 0.817$, mean shift +0.027) yet flips verdicts on 17.7% of modified criteria (vs. 7.3% re-grading noise) and reduces false penalties on Japan-adapted negative criteria by 7.1 percentage points, masking item-level clinical mismeasurement behind stable leaderboards. Axis-level and paired analyses further show that context awareness and Japan-specific clinical criteria remain primary bottlenecks, whereas Japanese continual pretraining and reasoning post-training substantially improve locally grounded performance. Datasets, physician revision logs, and evaluation code are available at https://github.com/horshohei/JHealthBench-L.
papers.summary: Rubric-based medical benchmarks such as `HealthBench` embed assumptions about the source region's institutions, medications, and care pathways, so machine-translating them can penalize answers that are correct in another country. `JHealthBench-L` adapts 79 patient-facing consultations and 1,022 criteria to Japan through source-cited LLM drafting, specialist revision, independent dual-physician review, and meta-review, with specialists rewriting only 4.4% of criteria from scratch. Across 18 LLMs, translation-only evaluation preserves coarse rankings (Kendall tau of 0.817) but **flips verdicts on 17.7% of modified criteria** against 7.3% re-grading noise. Context awareness and Japan-specific criteria remain the main bottlenecks, while Japanese continual pretraining and reasoning post-training help.

papers.title: Incorporating the Knowledge Distillation to Improve the EfficientNet Transfer Learning Capability
papers.abstract:
Due to the Deep Learning requirement for a large training dataset, Transfer Learning has become a central method in the field of Computer Vision, which heavily used Deep Learning. Since the adoption of transfer learning in the field, the performance of the models in computer vision is significantly upgraded. The common transfer learning practice in computer vision research is to use state-of-the-art architectures in the ImageNet dataset as the backbone network. The best performing architecture in ImageNet is currently held by EfficientNet, which is a set of architectures that were progressively grown from a baseline architecture.
  By observing the EfficientNet development approach, it is natural to hypothesize that the smaller EfficientNet architecture is capable to contain the knowledge of the larger architecture. This hypothesis comes from the fact that the larger EfficientNet architecture was grown from the smaller architecture. Therefore, in this study, we experimented if it is beneficial to transfer the knowledge from the larger architecture to the smaller architecture of the EfficientNet. To achieve this goal, we proposed a transfer learning method that uses Knowledge Distillation as the knowledge transfer mechanism from the larger to smaller architecture. We found that the proposed method is able to upgrade the performance of each of the EfficientNet architecture. Several smaller architectures are even able to outperform the larger architecture that was trained using the standard transfer learning method.
papers.summary: Since larger `EfficientNet` variants are grown from smaller ones, the authors hypothesize that a smaller variant can hold the knowledge of a larger one. They propose a transfer learning method that uses knowledge distillation to pass knowledge from larger to smaller `EfficientNet` architectures. The method reportedly improves every variant tested, and **several smaller architectures outperform larger ones trained with standard transfer learning**.

papers.title: Counter-DECEIVR: Counterfactual Explanations for Deepfake Detectors using Detector-Guided Rectified Flow Inversion
papers.abstract: Deep-learning-generated media are increasingly passed off as real, driving an arms race between image generators and deepfake detectors. Trust in the latter is limited by their often black-box nature; and, while region-based explanations can sometimes be extracted, these become less useful as generation quality improves. Counterfactual examples, which show the minimal change that flips a detector's decision, reveal what evidence drives a verdict, helping analysts decide whether to trust it. This work introduces Counter-DECEIVR (DEtector-guided reCtifiEd flow InVeRsion for counterfactuals), a novel training-free framework that generates counterfactual examples.
