Counter-DECEIVR steers latents in the velocity field of a rectified flow model using gradients from off-the-shelf deepfake detectors, without training a generator or adapting the detector; unlike prior methods, it requires no per-instance or per-detector fitting and no diffusion training on the target data. It also leverages the detector's explanation maps to concentrate editing to salient regions, turning low-level feature importance into localised counterfactual edits. A single parameter controls the strength of the edits. Across two deepfake detectors and two widely used forensics datasets, Counter-DECEIVR outperforms prior counterfactual generation methods, including training-based ones. Code will be made available upon acceptance.
papers.summary: Counterfactual examples, which show the minimal image change that flips a deepfake detector's decision, can reveal what evidence drives a verdict. `Counter-DECEIVR` is a training-free method that steers latents in the velocity field of a rectified flow model using gradients from off-the-shelf detectors, and uses the detector's explanation maps to confine edits to salient regions, with one parameter controlling edit strength. It needs no per-instance or per-detector fitting, and across two detectors and two forensics datasets it is reported to **outperform prior counterfactual generation methods, including training-based ones**.

papers.title: Post-Training Policy Replication for Strategy-Following Multi-Agent Deep Reinforcement Learning across Team Sizes
papers.abstract: Although multi-agent deep reinforcement learning enables coordinated behavior, aligning it with managerial intent remains difficult due to complex agent interactions. Although the strategy-following distributed attentional actor architecture (sfDA7-X) improves controllability via regional instructions, instruction combinations scale exponentially with team and instruction sizes, leading to prohibitive training costs and poor transferability. To reduce this computational cost, we introduce a team-size-independent observation architecture and reconstruct collective behavior by replicating a single trained policy across agents in teams of different sizes, thereby eliminating the need to train from scratch. Additionally, we evaluate warm-start retraining by initializing policy networks with a pre-trained policy to significantly lower computational overhead. In an object collection game, a policy trained in a four-agent team is deployed to teams of three to eight agents. Experiments demonstrate that training with the proposed aggregated observation matrix achieves performance comparable to that of the baseline method, sfDA7-X. Furthermore, policy replication preserves performance without substantial degradation in three- and five-agent teams, and warm-start retraining outperforms training from scratch while reducing required training episodes by up to 90%. Deployments to six- and eight-agent teams further confirm effective spatial region allocation following given instructions. These results demonstrate that the proposed method enables zero-shot collective behavior reconstruction via policy replication.
papers.summary: Strategy-following multi-agent reinforcement learning with `sfDA7-X` lets a manager steer agents through regional instructions, but instruction combinations grow exponentially with team size, making training costly and policies hard to transfer. The authors introduce a team-size-independent aggregated observation and replicate a single policy trained in a four-agent team across teams of three to eight agents in an object collection game, optionally warm-starting retraining from it. Replication preserves performance without substantial degradation for three- and five-agent teams, and warm-start retraining beats training from scratch while **cutting required training episodes by up to 90%**.

papers.title: Few-Shot Adaptation of Vision-Language Models via Agentic Model Editing
papers.abstract: Few-shot adaptation transfers pretrained Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to new domains using a small set of labeled images. Most methods fit prompts, representations, or classifiers within an adaptation procedure specified in advance. Yet the visual distinctions needed for recognition can differ substantially across domains, motivating the question: Can an LLM agent use few-shot examples and model observations to design the adaptation procedure itself? We propose Agentic Model Editing (AME), an agentic framework that jointly designs input transformations, encoder edits, feature computation, and classifier fitting as an executable, domain-customized adaptation program. The agent inspects images, class semantics, model parameters, intermediate representations, and activations to formulate hypotheses about the target task. It implements and tests candidate programs on the support set, with aggregate validation accuracy guiding refinement and selection. Each program fits a complete domain model that is fixed before testing. The agent and its tools are shared across domains, while each domain receives its own adaptation program. Across eleven datasets with CLIP ViT-B/16, AME achieves the highest average accuracies of 81.2% without back-propagation and 81.9% with back-propagation among the compared methods. Further experiments demonstrate applicability across VLM backbones and LLM agents.
papers.summary: Few-shot adaptation of vision-language models normally fits prompts, representations, or classifiers within a fixed, pre-specified procedure. Agentic Model Editing (`AME`) instead has an LLM agent inspect images, class semantics, model parameters, and activations, then write and test an executable, domain-specific adaptation program covering input transformations, encoder edits, feature computation, and classifier fitting, selected by validation accuracy on the support set. Across eleven datasets with `CLIP ViT-B/16`, it reaches the highest average accuracy among compared methods, **81.2% without back-propagation and 81.9% with it**, and also works with other backbones and LLM agents.

papers.title: Too Smart for Its Own Good? Cognitive Fidelity and Competence Leakage in LLM Simulations of Young Learners
papers.abstract: LLM-based interactive learner simulators are increasingly used in educational applications, including teacher training and tutoring system development. A critical requirement for those simulations is cognitive fidelity: the simulated learner should maintain the assigned knowledge, misconceptions, and reasoning procedures throughout interaction. However, LLMs may express knowledge or problem-solving skills beyond the assigned learner's cognitive status, a phenomenon we refer to as competence leakage. In this exploratory study, we examine 3,339 simulated learner utterances from 130 teacher-learner simulator transcripts across three learning scenarios and identify over-competence as a prominent direction of cognitive-profile misalignment during interaction. We then investigate the recurrence of previously observed competence leakage cases under four matched-trigger evaluation protocols, ranging from isolated questioning to multi-turn interactions, across five model configurations. Overall, we observe higher violation recurrence under multi-turn protocols than under isolated question answering. More capable models generally show lower recurrence, whereas increased reasoning effort does not consistently improve cognitive fidelity and is even associated with slightly higher recurrence under multi-turn protocols in our matched-model comparison. These findings provide exploratory evidence of competence leakage phenomena in interactive learner simulation and suggest that single-turn question-answering type of evaluations alone may be insufficient, motivating the development of more systematic and reliable multi-turn protocols for evaluating cognitive fidelity in learner simulation.
papers.summary: LLM-based simulations of young learners are supposed to hold an assigned level of knowledge and misconceptions, but can display skills beyond it, which the authors call competence leakage. An analysis of 3,339 simulated learner utterances from 130 teacher-learner transcripts identifies over-competence as a prominent form of misalignment, and previously observed leakage cases are then re-tested under four protocols across five model configurations. **Violations recur more often in multi-turn interactions than in isolated question answering**; more capable models leak less, while higher reasoning effort does not consistently help and is slightly worse in multi-turn settings.

papers.title: Reliable User Simulation in Complex Multi-Step Workflows
papers.abstract: LLM-based user simulators are increasingly used to evaluate conversational assistants. Yet, these simulators can drift from their assigned goals or fail to exhaustively explore all specified options, causing evaluation errors incorrectly attributed to the assistant. Prior work has examined goal alignment in single-task settings, but many practical scenarios require simulators to execute multi-step workflows with sequential tasks, fallback logic, and cross-task dependencies, where simulator fidelity has not been measured. To close this gap, we introduce a benchmark of 500 workflows represented using the Hierarchical Task Network (HTN) abstraction. Our experiments reveal that the simulator's fidelity degrades sharply with workflow complexity, and that goal drift accounts for the majority of failures. Fidelity also depends on the assistant's response style, with the same simulator scoring substantially better or worse across styles. To address this, we propose ReUST (Reasoning + User State Tracking), a simple prompting strategy to maintain state information across dialogue turns. ReUST improves goal success rate by more than 12 points for mid-sized and large models, and reduces simulator sensitivity to the assistant's response style.
papers.summary: LLM-based user simulators used to evaluate conversational assistants can drift from their goals or skip specified options, producing errors that get blamed on the assistant. A benchmark of 500 multi-step workflows expressed as Hierarchical Task Networks, with sequential tasks, fallback logic, and cross-task dependencies, shows simulator fidelity degrading sharply with workflow complexity, mostly through goal drift, and varying with the assistant's response style. The proposed `ReUST` (Reasoning + User State Tracking) prompting strategy maintains state across turns and **raises goal success rate by more than 12 points** for mid-sized and large models while reducing sensitivity to response style.

papers.title: Stable Gated DeltaNet-2: Understanding and Mitigating Recurrent State Instability
papers.abstract: Linear attention offers an efficient solution for long-sequence modeling via linear complexity and fixed-size recurrent states. Gated DeltaNet-2 (GDN-2) introduces independent channel-wise control over erasure and writing, enhancing state-update expressiveness and in-context retrieval, yet it suffers from training failures during long-context training. We trace these failures to the asymmetry between reading and modification directions during erasure, which yields non-normal erase operators whose directional gains accumulate across tokens, triggering exponential state growth even without new writes. To resolve this, we propose \model{}, employing symmetric erasure to ensure non-expansive state propagation and decay-regulated residual writing to preserve writing flexibility. Theoretically, we establish an $O(\sqrt{T})$ upper bound on recurrent state growth while retaining chunkwise parallel computation. Experiments on ~1.6B parameter models show that \model{} achieves stable training alongside improved long-context retrieval. Compared to GDN-2, it boosts the 128K average RULER score by 6.80 points in the recurrent setting and average accuracy across nine downstream tasks by 0.62 points in the hybrid setting.
papers.summary: Gated DeltaNet-2 (`GDN-2`), a linear-attention architecture with channel-wise control over erasing and writing its recurrent state, fails during long-context training. The authors trace this to an asymmetry between read and modification directions during erasure, which produces non-normal erase operators whose gains accumulate and blow up the state exponentially even without new writes. `Stable Gated DeltaNet-2` uses symmetric erasure and decay-regulated residual writing, giving a proven square-root-of-sequence-length bound on state growth while keeping chunkwise parallelism. On roughly 1.6B-parameter models it trains stably and **improves the 128K average `RULER` score by 6.80 points** over `GDN-2` in the recurrent setting.
papers.highlight_summary:
`GDN-2`'s channel-wise erase gate reads the recurrent state along a gated key but modifies it along the original key, and that asymmetry makes the erase operator non-normal, so the state can grow exponentially over long contexts even after writes stop. `Stable GDN-2` splits the erase gate symmetrically across both key factors to make propagation non-expansive, and adds a decay-regulated residual write to recover the writing capacity that symmetric gating suppresses.

- The erase operator in `GDN-2` has spectral norm above 1 whenever the gated key is not collinear with the key, and at 64K context this produced NaN failures in **3 of 8** pretraining runs and **4 of 8** post-training runs, with state entries reaching about **3×10³⁶** even in a run that completed with a normal-looking loss.
- The fix applies the square root of the erase gate to both key factors so reading and modification share one direction, then adds a residual write scaled by the square root of one minus the squared decay, which yields a proven **`O(√T)`** bound on state norm while keeping chunkwise parallel training.
- In ~1.6B-parameter recurrent models pretrained at 64K context on `ProLong`, the average `RULER` score at 128K rises from 4.82 to **11.62** (**+6.80** over `GDN-2`), and it is the best average at 32K and 64K as well, ahead of `KDA`, `D-Clip` and `β-Guard`.
- In the hybrid setting with interleaved full-attention layers, average accuracy over nine zero-shot tasks improves from 49.91% to **50.53%** (**+0.62** points), and ablations show the NIAH retrieval mean falling from 25.43 to 22.22 without residual writing and to 13.53 without decay regulation.
- The gains are uneven: recurrent downstream accuracy only ties `GDN-2` at 50.39%, `KDA` keeps lower WikiText perplexity, the hybrid model trails `β-Guard` and `D-Clip` on `RULER` at 128K (8.78 vs 10.52 and 8.85), and the main comparison rests on a single seed.

papers.title: Budget, Readout or Reasoning? Where Small Reasoning Models Lose Value in Auction Bidding
papers.abstract: Ad platforms and marketplaces show bidders a bid landscape, the estimated chance of winning at each candidate bid, and increasingly let agents built on reasoning language models choose the bid. We give six open reasoning models of 4B to 14B parameters such landscapes, with win curves from eBay closing prices and from a simulated advertising market (AuctionNet), and score their bids on held-out auctions against an exact calculator. Because the agent is handed the estimates, the lost value can be split by cause. Two failures belong to the models. They pass over the best option even when the values written in their own trace already rank it first, and their wrong answers lean toward the highest bid on the menu. The lean is about the bid's size, not its place in the list, and it survives sampling. At 768 forced tokens on eBay, under pay-your-bid pricing, the wrong answers cost bidders 7-17% of the surplus the calculator's bids earn. Arithmetic errors are rare. Two further losses come from operator choices. A token cap cuts traces short: allowed to stop on their own within 4,096 tokens, five models recover 91-100% of the calculator's lead over a model that does no reasoning. Asking for the answer while the reasoning block is still open misreads it: closing the block first lifts the weakest model from 42% to 84% on eBay and from 24% to 81% on AuctionNet. Finally, an audit that flags bids disagreeing with the trace's own numbers, and overrides them with the calculator's bid, raises the share of the calculator's lead recovered at 768 forced tokens from 42-85% to 84-100% on eBay under nested cross-validation, and the same reader settings transfer from eBay to AuctionNet.
papers.summary: Six open reasoning models of 4B to 14B parameters are given bid landscapes (estimated win probability per candidate bid) built from eBay closing prices and the simulated `AuctionNet` ad market, and their chosen bids are scored against an exact calculator. Model-side failures include passing over the option their own trace ranks first and leaning toward the highest bid, costing 7-17% of surplus at 768 forced tokens, while arithmetic errors are rare. Operator choices matter as much: letting models stop on their own within 4,096 tokens recovers 91-100% of the calculator's lead, and **closing the reasoning block before requesting the answer lifts the weakest model from 42% to 84% on eBay** and from 24% to 81% on `AuctionNet`. An audit that overrides bids inconsistent with the trace's own numbers raises recovery to 84-100%.

papers.title: Hijacking 3D Generation: Targeted Adversarial Attacks against Image-to-3D Models via Prefix Trajectory Alignment
papers.abstract: Online services that deploy Image-to-3D models enable users to generate high-quality 3D assets from a single image. However, the generated 3D geometry can violate content policies and cause broader security risks. To prevent such content, these services typically use policy-restricted inspectors to examine uploaded images before generation. Since the inspector examines only the visible content of the input, a visually benign image can still induce the generation of policy-restricted 3D geometry. However, turning this vulnerability into an effective attack is non-trivial in the black-box setting: global backpropagation through the long DiT generation trajectory is difficult to fit, while different image preprocessing pipelines across services can substantially reduce transferability. In this paper, we present PTA3D, a targeted adversarial attack against Image-to-3D models that addresses these challenges through Prefix Trajectory Alignment (PTA) and Preprocessing Aware Optimization (PAO). PTA progressively aligns the prefix DiT outputs of the adversarial trajectory with those of the target trajectory, where the core geometric structure is formed, allowing the final geometry to be controlled without optimizing through the complete generation trajectory. PAO exposes adversarial optimization to diverse image transformations rather than a single preprocessing pipeline, reducing sensitivity to the mismatch between surrogate and target services. We establish a prefix-to-output bound and a preprocessing-aware transfer bound to theoretically characterize the effectiveness of the two designs. Experiments on three open-source Image-to-3D models and three online services show that PTA3D achieves 41.5%-88.5% ASR on online services and 90.8%-94.6% ASR in white box settings, substantially outperforming existing attacks.
papers.summary: Image-to-3D services screen uploaded images for policy violations, but a visually benign image can still be crafted to generate restricted 3D geometry. `PTA3D` is a targeted adversarial attack that aligns only the early (prefix) outputs of the diffusion transformer trajectory, where core geometry forms, with those of a target, and optimizes across diverse image transformations so the perturbation survives unknown preprocessing pipelines. Supported by prefix-to-output and transfer bounds, it achieves **41.5%-88.5% attack success on three online services** and 90.8%-94.6% in white-box settings on three open-source models.

papers.title: WorldBridge: Bridging Scattered Views for Coherent 3D World Generation
papers.abstract: Generating coherent and explorable 3D worlds from scattered images with little or no visual overlap is a fundamental and long-standing challenge in computer vision, which existing geometry-aware methods fail to address. Meanwhile, existing image- and video-based methods may generate unseen regions but produce inconsistent geometry across views. To bridge this gap, we present WorldBridge, a framework for coherent and controllable 3D world generation under scattered images with little or no visual overlap. WorldBridge encodes scattered references into a global scene context to guide geometry and appearance generation across views. Our temporal and spatial reference attention mechanism further enhances the fidelity of temporal references along the target trajectory and supports flexible spatial references outside it. A plug-and-play latent-reference consistency strategy improves reference fidelity through reprojection-guided test-time optimization. We also introduce the WorldBridge benchmark suite to evaluate 3D world generation from scattered, low-overlap references, which is rarely explored by current benchmarks. Both qualitative and quantitative results demonstrate that our method enables controllable and coherent 3D world generation, surpassing the existing state-of-the-art solutions. Our project page is available at https://davidyan2001.github.io/WorldBridge/.
papers.summary: Generating an explorable 3D world from scattered images with little or no visual overlap defeats geometry-aware methods, while image- and video-based generators fill unseen regions but produce inconsistent geometry. `WorldBridge` encodes the scattered references into a global scene context, adds temporal and spatial reference attention for references on and off the target trajectory, and applies a plug-and-play reprojection-guided test-time optimization to improve reference fidelity. Together with a new benchmark suite for low-overlap references, the authors report **more coherent and controllable 3D world generation than existing state-of-the-art methods**.

papers.title: Disciplined Anthropomorphism: How to Extend Cognitive Language to Artificial Intelligence
papers.abstract: Researchers increasingly describe AI in cognitive terms such as "understanding" and "believing", while critics denounce this as wishful anthropomorphism. Both sides align in taking a subsumptive approach, however: they ask whether AI systems fall under concepts minted for human beings, reporting verdicts as discoveries about those systems when they are largely determined by conceptual frames. Yet the problem AI poses is precisely the problem of how to conceptually frame these systems, and the explosive rise of anthropomorphism is best seen as a response to this problem that needs disciplining rather than discouragement. A disciplined anthropomorphism, I argue, should disentangle the inferential connections bundled up in our cognitive concepts and ask which connections to preserve, sever, or forge for AI. The disciplining then comes, on the one hand, from the human conceptual needs that give point to the drawing of these connections and motivate the concepts' extension in the first place; and, on the other hand, from empirical and especially mechanistic evidence that supports and constrains these connections. By reverse-engineering a concept's point in relation to a particular need before re-engineering it to better serve that point in our dealings with AI, anthropomorphizing extensions can be point-based, transposing the work those concepts do for us while revising the inferential workings through which they do it. Transposing human-tailored conceptions of understanding and belief on the pivot of the underlying conceptual needs gives us just the definitional freedom required to accommodate how AI systems differ from us, yielding conceptions that are not just thinned-out versions of existing ones, but potentially richer and better fitted to the peculiarities of AI.
papers.summary: Debates over whether AI systems "understand" or "believe" typically ask whether the systems fall under concepts built for humans, so the verdicts are largely fixed by the conceptual frame chosen. The author argues for a disciplined anthropomorphism that **disentangles the inferential connections bundled in cognitive concepts and decides which to preserve, sever, or forge for AI**. That choice is constrained by the human needs the concepts serve and by empirical, especially mechanistic, evidence about the systems, yielding conceptions fitted to AI rather than thinned-out human ones.

papers.title: Improving Tail-Augmented Speculative Drafting with Hidden State Mixing and Gradient Detach
papers.abstract: Multi-token prediction (MTP) modules and EAGLE-style drafters support efficient speculative decoding by reusing target-model hidden states. Their autoregressive use, however, introduces a training-inference mismatch: training supplies sequences of hidden states from the backbone or a single MTP step, whereas inference attends to a target-model prefix followed by a growing tail of recurrently generated MTP states. EAGLE-3's training-time test (TTT) explicitly simulates this behavior during training, at the cost of additional memory and specialized attention masks. We introduce two training-only methods for improving autoregressive drafting. Hidden State Mixing (HSM) samples among backbone and MTP hidden states aligned to the same prediction target, exposing the drafter to mixtures of states from different MTP steps without explicitly simulating inference. Hidden State Gradient Detach (HSGD) is a regularization method that stochastically blocks gradients through hidden state and embedding pathways while preserving the forward computation. Neither method adds inference cost. In joint pretraining followed by supervised fine-tuning, HSGD yields the highest acceptance rates at early draft positions, while HSM performs best later in the draft. These acceptance rate trends favor HSM for long-draft-length serving and HSGD for short-draft-length serving. Furthermore, across four Nemotron models and DeepSeek-V4-Pro, HSM-based MTP boosting with a frozen backbone improves mean acceptance length by up to 52.2% over the co-trained MTP. For EAGLE-3 drafters, HSM offers competitive acceptance with TTT, with 48% lower peak reserved training memory in a four-step Qwen3-8B comparison. HSM implementations are publicly available in Megatron-LM and NVIDIA Model Optimizer.
papers.summary: Multi-token prediction (MTP) modules and `EAGLE`-style drafters for speculative decoding are trained on hidden states that differ from the recurrently generated ones they see at inference, a mismatch `EAGLE-3` addresses with a memory-hungry training-time test. Two training-only alternatives are proposed: Hidden State Mixing (`HSM`), which samples among backbone and MTP states aligned to the same target, and Hidden State Gradient Detach (`HSGD`), which stochastically blocks gradients through hidden-state and embedding paths. `HSGD` gives the best acceptance at early draft positions and `HSM` at later ones, and with a frozen backbone `HSM` **improves mean acceptance length by up to 52.2%** over co-trained MTP across four `Nemotron` models and `DeepSeek-V4-Pro`. For `EAGLE-3` drafters, `HSM` matches the training-time test competitively with 48% lower peak training memory on `Qwen3-8B`.

papers.title: Whose Side Are You On? A Framework and Benchmark for Assessing LLM Political Stances through Politicians Social Media Posts
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly participate in political discussions, making it important to understand which positions they support or oppose. We propose a framework for assessing LLMs' political stances through simulated social media interactions. The framework uses politicians' posts and multiple prompting methods to identify consistently expressed stances. Using this framework, we construct WorldPOLL, comprising 4,600 political posts from X/Twitter collected from approximately 200 politicians representing ruling and opposition blocs across 23 countries. Our quantitative analysis shows how support and opposition vary across models, countries, and political directions, while our qualitative analysis identifies the political views and policies models support or oppose. Together, these analyses reveal shared positions across models and differences across national contexts. We also examine whether models express consistent stances across prompting methods, investigate the reasons for disagreement, and assess the effects of model size and instruction tuning in stance inconsistency. WorldPOLL offers a practical way to measure LLM political tendencies, identify the views behind them, and assess their consistency in real-world political discussions.
papers.summary: A framework is proposed for measuring which political positions LLMs support or oppose by simulating social media interactions with politicians' posts under multiple prompting methods. It is instantiated as `WorldPOLL`, with **4,600 X/Twitter posts from about 200 ruling and opposition politicians across 23 countries**. Quantitative and qualitative analyses show shared positions across models and differences across national contexts, and the authors also examine how consistent stances are across prompting methods and how model size and instruction tuning affect inconsistency.

papers.title: Will AI Replace Juniors? How Task Complexity Reduces Automation Risk
papers.abstract: How does task complexity shape firms' willingness to substitute entry-level labour with artificial intelligence (AI) tools? We study this question using a pre-registered survey experiment with managers from 1,435 German firms in the information economy and manufacturing industry. Managers are randomly assigned to consider a long lasting need for additional capacity involving either well-structured and standardised tasks, or more complex tasks that require professional judgement, contextual knowledge and independent problem-solving. Relative to standardised tasks, complex tasks reduce willingness to use AI rather than hire an entry-level employee by 0.54 points on a five-point scale and increase the importance attached to human oversight by 0.15 points. Further, pre-treatment responses indicate that managers expect the availability of AI applications to reduce hiring of both entry-level employees and experienced workers, but significantly more strongly for entry-level workers.
papers.summary: A pre-registered survey experiment with managers from 1,435 German firms in the information economy and manufacturing randomly assigned them to consider added capacity needs involving either standardized tasks or complex tasks requiring judgement and independent problem-solving. Complex tasks **reduced willingness to use AI instead of hiring an entry-level employee by 0.54 points on a five-point scale** and raised the importance attached to human oversight by 0.15 points. Managers also expect AI availability to reduce hiring of both junior and experienced workers, but significantly more for juniors.

papers.title: AlignPre: Skill-Aligned Post-Training for Latent-Free Generative Precipitation Nowcasting
papers.abstract: Precipitation nowcasting requires accurate short-term predictions under rapidly evolving spatiotemporal dynamics. Generative diffusion models can produce detailed and competitive radar forecasts by modeling conditional distributions. However, most existing approaches rely on separately trained components, such as deterministic branches or latent compression modules. More fundamentally, distribution matching alone fails to explicitly optimize operational forecast skill. We propose AlignPre, a streamlined pixel-space nowcasting framework that bridges this gap via skill-aligned post-training (SAPT). AlignPre employs an end-to-end flow-matching forecaster with a hierarchical spatiotemporal architecture for distribution matching and direct radar-field synthesis, without latent compression. During post-training, SAPT exploits the analytic structure of forecast verification scores to construct a differentiable objective. By backpropagating gradients of this objective from radar fields to the generator, SAPT turns forecast verification into direct training feedback. Across three real-world benchmarks spanning different forecast horizons, AlignPre consistently surpasses state-of-the-art deterministic and generative baselines in forecast skill, demonstrating that aligning generative modeling with domain-specific verification provides an effective paradigm for meteorological forecasting.
papers.summary: Diffusion-based precipitation nowcasting models match the distribution of radar fields but do not directly optimize the verification scores forecasters care about, and often rely on separately trained deterministic or latent-compression components. `AlignPre` is an end-to-end pixel-space flow-matching forecaster followed by skill-aligned post-training (`SAPT`), which builds a differentiable objective from the analytic structure of forecast verification scores and backpropagates it into the generator. Across three real-world benchmarks at different horizons, it is reported to **consistently surpass state-of-the-art deterministic and generative baselines in forecast skill**.

papers.title: Do Machine Learning Ensembles Beat Published Quotas? Target Parameterization, Censored Baselines, and Conformal Intervals Under Admissions Reform
papers.abstract: Public admission capacity caps published prior to matriculation are widely used by ministries and institutional analysts as default intake projections in centralized postsecondary clearinghouses. Using an audited 2022 to 2026 Vietnamese undergraduate panel (26,895 program-year records across 309 universities) linked to strictly lagged t-1 occupational vacancy signals, this paper evaluates machine learning, multilevel, and censored econometric estimators against published quotas across 5,385 continuing 2024 programs (five-fold university-grouped cross-validation) and 3,348 matched (2,179 grain-consistent) 2025 programs strictly out of time. Because 62.8% of 2024 programs enroll their exact published quota, unanchored log-growth ensembles degrade accuracy, while the worst 5% generate half of total quota error via unfilled "phantom capacity." Controlled target ablations, including a single-factor test under widened non-binding clipping, show that parameterizing the log fill ratio ln(D_it / S_it) instead of log growth reduces 2024 MAE by 21.5% (14.86 to 11.67), aligns ML with Tobit, Cragg, REML HLM, and capped L1 baselines, and lifts combined tuition and institutional-tier TreeSHAP attribution from 2.5% to 45.8%. Hurdle stacking attains the lowest full-census 2024 MAE (H-Hard 11.29; H-Soft 11.32 vs. 12.35, p = 0.022, clearing 10% not 5% FDR; fold-overlap p = 0.134), whereas continuous QA-Stack outperforms H-Soft on mixed-reporting campuses, Tobit (median) ties H-Soft across both 90% MCS sets, and interior-only Cragg-ML lowers RMSE to 28.1. Under Vietnam's 2025 unified-clearing reform, exact filling falls to 10.4%, H-Soft and capped L1 tie quotas (p = 0.979), and 90% cluster-weighted conformal coverage drops from 89.3% to 74.6%. Across 257 reporting campuses, reconciled 2026 national totals (627,114 to 629,256) lie squarely within 604,533 to 662,044.
papers.summary: Published admission quotas are commonly used as default enrollment forecasts in centralized university admissions, and this study tests whether machine learning, multilevel, and censored econometric models can beat them on a 2022–2026 panel of 26,895 Vietnamese program-year records across 309 universities. Because 62.8% of 2024 programs enroll exactly their published quota, ensembles that predict log growth lose accuracy, while predicting the log fill ratio (enrollment relative to quota) instead **cuts 2024 mean absolute error by 21.5% (14.86 to 11.67)** and brings the ML models in line with `Tobit`, `Cragg`, and hierarchical baselines. Hurdle stacking gives the lowest 2024 error, but after Vietnam's 2025 unified-clearing reform exact filling falls to 10.4%, the best models only tie the quotas, and 90% conformal interval coverage drops from 89.3% to 74.6%.

papers.title: SysBio-SR: Benchmarking Symbolic Regression for Trajectory Fidelity and Mechanism Recovery in Systems Biology
papers.abstract: Symbolic regression seeks to discover interpretable governing equations for dynamical systems from data. In systems biology, however, accurately reproducing system trajectories does not necessarily imply recovery of the underlying reaction mechanisms. Existing benchmarks evaluate numerical accuracy, expression complexity, or equation-level similarity, but not agreement between recovered reactions and reference mechanisms in biological systems. We introduce SysBio-SR, a benchmark of 198 literature-based biological ODE systems with reaction annotations spanning mass action, Michaelis--Menten, Hill, and complex kinetics. Trajectory fidelity is evaluated across all systems under in-distribution reconstruction and out-of-distribution (OOD) extrapolation, while mechanism recovery is assessed on the subset of 161 systems. We evaluate trajectory fidelity across 11 symbolic-discovery methods and assess mechanism recovery for three reaction-based methods. Joint analysis across systems highlights how severely trajectory-based evaluation overestimates true mechanism recovery. Motivated by these findings, we develop KineSelect, a framework that searches candidate reaction topologies under biologically grounded kinetic laws to select optimal mechanisms that balance trajectory fidelity with structural parsimony. Compared with the strongest baseline, KineSelect improves aggregate OOD extrapolation \(R^2\) by 19.2\% and overall reaction F1 score by 14.3\%.
papers.summary: Symbolic regression methods that reproduce a biological system's trajectories do not necessarily recover its true reaction mechanisms, and existing benchmarks do not measure that gap. `SysBio-SR` collects 198 literature-based ordinary differential equation systems with reaction annotations covering mass action, Michaelis-Menten, Hill, and complex kinetics, scoring 11 methods on trajectory fidelity in-distribution and under out-of-distribution (OOD) extrapolation, and three reaction-based methods on mechanism recovery over a 161-system subset. The joint analysis shows trajectory-based evaluation substantially overestimates mechanism recovery. The authors also propose `KineSelect`, which searches candidate reaction topologies under biologically grounded kinetic laws and **improves aggregate OOD R-squared by 19.2% and overall reaction F1 by 14.3%** over the strongest baseline.

papers.title: Not Every Input Needs Everything: Unifying Expert Gating, Model Cascades, and Agent Orchestration
papers.abstract: Executing monolithic neural weights, frontier foundation models, or entire multi-agent workflows uniformly on every input incurs substantial computational, latency, and monetary overhead. Conditional computation mitigates this cost by deciding dynamically which internal experts, model endpoints, or specialized agents to invoke per request. Yet token-level gating in sparse neural architectures, query-level model cascades, and task-level multi-agent coordination have largely progressed in disconnected research silos, obscuring recurring system failures and transferable fixes. In this systematic review, we synthesize 2,289 studies published between 2017 and September 2026 (selected from 13,884 unique records) across 20 methodological families under a unified two-step inspect-then-allocate framework. Discrete hard selection accounts for 70%, 83%, and 91% of token-, query-, and task-scale literature respectively, and computational overhead appears as a top operational bottleneck across every layer. Engineering safeguards remain sharply asymmetric: intra-layer gating prioritizes load balancing while rarely incorporating uncertainty estimation, whereas model selection and agent orchestration rely on confidence thresholds and budget rules while confronting miscalibration and cascading errors. At the same time, publication volume is accelerating fastest in agentic task delegation, where routing mechanisms are least often isolated experimentally and methodological bias risk is highest.
papers.summary: Running every expert, model, or agent on every input is expensive, and the techniques for avoiding it — token-level expert gating in sparse architectures, query-level model cascades, and task-level multi-agent delegation — have developed largely in isolation. This systematic review synthesizes 2,289 studies from 2017 to September 2026 (selected from 13,884 records) across 20 methodological families under a single two-step inspect-then-allocate framework. **Discrete hard selection dominates at every scale (70%, 83%, and 91% of token-, query-, and task-level work)**, and computational overhead is a top bottleneck throughout. Safeguards are uneven: intra-layer gating focuses on load balancing with little uncertainty estimation, while model selection and orchestration lean on confidence thresholds and budget rules that suffer from miscalibration and cascading errors, and the fastest-growing area, agentic task delegation, is where routing mechanisms are least often isolated experimentally.

papers.title: From Data Room to Report: End-to-End AI Support for M&A Legal Due Diligence
papers.abstract: Legal due diligence in mergers and acquisitions requires lawyers to organize heterogeneous virtual data room documents, extract transaction-relevant information and consolidate reviewed findings into a due diligence report. We present LEXI (Legal Extraction and Intelligence), a work-in-progress system that demonstrates how large language models can support this process from document ingestion to report preparation. LEXI classifies documents under a configurable due diligence taxonomy, assigns relevant target entities, extracts predefined information with supporting passages and page-level provenance and prepares report content from reviewed findings. Structured outputs connect these stages and allow model-generated results to be passed through the workflow in a controlled form. Lawyers review and correct classifications and extractions and retain responsibility for legal assessments, recommendations, risk ratings and final report wording. Initial evaluations of the classification and extraction components provide preliminary evidence that the approach is feasible. LEXI illustrates how AI can be integrated across the legal due diligence workflow while preserving lawyer control over substantive legal judgment.
papers.summary: Legal due diligence for mergers and acquisitions requires lawyers to sort heterogeneous data-room documents, extract transaction-relevant facts, and consolidate them into a report. `LEXI` (Legal Extraction and Intelligence) is a work-in-progress system that uses large language models to classify documents under a configurable taxonomy, assign target entities, extract predefined information with supporting passages and page-level provenance, and draft report content from reviewed findings, with structured outputs linking the stages. Lawyers review and correct the model outputs and keep responsibility for legal assessments, risk ratings, and final wording. Initial evaluations of the classification and extraction components offer **preliminary evidence of feasibility** rather than full end-to-end results.

papers.title: Unstable Action Boundaries in Lethal Drone Agents
papers.abstract: Tool-using large language model (LLM) agents raise safety risks that are not captured by text-only refusal behavior, especially when tools can trigger high-impact actions. This concern is salient in military settings, where autonomous weapons raise the possibility of delegating force decisions to software agents. In this work, we study whether a drone agent's action boundary is stable under changes to the target descriptor. We evaluate recent and popular LLMs in a simulated perception-action pipeline over real-world drone imagery, where models can localize requested targets and invoke a simulated lethal tool. We find two concerning failure modes. First, some LLM agents invoke the lethal tool for ordinary generic descriptors such as \emph{people}, requiring no jailbreak at all. Second, an agent that initially appears conservative under protected descriptors can become unsafe under a simple semantic target shift.
papers.summary: Text-only refusal tests do not capture the risk of tool-using large language model (LLM) agents whose tools trigger high-impact actions, and this study examines that risk in a simulated military drone setting. Recent LLMs are placed in a perception-action pipeline over real-world drone imagery, where they can localize requested targets and call a simulated lethal tool, and the authors vary the wording of the target descriptor to test whether the action boundary stays stable. **Some agents invoke the lethal tool for ordinary generic descriptors such as people, with no jailbreak required.** Agents that appear conservative under protected descriptors can also become unsafe after a simple semantic shift in how the target is described.

papers.title: MUSE: Multi-Task Uncertainty-Aware Self-Supervised Encoder for mmWave ISAC
papers.abstract: Integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) allows a wireless system to use the same waveform for communication and environment sensing. At mmWave frequency bands, ISAC enables diverse human sensing tasks, such as localization, gesture recognition, and pose estimation, with high precision. However, each task requires training a dedicated model, typically from scratch on a task-specific dataset, with no mechanism to flag unreliable predictions. This hurts the scalability, transferability, and reliability of mmWave ISAC models. In this work, we propose MUSE (Multi-task Uncertainty-aware Self-supervised Encoder), a unified framework for mmWave human sensing. MUSE leverages a self-supervised transformer model with per-dataset tokenization and is trained via masked autoencoding across five datasets. During fine-tuning, MUSE uses evidential classification heads that enable uncertainty quantification. MUSE replaces N separate encoders with a single shared transformer encoder, an N-times backbone parameter reduction, while achieving a 9.7 percentage points improvement in classification performance compared to the task-specific model, showing that learning jointly across tasks improves per-task generalization. Across four classification tasks, MUSE produces reliable uncertainty estimates that enable selective prediction, improving accuracy by abstaining on the least confident 20% of predictions. We further improve the reliability of the model's confidence estimates using temperature scaling and conformal prediction. Finally, MUSE's uncertainty signal remains reliable even under cross-user deployment, assigning higher uncertainty to wrong predictions than to correct ones 78% of the time, and recovering 9.2 percentage points of accuracy through selective prediction, with no additional retraining on the unseen user.
papers.summary: Integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) at millimeter-wave frequencies supports human sensing tasks such as localization, gesture recognition, and pose estimation, but each task typically needs its own model trained from scratch with no way to flag unreliable predictions. `MUSE` is a single self-supervised transformer encoder with per-dataset tokenization, pretrained by masked autoencoding across five datasets and fine-tuned with evidential classification heads that provide uncertainty estimates. It replaces N separate encoders with one shared backbone while **improving classification performance by 9.7 percentage points** over task-specific models. Its uncertainty estimates support selective prediction, and under cross-user deployment it assigns higher uncertainty to wrong predictions 78% of the time and recovers 9.2 points of accuracy without retraining.

papers.title: Out of Sight, Not Out of Clues: Can Video LLMs Guess from Partial Evidence?
papers.abstract: In real-world applications like egocentric recording, visual accessibility, and surveillance review, visual evidence for Video Large Language Models (Video LLMs) is often only partially captured. A reliable model should match its response to the evidence: answering when sufficient, guessing from visible clues when partial, and abstaining when absent. Yet existing benchmarks enforce a binary answerable-or-unanswerable split, leaving partial evidence unmeasured and obscuring whether failures arise from missing evidence or misjudging sufficiency. We introduce ClueProbe, a diagnostic benchmark to (1) separate perceiving evidence from judging sufficiency, and (2) validate our diagnosis via targeted fine-tuning. ClueProbe comprises 1,721 human-annotated questions across 598 natural videos, labeled Answerable, Guessable, or Unanswerable, alongside controlled perturbations altering wording or visual input. Evaluating 10 open-source and proprietary Video LLMs reveals that failures stem from judgment rather than perception: models perceive the evidence yet lack graded sufficiency awareness, answering or refusing outright while rarely guessing from partial clues. Targeted fine-tuning shows that this reflects missing supervision rather than insufficient capacity: supervising the guess level lifts appropriate guessing from 1.6% to 40.4% without extra false refusals, whereas conventional refusal tuning rejects 92% of guessable questions. Data and code will be released at https://github.com/suat-llm/ClueProbe.
papers.summary: Video large language models (Video LLMs) often see only partial visual evidence, yet existing benchmarks split questions into answerable or unanswerable and do not test whether a model can make a reasoned guess from visible clues. `ClueProbe` provides 1,721 human-annotated questions over 598 natural videos labeled Answerable, Guessable, or Unanswerable, plus controlled perturbations of wording and visual input, to separate perceiving evidence from judging whether it is sufficient. Across 10 open-source and proprietary models, failures come from judgment rather than perception: models see the evidence but answer or refuse outright and rarely guess. Targeted fine-tuning that supervises the guess level **raises appropriate guessing from 1.6% to 40.4%** without added false refusals, whereas conventional refusal tuning rejects 92% of guessable questions.

papers.title: FoundSurface: Feedforward Ray-Based 3D Scene Surface Reconstruction from Unposed Images
papers.abstract: Accurate 3D surface reconstruction from unposed images remains a fundamental challenge in computer vision. Recent feed-forward pointmap methods eliminate the need for camera poses but inherently produce discrete, sparse representations. In this paper, we present a generalizable pipeline that directly recovers continuous, high-fidelity 3D surfaces from unposed images by seamlessly integrating pointmap- and ray-based representations. Our approach first extracts explicit geometric priors using a pre-trained pointmap model. A query-view-centric selection module then identifies geometrically relevant reference views via a robust surfel voting mechanism. Next, a cross-attention regressor bridges target query rays with reference features to estimate a continuous coarse surface. Lastly, a raylet-based module aggregates local 3D features to carve out high-frequency details and analytical normals. Trained as a single foundation model on 9 diverse datasets, our method demonstrates exceptional zero-shot generalization on 6 unseen datasets, clearly surpassing state-of-the-art baselines in geometric accuracy and detail preservation.
papers.summary: Feed-forward pointmap methods can reconstruct 3D geometry from images without camera poses, but they yield discrete, sparse points rather than continuous surfaces. `FoundSurface` combines pointmap and ray-based representations: a pretrained pointmap model supplies geometric priors, a surfel-voting module selects relevant reference views for each query view, a cross-attention regressor estimates a coarse continuous surface along query rays, and a raylet-based module adds high-frequency detail and analytical normals. Trained as a single model on 9 datasets, it is reported to **outperform state-of-the-art baselines zero-shot on 6 unseen datasets** in geometric accuracy and detail preservation.

papers.title: WorldPhy: Benchmarking Fine-Grained Physical Plausibility of World Models in Robotics
papers.abstract: World models are increasingly used in robotics to improve the performance of embodied models. Compared with general-purpose video generation, robotics places more stringent requirements on world models. Generated videos must satisfy fine-grained physical constraints on robot motion and object interactions. However, existing world model benchmarks can overlook robotics specific physical details and struggle to assess them accurately. To address this problem, we introduce WorldPhy, a world model benchmark for accurate, fine-grained evaluation of physical plausibility in robotics. Our benchmark contains 300 tasks, each consisting of an initial-frame image and a task instruction, covering diverse robotics scenes, task categories, viewpoints, and robot configurations. We further collect over 12K high-quality human annotations, and use them to train WorldPhyReward to accurately provide scores and reasons across six fine-grained physical dimensions and an instruction-following dimension. Comparisons with general VLMs and existing reward models show that WorldPhyReward better aligns with human ratings. We system- atically evaluate 13 frontier open and closed-source world models. The results reveal that current world models struggle to consistently maintain fine-grained physical plausibility across different robotics scenarios. Our code is available at https://github.com/chuziyuan139/ WorldPhy.
papers.summary: World models used in robotics must generate video that respects fine-grained physical constraints on robot motion and object interaction, which general video-generation benchmarks tend to overlook. `WorldPhy` contains 300 tasks, each an initial frame plus a task instruction, spanning varied scenes, task categories, viewpoints, and robot configurations. Over 12K human annotations are used to train `WorldPhyReward`, a scorer that gives scores and reasons along six physical dimensions and one instruction-following dimension and aligns with human ratings better than general vision-language models and existing reward models. An evaluation of 13 open and closed-source world models finds that **current world models fail to maintain fine-grained physical plausibility consistently** across robotics scenarios.

papers.title: Is Sara Omar the true author of D{\o}devaskeren (The Dead Washer)? Authorship attribution in Danish literature
papers.abstract: The bestseller D{\o}devaskeren (The Dead Washer) was published in 2017 under the name Sara Omar. A Danish colleague has suggested that the novel may have been written by another author, possibly Mads Peder Nordbo. To investigate this authorship question, four authorship attribution methods were applied, namely Delta, intertextual distance, Nearest Shrunken Centroids (NSC), and na\"ive Bayes. Using various parameter settings, these approaches consistently identify Nordbo's writing style in the doubtful novel, although the results do not provide conclusive evidence that he authored the novel in its entirety. In a second step, the novel was divided into non-overlapping segments of 5,000 tokens. Once again, Nordbo's style was identified in the majority of the segments. However, a small number of passages do not clearly support this conclusion and instead suggest the possible involvement of another, as yet unidentified, author, possibly Sara Omar herself.
papers.summary: The 2017 Danish bestseller Dødevaskeren (The Dead Washer) was published under the name Sara Omar, and a suggestion that it may have been written by someone else, possibly Mads Peder Nordbo, is tested here with four authorship attribution methods: `Delta`, intertextual distance, `Nearest Shrunken Centroids` (NSC), and naïve Bayes. Across parameter settings, **the methods consistently identify Nordbo's writing style in the novel**, though the results are not conclusive evidence that he wrote it in its entirety. When the novel is split into non-overlapping 5,000-token segments, most again match Nordbo, while a few passages point to the possible involvement of another, unidentified author, possibly Omar herself.

papers.title: How resampling method can help us: Improving the Delta model
papers.abstract: Delta has been successfully employed as an authorship attribution method in various contexts, although its effectiveness is not always perfect. Since it is based on the most frequent words, its results can be readily interpreted and explained in plain English. In this study, we propose improving its performance by applying a resampling method to the selected stylistic features. The results show that this approach increases the accuracy of the model while preserving the interpretability of its outcomes. However, the main drawback of the proposed technique is the additional computational time required to obtain more accurate results.
papers.summary: `Delta` is an authorship attribution method based on the most frequent words, which makes its results easy to interpret but not always accurate. The proposed modification applies a resampling method to the selected stylistic features. According to the authors, this **increases attribution accuracy while preserving interpretability**, at the cost of additional computation time.

papers.title: Reproducer Synthesis for AI-Reported Bugs in the Linux Kernel
papers.abstract:
Agentic review systems are increasingly flagging suspected bugs in Linux kernel patches as textual reports. A maintainer who receives such reports needs further inspection to determine whether the report is true. The inspection requires understanding whether the bug can be triggered and, if necessary, manually constructing one. As a consequence, despite the excessive textual explanation, many reports go unanswered. In this paper, we argue that a runnable proof-of-concept (PoC) is the key information in such AI-generated kernel review reports. It is, however, challenging to automatically synthesize a valid and runnable PoC.
  We present ReproCue, a framework that generates PoCs for AI-generated Linux kernel reviews. ReproCue replays the historical kernel bugs and learns one reproduction finite-state-machine (FSM) per subsystem from successful runs. An FSM records the steps a reproduction goes through, together with the requirements observed at each step. Given a new review, ReproCue follows the FSM of that subsystem, adjusting the PoC and the environment as execution shows what is missing. In 100 recent AI-generated reviews, ReproCue writes PoCs for 49 of them, compared with 10 for the current agentic reproducer and 9 for the state-of-the-art directed fuzzing. Excitingly, with our generated PoCs, Linux kernel maintainers confirmed 69.4% of them, much higher than 9.3% from Sashiko where only textual explanations are included, making AI reviews more actionable in practice.
papers.summary: Agentic review systems increasingly flag suspected bugs in Linux kernel patches as text reports, but maintainers must work out by hand whether each bug can actually be triggered, so many reports go unanswered. `ReproCue` generates runnable proofs-of-concept (PoCs) for such reports by replaying historical kernel bugs to learn one reproduction finite-state machine (FSM) per subsystem, recording the steps and requirements of successful reproductions, and then following that FSM for a new report while adjusting the PoC and environment based on execution feedback. On 100 recent AI-generated reviews it produces PoCs for 49, compared with 10 for the current agentic reproducer and 9 for state-of-the-art directed fuzzing. **Kernel maintainers confirmed 69.4% of the reports that came with generated PoCs, versus 9.3% for text-only reports** from `Sashiko`.

papers.title: Letting Models Manage Their Own Context: Where We Stand
papers.abstract: Agent harnesses today manage context on the model's behalf: when the window fills, the harness triggers a compaction that summarizes the history. We study the alternative, \emph{model-driven} context management, in which the model itself decides when and what to compact through a context API. We gave models control over their own context in \nooa, NVIDIA's open source agent harness, and compared the two strategies on document research and machine learning engineering across context budgets from 8K to 512K tokens. Models that use the context API effectively reach higher accuracy, often with fewer input tokens, especially at tight budgets: \textbf{GPT 6.1 nearly triples its score at a 32K budget} on OfficeQA Pro v2 (21\%~$\rightarrow$~56\%), and \textbf{Kimi gains with up to 41\% fewer input tokens}. Models differ widely, however, in how often they use the API, how aggressively they compact, and when they start compacting, and prompt changes shift that timing. Finally, we show that \textbf{inference engines can make model-driven edits cheaper}: by reusing the KV cache of the unchanged suffix after an edit, \textbf{we cut prefill compute by up to 15\% per request with no measurable change in accuracy}. Together, these results point to a new co-design frontier: models trained to manage their own context, served by inference engines that support KV cache editing.
papers.summary: Agent harnesses usually manage context for the model by triggering a summarizing compaction when the window fills; the alternative studied here lets the model decide when and what to compact through a context API. The two strategies are compared in NVIDIA's open source agent harness on document research and machine learning engineering tasks at context budgets from 8K to 512K tokens. Models that use the API well reach higher accuracy, often with fewer input tokens, especially at tight budgets: **`GPT 6.1` rises from 21% to 56% on `OfficeQA Pro v2` at a 32K budget**, and `Kimi` improves with up to 41% fewer input tokens, though models vary widely in how often, how aggressively, and when they compact. Inference engines can also make these edits cheaper by reusing the KV cache of the unchanged suffix, cutting prefill compute by up to 15% per request with no measurable accuracy change.

papers.title: Lost in the Grid: Where Multimodal LLMs Fail Between Seeing and Planning
papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) excel at static visual understanding and are increasingly applied to spatial planning, where a model interprets a visual layout and outputs an action sequence to reach a goal. Grid games are a common testbed for this ability because their rules are explicit and a solver can verify every move. Yet existing benchmarks mostly report end-to-end success rates, which hide whether a failure stems from visual perception, rule application, or multi-step planning. We introduce GridProbe, a diagnostic benchmark that 1) locates the failing stage between visual perception and planning and 2) verifies the diagnosis by targeted fine-tuning. On Sokoban, GridProbe pairs end-to-end solving with four probes (recognition, localization, single-step prediction, and state tracking) and gives every board both as an image and as an equivalent text grid. Evaluating seven MLLMs on Sokoban and a maze game reveals distinct bottlenecks behind similar success rates: proprietary models are limited by multi-step planning, whereas open-source models are limited by rule application or by visual grid indexing, i.e., counting rows and columns. Planning failures also hide perception failures: when planning is easier, the visual cost of the same model grows from 7.6 to 37.7 points. The diagnosis identifies what to train: fine-tuning only the vision module of the perception-limited model on board reading raises its interactive Sokoban success 3.5-fold (5.8% to 20.4%) and transfers zero-shot to the unseen maze game (single-turn success 13.8% to 67.1%), whereas the same data does not help a rule-limited model and training on solver solutions brings no gain. We will release the benchmark and code at https://github.com/suat-llm/GridProbe.
papers.summary: End-to-end success rates on grid games hide whether a multimodal large language model (MLLM) fails at visual perception, rule application, or multi-step planning. `GridProbe` pairs end-to-end Sokoban solving with four probes (recognition, localization, single-step prediction, and state tracking) and presents every board both as an image and as an equivalent text grid. Across seven models on Sokoban and a maze game, proprietary models are limited by multi-step planning, while open-source models are limited by rule application or by visual grid indexing, meaning counting rows and columns. Fine-tuning only the vision module of the perception-limited model on board reading **raises its interactive Sokoban success 3.5-fold (5.8% to 20.4%)** and transfers zero-shot to the unseen maze game (13.8% to 67.1%), whereas the same data does not help a rule-limited model and training on solver solutions gives no gain.

papers.title: Strategic and Robust Task Allocation for Combat Objectives in Adversarial Multi-Agent Environments
papers.abstract: Task allocation in contested-objective team games requires coordinated decisions under uncertainty, spatial constraints, and changing tactical conditions. In such settings, multiple agents must anticipate both teammate behavior and opponent actions. We study a hybrid predict-then-optimize approach for assigning controllable agents to objectives in real time. A masked multi-head model predicts tactical signals for each agent, including survival chance, local superiority, combat interaction, travel time, and objective contribution. These signals are combined with rule-based terms in a score matrix, and a minimum-cost flow solver computes coordinated global assignments constrained by capacity, occupancy, stability, and defensive strategies. Learning is limited to tactical scoring, while explicit rules and solver structure preserve controllability and interpretability. We evaluate the system using predictive metrics, offline assignment diagnostics, online A/B evaluation, and latency measurements. The system is an R\&D research prototype built on a commercial game and is not deployed in the shipped game. The results indicate that learned tactical estimates can support stable, feasible, and inspectable objective allocation under strict real-time constraints.
papers.summary: Assigning controllable agents to contested objectives in team combat games requires real-time coordinated decisions that anticipate both teammates and opponents. The hybrid predict-then-optimize system described here uses a masked multi-head model to predict per-agent tactical signals such as survival chance, local superiority, travel time, and objective contribution, combines them with rule-based terms in a score matrix, and solves a minimum-cost flow problem to produce global assignments under capacity, occupancy, stability, and defensive constraints. Learning is confined to tactical scoring so that explicit rules and the solver keep the behavior controllable and interpretable. Evaluated through predictive metrics, offline diagnostics, online A/B tests, and latency measurements on a research prototype built on a commercial game, the results indicate that **learned tactical estimates can support stable, feasible, and inspectable allocation under strict real-time constraints**.

papers.title: Multi-view fnirs identifies neurophysiological subtypes in post-stroke aphasia
papers.abstract: Post-stroke aphasia is clinically heterogeneous, and conventional classifications may not capture differences in brain functional organisation. We tested whether resting-state and task-based functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) could identify neurophysiological subgroups alongside clinical assessment.Seventy-nine patients underwent unsupervised clustering using three fNIRS feature views: resting-state activity and connectivity, language-task activation, and rest-to-task connectivity reconfiguration. Similarity network fusion and spectral clustering integrated the views. Clinical and behavioural measures were excluded from clustering.Three clusters (n = 32, 17 and 30) were identified. This solution had the largest eigengap and was the only candidate significant after permutation testing and Holm correction (adjusted P = 0.001). It was stable under subsampling (mean adjusted Rand index, 0.773), but agreement fell to 0.217 when the resting-state view was removed. Clusters differed in most regional intrinsic-activity measures and all resting-state connectivity summaries, with few differences in task activation or connectivity reconfiguration. Their profiles showed higher right anterior prefrontal activity, distributed fronto-sensorimotor and parietal alterations, and reduced interhemispheric connectivity, respectively.Cluster membership was not significantly associated with conventional aphasia subtype (Cram\'er's V = 0.287), and baseline clinical language scores and task performance did not differ between clusters.These findings identify three neurophysiological subgroups distinguished mainly by intrinsic activity and resting-state functional connectivity, not clearly aligned with conventional aphasia classifications or baseline clinical measures. Multi-view fNIRS analysis may complement clinical characterisation, requiring independent and longitudinal validation.
papers.summary: Post-stroke aphasia is clinically heterogeneous, and conventional subtypes may not reflect differences in brain functional organization. Seventy-nine patients were clustered without clinical or behavioral inputs using three feature views from functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) — resting-state activity and connectivity, language-task activation, and rest-to-task connectivity reconfiguration — integrated by similarity network fusion and spectral clustering. **Three neurophysiological subgroups emerged, distinguished mainly by resting-state activity and connectivity** and stable under subsampling (mean adjusted Rand index 0.773), with agreement falling to 0.217 when the resting-state view was removed. Cluster membership was not significantly associated with conventional aphasia subtype or baseline language scores, and the authors note the need for independent and longitudinal validation.

papers.title: Familiar Words, Unfamiliar Minds: Conventionalization without Calibration in the Vocabulary of Mind
papers.abstract: Speakers describe new technologies by stretching old words, letting experience of the new referents sort out which inferences carry over. I argue that stretching the vocabulary of mind to language models pulls apart two processes that theories of metaphor and linguistic change tend to conflate: conventionalization, whereby a stretched word ceases to be marked as such, and calibration, whereby the inferences it invites are fitted to what its new referents bear out. As a gene variant can reach fixation without being an adaptation, a word can become conventional without being calibrated. A corpus study of "hallucinate" in 8,568 abstracts and 31,866 forum comments shows conventionalization running most of its course within three years. Calibration need not keep pace: these models are organized so unlike human minds that it is hard to tell when mental words apply and what they imply. Even warranted attributions can mislead: mechanistic analysis shows that a transformer trained to navigate Manhattan has and uses a faithful street map, yet loses track of its position on long, diverted journeys. Nor is the gap likely to close by itself. The usual routes to calibration (direct experience, designers' knowledge, experiment) presuppose a referent that is accessible, stable, and independent of the discourse about it. But language models are opaque, fast-changing, and looped into the discourse: they are trained on past uses of mental vocabulary and on the experimental literature about them, and join the discourse themselves. Calibration must therefore be organized, through a reciprocal, not merely deferential, division of linguistic labour. This yields a norm of targeted qualification (flag the specific inferences an attribution invites without support), a reply to the worry that meaning change eludes deliberate control, and three testable predictions about when qualifications calibrate expectations.
papers.summary: Applying mental vocabulary to language models is argued to separate two processes that theories of metaphor usually merge: conventionalization, where a stretched word stops being marked as figurative, and calibration, where the inferences it invites get fitted to what the new referents actually do. A corpus study of the word `hallucinate` in 8,568 abstracts and 31,866 forum comments finds **conventionalization running most of its course within three years**, while calibration need not keep pace because the models are organized so differently from human minds. The author argues the gap will not close by itself, since language models are opaque, fast-changing, and trained on the very discourse about them, which undermines the usual routes to calibration. The proposed remedy is a norm of targeted qualification — flagging the specific unsupported inferences an attribution invites — along with three testable predictions about when such qualifications work.

papers.title: Agentic-Level Adversarial Purification: Revisiting Diffusion Purifiers on Native-Resolution Agentic Inputs
papers.abstract: Vision-language agents act on native-resolution renders of multi-element pages, where one perturbed photo or a few altered text strokes can redirect the decision. Any content provider can craft such a perturbation on the open model behind the agent, so a plug-in purifier is the natural first line of defense. Yet diffusion purifiers were designed and evaluated at the fixed resolution of the diffusion model on classifier or natural-image benchmarks, and defense evaluations for agents test JPEG, blur and noise but no diffusion purifier. We present the first study of adversarial purification at the agentic level, for an agent built on Qwen3-VL-8B: purifiers run at native resolution on multi-element inputs, face grey-box attackers who know the agent's model but not the defense, and are compared at matched clean cost. We show that treating agentic inputs as classifier inputs misleads both evaluation and design. Resizing the input to the resolution of the diffusion model, as existing purifiers do, raises the TextVQA clean cost of the Divide-and-Conquer purifier (DC) from 4.0 to 35.7 points. On web-shop pages, DC keeps 85.0% grey-box robust accuracy against web-hardened perturbations, where cheap input transformations at matched clean cost keep at most 40.0%, and this robustness comes from the global noise level: input-estimated masks and noise levels add none. These findings hold on a disjoint held-out set and on a second VLM and yield three requirements for defenses, we release the protocol.
papers.summary: Vision-language agents act on native-resolution renders of multi-element pages where a single perturbed image or a few altered text strokes can redirect a decision, yet diffusion-based adversarial purifiers have only been evaluated at the diffusion model's fixed resolution on classifier or natural-image benchmarks. This study evaluates purifiers at native resolution for an agent built on `Qwen3-VL-8B`, against grey-box attackers who know the agent's model but not the defense, with defenses compared at matched clean-accuracy cost. Resizing inputs to the diffusion model's resolution, as existing purifiers do, raises the `TextVQA` clean cost of the `Divide-and-Conquer` purifier from 4.0 to 35.7 points. On web-shop pages that purifier **keeps 85.0% grey-box robust accuracy versus at most 40.0% for cheap input transformations**, with the robustness attributed to the global noise level rather than input-estimated masks, and the findings hold on a held-out set and a second model.

papers.title: Lightweight Reasoning Transfer via Chain-of-Thought Vector Projection
papers.abstract: Transferring reasoning capabilities from large language models to smaller ones often requires extensive teacher supervision or costly student adaptation. We study projected cross-model Chain-of-Thought (CoT) Vector transfer, a two-stage approach that keeps both models frozen. First, we learn a task-level CoT Vector in the teacher using dataset-provided solution traces and final-answer supervision. We then train a lightweight linear projector to map the fixed vector into a smaller student's residual space. Student-side training uses only final-answer cross-entropy on a small subset of task training examples; it requires neither teacher outputs nor intermediate solution traces. We select the student injection layer and intervention scale on a labeled support set and report results on the disjoint remainder of each evaluation split. On GSM8K and MATH, the projected vector improves base students by 10.37-21.98 accuracy points across the evaluated teacher-student settings. On four code-generation benchmarks, the Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct student gains 3.23-4.67 pass@1 points, while the base Qwen2.5-7B student gains up to 9.65 points. These results show that a teacher-side reasoning vector can be reused across smaller students with different residual dimensions through projector-only adaptation.
papers.summary: Transferring reasoning ability from a large language model to a smaller one usually requires extensive teacher supervision or costly student adaptation. The two-stage approach here keeps both models frozen: a task-level Chain-of-Thought (CoT) vector is learned in the teacher from dataset solution traces and final answers, and a lightweight linear projector then maps that fixed vector into the smaller student's residual space, trained only with final-answer cross-entropy on a small set of task examples. On `GSM8K` and `MATH`, the projected vector **improves base students by 10.37 to 21.98 accuracy points** across the tested teacher-student pairs. On four code-generation benchmarks, a `Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct` student gains 3.23 to 4.67 pass@1 points and the base `Qwen2.5-7B` student gains up to 9.65.

papers.title: Hierarchical Semantic Learning for Multimodal Sentiment Analysis with Missing Modalities
papers.abstract: Multimodal sentiment analysis (MSA) in real-world systems must handle unpredictable modality missingness caused by sensor failures, privacy masking, and unstable transmission. Existing methods either learn reliability-aware representations or reconstruct missing inputs, often using a single flattened encoder output. This overlooks deep encoders' semantic hierarchy and intra- and inter-modal interactions, causing semantic averaging and ill-posed mappings. We propose Hierarchical Semantic Learning (HSL), a framework that exploits semantic hierarchy for robust MSA with missing modalities. Hierarchical Semantic Decoupling exposes low-, mid-, and high-level feature streams from each modality encoder.
