Across four LLMs it gives the best accuracy among multi-precision methods at 2 and 3 bits, **retaining 69% of FP16 accuracy at 2 bits**, and is within one point of the best at 4 bits. Decoding is about as fast as existing kernels, and an LPDDR memory energy model estimates up to 27% less energy at equal accuracy.

papers.title: Agentic Waterfall: An Intent-Driven Information Discovery Framework for Reclaiming User Control in the Attention Economy
papers.abstract: We formalize Agentic Waterfall Feed, a new problem of personalized information discovery in which users actively direct recommendations and the system adapts to evolving needs inferred from both explicit requests and browsing behavior. We address this problem with the Agentic Waterfall framework, whose language-model controller maintains persistent user state and coordinates content retrieval, ranking, and state updates. To evaluate systems on this task, we contribute the Agentic Waterfall Dataset and a replay-based evaluation protocol. The dataset combines real content metadata with simulated interaction histories. The protocol compares systems under shared histories using relevance scores and blind judgments of how well recommendations satisfy current user goals and constraints. Agentic Waterfall remains competitive with strong baselines on conventional recommendation tasks across five public benchmarks. On the Agentic Waterfall Dataset, it outperforms the strongest baseline in both evaluations, with relative improvements of up to 16.1%.
papers.summary: The authors formalize a recommendation setting, the Agentic Waterfall Feed, in which users actively direct what they are shown and the system adapts to needs inferred from both explicit requests and browsing behavior. Their framework uses a language-model controller that maintains persistent user state and coordinates content retrieval, ranking, and state updates. They contribute the `Agentic Waterfall Dataset`, combining real content metadata with simulated interaction histories, and a replay-based protocol using relevance scores and blind judgments of goal satisfaction. The system stays competitive with strong baselines on five public recommendation benchmarks and beats the strongest baseline on the new dataset by **up to 16.1% relative improvement**.

papers.title: SemProxy: Semantic 3D Proxies for Controllable Agentic 3D Modeling
papers.abstract: Coding agents are increasingly capable of generating 3D models, yet enabling users to effectively control the modeling process remains challenging. Existing workflows rely primarily on text prompts and reference images, which often struggle to convey precise spatial intentions and require iterative corrections. We introduce SemProxy, a lightweight intermediate representation that bridges intuitive human interaction and agentic 3D modeling. Instantiated as labeled 3D bounding boxes, semantic 3D proxies allow users to directly specify object parts and spatial arrangements while leaving geometric details to coding agents. These proxies can be serialized into structured text and rendered as images, making them directly accessible to existing coding agents without additional training or modifications. We further develop ProxyStudio, a user interface that integrates text, image references, and interactive 3D proxy editing into agentic modeling workflows. We demonstrate the versatility of SemProxy across object- and scene-level modeling tasks with different coding agents, and evaluate its effectiveness in supporting controllable human-agent collaborative 3D modeling through a user study.
papers.summary: Coding agents can generate 3D models, but text prompts and reference images convey precise spatial intent poorly and force iterative corrections. `SemProxy` introduces labeled 3D bounding boxes as an intermediate representation with which users specify object parts and spatial arrangement while the agent fills in geometric detail. Because the proxies **serialize to structured text and render as images, existing coding agents can use them without additional training or modification**. A companion interface, `ProxyStudio`, combines text, image references, and interactive proxy editing, and the approach is demonstrated on object- and scene-level tasks with different agents and evaluated in a user study.

papers.title: CHASE: Curiosity-Guided Skill Acquisition for Embodied Task Execution
papers.abstract: Robots executing tasks in partially observed environments must resolve uncertainty while operating with incomplete skills. Inspired by human curiosity, we investigate how robots can formulate task-relevant hypotheses, seek evidence, and acquire missing skills during task execution. We propose CHASE, a Curiosity-guided Harness for Acquiring Skills from Evidence, which operationalizes curiosity as selecting investigations that resolve task uncertainty and expand executable capabilities. Four modules connect dynamic scene understanding, hypothesis-driven planning, on-demand skill acquisition, and verified execution. The planner balances information value, skill reuse, and acquisition/execution cost. Missing skills trigger bounded exploration, learning from verified segments, and held-out admission during acquisition; separate checks verify physical effects and acquired evidence. Newly admitted skills expand the executable investigation set, closing the loop between resolving uncertainty and acquiring capabilities. Simulation and real-robot experiments evaluate investigation, skill acquisition, and task execution. CHASE achieves 50-80% task success under combined information and capability gaps, with 70-90% evidence resolution.
papers.summary: Robots in partially observed environments often face both missing information and missing skills at the same time. `CHASE` (Curiosity-guided Harness for Acquiring Skills from Evidence) treats curiosity as choosing investigations that both resolve task uncertainty and expand what the robot can execute, linking dynamic scene understanding, hypothesis-driven planning, on-demand skill acquisition, and verified execution. Its planner balances information value, skill reuse, and acquisition and execution cost, and missing skills trigger bounded exploration, learning from verified segments, and held-out admission tests before a skill is added. In simulation and real-robot experiments it achieves **50-80% task success under combined information and capability gaps**, with 70-90% evidence resolution.

papers.title: DocSEAM: Bidirectional Cross-Page Encoding for Multi-Page Document Understanding
papers.abstract: Multi-page document vision-language models encode each page independently, creating a feature-level discontinuity at page boundaries: visual tokens are formed without access to content on adjacent pages, and the language model must reason over these page representations formed in isolation. We introduce DocSEAM (Document Selective Enrichment via Anchored Masking), a lightweight module inserted between a pretrained vision encoder and the language model that injects the inductive bias of local cross-page context into visual representations. For each page, DocSEAM forms a local triplet with its two neighbors, applies center-anchored masked self-attention with directional salience gates to fuse information from neighbor pages, and returns only the enriched center-page tokens, leaving the visual token count unchanged. After a supervised cross-page warm-up and multi-page fine-tuning with DocSEAM frozen, our 9B-parameter model achieves state-of-the-art results among the evaluated open-weight models of up to 10B parameters on five multi-page document VQA benchmarks. We further show that under controlled re-pagination, DocSEAM reduces sensitivity to boundary placement and improves cross-page span localization
papers.summary: Vision-language models for multi-page documents encode each page independently, so visual tokens are formed without access to content on adjacent pages. `DocSEAM` (Document Selective Enrichment via Anchored Masking) is a lightweight module placed between a pretrained vision encoder and the language model that groups each page with its two neighbors, fuses neighbor information through center-anchored masked self-attention with directional salience gates, and returns only the enriched center-page tokens, leaving the token count unchanged. The resulting 9B-parameter model achieves **the best results among evaluated open-weight models of up to 10B parameters on five multi-page document question-answering benchmarks**. Under controlled re-pagination, it is also less sensitive to where page boundaries fall and better at localizing spans that cross pages.

papers.title: Mitigating Hallucinations in Medical Question Answering on ESC Cardiology Guidelines: Evaluation and Retrieval Optimization
papers.abstract: Background: Large language models produce hallucinations in medical question answering (QA). Verify-and-revise pipelines that check atomic claims against retrieved guideline evidence are a standard mitigation, but evaluations almost universally treat the verifier's output as ground truth, an assumption rarely tested. Objective: To measure, claim by claim against human judgement, how such a pipeline fails in a guideline-grounded clinical setting. Methods: We built a dataset of 160 questions (100 patient vignettes from 89 de-identified cases, 60 fact-based) over four recent ESC cardiology guidelines, all approved by a practising internist, and a retrieval corpus of 627 hand-verified guideline records at two chunk granularities. A five-stage pipeline was run under four retrieval configurations and three independent runs (1920 arm-runs); all 606 first-pass refuted claims were manually audited, an independent judge re-judged 906 decisions, and the expert blindly reviewed 100 accepted claims. Results: Only 44.7-50.6% of flagged claims were true hallucinations. Correction loops converged in 85.2-95.1% of cases, yet 35% of genuine final errors were introduced by correction. Single-run true-hallucination recall was 35.6-41.2%, the three-run union 71-80%; verifier agreement was moderate (kappa = 0.505). The blind probe estimated the accepted-claim miss rate at 3.2% (95% CI 0.7-6.7%). Final genuine-error rate: 1.7% of answers. Conclusion: Claim-level verification reduces hallucinated content by an order of magnitude, but verifier reliability, not generation, is the limiting factor and must be measured, not assumed.
papers.summary: Verify-and-revise pipelines that check atomic claims against retrieved guideline evidence are a standard hallucination mitigation in medical question answering (QA), but evaluations usually treat the verifier's output as ground truth. The authors audit such a pipeline claim by claim against human judgment using 160 questions over four European Society of Cardiology (`ESC`) guidelines and 627 hand-verified guideline records, across four retrieval configurations and three runs. **Only 44.7-50.6% of claims flagged by the verifier were true hallucinations**, single-run recall of true hallucinations was 35.6-41.2%, and 35% of genuine final errors were introduced by the correction step itself. The final genuine-error rate was 1.7% of answers, leading the authors to conclude that verifier reliability rather than generation is the limiting factor.

papers.title: Calibration of Neuromusculoskeletal Models Using Differentiable Physics: Recommendations for Improving Model Accuracy
papers.abstract: Differentiable physics has shown potential to usher in a new paradigm in human neuromusculoskeletal (NMS) model calibration. Early results from pioneering works have demonstrated that auto-differentiable NMS models can greatly reduce NMS model calibration time while achieving comparable accuracy compared to traditional calibration methods. The efficient gradient-based optimizers have enabled calibration of increasingly sophisticated human models with a large number of parameters, which seek to narrow the gap between simulation and reality. Several modules have been evaluated separately in different studies, but have never been directly compared within the same study. In this work, these modules are compared on the same differentiable upper limb model with a 3-DoF shoulder, a 2-DoF elbow, and 11 superficial and 5 deep muscles in the calibration to find an optimal pipeline for improving model accuracy. The considered modules include muscle synergy, learnable bone parameters, optimizable geometry of wrap objects, and constraint torque of the differentiable arm model. To evaluate the effect and interplay between the modules on calibration accuracy, one or more modules were used in each of 16 calibration configurations, which were compared in terms of the error between two joint torques calculated by the forward and inverse dynamics with the calibrated model on 9 distinctive testing movements across 4 subjects. Results showed that torque loss was reduced by 23.6% on average using muscle synergy extrapolation to estimate deep muscle activities, and by 10.9% on average through bone dynamic parameter optimization, which are both recommended to be incorporated in the calibration.
papers.summary: Differentiable physics enables fast gradient-based calibration of human neuromusculoskeletal (NMS) models, but the modules proposed in separate studies have never been compared directly. Using one differentiable upper-limb model with a 3-degree-of-freedom shoulder, 2-degree-of-freedom elbow, and 16 muscles, the authors test 16 calibration configurations combining muscle synergy, learnable bone parameters, optimizable wrap-object geometry, and constraint torque, across 9 test movements and 4 subjects. Torque loss fell by **23.6% on average when muscle synergy extrapolation was used to estimate deep muscle activity**, and by 10.9% with bone dynamic parameter optimization, and both are recommended for calibration pipelines.

papers.title: One Representation to Rule Them All -- Open-Vocabulary Change Detection from Text or Visual Examples
papers.abstract: Open-vocabulary change detection (OVCD) aims to localise user-specified changes without retraining for predefined categories. Existing approaches typically rely on textual descriptions and combine separate models for region proposal, semantic recognition, and temporal comparison. This limits how target concepts can be expressed and makes detection dependent on several intermediate predictions. We introduce OVTSID3, a training-free framework that unifies region grouping, concept identification, and temporal comparison in the representation space of DINOv3. OVTSID3 supports two complementary modes of concept specification: zero-shot textual queries or one-shot visual prompting through a masked reference pair. OVTSID3 outperforms all prior training-free OVCD methods on two building and two natural-disaster benchmarks, raising the average F1 by 8.9 points. OVTSID3 also supports semantic change detection and achieves state-of-the-art on SECOND. These results demonstrate the flexibility of a unified representation for text- or example-guided change detection without task-specific model training.
papers.summary: Open-vocabulary change detection (OVCD) localizes user-specified changes between images without retraining for fixed categories, but existing approaches rely on text descriptions and chain separate models for region proposal, recognition, and temporal comparison. `OVTSID3` is a training-free framework that performs all three steps in the representation space of `DINOv3`, accepting either zero-shot text queries or a one-shot visual prompt given as a masked reference pair. It outperforms prior training-free OVCD methods on two building and two natural-disaster benchmarks, **raising average F1 by 8.9 points**, and also achieves state-of-the-art semantic change detection on `SECOND`.

papers.title: Evaluating Aviation Safety Knowledge Extraction with SmolLM2: From Zero-Shot to Retrieval-Grounded Prompting
papers.abstract: Aviation accident narratives contain safety knowledge that is difficult to capture using structured occurrence fields alone. This study evaluates prompting-based knowledge extraction across four dimensions: concept accuracy, verbatim evidence grounding, structural compliance, and directed relation extraction. SmolLM2-1.7B-Instruct was evaluated under zero-shot, one-shot, fixed few-shot, and retrieval-grounded prompting using 300 National Transportation Safety Board narratives from 2000-2020, containing 3,763 reference concepts and 467 directed relations. Evaluation combined structural checks, verbatim evidence matching, expert-reviewed semantic matching, and paired bootstrap confidence intervals. No prompting strategy performed best across all dimensions. Retrieval-grounded prompting achieved the highest concept micro-F1 of 32.27%, although its advantage over fixed few-shot prompting was uncertain (95% CI: -0.92 to 2.40 percentage points). One-shot prompting achieved the highest relation F1 of 6.95%, identifying directed relation extraction as the principal SmolLM2 bottleneck. Compared with fixed few-shot prompting, retrieval improved verbatim grounding (59.45% vs. 54.02%) but reduced complete structural compliance (33.3% vs. 42.7%). Verbatim matching establishes source presence rather than evidential relevance. An exploratory comparison using 35 benchmark narratives showed that Qwen3-8B achieved higher concept micro-F1 across all prompting conditions and higher relation F1 under demonstration-based prompting, reaching 51.37% and 34.62%, respectively, under one-shot prompting. The small subset limits generalization. These findings support evaluating semantic correctness, source traceability, structural reliability, and directed relation accuracy separately.
papers.summary: Extraction of safety concepts and directed relations from aviation accident narratives is evaluated for `SmolLM2-1.7B-Instruct` under zero-shot, one-shot, fixed few-shot, and retrieval-grounded prompting, using 300 National Transportation Safety Board narratives with 3,763 reference concepts and 467 relations. No prompting strategy was best across all dimensions: retrieval-grounded prompting gave the highest concept micro-F1 at 32.27% with an uncertain edge over few-shot, and improved verbatim grounding while reducing structural compliance. Directed relation extraction was the main bottleneck, with **relation F1 peaking at only 6.95%** under one-shot prompting. In an exploratory 35-narrative comparison, `Qwen3-8B` reached 51.37% concept micro-F1 and 34.62% relation F1 under one-shot prompting.

papers.title: Most of the Way There: Turning a Strong Video Prior into an Action-Conditioned World Model
papers.abstract: Modern video generators excel at producing visually plausible futures guided by text and image prompts. Yet their emphasis on semantic plausibility does not guarantee fidelity to the physical consequences of specific actions. Action-conditioned world models (ACWMs), in contrast, aim to simulate how the world responds to robot actions, enabling scalable policy evaluation and improvement without costly real-world rollouts. The challenge is not merely to generate a plausible future, but to predict what follows from a specific physical action. As video priors grow stronger, we ask how little adaptation is truly needed to bridge this gap. We introduce Dianjing, a minimal recipe that preserves and unlocks the capabilities of strong video priors through unified physical action conditioning, training concentrated at the high noise levels where motion and layout, and thus the consequences of actions, are decided, and native history conditioning. Built upon MiniMax H3, a 33B video foundation model, Dianjing freezes the pretrained backbone and trains only 0.34% of its parameters using approximately 65 hours of robot video across two embodiments, without additional robot-specific pretraining or camera calibration. Controlled ablations show that where training is allocated across noise levels matters more than how actions enter the network. On WorldOracle, which evaluates predictions against paired real-world executions, Dianjing achieves the best scores on four of the five evaluation tracks and ranks second on AgiBot-Long. Our findings suggest that strong video priors already bring us most of the way to world modeling; lightweight physical action grounding can unlock their potential for real-world prediction.
papers.summary: Video generators produce plausible futures but do not reliably predict the consequences of specific robot actions, which is what action-conditioned world models (ACWMs) need for policy evaluation. `Dianjing` adapts the frozen 33B `MiniMax H3` video model by adding unified physical action conditioning and native history conditioning, and by concentrating training at the high noise levels where motion and layout are decided. It trains **only 0.34% of the parameters on about 65 hours of robot video** across two embodiments, with no robot-specific pretraining or camera calibration. On `WorldOracle` it scores best on four of five tracks and second on `AgiBot-Long`, and ablations indicate that the allocation of training across noise levels matters more than how actions enter the network.

papers.title: vSFT: Learning to Verbally Tune Agents at Test Time
papers.abstract: Large language model agents are increasingly improved via agentic reinforcement learning, which can be on-policy but suffers from expensive rollouts and sparse rewards, limiting its application at test time. In this paper, we present a verbally Supervised Fine-Tuning (vSFT) framework that enables the conjunction of dense feedback in natural language and weight updates at test time. Specifically, our vSFT forms a closed loop between an agent and a supervisor via a hypernetwork, in which the supervisor generates verbal supervision from the agent's failed trajectories, and the hypernetwork converts that supervision into low-rank weight updates to tune the agent. We validate that this test-time in-parameter evolving process outperforms both its in-context counterparts and prevalent reinforcement learning methods. In particular, our vSFT using Qwen3-4B outperforms GRPO and Reflexion by 8.7% and 13.9% in success rate on ALFWorld, and by 4.8% and 18.2% on WebShop, respectively. We believe that learning how to adapt a model, rather than an adapted model, offers a promising path towards more capable agents that improve themselves.
papers.summary: Agentic reinforcement learning for large language model agents is costly at test time because rollouts are expensive and rewards are sparse. Verbally Supervised Fine-Tuning (`vSFT`) closes a loop in which a supervisor writes natural-language feedback on the agent's failed trajectories and a hypernetwork converts that feedback into low-rank weight updates for the agent. With `Qwen3-4B`, the method **beats `GRPO` and `Reflexion` by 8.7% and 13.9% in success rate on `ALFWorld`**, and by 4.8% and 18.2% on `WebShop`.

papers.title: ProxyGenBench: Benchmarking Proxy-Guided Video Generation
papers.abstract: Recent video generators produce realistic videos, yet controlling how scenes unfold remains challenging. Structural proxies, such as animated 3D blockouts, guide generation by specifying scene layout, motion, camera behavior, and event order. However, these coarse inputs leave details unspecified and may contain artifacts that should not be reproduced. Successful proxy-guided generation must therefore Preserve intended structure, Complete missing content and correct proxy artifacts, and Bind text, image, and audio conditions to the right entities and events. We introduce ProxyGenBench to study these interacting requirements, with 312 evaluation cases from 60 scenes across three scene tasks and controlled variations in proxy fidelity, text detail, and multimodal inputs. We evaluate five video generators using verified, case-specific checklists. Experiments show that proxies improve spatiotemporal control, but greater proxy detail can coincide with poorer completion, while strong structural adherence does not ensure correct binding.
papers.summary: Structural proxies such as animated 3D blockouts let users specify layout, motion, camera behavior, and event order for video generation, but they are coarse and may contain artifacts that should not be copied. `ProxyGenBench` tests whether generators preserve intended structure, complete missing content and correct proxy artifacts, and bind text, image, and audio conditions to the right entities, using 312 cases from 60 scenes with controlled variation in proxy fidelity, text detail, and multimodal inputs. Evaluating five video generators with verified case-specific checklists shows that proxies improve spatiotemporal control, but **more detailed proxies can coincide with poorer completion, and strong structural adherence does not ensure correct binding**.
papers.highlight_summary:
Structural proxies such as animated 3D blockouts give video generators explicit control over layout, motion, camera and event order, but they are coarse and carry artifacts that should not be copied into the final video. `ProxyGenBench` tests whether generators can simultaneously Preserve the intended structure, Complete or correct what the proxy leaves unfinished, and Bind text, image and audio conditions to the right entities and events.

- The benchmark has **312 cases from 60 scenes** across dynamic action, multi-shot and multi-view tasks, varying proxy fidelity (`Pr0`–`Pr2`) and text detail (`T0`–`T2`), and scores five generators on 32 criteria using case-specific checklists written by `Gemini-3.1-Pro` and verified by `Qwen3.5`.
- On small matched proxy/no-proxy subsets, adding a proxy lifts action-transition accuracy from 0.894 to **1.000** and cross-shot spatial consistency from 0.833 to **0.952**, cuts `MEt3R` error from 0.464 to **0.337**, and wins **35 of 50** pairwise VLM preferences when both presentation orders are aggregated.
- Average structural scores hide joint failures: without audio references `Seedance-2.5` leads the structure-weighted Strict score at **0.450**, yet only **7.2–17.4%** of outputs across the five models pass all critical Preserve checks at once.
- Moving from blockout to detailed proxies on 31 shared scenes raises Preserve by 1.1–6.7 points but lowers Complete by **4.8–7.9 points for all five models**, and structure does not imply binding, with the 12 Studio 3D cases scoring 0.848–0.962 on Preserve against only **0.182–0.500** on Bind and audiovisual timing alignment averaging 0.513 versus 0.768 for voice matching.
- Scoring depends on a VLM judge that agrees with humans on **92.9%** of 3,199 audited judgments but drops to 89.7% on Preserve and 84.0% on judge-labelled Bind failures, and several headline comparisons rest on small subsets of 12 to 50 cases.

papers.title: EgoUseBench: Benchmarking Computer-Use Agents under Evolving First-Person Contexts
papers.abstract: AI wearables, such as smart glasses, extend the context available to agents beyond digital environments to users' physical surroundings. With these devices, computer tasks can originate from users' ongoing activities rather than solely from explicit instructions. Through first-person observations, agents can identify objects and activities relevant to user requests and ground digital tasks in the surrounding context. We call this interaction paradigm Ego Use. However, first-person observations are limited by the wearer's viewpoint and may provide incomplete or ambiguous evidence of ongoing activities. As new observations arrive, agents may need to revise their understanding of the physical context and user intent, and reassess whether prior digital actions remain valid. Whether current agents can reliably handle these changes remains insufficiently evaluated. We introduce EgoUseBench, a benchmark for evaluating Ego Use across three interaction settings with different levels of first-person context. Computer-Use relies on explicit instructions, Offline Ego Use provides prerecorded first-person context before execution, and Online Ego Use provides continuous observations as user intent evolves. Based on over 74 hours of real-world first-person recordings, we construct 693 tasks across the three interaction settings. To capture task evolution, we track first-person observations, user requirements, and website state separately. We further group tasks by how information changes during execution, resulting in three types: Graft (revised user requirements), Refresh (new first-person observations), and Clarify (agent-initiated information seeking). We evaluate advanced models and find that average success rates in Online Ego Use are 26.3% lower than in Computer-Use. This result reveals the difficulty of keeping task execution aligned with evolving first-person context and user intent.
papers.summary: Smart glasses and other wearables let computer tasks arise from a user's ongoing physical activity, but first-person observations are partial and an agent may have to revise its understanding and its earlier digital actions as new evidence arrives. `EgoUseBench` builds 693 tasks from over 74 hours of real first-person recordings across three settings: instruction-only computer use, offline use with prerecorded context, and online use with continuous observations as intent evolves. Tasks are grouped by how information changes, covering revised user requirements, new observations, and agent-initiated clarification. Advanced models show **average success rates 26.3% lower in the online setting than in standard computer use**.

papers.title: Noise threshold for learning with quantum memory
papers.abstract: A quantum memory can reduce exponentially the number of experiments needed to learn a physical process, but real memories are noisy. Here we show that, for Pauli memory noise with eigenvalues $\lambda_X,\lambda_Y,\lambda_Z$, the advantage is governed by $\lambda_X^2+\lambda_Y^2+\lambda_Z^2$. We prove that no protocol with an entangled probe gains an exponential advantage when this sum is at most one, reduce the general case to the additivity of a R\'enyi-2 coherent information, and find coded memories that retain a growing advantage within 1% of this threshold. On a superconducting processor, nine simultaneously operated Bell pairs show an advantage that grows or shrinks exponentially with system size, reversing where a parameter-free model predicts. A three-qubit repetition code turns a shrinking advantage into a growing one with all processor and readout errors included, and under dephasing its memory performs better than Bell sampling in any memory frame on a perfect processor.
papers.summary: Quantum memory can exponentially reduce the number of experiments needed to learn a physical process, but real memories are noisy. For Pauli memory noise, the advantage is shown to be governed by the sum of the squares of the three Pauli eigenvalues: **no entangled-probe protocol gains an exponential advantage when that sum is at most one**, while coded memories retain a growing advantage within 1% of the threshold. On a superconducting processor, nine simultaneously operated Bell pairs show an advantage that grows or shrinks exponentially with system size, reversing where a parameter-free model predicts. A three-qubit repetition code turns a shrinking advantage into a growing one with all processor and readout errors included.

papers.title: Where Does the Asymmetry Enter? Staging a Fairness Audit Across a Fused Multimodal Moderation Pipeline
papers.abstract: Almost every short-video upload now passes through a classifier that fuses video, speech, and on-screen text into one decision about whether it may be seen. It moderates every language community on the platform at once, and fairness across them is judged, if at all, from one accuracy score. That score is compatible with error falling almost entirely on one language group. An audit that goes looking reads the model's decisions, the last stage of a long pipeline and the one whose test has the fewest items. We ask where in a fused pipeline a subgroup asymmetry can be detected at all: in what the classifier may read, in what its branches encode, or in what it decides. We answer this with a post-hoc audit of a published TikTok classifier, holding all three stages to one significance standard using only its logged decisions, labels, and pre-fusion features, with source language as the subgroup axis. The asymmetry is significant at the stage deciding what the model may read, and again in what the text branch encodes. At the earlier stage, a language-blind cap admits less of a Vietnamese clip than an English one, for reasons of segmentation, not verbosity. The asymmetry is undetectable at the decision, where the smallest subgroup leaves twelve items to test. An audit reading only decisions looks where its evidence is thinnest; the same test staged upstream recovers a disparity the decision-level view returns as noise.
papers.summary: Short-video moderation classifiers fuse video, speech, and on-screen text into one decision, and fairness across language communities is typically judged from a single accuracy score that can hide errors concentrated in one group. A post-hoc audit of a published TikTok classifier applies one significance standard at three stages, namely what the model may read, what its branches encode, and what it decides, using only logged decisions, labels, and pre-fusion features with source language as the subgroup axis. **The language asymmetry is significant at the input stage and in the text branch but undetectable at the decision stage**, where the smallest subgroup leaves only twelve items to test. At the input stage, a language-blind cap admits less of a Vietnamese clip than an English one because of segmentation rather than verbosity.

papers.title: FlyingStart: Learned Cross-Token Warm Starts for Fixed-Point Decoding in Recurrent-Depth Language Models
papers.abstract: Recurrent-depth language models generate each token by iterating a shared block of layers until its hidden state converges. Inference methods for these models decide when to stop the iteration, yet every token still starts from random noise and pays the full cost of converging. We show that where the iteration starts is a second, independent lever. A token's fixed point is predictable from the state at which the previous token stopped, after a learned change of coordinates, and we introduce FlyingStart, a linear warm start that is fitted in closed form on the frozen model and costs under 5% of one loop. The iteration and its stopping rule are unchanged, so the exit criterion certifies the same distance to the fixed point from any start: a better start removes loops at unchanged accuracy. On Huginn-0125, FlyingStart matches the accuracy of the strongest training-free baseline with 14--19% fewer decoding layers, raises batched throughput by 16--18% in two serving engines, and adds a further 10--14% on top of self-speculative decoding. A contraction analysis predicts the number of loops saved on all four models we study, including one where the prediction was recorded before any evaluation, and token by token on Huginn, and it identifies when a warm start pays off: the saving grows with the number of loops a model needs to converge.
papers.summary: Recurrent-depth language models produce each token by iterating a shared block of layers to a fixed point, and existing inference methods only decide when to stop while every token still starts from random noise. `FlyingStart` is a linear warm start, fitted in closed form on the frozen model and costing under 5% of one loop, that predicts a token's fixed point from the state at which the previous token stopped. On `Huginn-0125` it **matches the strongest training-free baseline's accuracy with 14-19% fewer decoding layers**, raises batched throughput by 16-18% in two serving engines, and adds a further 10-14% on top of self-speculative decoding. A contraction analysis predicts the loops saved on all four models studied and shows that the saving grows with the number of loops a model needs to converge.

papers.title: Know the Design, Pick the Attack: Sentence-Keyed Watermarks for LLMs
papers.abstract: A watermark lets the provider of a language model recognise the text its model wrote, which matters more as generated text becomes hard to tell from human writing: provenance underpins academic integrity, the fight against misinformation and new regulation. Providers have started to watermark the text of their models, and to explain how their watermarks work. Explaining a watermark, however, also tells an attacker how to break it, and there are two ways to do so: reword the text to erase the mark, or learn the mark and copy it onto text the model never wrote. Each attack has been studied on its own. We study an attacker that reads the published design to choose between them: it erases the watermarks that are hard to learn and forges the ones that survive rewording. Against it, every existing watermark we compare fails. We propose KeyedLex, which reads its secret key from the grammar of the previous sentence, which rewording changes little, and whose detector does not need to recover the key exactly. It outperforms every watermark we compare on both models we test, losing about half of its signal where the best alternative loses two thirds, at no extra cost in text quality over the best-known watermarks.
papers.summary: Publishing how a language-model watermark works also tells an attacker how to defeat it, either by rewording text to erase the mark or by learning the mark and forging it onto text the model never wrote. The study considers an attacker who reads the published design and picks whichever attack suits it, and finds that every existing watermark compared fails against this adaptive strategy. The proposed `KeyedLex` derives its secret key from the grammar of the previous sentence, which rewording changes little, and its detector does not need to recover the key exactly. On both models tested it **loses about half of its signal where the best alternative loses two thirds**, with no extra cost in text quality over the best-known watermarks.

papers.title: Angular Interpolation in Sparse-View Low-Dose CT Reconstruction: Placement Effects and Data-Consistency Step-Size Scaling
papers.abstract: Dual-domain networks combine projection and image processing for sparse-view low-dose computed tomography (CT). We quantify the contribution of angular interpolation before learning and distinguish its roles in sinogram initialisation and the image residual base. On synthetic parallel-beam data, parameter-free interpolation reduces noise-free missing-view mean absolute error by 99.7% relative to zero filling at 60 views. Full-view filtered back-projection (FBP) of the jointly learned completed sinogram adds 1.27 dB of peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) over interpolated FBP. In a data-consistency dual-domain network (DC-DuNet), a 2x2 configuration ablation controls branch width, depth and training schedule while varying these placements and their associated input channels. After 20 epochs, the PSNR contrasts are +1.98 dB for sinogram initialisation and -2.16 dB for the interpolated image base; the image-base ranking also reverses during training. The sinogram-initialised variant exceeds an image-only U-Net by 0.96 dB at 60 views and 10% dose, and by 1.28 dB on independently generated synthetic data. The U-Net leads at higher view counts and with a shared interpolated image base. Without retraining, the variant retains a 0.12 dB advantage on held-out CHAOS abdominal CT under simulated degradation; the image-base contrast rounds to zero. The implemented projection/backprojection pair has empirical dominant gain of approximately 0.85NK, where N is image-grid width and K acquired view count. These results distinguish interpolation placement from network architecture and support NK normalisation for step calibration.
papers.summary: Dual-domain networks for sparse-view, low-dose computed tomography combine projection and image processing, and this study isolates what angular interpolation contributes when used for sinogram initialisation versus as the image residual base. In a controlled 2x2 ablation of a data-consistency dual-domain network (`DC-DuNet`), **sinogram initialisation adds 1.98 dB of peak signal-to-noise ratio while an interpolated image base costs 2.16 dB** after 20 epochs. The sinogram-initialised variant beats an image-only `U-Net` by 0.96 dB at 60 views and 10% dose, though the `U-Net` leads at higher view counts, and it keeps a 0.12 dB edge on held-out `CHAOS` abdominal scans without retraining. The measured gain of the projection and backprojection pair supports normalising the data-consistency step size by image-grid width times view count.

papers.title: Long-Horizon Planning with Latent World Models via Graph Anchors
papers.abstract:
Latent world models plan in a compact latent space by predicting the outcomes of actions. Their planners judge a plan by the latent distance between its
  predicted end state and the goal image. We show that this distance fails in two distinct ways. First, it loses directional signal a few steps from the
  goal, causing distant goals to fail. Second, it weighs the robot arm over the manipulated object, causing manipulation to fail at contact. We measure
  both failures directly on recorded data by asking whether a lower latent distance corresponds to true progress toward the goal. Across five
  environments, six visual representations (including raw pixels and V-JEPA 2), and nine Meta-World tasks, this ranking test cleanly separates the two
  failures, and the graph distance to a goal predicts where closed-loop planning breaks down. Both failures share a single remedy: replacing the distant
  goal with a nearby target that lies on a recorded trajectory. We realize this principle with Graph Anchors, a training-free planner for frozen latent
  world models. It builds a sparse graph once over the model's own training frames and aims each planning step at a node a few moves ahead along the
  shortest path to the goal, keeping paths on recorded transitions wherever contact matters. On goals up to 400 steps away, Graph Anchors raise LeWM's
  success from 13% to 85% on PointMaze-Medium, from 8% to 87% on PointMaze-Large, and from 5% to 71% on Push-T, where stronger search toward the goal
  fails and where prior training-free planners break down under missing step horizons, subsampling shortcuts, or fragmented contact.
papers.summary: Planners for latent world models score a plan by the latent distance between its predicted end state and the goal image, and this distance is shown to fail in two ways: it loses directional signal a few steps from the goal, and it weighs the robot arm over the manipulated object. A ranking test on recorded data across five environments, six visual representations including `V-JEPA 2`, and nine `Meta-World` tasks separates the two failures. `Graph Anchors`, a training-free planner for frozen world models, builds a sparse graph over the model's training frames and aims each planning step at a node a few moves ahead on the shortest path to the goal. On goals up to 400 steps away it **raises `LeWM`'s success from 13% to 85% on `PointMaze-Medium`**, from 8% to 87% on `PointMaze-Large`, and from 5% to 71% on `Push-T`.

papers.title: PURA: Video Token Pruning via Unified Spatiotemporal Redundancy Assessment
papers.abstract: Video large language models incur substantial inference costs from long visual token sequences. Existing video token compression methods mitigate these costs by exploiting spatial redundancy within frames and temporal redundancy across frames. However, many approaches impose predefined processing orders or fixed allocation ratios for spatial and temporal compression, limiting their ability to adapt to the varying balance of spatiotemporal redundancy across videos. To address this limitation, we propose PURA, a training-free method that prunes visual tokens through unified spatiotemporal redundancy assessment. For each token, PURA constructs spatial and temporal reference candidates and selects the reference with the lowest representation error across the two dimensions. The representation error is combined with token importance to determine each token's removal cost. To avoid the time overhead of removing the lowest-cost token one by one, we introduce Coordinated Pruning, which iteratively groups mutually compatible low-cost removals into batches for simultaneous execution and updates the pruning state after each batch until the target budget is reached. Extensive experiments on three video large language models and five video understanding benchmarks demonstrate that PURA achieves a favorable trade-off between task performance and inference efficiency.
papers.summary: Video large language models are expensive at inference because of long visual token sequences, and existing compression methods fix the order or ratio of spatial versus temporal pruning in advance. `PURA` is a training-free method that, for each token, builds spatial and temporal reference candidates, picks whichever gives the lowest representation error, and combines that error with token importance into a removal cost. A batching scheme called Coordinated Pruning removes groups of mutually compatible low-cost tokens at once instead of one by one. Across three video large language models and five video understanding benchmarks, the authors report that it **achieves a favorable trade-off between task performance and inference efficiency**.

papers.title: AliceAI-Foundation-80B-A3B-Base
papers.abstract: We present AliceAI-Foundation-80B-A3B-Base, a mixture-of-experts language model with 80 billion total parameters and approximately 3 billion active parameters per token, trained from scratch at Yandex and released under the Apache 2.0 license. The model combines Kimi Delta Attention with full attention, uses Attention Residuals, and is trained with Muon. Training comprises general pretraining on 17.5 trillion tokens, two context-extension stages, and a dedicated stage for reasoning and agentic interaction. We describe the data collection and augmentation pipelines, evaluation protocols, architectural ablations, and scaling-law experiments. We identify the limitations of held-out training loss as a proxy for downstream performance and introduce an auxiliary loss on mixture-of-experts outputs to stabilize training at the predicted learning rate. Domain-specific data selection and augmentation improve factual knowledge, mathematics, and programming skills, while agent trajectories introduced during pretraining improve performance on agentic benchmarks after supervised fine-tuning. In zero-shot reasoning evaluation, the model achieves leading results among open base models of comparable size, with 88.7% pass@8 on IMO-AnswerBench and 82.9% pass@8 on LiveCodeBench v5-v6. To evaluate Russian-language factual knowledge, we introduce and release two benchmarks with their evaluation protocols: WikiWebFacts, which tests short factual questions drawn from encyclopedic sources and search queries, and HardMultiQA, which tests more demanding factual questions inspired by user interactions. Our model scores 86.5% on WikiWebFacts and 67.9% on HardMultiQA, compared with 83.2% and 65.4% for DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base (284B total and 13B active parameters) and 72.8% and 54.5% for Nemotron-3-Super-120B-A12B-Base (120B total and 12B active parameters), outperforming both larger models on these benchmarks.
papers.summary: `AliceAI-Foundation-80B-A3B-Base` is a mixture-of-experts language model from Yandex with 80 billion total and roughly 3 billion active parameters per token, trained from scratch on 17.5 trillion tokens and released under Apache 2.0. It combines `Kimi Delta Attention` with full attention, uses Attention Residuals, and is trained with `Muon`, with an auxiliary loss on mixture-of-experts outputs to stabilize training; the report also covers data pipelines, ablations, scaling-law experiments, and the limits of held-out loss as a proxy for downstream performance. The model reaches **88.7% pass@8 on `IMO-AnswerBench` and 82.9% pass@8 on `LiveCodeBench` v5-v6**, reported as leading among open base models of comparable size. On two newly released Russian factual benchmarks, `WikiWebFacts` and `HardMultiQA`, it scores 86.5% and 67.9%, ahead of the larger `DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base` and `Nemotron-3-Super-120B-A12B-Base`.

papers.title: EPPC-CARE: Staged Hierarchical Annotation of Communication Behaviors in Secure Patient-Provider Messages
papers.abstract: Objectives: Patient portal messages provide invaluable information about communication dynamics between patients and healthcare providers, but extracting it manually is labor-intensive. We developed and evaluated EPPC-CARE, an automated framework for identifying communication behaviors together with the supporting text for each classification. Materials and Methods: From 867 messages, we obtained 5,516 reference standard annotations. Each annotation is a triplet of communication-related text (span), a broader communication category (Code), and a specific subcategory (Sub-code). We evaluated EPPC-CARE's identified triplets across six open-weight large language models (LLMs) against supervised fine-tuning and communication-based models such as EPPC-OASIS. We also compared EPPC-CARE with human expert annotations on 100 messages. Results: EPPC-CARE improved performance over EPPC-OASIS across all six models. EPPC-CARE's Triplet F1 improved by 2.90 percentage points on average, with a best score of 64.4%. On the human expert evaluation subset, EPPC-CARE and the human expert showed comparable agreement with the reference standard, with differences favoring EPPC-CARE. Discussion: These findings suggest that identifying triplet components (span, code, subcode) sequentially can improve performance across model families while preserving the supporting text behind each identification. EPPC-CARE links the communication code and subcode with the source text (span), supporting human verification of automated annotations in clinical informatics. EPPC-CARE may therefore make larger-scale studies of patient-provider communication more feasible and provide a foundation for human-in-the-loop annotation workflows. Conclusion: EPPC-CARE offers a more reliable and reviewable approach for automated characterization of communication behaviors in secure patient-provider messaging.
papers.summary: Patient portal messages reveal how patients and healthcare providers communicate, but coding them by hand is labor-intensive. `EPPC-CARE` is an automated framework that identifies, in sequence, the supporting text span, a broad communication category, and a specific subcategory, and it was evaluated on 5,516 reference annotations from 867 messages across six open-weight large language models. It improved on the earlier `EPPC-OASIS` approach for all six models, **raising Triplet F1 by 2.90 percentage points on average to a best score of 64.4%**. On a 100-message subset, its agreement with the reference standard was comparable to that of a human expert.

papers.title: HAS: Hierarchical Adaptive Frame Sampling for Video Understanding
papers.abstract: Due to context-length constraints, most MLLMs cannot process full-length videos and therefore rely on sampling a subset of frames as input. However, existing sampling methods, ranging from uniform sampling to relevance-based selection, are often driven by a single sampling principle and thus struggle to accommodate the heterogeneous evidential requirements of different queries: some demand a holistic understanding of how the video unfolds over time, while others hinge on fine-grained events within a short temporal window. To address this limitation, we propose \textbf{Hierarchical Adaptive Frame Sampling (HAS)}, a two-stage frame sampling framework. In the first stage, \emph{Backbone Frame Construction}, we apply a Determinantal Point Process (DPP) to sample frames that are both query-relevant and non-redundant. These selected frames capture key moments across the video and form the backbone of the sampling set, providing a foundation for subsequent enrichment. In the second stage, \emph{Adaptive Contextual Enrichment}, we analyze the temporal distribution of the backbone frames to infer the query's requirements and adaptively allocate the remaining frame budget between Local and Global Context. The Local Context enriches the backbone with fine-grained temporal dynamics and short-range causal relations, whereas the Global Context connects temporally isolated evidence and provides a holistic view of the entire video to support global understanding. Through such a hierarchical two-stage process, HAS effectively addresses diverse query requirements. Incorporated into three leading MLLMs, it demonstrates consistently superior performance across the Video-MME, LongVideoBench, and MLVU benchmarks.
papers.summary: Multimodal language models cannot ingest full-length videos and must sample frames, yet a single sampling principle fits poorly because some queries need a holistic view of the video while others hinge on a short window. Hierarchical Adaptive Frame Sampling (`HAS`) first uses a Determinantal Point Process to pick backbone frames that are query-relevant and non-redundant. It then reads the temporal distribution of those frames to infer what the query needs and splits the remaining frame budget between local context around the backbone and global context spanning the video. Added to three leading models, it is reported to give **consistently superior performance on `Video-MME`, `LongVideoBench`, and `MLVU`**.

papers.title: Recalling the Past to Answer the Present: Context-Aware Multi-Evidence Reasoning for Streaming Video Question Answering
papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have achieved remarkable progress in video understanding, yet existing video question answering (VQA) benchmarks mainly evaluate models in offline settings. Real-world streaming scenarios instead require models to answer context-dependent queries by retrieving and reasoning over evidence distributed across the video history. We introduce StreamRecall, a benchmark for context-aware Multi evidence reasoning in streaming video QA. StreamRecall requires models to retrieve, associate, and reason over temporally scattered evidence to answer queries at the appropriate moment. It contains 4,983 questions over 462 videos, with context-aligned query times and fine-grained temporal evidence annotations. We further propose the Evidence Utilization Cascade to diagnose model reasoning through evidence localization, grounding, chain completion, and answer derivation. To enable efficient long-term streaming reasoning, we present EviStream, a training-free causal visual memory mechanism that preserves reasoning-critical evidence under a fixed KV budget. Experiments reveal substantial gaps between current VLMs and realistic streaming requirements, establishing StreamRecall as a foundation for developing evidence-aware streaming video intelligence.
papers.summary: Video question answering benchmarks mostly test offline settings, whereas streaming use requires answering context-dependent queries from evidence scattered across the video history. `StreamRecall` provides 4,983 questions over 462 videos with context-aligned query times and fine-grained temporal evidence annotations, along with an `Evidence Utilization Cascade` that diagnoses models through evidence localization, grounding, chain completion, and answer derivation. The authors also present `EviStream`, a training-free causal visual memory mechanism that keeps reasoning-critical evidence under a fixed key-value cache budget. Experiments reveal **substantial gaps between current vision-language models and realistic streaming requirements**.

papers.title: An Information-Theoretic Analysis of Information Hiding in Semantic Communication
papers.abstract: Semantic communication shifts the transmission goal from the accurate recovery of syntactic symbols to the reliable conveyance of semantic content, yet a systematic information-theoretic characterization of information hiding at the semantic layer is still missing. Building on the semantic information theory of Niu-Zhang and the classical information hiding theory of Moulin-O'Sullivan, this paper establishes an information-theoretic framework for information hiding under semantic communication. The classical hiding model is extended to a two-layer structure (semantic host, syntactic host, syntactic composite signal, syntactic received, semantic received) bridged by synonymous mappings f_s, f_x and the inverse mapping f_y^{-1}, subject to four distortion constraints: syntactic transparency, semantic fidelity, syntactic perturbation, and semantic destruction. The capacity is cast as a Stackelberg game with the hider moving first and the payoff J(Q,A) = I(U~; Y~ | K) - I(U~; S~ | K), yielding the single-letter maximin C^s = max_Q min_A J(Q,A), whose achievability and converse follow from random coding and joint typicality decoding. Relative to the classical capacity, comparison payoffs built from the up/down semantic mutual information give the endpoint sandwich C^s_end(0,1) <= C^s <= C^s_end(1,0) with the classical value C in the same interval, while closing semantic tolerance yields C^s_no-tol <= C_cl under a fair comparison. These results clarify that semantic hiding is not unconditionally superior to classical hiding. Binary, ternary, and Gaussian examples confirm the degeneration under one-to-one mappings and the capacity loss under coarsening.
papers.summary: Semantic communication aims to convey meaning rather than recover exact symbols, and no systematic information-theoretic account of hiding information at the semantic layer has existed. Building on the semantic information theory of Niu-Zhang and the hiding theory of Moulin-O'Sullivan, the work extends the classical model to a two-layer semantic and syntactic structure linked by synonymous mappings under four distortion constraints. Hiding capacity is cast as a Stackelberg game with the hider moving first, giving a single-letter maximin expression proved by random coding and joint typicality decoding. The resulting bounds show that **semantic hiding is not unconditionally superior to classical hiding**, and binary, ternary, and Gaussian examples confirm the capacity loss under coarsening.

papers.title: On Utilization of Edge-AI for condition monitoring towards predictive maintenance: A use case in dairy processing using explainable AI
papers.abstract: The Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) are driving Industry 4.0, enhancing productivity, automation, and efficiency in manufacturing systems. This study develops an Edge-AI-based condition monitoring framework, as a step towards predictive maintenance, for a rotary valve in a dairy processing pilot plant, using vibration data collected via a low-power IIoT sensor node and processed on an edge device.
papers.summary: Condition monitoring is treated as a step toward predictive maintenance in Industry 4.0 manufacturing, using the Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT). The study **develops an Edge-AI framework that monitors a rotary valve in a dairy processing pilot plant**, using vibration data collected by a low-power IIoT sensor node and processed on an edge device. The abstract reports no quantitative results.

papers.title: Sage-Med: Scaling Medical Multimodal Intelligence
papers.abstract: Establishing effective scaling laws for medical multimodal large language models (MLLMs) remains a persistent and fundamental challenge. Our systematic evaluation shows that existing medical MLLMs tend to underperform frontier general-purpose MLLMs across a range of medical tasks, while scaling model size primarily improves text capabilities rather than multimodal perception, and enabling reasoning modes fails to close this visual gap. To investigate how medical multimodal intelligence scales in practice, we introduce Sage-Med-Preview, a 35B-parameter medical multimodal model with 3B activated parameters, built by combining stage-specific curation over 322.7 million candidate records with a progressive training curriculum spanning medical pretraining, staged supervised fine-tuning, and adaptive reinforcement learning. Across this curriculum, progressive supervised refinement and adaptive reinforcement learning yield consistent stage-wise gains, substantially advancing both specialized visual understanding and medical language capabilities. Evaluated against 77 competing models across 238 clinical tasks spanning 61 public and 13 private multi-center benchmarks in more than 40 modalities, Sage-Med-Preview achieves an average score of 58.26% on the 31 public multimodal benchmarks. It outperforms the state-of-the-art open-source medical model Hulu-Med-235B-A22B at 50.99% and the general scientific model Intern-S2-Preview at 52.24%, and approaches the advanced proprietary model GPT-6.2-Sol across multiple tasks such as comprehensive multimodal understanding, report generation, and visual grounding. Although substantial challenges remain in complex medical reasoning and multi-step clinical workflows, this report provides empirical evidence, actionable data and training recipes, and a rigorous benchmark toward scalable clinical multimodal intelligence.
papers.summary: A systematic evaluation finds that medical multimodal large language models (MLLMs) tend to underperform frontier general-purpose ones, that scaling model size mainly improves text rather than visual perception, and that reasoning modes do not close the visual gap. `Sage-Med-Preview` is a 35B-parameter medical multimodal model with 3B activated parameters, built from curation over 322.7 million candidate records and a curriculum of medical pretraining, staged supervised fine-tuning, and adaptive reinforcement learning. Compared with 77 models on 238 clinical tasks, it **averages 58.26% on 31 public multimodal benchmarks, ahead of `Hulu-Med-235B-A22B` at 50.99%** and `Intern-S2-Preview` at 52.24%, and approaches `GPT-6.2-Sol` on several tasks. The authors note that complex medical reasoning and multi-step clinical workflows remain difficult.

papers.title: Procedure Inference as Memory: Learning Recruiter Decision Procedures from OKF-Structured Episodes in Multi-Session Hiring Assistants
papers.abstract:
Multi-session hiring assistants must infer evolving recruiter preferences and decision patterns across projects and time. We introduce Open Knowledge Format (OKF)-indexed episodic memory to organize interactions and retrieve related events through their lineage. We also introduce Procedure Memory, which learns reusable decision procedures from these episodes through prompted reflection or reinforcement learning. We compare these approaches with no memory, full-history context, and conversation search, and evaluate Jev-class models for index navigation and GPT-5.6 Luna as a lower-cost alternative to GPT-5.4.
  In our evaluation, OKF-indexed retrieval achieves low-priority preference F1 scores of 0.93-0.95 at medium and high preference overlap between hiring projects. It significantly outperforms full-history context and conversation search in both settings, and no memory at high overlap, while using 69% fewer context tokens than full history. Procedure Memory reduces conversational turns by up to 39% relative to no memory. Qualitative and long-horizon evaluations provide evidence of temporal reasoning, with RL-learned procedures achieving 60% on both correct abstention and exact-field identification. Jev-class models improve conversational efficiency but more frequently miss temporally relevant evidence, highlighting the importance of evidence selection.
  On PersonaMem-v2, Procedure Memory with OKF retrieval achieves 50.2% accuracy versus 48.6% for full-history context and 29.0% for no memory, using 90.5% fewer reader input tokens than full history. GPT-5.6 Luna performs comparably to GPT-5.4 at lower cost. These findings highlight the value of structured episodic memory and learned decision procedures for efficient personalization and temporal reasoning.
papers.summary: Hiring assistants that work across many sessions must infer recruiter preferences and decision patterns that evolve over projects and time. The system organizes interactions in an episodic memory indexed by Open Knowledge Format (`OKF`), retrieves related events through their lineage, and adds `Procedure Memory`, which learns reusable decision procedures from episodes by prompted reflection or reinforcement learning. `OKF`-indexed retrieval reaches low-priority preference F1 of 0.93-0.95 at medium and high overlap between projects while using 69% fewer context tokens than full history, and `Procedure Memory` cuts conversational turns by up to 39% versus no memory. On `PersonaMem-v2` the combination achieves **50.2% accuracy versus 48.6% for full-history context, with 90.5% fewer reader input tokens**.

papers.title: Tune for Retention, Not Just Gain: SFT Forgets Far Less than You Think
papers.abstract: Catastrophic forgetting, the drastic loss of previously acquired capabilities when learning new ones, is a central challenge in language model fine-tuning. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is widely believed to be prone to such forgetting. Recent works have attributed this to the off-policy nature of SFT, arguing that on-policy learning is key to continual learning. In this paper, we challenge this premise. We show that while maximizing new-task performance can induce catastrophic forgetting, alternative hyperparameter choices (lower learning rate and batch size) can yield similar gains with little to no forgetting. With hyperparameters selected jointly for gain and retention, vanilla SFT retains prior capabilities far better than previously suggested and can be competitive with Self-Distillation Fine-Tuning (SDFT), an on-policy approach designed to mitigate forgetting. While SDFT can be more robust to hyperparameter choices, it also requires a retention-aware criterion to identify hyperparameter configurations that avoid catastrophic forgetting. Our results challenge the view that on-policy training is what enables learning with retention and raise broader questions about what drives catastrophic forgetting during fine-tuning.
papers.summary: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) of language models is widely believed to cause catastrophic forgetting, which recent work attributes to its off-policy nature. The experiments here show that although tuning purely for new-task performance can induce forgetting, **a lower learning rate and batch size yield similar gains with little to no forgetting**. With hyperparameters chosen jointly for gain and retention, vanilla SFT is competitive with Self-Distillation Fine-Tuning (`SDFT`), an on-policy method designed to reduce forgetting. `SDFT` is more robust to hyperparameter choices but also needs a retention-aware selection criterion to avoid catastrophic forgetting.

papers.title: VisualMontage: Manipulating the Beliefs of Vision-Language Agents with Authentic Image Sequences
papers.abstract: As agents based on vision-language models (VLMs) increasingly interpret social-media content, errors in their analysis may lend credibility to rumors and amplify their spread. In this paper, we study the problem of visual cognitive collusion, in which coordinated posts combine authentic images and locally faithful captions to induce VLM agents to infer and accept attacker-chosen target claims through their own reasoning. To enable systematic evaluation of this cognitive threat, we introduce a new benchmark comprising 544 target cases and 33.2K candidate images across eight application domains. We further propose VisualMontage, a multi-agent framework for simulating such attacks through narrative planning, image selection and ordering, and caption assignment under iterative review. We evaluate this threat through extensive experiments across 12 vision-language models, examining modality effects, production-team components, and downstream defenses. Using identical attack feeds across models without victim-specific optimization, we demonstrate cross-model transferability, achieving mean attack success rates of 61.93% for proprietary models and 68.71% for open-weight models. Moreover, 92.65% of generated feeds pass independent model-based validity auditing. Even after downstream review, residual attack success rates range from 35.3% to 76.7% across the evaluated configurations. Our additional controlled comparisons further reveal that captions can improve model-rated posting naturalness while reducing attack success. Together, these findings reveal a novel cognitive threat in social-media interpretation and motivate safeguards that assess how authentic posts jointly shape agents' reasoning and conclusions.
papers.summary: Vision-language model (VLM) agents that interpret social-media content can be steered toward attacker-chosen claims by coordinated posts that use only authentic images and locally faithful captions, a threat the authors call visual cognitive collusion. They build a benchmark of 544 target cases and 33.2K candidate images across eight domains, plus `VisualMontage`, a multi-agent framework that simulates the attack through narrative planning, image selection and ordering, and caption assignment under iterative review. Using identical feeds across 12 models with no victim-specific optimization, the attack reaches **mean success rates of 61.93% on proprietary models and 68.71% on open-weight models**, and residual success after downstream review still ranges from 35.3% to 76.7%. Controlled comparisons also show that captions raise model-rated naturalness of the posts while lowering attack success.

papers.title: Do We Really Need an LLM for Weight-Space Programming? A Deterministic Forward-Only Paradigm and Its Capability Boundaries
papers.abstract: Recent work on Weight-Space Programming uses LLMs to edit neural weights with forward passes only, conflating LLM scripting with the underlying algebra of forward-only editing. We show that for core structured editing regimes, an LLM optimizer is unnecessary, and introduce Forward Weight-Space Programming (FWSP): a deterministic pipeline combining probing, localization, stratified operators (O1-O4), automatic blind routing (83.3% vs. 33.3% for a 27B LLM with the same tool library), and paired verification with zero additional per-token computation. For reasoning LLMs, we propose Protected FisherGate, a closed-form covariance-whitened readout edit orthogonal to normal-reasoning states: on DeepSeek-R1-0528-8B, a single frozen math-calibrated patch achieves 84.2% HumanEval pass@1 (1K budget; 75.4 +/- 9.4% across 3/5 Stage-4-passing subsets), beating 512-token-reserved budget forcing by +14.6 pp (-23.4% tokens) while transferring across HF-to-vLLM backends on full GSM8K and MATH-500. Across five modalities and thirteen models (50K to 27B dense and FP8 MoE), we further prove and verify two operator boundaries, subspace entanglement and frozen representation span, where FWSP-localized LoRA bridges forward-only and gradient adaptation.
papers.summary: Prior work on Weight-Space Programming uses a large language model to edit neural network weights with forward passes only, and the authors argue that for core structured editing regimes the LLM optimizer is unnecessary. Their Forward Weight-Space Programming (`FWSP`) is a deterministic pipeline of probing, localization, four stratified operators, automatic routing, and paired verification, whose blind routing is 83.3% accurate versus 33.3% for a 27B LLM given the same tool library. For reasoning models they add `Protected FisherGate`, a closed-form covariance-whitened readout edit, and on `DeepSeek-R1-0528-8B` a single frozen math-calibrated patch reaches **84.2% `HumanEval` pass@1, 14.6 points above budget forcing with 23.4% fewer tokens**. Across five modalities and thirteen models they also prove and verify two limits of forward-only editing, subspace entanglement and frozen representation span, where `FWSP`-localized `LoRA` bridges to gradient-based adaptation.

papers.title: From Models to Services: Systematizing Security Assurance for Model-as-a-Service
papers.abstract: Large language models are mainly delivered as cloud services, in which the assets of different principals are coupled within a single service pipeline, while the related security research is scattered across several fields with differing threat models. This paper systematizes this research from a service perspective. We decompose Model-as-a-Service (MaaS) into a five-layer stack and five trust boundaries, define six adversary classes and six security goals, use them to code 120 studies, and evaluate 50 defenses under a unified set of criteria. The results show that 44.2% of the studies concentrate on behavioral integrity, while service integrity, availability and cost, and accountability together account for only 13.3%. Defenses are evaluated on production services at less than half the rate of attacks, and none of the cryptographic or hardware mechanisms that protect against the provider can be adopted unilaterally by customers. Finally, we propose a research agenda by comparison with current standards and regulations.
papers.summary: Security research on large language models delivered as cloud services is spread across fields with differing threat models, so the authors systematize it from a service perspective. They decompose Model-as-a-Service (MaaS) into a five-layer stack with five trust boundaries, define six adversary classes and six security goals, code 120 studies against them, and evaluate 50 defenses under unified criteria. They find that **44.2% of studies concentrate on behavioral integrity, while service integrity, availability and cost, and accountability together account for only 13.3%**. Defenses are evaluated on production services at less than half the rate of attacks, and none of the cryptographic or hardware mechanisms that protect against the provider can be adopted unilaterally by customers.

papers.title: HoMe: Toward Practical Harness Optimization of Memory Systems for AI Assistants
papers.abstract: The behavior of memory systems for long-running AI assistants is governed by a harness, which consists of the code, prompts, and configurations for memory construction, maintenance, retrieval, and answer generation. However, optimizing the harness of a memory system remains largely manual, and unrestricted editing alone does not ensure structural improvements. In this paper, we introduce HoMe, an evaluation-driven framework that iteratively evaluates candidate harnesses and derives each new candidate from any previously evaluated harness by editing any part of it. HoMe combines session-level memory versioning with execution traces to identify shared failure mechanisms across cases and localize them to the responsible sessions and harness components. It encourages early structural exploration through candidate gating and reduces evaluation cost through smoke tests, adaptive sampling, and the reuse of constructed memory. We validate HoMe with the open-source memory system ReMe on two large-scale long-horizon memory benchmarks, LongMemEval-S and BEAM. With six formal candidate evaluations per benchmark, after a full initial evaluation, HoMe discovers harnesses that improve end-task performance over the originally strong harness while consuming far fewer query-time tokens. The code is available at https://github.com/agentscope-ai/ReMe.
papers.summary: The harness of an AI assistant's memory system, meaning the code, prompts, and configuration for memory construction, maintenance, retrieval, and answer generation, is still tuned largely by hand. `HoMe` is an evaluation-driven framework that iteratively evaluates candidate harnesses and derives each new one by editing any part of any earlier candidate, using session-level memory versioning and execution traces to trace shared failures to the responsible sessions and components. It cuts evaluation cost with smoke tests, adaptive sampling, and reuse of constructed memory, and uses candidate gating to encourage early structural exploration. Applied to the open-source memory system `ReMe` on `LongMemEval-S` and `BEAM`, six formal candidate evaluations per benchmark yield harnesses that **improve end-task performance over an already strong baseline while consuming far fewer query-time tokens**.

papers.title: DecisionReplay: A Corpus and Offline Simulator for Ensembling Decision Models
papers.abstract: Comparing ensembles, routers and cascades requires the output of every model on every item, and its cost. Stored collections built for routing keep no per-option probabilities. We provide a dataset on which ensemble methods, routers and cascades are simulated quickly, without new model calls. DecisionReplay holds the probability vectors of 17 commercial decision models, endpoints that return a probability for every answer option, on 35 benchmarks, with the token counts, billed cost and measured latency of every call, all released. A deterministic simulator replays any policy that selects, combines or cascades them. One well-chosen model per benchmark is hard to beat: pooling all models loses 2.7 accuracy points to it, and stacking gains 1.0 points at 3.4 times its cost. The models are wrong together: two that are both wrong choose the same wrong option in 72% of cases. The best router matches that model at 64% of its cost, and certified early exit cuts the cost of a stacked ensemble by 43% without changing an answer. DecisionReplay makes it cheap and fast to test whether a new method changes these results.
papers.summary: Comparing ensembles, routers, and cascades requires every model's output and cost on every item, yet existing routing collections store no per-option probabilities. `DecisionReplay` releases the probability vectors of 17 commercial decision models on 35 benchmarks together with token counts, billed cost, and measured latency for every call, plus a deterministic simulator that replays any selection, combination, or cascade policy without new model calls. The replay shows that **one well-chosen model per benchmark is hard to beat: pooling all models loses 2.7 accuracy points to it and stacking gains only 1.0 point at 3.4 times the cost**. Models also fail together, picking the same wrong option in 72% of cases where two are both wrong, while the best router matches the single best model at 64% of its cost and certified early exit cuts a stacked ensemble's cost by 43% without changing an answer.

papers.title: LatentRL-QAS: Transfer via Latent Reinforcement Learning for Quantum Architecture Search
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) emerges as a prominent approach to quantum architecture search (QAS), the automated design of quantum circuits. However, transferring what an agent has learned from one number of qubits to another is still weakly explored: the state, the action space and the neural network of a state-of-the-art RL-QAS agent all grow with the number of qubits, which makes transfer learning across qubit counts prohibitive. We make this transfer possible by introducing LatentRL-QAS, a latent space transfer and refresh framework for RL-based QAS.
