At its core, a circuit variational autoencoder encodes a circuit as one token per gate and maps circuits on any number of qubits into the same latent space. An RL agent navigates this space instead of adding gates, so its state, actions and network have the same size at every qubit count. The latent space is periodically refreshed with the agent's new discoveries and, for a larger system, grown from the solutions of the smaller one, so what is transferred is the representation of circuits, not network weights or past experience. To show transfer, we consider absolutely maximally entangled (AME) states, a resource for quantum error correction. LatentRL-QAS discovers the five- and six-qubit AME states without being shown them and prepares them in 89-99% of evaluation episodes, whereas the baseline RL-QAS fails to find them with the same budget, even with a network 10 to 17 times larger. LatentRL-QAS remains robust under depolarizing noise with single-qubit gate errors amplified 10x and two-qubit gate errors 5x compared with IBM quantum hardware. By decoupling the RL agent from the number of qubits, LatentRL-QAS lets quantum architecture search reuse circuit representations learned on smaller problems, providing a foundation for the transferable design of circuits across quantum optimization problems.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) agents for quantum architecture search (QAS), the automated design of quantum circuits, have state, action space, and network sizes that grow with qubit count, which blocks transfer between problem sizes. `LatentRL-QAS` uses a circuit variational autoencoder that encodes one token per gate and maps circuits on any number of qubits into a shared latent space, which the agent navigates instead of adding gates, and the space is periodically refreshed with new discoveries and grown from smaller-system solutions. On absolutely maximally entangled (AME) states, it **discovers the five- and six-qubit states unaided and prepares them in 89-99% of evaluation episodes**, whereas a baseline RL-QAS agent fails with the same budget even with a network 10 to 17 times larger. The method stays robust under depolarizing noise with gate errors amplified 5x to 10x relative to IBM hardware.

papers.title: ZeroHero: Training Small Language Agents from Scratch
papers.abstract: Large pretrained language models provide capable policies for interactive tasks, but how much model capacity is necessary for a specialized language agent? We introduce ZeroHero, a framework for training small language agents (SLAs) from scratch. In each environment, a large language model acts as the expert, and we collect its successful trajectories. We pretrain each SLA, which has fewer than 50 million parameters, to predict the expert's responses given the interaction history. We then post-train the agent on its own interactions using proximal policy optimization (PPO). During post-training, reasoning alignment supplements environment rewards with expert supervision on the language the agent generates alongside its actions. We evaluate the agents in three multistep environments where acting requires both understanding and generating language. In Crafter, agents interpret textual observations and generate reasoning before acting. In WebShop, they translate shopping instructions into search queries. In Alfworld-Dialogue, they ask clarifying questions and use the answers to guide household actions. The agents approach expert performance on WebShop and surpass their respective demonstration experts on Crafter training rollouts and held-out Alfworld-Dialogue tasks. An interactive demo is available at https://zoyav.github.io/-ZoyaV-zerohero-demo.
papers.summary: How much model capacity a specialized language agent needs is tested with `ZeroHero`, a framework for training small language agents (SLAs) of **fewer than 50 million parameters** from scratch. Each agent is first pretrained to predict a large language model expert's responses from successful trajectories, then post-trained on its own interactions with proximal policy optimization (`PPO`), with a reasoning-alignment term that adds expert supervision on the language the agent generates alongside its actions. Evaluated on `Crafter`, `WebShop`, and `Alfworld-Dialogue`, the agents approach expert performance on `WebShop` and surpass their demonstration experts on `Crafter` training rollouts and held-out `Alfworld-Dialogue` tasks.

papers.title: Carrying Feature Ablations Across Sparse Autoencoder Seeds
papers.abstract: A vision encoder turns an image into one vector per patch, refined layer by layer. A sparse autoencoder (SAE) writes each vector of one layer as a sum of learned directions, most with a coefficient of zero. Researchers call each direction a feature and edit the encoder by removing one feature. An SAE trained from another random seed learns different features. Earlier work matches the two SAEs' features one to one by how closely their directions agree. Matched features can point alike yet respond to different image parts, so removing them may change the encoder differently. We remove a feature and, separately, its match, then compare the changes in the encoder's output on the same held out images. When the second change nearly reproduces the first, we say the removal carries across seeds. A setting fixes a DINOv2 or SigLIP layer and its SAE feature count. At our tolerance, the removal carries for 12% to 70% of matched pairs across three settings. The share is 0% in two controls: an SAE whose directions stay random and, post hoc, matches shuffled among trained features. Post hoc, predicting which removals carry is more accurate with layer contributions than with directions. Some incorrect predictions remain. One persists on independent images. So pairs can be screened at the layer. Measuring the output detects errors this screen misses.
papers.summary: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) trained from different random seeds learn different features, and matching features across seeds by direction similarity does not guarantee that removing matched features changes a vision encoder in the same way. The authors ablate a feature and, separately, its matched counterpart, then compare the resulting changes in encoder output on held-out images, saying the removal carries across seeds when the second change nearly reproduces the first. Across three settings on `DINOv2` and `SigLIP` layers, **the removal carries for only 12% to 70% of matched pairs**, and for 0% in two controls using random directions or shuffled matches. Layer contributions predict which removals carry more accurately than directions do, though some errors remain that only measuring the output detects.

papers.title: Motion Beyond Pixels: Learning Future Visual Representations for Object-Centric Dynamics
papers.abstract: Many embodied world models predict future states in latent spaces optimized for RGB reconstruction, which do not explicitly prioritize object-level semantics and geometry relevant to motion generation. We present MotionRep, a visual representation world model that jointly generates future DINO representations and 3D object flow, coupling semantic and geometric information with object-centric dynamics. To make high-dimensional DINO features amenable to generative modeling, we introduce DINO-VAE, which combines temporal and channel compression with latent regularization to produce compact latents while preserving semantic and geometric information. Conditioned on an initial observation, object query points, and a language instruction, a unified diffusion transformer predicts future visual representations and 3D object flow through joint attention. MotionRep employs asymmetric modality-specific noise schedules to keep the visual stream ahead of 3D object flow during joint denoising, allowing progressively refined future visual representations to guide flow generation. Experiments on simulated and real-world manipulation benchmarks demonstrate that MotionRep outperforms pixel-based baselines in 3D object flow accuracy and generalization to unseen scenes, while requiring only three denoising steps for inference. These results support predictive visual representations as an effective future-state space for object-centric dynamics modeling.
papers.summary: Embodied world models often predict the future in latent spaces tuned for RGB reconstruction, which do not prioritize the object-level semantics and geometry that matter for motion. `MotionRep` instead jointly generates future `DINO` representations and 3D object flow with a unified diffusion transformer conditioned on an initial observation, object query points, and a language instruction, using a `DINO-VAE` to compress the features and asymmetric noise schedules that keep the visual stream ahead of the flow during denoising. On simulated and real-world manipulation benchmarks it **outperforms pixel-based baselines in 3D object flow accuracy and generalization to unseen scenes while needing only three denoising steps** at inference.

papers.title: REE: A Scientific Research Entrance Exam for AI Agents
papers.abstract: Autonomous research agents are emerging as a promising approach to scientific problem-solving across disciplines, owing to their growing ability to improve a solution through repeated experiments. Evaluating this ability requires benchmarks that pose open-ended research problems and measure improvements over established scientific methods. We introduce REE (Research Entrance Exam), a benchmark that tests AI agents on scientific research. It consists of 100 open-ended research problems spanning five broad scientific areas and 23 domains. To ensure high quality, every problem is drawn from active research in its field and individually reviewed by domain experts. Each problem is posed as a task of iterative improvement: an agent has up to 12 hours to improve a working starter solution, and REE scores the result on a common scale against an established expert solution evaluated under comparable conditions. By this measure, two of the four frontier agents we evaluate, Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol, outperform the expert solutions on 86% and 81% of problems, across all five scientific areas. Their runs also show how they do so: both agents surpass the expert solutions within the first two hours on average, and their best solutions mostly tailor or combine established methods of the field. REE thus provides a unified framework for evaluating autonomous scientific research, capturing both improvements over established methods and the research processes behind them.
papers.summary: `REE` (Research Entrance Exam) is a benchmark of 100 open-ended research problems across five scientific areas and 23 domains, each drawn from active research and reviewed by domain experts. Every problem is framed as iterative improvement: an agent gets up to 12 hours to improve a working starter solution and is scored on a common scale against an established expert solution evaluated under comparable conditions. Two of the four frontier agents tested, `Claude Opus 5.5` and `GPT-6.1 Sol`, **outperform the expert solutions on 86% and 81% of problems** across all five areas. Both surpass the expert solutions within the first two hours on average, and their best solutions mostly tailor or combine established methods of the field.

papers.title: Do We Still Need Reinforcement Learning When We Can Read the World Model?
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning has achieved remarkable success in sequential decision-making, but learning effective policies often requires substantial interaction experience. Model-based reinforcement learning alleviates this dependence by leveraging world models, which are typically used to support planning or policy optimization. In this paper, we investigate an alternative paradigm in which autonomous LLM-based coding agents directly synthesize control policies by reasoning over readable world models. By examining environment source code, these agents translate environmental knowledge into executable decision rules and iteratively refine their policies using online feedback or offline data, without task-specific RL training. Experiments across diverse decision-making benchmarks show that synthesized policies match or outperform conventional RL methods while requiring substantially less experience. Further analyses reveal interpretable decision rules and how they evolve through feedback-driven refinement. Comparisons with policies generated without source code access and experiments under challenging conditions further demonstrate the benefits of readable world models. These findings suggest that direct policy synthesis can reduce reliance on trial and error, challenging the necessity of task-specific RL training.
papers.summary: Instead of training policies through trial and error, LLM-based coding agents here synthesize control policies directly by reading an environment's source code as a readable world model. The agents translate that knowledge into executable decision rules and refine them with online feedback or offline data, with no task-specific reinforcement learning training. Across diverse decision-making benchmarks, the synthesized policies **match or outperform conventional reinforcement learning methods while requiring substantially less experience**. Policies generated without source code access perform worse, and the analysis shows interpretable decision rules that evolve through feedback-driven refinement.

papers.title: Multi-Party Authorization of Maintenance Prescriptions on a Permissioned Blockchain
papers.abstract: In industrial prescriptive maintenance, an equipment supplier's model may recommend an intervention that a plant schedules, a contractor executes, and a quality or safety function approves. A shared ledger records who submitted the prescription, yet cannot check whether the agreed model and decision rule produced it. We require permissioned-blockchain endorsers to verify a succinct proof of that calculation before releasing a work order. On a four-organization Hyperledger Fabric testbed using a public engine benchmark, this stopped all nine contested or mis-operated prescriptions, whereas hash checks accepted four that either raised simulated maintenance cost or reintroduced late failures.
papers.summary: In industrial prescriptive maintenance, a shared ledger can record who submitted a maintenance prescription but cannot check whether the agreed model and decision rule actually produced it. The authors require permissioned-blockchain endorsers to verify a succinct proof of that computation before a work order is released. On a four-organization `Hyperledger Fabric` testbed using a public engine benchmark, this **stopped all nine contested or mis-operated prescriptions, whereas hash checks accepted four** that either raised simulated maintenance cost or reintroduced late failures.

papers.title: DemoFoundry: Toward Scalable Photorealistic Robot Data with Coding Agents and Generative Rendering
papers.abstract: Scaling robot learning requires demonstrations that combine realistic visual observations with reliable action supervision. Simulation-based synthesis faces a substantial visual gap relative to real environments, while video-only generation struggles to maintain physically consistent interactions and provide aligned action labels. We present DemoFoundry, an automated framework that couples coding agents with generative rendering to synthesize photorealistic and physically grounded robot demonstrations. Coding agents both construct aligned real--proxy video pairs from existing robot episodes to train a video renderer and write executable interaction programs to generate new demonstrations. Given a scene reference and task instruction, an agent reconstructs task-relevant geometry and writes a control program without requiring target-task human demonstrations. Program execution in a physics simulator produces proxy videos with aligned robot states and actions. The video renderer translates these proxy videos into scene-consistent, photorealistic observations, reducing the need for detailed appearance modeling in each scene. Automated task-execution checks select successful trajectories for rendering and policy learning. Experiments show improved visual quality and action--video consistency. Policies trained on the generated demonstrations outperform raw-simulation training and approach the performance of training on an equal number of real demonstrations.
papers.summary: Robot demonstration data from simulation suffers a visual gap to real environments, while video-only generation struggles with physical consistency and aligned action labels. `DemoFoundry` couples coding agents with generative rendering: given a scene reference and task instruction, an agent reconstructs task-relevant geometry and writes a control program that runs in a physics simulator, and a video renderer trained on agent-built real-proxy video pairs translates the resulting proxy videos into photorealistic observations with aligned states and actions. Automated task-execution checks filter for successful trajectories, and no human demonstrations of the target task are needed. Policies trained on the generated data **outperform raw-simulation training and approach the performance of training on an equal number of real demonstrations**.

papers.title: RoboEvo$^2$: Recursive Robot Self-Improvement via Harness-Policy Co-Evolution
papers.abstract: Robots should adapt to unfamiliar environments and acquire new skills through interaction, then execute those skills efficiently with practice. Vision-language-action policies provide efficient control, but often need additional human demonstrations to handle unfamiliar settings; reasoning agents can discover solutions using broad prior knowledge and robot-control APIs, but repeated deliberation and repair are costly. Inspired by human learning through reasoning and practice, we propose RoboEvo$^2$, a framework for recursive harness-policy co-evolution. In Policy-to-Harness (P2H) evolution, policy failures guide a coding agent to search complementary Code, Code+ICL, and Code+Policy routes, consolidating verified solutions into reusable skills, routing strategies, and experience memory. In Harness-to-Policy (H2P) evolution, verified trajectories provide supervised training, while Counterfactual Preference Distillation (CPD) teaches the policy to favor successful corrections over failures from the same starting state. The improved policy provides stronger motor skills for subsequent search, while its remaining failures redirect harness evolution, closing the reciprocal loop. Through recursive co-evolution without additional human demonstrations, RoboEvo$^2$ improves standalone success from 11.0% to 84.1% and hybrid success from 30.4% to 90.5% on LIBERO-PRO, with similar gains and reduced agentic costs on RoboTwin C2R. Further experiments demonstrate autonomous task acquisition, cross-embodiment harness transfer, and 95.0% hybrid success on the Unitree G1-D. Our models and code will be publicly released.
papers.summary: Vision-language-action policies control robots efficiently but need new human demonstrations for unfamiliar settings, while reasoning agents can find solutions through robot-control APIs at a high cost in repeated deliberation. `RoboEvo$^2$` alternates two phases: in Policy-to-Harness (P2H) evolution, policy failures guide a coding agent to search code-based, in-context, and policy-assisted routes and consolidate verified solutions into reusable skills, routing strategies, and memory, and in Harness-to-Policy (H2P) evolution, verified trajectories supervise the policy while Counterfactual Preference Distillation (CPD) teaches it to prefer successful corrections over failures from the same starting state. Without additional human demonstrations, this loop **raises standalone success from 11.0% to 84.1% and hybrid success from 30.4% to 90.5% on `LIBERO-PRO`**, with similar gains and lower agentic cost on `RoboTwin C2R`. It also reaches 95.0% hybrid success on a `Unitree G1-D` robot and transfers harnesses across embodiments.

papers.title: Neural Rendering Compiler: Generative Video Models as Programmable Renderers
papers.abstract: Generative video models are becoming powerful renderers, yet lack the predictable control interfaces of conventional systems such as HTML/CSS engines or Blender. Their capabilities emerge implicitly from training, making it difficult to determine what they can reliably execute. We present Neural Rendering Compiler (NeurCo), which automatically probes frozen video models to construct model-specific capability manuals describing which semantic requirements they can reliably satisfy. NeurCo represents user intent in a model-agnostic intermediate representation of objects, constraints, events, and cameras, then compiles it into model-specific execution strategies. Reliable requirements remain unchanged, while unreliable ones are selectively rewritten or compiled into alternative execution strategies. We introduce VComBench, a benchmark of 380 compositional, multi-requirement tasks spanning text-to-video, image-to-video, and reference-to-video generation. NeurCo improves requirement satisfaction from 46.8% to 52.3% on Wan and from 66.5% to 69.3% on Minimax H3, and achieves further gains when combined with prompt enhancers, including on Seedance 2.5. Our analysis reveals model-specific differences in control capabilities and trade-offs between controllability and photorealism, highlighting capability-guided compilation as a promising approach to programmable generative video rendering.
papers.summary: Generative video models lack the predictable control interfaces of conventional renderers, making it hard to know which requests they will reliably execute. The Neural Rendering Compiler (`NeurCo`) automatically probes a frozen video model to build a model-specific capability manual, expresses user intent in a model-agnostic intermediate representation of objects, constraints, events, and cameras, and compiles it into model-specific execution strategies that rewrite only the unreliable requirements. On `VComBench`, a new benchmark of 380 compositional multi-requirement tasks, it **raises requirement satisfaction from 46.8% to 52.3% on `Wan` and from 66.5% to 69.3% on `Minimax H3`**, with further gains when combined with prompt enhancers. The analysis also shows model-specific differences in control capability and a trade-off between controllability and photorealism.

papers.title: Find the Clue, Not the Scene: Rethinking Reasoning for Entity Recognition in Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Answering a knowledge-based visual question requires first recognizing the entity in the image and then recalling knowledge about it. Thinking vision-language models (VLMs) reason for thousands of tokens before answering, yet it remains underexplored how well such thinking VLMs perform each of these two steps. We therefore analyze thinking VLMs on this task and make two key observations. (1) Recognition is the bottleneck, since 76.3% of errors across four models on ViQuAE stem from misrecognizing the entity, and 84.9% of these failures are resolved once the entity name is provided in the question. (2) Recognition is driven by entity-recall clues rather than by general descriptions of the image. An entity-recall clue is a distinctive visual detail that helps the model recall the entity, such as keys, a traditional attribute of Saint Peter. Based on these findings, we propose ClueRL, a reinforcement learning approach that extends Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with an advantage localized to the entity-recall clue in the thinking trace. Rather than injecting new entity knowledge, ClueRL changes how VLMs think: it leads them to attend more closely to visual details and spot these clues, helping them use the knowledge they already have. Consequently, it outperforms both GRPO and a perception-reward baseline on three entity recognition benchmarks. Moreover, this clue-seeking behavior generalizes beyond entity recognition, the only task used for training. Since recognition is the bottleneck, the gains carry over to knowledge-based visual question answering. They even extend to general multimodal reasoning, raising Qwen3.5-4B by 4.4 and 4.0 points on the ScienceQA and MMMU subsets of MMStar, respectively.
papers.summary: An analysis of thinking vision-language models (VLMs) on knowledge-based visual question answering finds that entity recognition is the bottleneck: **76.3% of errors across four models on `ViQuAE` come from misrecognizing the entity**, and 84.9% of those are fixed when the entity name is supplied. Recognition turns out to depend on distinctive visual details called entity-recall clues rather than general image descriptions. The proposed `ClueRL` extends Group Relative Policy Optimization (`GRPO`) with an advantage localized to the clue in the thinking trace, and it outperforms `GRPO` and a perception-reward baseline on three entity recognition benchmarks. Although trained only on entity recognition, the gains carry over to knowledge-based question answering and general multimodal reasoning, raising `Qwen3.5-4B` by 4.4 and 4.0 points on the `ScienceQA` and `MMMU` subsets of `MMStar`.

papers.title: Technical Report MEG2text: Beyond Alignment in Non-Invasive Brain-to-Text
papers.abstract: Non-invasive brain-to-text seeks to recover language from brain activity without surgery. A central challenge is turning learned brain-language representations into accurate word predictions. We present MEG2text, a decoding system that combines corrected training and evaluation, brain-text alignment, a class-balanced word readout, and target-word language-model fusion. On LibriBrain100's word-ranking task, MEG2text reaches 64.12% mean Top-10 balanced accuracy, improving on published MEG-XL by 16.92 percentage points across four corpora, with gains on each corpus. Controlled comparisons show that both implementation corrections and a learned readout contribute to this improvement. Candidate-level analysis reveals that some words receive informative scores yet consistently lose to competing candidates, while an identical-feature comparison shows that learning the classification rule improves decoding without changing the representation. These findings identify the decoding rule as a consequential part of non-invasive brain-to-text and show how system improvements can make better use of aligned neural features.
papers.summary: Non-invasive brain-to-text decoding must turn learned brain-language representations into accurate word predictions. `MEG2text` combines corrected training and evaluation, brain-text alignment, a class-balanced word readout, and target-word language-model fusion. On the `LibriBrain100` word-ranking task it reaches **64.12% mean Top-10 balanced accuracy, 16.92 percentage points above the published `MEG-XL`** across four corpora. Controlled comparisons attribute the gain to both implementation corrections and the learned readout, and an identical-feature comparison shows that learning the classification rule improves decoding without changing the representation.

papers.title: Evacuation Traffic Prediction for Dynamic Transportation Networks over Multiple Hurricanes: A Generalized Graph Learning Approach
papers.abstract: High traffic demand during hurricane evacuations causes severe congestion on major highways, leading to delays and safety risks for evacuees. Predicting evacuation traffic in real-time can significantly enhance evacuation management efforts. However, evacuation traffic is highly dynamic and uncertain due to evolving hurricane characteristics and diverse population response. Each hurricane has unique characteristics and evacuation contexts, resulting in different spatial-temporal traffic patterns. Moreover, the structure of detector-based transportation networks varies across multiple hurricanes. Hence, a model trained on the data from one hurricane may not generalize well for others. This study proposes a generalized dynamic graph learning framework using traffic detectors and evacuation data from 12 historical hurricanes. Leveraging the dynamic nature of transportation network, we develop a Graph Convolutional Long Short-Term Memory (GCN-LSTM) model that predicts evacuation traffic up to 6 hours in advance. For an unseen hurricane (Milton, 2024), the model shows strong generalizability, achieving an RMSE of 280.6 and R2 of 0.96 for 1-hour prediction, and an RMSE of 459.8 and R2 of 0.89 for overall 6-hours prediction. We also introduce a modular training approach, where we evaluate performance improvements by sequentially incorporating data from multiple hurricanes. The proposed model outperforms state-of-the-art baseline models for overall 6-hour prediction horizons. Ablation experiments show an 8.4% improvement in RMSE for the proposed dynamic GCN-LSTM model compared to its static counterpart. Traffic management officials can use the developed model to understand future traffic conditions during hurricane evacuation in advance and take proactive measures to reduce delays during evacuation.
papers.summary: Traffic patterns and detector network structure differ from one hurricane evacuation to the next, so models trained on a single storm generalize poorly. The authors train a dynamic Graph Convolutional Long Short-Term Memory (`GCN-LSTM`) model on traffic detector and evacuation data from 12 historical hurricanes to forecast evacuation traffic up to 6 hours ahead. On the unseen Hurricane Milton (2024), it achieves **an R2 of 0.96 for 1-hour prediction** and 0.89 over the full 6-hour horizon, outperforming baseline models. The dynamic graph formulation improves RMSE by 8.4% over a static counterpart.

papers.title: PoVi: Agentic Poetry-to-Video Generation with Knowledge Grounding and Figurative Understanding
papers.abstract: Poetry-to-video generation requires more than translating text into visual scenes. Poetic language is highly compressed, often depends on historical and cultural knowledge, and frequently conveys meaning through metaphor, imagery, and other non-literal expressions. We introduce PoVi, a benchmark and agentic framework for grounded poetry-to-video generation, evaluating semantic grounding, discourse coherence, and audiovisual realization. PoVi reconstructs poem semantics into an evidence-bounded representation and progressively transforms them into narration, interpretation, character assets, and shot-level visual plans, followed by narration-aligned video generation. Across three planning backbones and four video generators, PoVi consistently improves over single-call generation, with the largest gains on implicit background knowledge and metaphorical relations. PoVi provides a testbed for studying knowledge-grounded, long-horizon multimodal generation beyond direct text-to-video synthesis.
papers.summary: Turning poems into video is hard because poetic language is compressed, leans on historical and cultural knowledge, and conveys meaning through metaphor and imagery. `PoVi` is both a benchmark and an agentic framework that reconstructs a poem's semantics into an evidence-bounded representation and progressively turns it into narration, interpretation, character assets, and shot-level visual plans before narration-aligned video generation. Across three planning backbones and four video generators, it **consistently improves over single-call generation, with the largest gains on implicit background knowledge and metaphorical relations**.

papers.title: A Failure-Driven Data Flywheel for Post-Training Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.abstract: Pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) models rarely satisfy all behavioral requirements of a new platform, and teams without a large deployed fleet lack the data to address the resulting failures. We propose a failure-driven data flywheel for post-training such models. It constructs target scenarios absent from the available data by inserting task-relevant entities into reconstructed real-world scenes, and evaluates the model against each behavioral requirement of the target task. Failure rates form a failure map across task conditions and difficulty levels, which is re-evaluated after each round and assigns larger data generation quotas to conditions where the model still fails. We instantiate the framework in autonomous driving for occluded-pedestrian emergence and yielding at stop-sign-controlled intersections, and evaluate it on two VLA models and one non-VLA planner in simulation and on a real vehicle. For occluded-pedestrian emergence, five rounds of post-training improve the critical-phase collision-free rate on the sealed test set from 0.261 to 0.579 for AutoVLA and from 0.390 to 0.765 for ReCogDrive, while the unnecessary braking rate in paired control scenarios never exceeds 0.013. On a full-scale vehicle without real-world training, post-trained ReCogDrive achieves 4 of 5 safe passages, versus 1 of 5 for the base model. Fine-grained evaluation reveals a pattern obscured by the collision-free rate alone: both VLA models learn anticipatory deceleration before reaching the occluding vehicle, while braking after pedestrian emergence remains limited. For stop-sign yielding, the stop-before-line rate rises from 0.100 to 0.897 for AutoVLA and from 0.000 to 0.667 for ReCogDrive. With sequential training from the pedestrian-capability models, it reaches 0.599 and 0.358, respectively, while the pedestrian collision-free rate decreases by at most 0.032.
papers.summary: Pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) models rarely meet every behavioral requirement of a new platform, and teams without a large deployed fleet lack data to fix the failures. The proposed data flywheel builds missing scenarios by inserting task-relevant entities into reconstructed real-world scenes, evaluates the model against each behavioral requirement, and maintains a failure map that assigns larger data-generation quotas to conditions where the model still fails. Applied to autonomous driving, five rounds of post-training **raise the critical-phase collision-free rate for occluded-pedestrian emergence from 0.261 to 0.579 for `AutoVLA` and from 0.390 to 0.765 for `ReCogDrive`**, with unnecessary braking never above 0.013. On a full-scale vehicle with no real-world training, post-trained `ReCogDrive` achieves 4 of 5 safe passages versus 1 of 5 for the base model, and stop-before-line rates at stop signs rise to 0.897 and 0.667 for the two models.

papers.title: Maco-RL: Scaling Agent Capabilities with Mixed-Task Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Mixed-task reinforcement learning (MixRL) directly trains a unified policy across domains to continually expand agent capabilities without training separate specialists or requiring an extra distillation stage. Despite its appeal, scaling MixRL poses significant challenges in achieving stable and efficient mixed-task learning, effectively allocating rollout compute, and supporting continual domain expansion. To address these challenges, we propose Maco-RL, an approach that effectively scales MixRL. Specifically, Maco-RL employs a quota-based scheduler for asynchronous rollouts across multiple task domains, thereby stabilizing training by balancing gradient contributions and mitigating off-policy effects. Along an orthogonal axis, Maco-RL further introduces Tri-Buffer Sampling (TBS) to allocate compute among samples with varying levels of mastery, promoting sustained frontier exploration while preserving acquired capabilities. Experiments on five benchmarks show Maco-RL raises Qwen3.5-27B's overall score from 43.6 to 54.2 and then to 60.1 with continual expansion, reaching the frontier held by Qwen3.8-27B, which is further pushed outward by +5.7. Maco-RL also outperforms single-task RL with less compute for policy updates. These results support MixRL as a practical and compute-efficient post-training approach with substantial potential to strengthen general agent capabilities.
papers.summary: Mixed-task reinforcement learning (MixRL) trains one unified agent policy across several domains instead of training separate specialists and distilling them, but it is hard to keep stable, to allocate rollout compute well, and to extend to new domains. `Maco-RL` uses a quota-based scheduler for asynchronous rollouts that balances gradient contributions across domains, plus Tri-Buffer Sampling (TBS), which splits compute among samples by level of mastery to keep exploring the frontier while preserving learned skills. On five benchmarks it raises the overall score of `Qwen3.5-27B` **from 43.6 to 54.2, and then to 60.1 with continual domain expansion**, matching `Qwen3.8-27B`, which it improves by a further 5.7 points. It also outperforms single-task reinforcement learning while using less compute for policy updates.

papers.title: When the Proxy Is Wrong: Mismatch-Corrected Bandits for Adaptive Data Sampling
papers.abstract: Data allocation methods often use a small proxy model to select training data for a larger target model. However, this proxy can rank data differently from the target, leading to suboptimal training performance. To address this problem, we model the mismatch between the proxy and target models and incorporate it into the allocation decision. To do so, the problem is cast as a multi-fidelity bandit, where each arm is a data intervention. The proxy reward is observed every round, whereas the target reward is revealed only on rare audits of the same update. These paired observations identify arm-wise mismatches without assuming a shared offset or preservation of rankings. Mismatch-corrected bandits correct the proxy with paired residuals, audit only uncertain decisions, and pace the audit budget over training. From a theoretical viewpoint, we prove a regret decomposition and lower bounds under stationarity. These bounds show that proxy-only allocation can incur linear regret and that a minimum number of paired audits is necessary. Under abrupt changes, using the audit budget early can also incur linear regret. A sliding-window policy that spreads audits over training achieves regret of order $\sqrt{\Gamma_T T\log T}$ where $\Gamma_T$ denotes the number of change points. Experimentally, we test the approach in a closed-loop proof of concept on CivilComments-WILDS, where BERT-Small guides the training of BERT-Large. Mismatch correction improves worst-group accuracy over a target-only policy with the same target-model budget. Spreading audits over training improves worst-group accuracy by 6.3 to 10.5 percentage points at the same audit count.
papers.summary: Small proxy models are often used to pick training data for a larger target model, but the proxy can rank data differently from the target. The authors cast data allocation as a multi-fidelity bandit in which the proxy reward is seen every round and the target reward only on rare paired audits, then correct the proxy with per-arm residuals, audit only uncertain decisions, and pace the audit budget over training. They prove that proxy-only allocation can incur linear regret, that a minimum number of audits is necessary, and that a sliding-window policy achieves regret on the order of the square root of the number of change points times T log T. In a proof of concept on `CivilComments-WILDS` with `BERT-Small` guiding `BERT-Large`, spreading audits over training improves worst-group accuracy by **6.3 to 10.5 percentage points** at the same audit count.

papers.title: From Shared Patterns to Individual Evidence: Two-Stage Reasoning for Emerging Entities in Temporal Knowledge Graphs
papers.abstract: Temporal knowledge graphs (TKGs) continually introduce emerging entities whose interaction histories evolve from zero-shot debuts into sparse, bursty few-shot trajectories. However, current paradigms are fragmented: pattern-transfer methods lack catalog-wide event memory, whereas online memory models suffer from endpoint-role asymmetry that degrades unseen-answer ranking. Furthermore, sparse early interactions exhibit both long-range dispersion and local redundancy under skewed distribution. To address these challenges, we propose INSPIRE (Integrating Shared Patterns and Individual Evidence for Reasoning), a two-stage forecasting framework over a known catalog. In Stage I, INSPIRE learns an availability-aware shared-pattern predictor that fuses event-updated memory across the full candidate catalog while applying coordinated query- and catalog-side masking. Subsequently, Stage II freezes this predictor and optimizes a lightweight individual-evidence adapter (EA) combining textual semantic priors with correlation-weighted long-range event statistics under support- and role-balanced co-answer supervision with prior-odds debiasing and soft residual alignment. In addition, we decompose evaluation by endpoint roles and track longitudinal emerging-answer cohorts via query-micro and answer-entity macro metrics. Across four benchmarks based on the ICEWS and GDELT event datasets, INSPIRE improves Emerging MRR by 16.73%-88.83% over the strongest baselines. Relative to paired Stage I predictors, EA further increases Emerging MRR by 8.28%-32.63%, Answer-new MRR by 7.81%-41.24%, and cohort macro MRR by 9.64%-39.94%, gains attributed to semantic priors and candidate-level score competition suppressing mismatched established competitors without zero-support prior shortcuts. The official code is publicly available at https://github.com/KcAcoZhang/INSPIRE.
papers.summary: Temporal knowledge graphs (TKGs) keep gaining new entities that start with no interaction history and then accumulate only sparse, bursty events, which existing forecasting methods handle poorly. `INSPIRE` works in two stages: it first trains a shared-pattern predictor that fuses event-updated memory across the full candidate catalog, then freezes it and trains a lightweight individual-evidence adapter (EA) that combines textual semantic priors with correlation-weighted long-range event statistics. The authors also break evaluation down by endpoint role and by cohorts of emerging answers. On four benchmarks built from the `ICEWS` and `GDELT` event datasets, it improves mean reciprocal rank on emerging entities by **16.73% to 88.83%** over the strongest baselines.

papers.title: Bigger Model or Bigger Table? How Much Backbone a Chorus N-gram Module Replaces
papers.abstract: We ask how much of a transformer's backbone the Chorus N-gram module replaces. Chorus adds hashed tables of token bigrams and trigrams to its input and attention. We train models of 16M to 349M parameters on 1.34 billion tokens of Polish printed before 1918 and find the size of a plain model with the same held-out loss. A separate learning-rate search for each kind of model cuts Chorus's gain at 47M by about a third. With tables about as large as the backbone, Chorus then matches a plain model 1.34 times its size at 16M and 1.16 to 1.20 times from 107M to 349M. With these tables, each added parameter replaces at most 0.31 backbone parameters. Chorus trains slower than a plain model of its size and faster than one of the same loss. On a fact quiz the two differ about as much as two seeds of one model. The results rest on one corpus, one 8,000-token vocabulary and a fifth of an epoch.
papers.summary: The `Chorus` N-gram module adds hashed tables of token bigrams and trigrams to a transformer's input and attention, and the question here is how much backbone capacity those tables stand in for. Models of 16M to 349M parameters were trained on 1.34 billion tokens of Polish printed before 1918, and each `Chorus` model was matched to the plain model with the same held-out loss. With tables about as large as the backbone, `Chorus` matches a plain model 1.34 times its size at 16M and 1.16 to 1.20 times from 107M to 349M, so **each added table parameter replaces at most 0.31 backbone parameters**. Tuning the learning rate separately for each model type cut the apparent gain at 47M by about a third, and the results rest on one corpus, one 8,000-token vocabulary, and a fifth of an epoch.

papers.title: How Well Do Vision-Language Scene Graphs Serve as Memory for Embodied Question Answering?
papers.abstract: Embodied QA needs memory, but answer accuracy mixes retained evidence, reading errors and question priors. For a simulated multi-room scene-graph pipeline we define answerability: the fraction of questions a fixed rule-based reader answers correctly from the graph alone. The baseline recovers 24.1% of visible object types and its room labels flicker. Four targeted repairs double recall, raise answerability from 27.2% to 37.4%, and improve retrained QA from 71.4% to 75.9%, yet better object F1 can lower answerability. A question-type prior beats this reader on every predicted graph. In one real-video test, graph memory lowers accuracy. These exploratory findings favour scoring retained evidence alongside accuracy.
papers.summary: Answer accuracy in embodied question answering mixes together what a memory actually retains, errors in reading it, and priors over question types. For a simulated multi-room scene-graph pipeline, the authors define answerability as the fraction of questions a fixed rule-based reader answers correctly from the graph alone, and find the baseline recovers only 24.1% of visible object types with unstable room labels. Four targeted repairs double recall and raise **answerability from 27.2% to 37.4%**, lifting retrained question-answering accuracy from 71.4% to 75.9%, although better object F1 can lower answerability. A question-type prior beats the reader on every predicted graph and graph memory lowers accuracy in one real-video test, findings the authors describe as exploratory.

papers.title: What Is a Theory Worth to an LLM Solver? Measuring, Inducing, and Merging Theories in Context
papers.abstract: Mathematicians solve problems faster when they know the right theory. We ask how much a stated theory is worth to a large language model (LLM) solver, and whether a model can write that theory itself. In a length-matched protocol, adding the right theory to the context of Qwen3-14B raises pass@1 on pattern waiting-time problems from 0.37 to 0.83 and cuts the median tokens of correct solutions from 10.2k to 6.3k, while worked examples of the same length do not help. The gain shrinks as the solver and its token budget grow (+0.46, +0.26, +0.07), and at a long budget it comes almost entirely from finishing within budget: solutions that finish are correct 98--100\% of the time in every condition. To separate induction from recall, we plant unpublished theorems in custom probability families and measure how much of the oracle theory's gain an induced theory recovers. A strong open model, required to explore the training problems with code before writing, recovers 60\% of the gain on one planted family, 48\% on a second, and almost none on a third, where it finds the right form but not the condition that makes the form computable. No single induced note is complete, but a strong model that merges several notes recovers 61\% of the gain on the classic family, above the best single note (47\%). Theories are worth the reasoning they save, and models can find their pieces before they can assemble them.
papers.summary: The study measures how much a stated mathematical theory helps a large language model (LLM) solve problems, and whether a model can write that theory itself. In a length-matched protocol, adding the right theory to the context of `Qwen3-14B` raises **pass@1 on pattern waiting-time problems from 0.37 to 0.83** and cuts the median tokens of correct solutions from 10.2k to 6.3k, while worked examples of the same length do not help; the gain shrinks as the solver and its token budget grow. To separate induction from recall, the authors plant unpublished theorems in custom probability families, where a strong open model recovers 60% of the oracle theory's gain on one family, 48% on a second, and almost none on a third. Merging several incomplete induced notes recovers 61% of the gain on the classic family, above the best single note at 47%.

papers.title: Collect for Coverage, Replay with Evidence: Adaptive and Efficient On-Policy Distillation for Long-Horizon Agents
papers.abstract: Fully online on-policy distillation (OPD) is costly for long-horizon agents because each update depends on fresh environment rollouts. Prefix replay offers an efficient alternative by sampling current-student responses from stored histories, reducing idle time for long-tail rollouts and allowing each collected trajectory to support multiple updates. However, our analysis of the complete prefix replay pipeline identifies two limitations in long-horizon settings. In trajectory collection, teacher-only trajectories miss student-induced histories, while broader history coverage can reduce teacher reliability. In trajectory reuse, fixed position-based schedules cannot identify critical decisions that may occur at any trajectory depth. We introduce CARE-OPD (Collect for coverAge, Replay with Evidence) to address both limitations. Student-seeded teacher completions and response-level confidence gating expand history coverage while filtering unreliable updates. Hindsight replay allocation then uses downstream execution evidence to select consequential turns. Across long-horizon tasks Software Engineering and Deep Research, CARE-OPD outperforms online OPD and prior prefix replay baselines. On SWE-bench Verified, it raises task success to 59.5% while reducing end-to-end training time by 45% and environment actions by 44% relative to asynchronous online OPD.
papers.summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) for long-horizon agents is expensive when every update needs fresh environment rollouts, and prefix replay, which resamples student responses from stored histories, misses student-induced histories and uses fixed position-based schedules that cannot find the critical decisions. `CARE-OPD` has the teacher complete trajectories seeded by the student, gates updates on response-level teacher confidence, and uses downstream execution evidence to choose which turns to replay. It outperforms online OPD and earlier prefix replay baselines on software engineering and deep research tasks. On `SWE-bench Verified` it reaches **59.5% task success while cutting end-to-end training time by 45%** and environment actions by 44% relative to asynchronous online OPD.

papers.title: Reading Fine-Tuning Diffs Through Lenses: Model Diffing for Backdoor Detection
papers.abstract: We introduce a common scoring system based on token readouts to evaluate weight, activation and output-based model diffing methods for backdoor detection in fine-tuning processes. We also improve existing weight and activation based methods by incorporating the $J$-lens and its refinement, the $J{+}{+}$-lens. We test our setup in experiments where we compare a backdoored model with the base model from which it was fine-tuned. Our results show that incorporating the $J{+}{+}$-lens improves the weight-based method in all our settings, while the $J$-lens improves its ranks within single layers. The strongest single method is $\Delta W J{+}{+}$, the weight difference decoded through the $J{+}{+}$-lens of the base model, which ranks a token naming the backdoor among its first ten tokens in 11 of our 12 settings. Moreover, we show that output and activation based methods such as ADL and Diff Mining can easily break if the backdoored model is penalised during fine-tuning for giving the backdoor's words probability on clean inputs, whereas the weight-based methods are not affected. Conversely, permuting the hidden units or training only the layers that read the residual stream hides the backdoor from the weight-based methods but not from ADL and Diff Mining. No single method resists both attacks.
papers.summary: Model diffing compares a fine-tuned model with its base model to find what changed, and here it is used to detect backdoors inserted during fine-tuning. The authors define a common token-readout score for weight-, activation-, and output-based diffing methods and improve the weight and activation methods by decoding through the `J-lens` and its refinement, the `J++-lens`. The strongest single method, the weight difference decoded through the `J++-lens` of the base model, ranks a token naming the backdoor among its first ten tokens in **11 of 12 settings**. Output and activation methods such as `ADL` and `Diff Mining` break when the backdoored model is penalised for giving the backdoor's words probability on clean inputs, while permuting hidden units or training only layers that read the residual stream hides the backdoor from weight-based methods, so no single method resists both attacks.

papers.title: One Model, Many Modes: Evolving System Prompt Ensembles for Creative Generation
papers.abstract: Preference-aligned LLMs can exhibit mode collapse, concentrating their output distributions around a narrow set of high-reward responses. This limits creative generation, which requires quality, novelty, and diversity. Existing test-time methods often emphasize diversity, giving less attention to whether individual responses are both high-quality and novel. This distinction matters in practical use, where users may seek a single compelling, original response. We formalize creative generation as a multi-objective distributional optimization problem and introduce SEPO, a training-free framework for System Prompt Ensemble Optimization. The framework combines prompt evolution with greedy max-min selection to identify behaviorally distinct system prompts under a quality constraint, then uniformly samples one prompt per response at inference time. Across four creative generation tasks with increasing quality requirements and three open-weight models, SEPO ranks first in 8 of 12 settings on the harmonic mean of quality, diversity, and novelty, while no baseline leads in more than two. On average, it raises LLM-judged diversity from 1.92 to 3.43 and novelty from 1.00 to 3.34 over base sampling (1-5 scale), with quality decreasing from 3.72 to 3.30. We further show that expanding the optimized ensemble increases separation among prompt-conditioned response distributions. These results support system prompt ensemble optimization as a promising approach to improving LLM creativity at inference time.
papers.summary: Preference-aligned language models tend to collapse onto a narrow set of high-reward responses, which hurts creative generation that needs quality, novelty, and diversity together. `SEPO`, short for System Prompt Ensemble Optimization, is a training-free method that evolves system prompts, uses greedy max-min selection to pick behaviourally distinct ones under a quality constraint, and samples one prompt uniformly per response at inference time. Across four creative tasks and three open-weight models it **ranks first in 8 of 12 settings** on the harmonic mean of quality, diversity, and novelty, while no baseline leads in more than two. On a 1-5 scale judged by a language model, average diversity rises from 1.92 to 3.43 and novelty from 1.00 to 3.34, while quality falls from 3.72 to 3.30.

papers.title: TASK Memory: Beyond Text-Only Memory with Activation Steering and Knowledge Editing against Memory Hallucination
papers.abstract: LLM agents increasingly rely on external memory, yet they still hallucinate about what they remember. Often the correct memory is retrieved and placed in the prompt, but the answer contradicts it or the memory is applied to the wrong question. We call these use-time memory hallucinations. Across five open models, we find that they arise from the conflict between parametric knowledge and external memory and take three forms: memory-ignoring, where the model returns to a stale fact in its weights (up to 46% of queries); memory-misapplying, where it attributes the memory to unrelated entities (up to 24%, and 49% when retrieval is combined with weight editing); and version confusion, where 53% of answers about revised facts assert the superseded value when both versions remain stored. We propose TASK memory, which goes beyond text-only memory by combining a Text note with Activation Steering and Knowledge editing that share one in-model address. The text holds the content. A removable knowledge edit supplies the address through its subject key and supports multi-hop composition. A pair of steering vectors decides, query by query, whether the model adopts the memory or keeps its own answer; the vectors store no content and control how the text memory is used. On frozen models under a pre-registered, test-once protocol, TASK reduces memory-ignoring hallucinations to at most 1.5% in all ten model-dataset cells and cuts neighbour misuse from 39.2% to 7.5% (+10.8 pp composite on CounterFact). It improves a 300-memory library over BM25 RAG by 16.4 pp, an advantage that holds at 3,000 memories, resolves fact revisions without fact IDs, and adds 7.5 pp of multi-hop accuracy on MQuAKE. 21 of 23 cross-model comparisons (8B-27B, four families) are significant, and TASK beats three recent context-steering methods in 9 of 10 model-dataset cells.
papers.summary: Language model agents with external memory often retrieve the correct memory and still answer against it or apply it to the wrong question, which the authors call use-time memory hallucinations. Across five open models they trace these to conflict between knowledge in the weights and external memory, in three forms: ignoring the memory (up to 46% of queries), misapplying it to unrelated entities (up to 24%), and version confusion, where 53% of answers about revised facts give the superseded value. `TASK` memory pairs a text note holding the content with a removable knowledge edit that provides an in-model address and a pair of steering vectors that decide per query whether the model adopts the memory. On frozen models it cuts **memory-ignoring hallucinations to at most 1.5% in all ten model-dataset cells**, reduces neighbour misuse from 39.2% to 7.5%, and beats `BM25` retrieval on a 300-memory library by 16.4 percentage points.

papers.title: InterConRank: Joint Node Centrality in Interconnected Heterogeneous Networks
papers.abstract: Two nodes with identical connections within their own layer can differ in importance if their neighbors in another layer occupy different positions in the network. We introduce InterConRank, a centrality algorithm that computes a separate node ranking for each layer of an interconnected network. Directed dependencies specify which layers supply scores to each receiving layer. InterConRank normalizes each type of link separately and updates all layers together, so a score can cross into a layer in one iteration and propagate along its internal links in the next. We prove convergence of this joint update and evaluate the resulting rankings on four scholarly networks. On all four networks, InterConRank gives the highest rank correlations with both h-index and total citations for nodes in the collaboration layer.
papers.summary: In networks made of several interconnected layers, two nodes with identical connections inside their own layer can still differ in importance because of where their neighbours sit in another layer. `InterConRank` computes a separate ranking for each layer, with directed dependencies specifying which layers supply scores to which, normalising each link type separately and updating all layers together. The authors prove that this joint update converges. On four scholarly networks it gives the **highest rank correlations with both h-index and total citations** for nodes in the collaboration layer.

papers.title: Make the Adversary Spend More: Stateful Deception as a Cost-Exchange Primitive for AI-Era Cyber Defense
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are transforming the economics of intrusion by reducing the attacker's cost to scan and adapt, while tempting defenders into unbounded compute. We argue that cyber deception should be judged by the cost exchange it imposes, not by realism or detection, and that the primitive making that exchange favorable is adversary-specific persistent state. Rather than a honeypot that resets or merges sessions, each recognized adversary re-enters the world it believes it has compromised, kept coherent with its own past actions and isolated from every other adversary, while the language model acts only as a constrained renderer of explicit state, never as its store. We formalize the trade-off as a Deception Exchange Rate (DER), relating mission-weighted adversary effort burned to defender resources spent, and instantiate it in an SSH honeypot pairing Cowrie with a local LLM. In this paper, we focus on the defender-side evaluation of that exchange, while specifying, but not yet measuring, per-adversary state and the adversary side of the DER. Across five open-weight models, deterministic-layer and prompt optimizations cut per-session defender cost by around 63% against a naive all-LLM decoy.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) lower an attacker's cost to scan and adapt, and the authors argue that cyber deception should be judged by the cost exchange it imposes rather than by realism or detection. Their proposed primitive is persistent state per adversary: each recognised attacker re-enters a fake world kept consistent with its own past actions and isolated from other attackers, with the language model only rendering explicit state rather than storing it. They formalise the trade-off as a Deception Exchange Rate (DER), relating adversary effort burned to defender resources spent, and build an SSH honeypot pairing `Cowrie` with a local LLM. Only the defender side is measured so far: across five open-weight models, deterministic-layer and prompt optimisations cut **per-session defender cost by around 63%** against a naive all-LLM decoy, while per-adversary state and the adversary side of the rate are specified but not yet evaluated.

papers.title: DFly2: Turbocharging Long-Context Speculative Decoding by Sharing the Target's Sparsity
papers.abstract: To avoid the quadratic cost of dense attention over long contexts, models such as DeepSeek-V4 and Hy4 have turned natively sparse, and speculative decoding, which matters most where decoding is slowest, increasingly runs on them. Their drafters, however, still keep a context cache of their own, over the whole prompt or a sliding window. Beyond memory, such a cache costs prefill time, prefix-cache hits and decode concurrency. Drafters that read the target's cache avoid one of their own, but settle only which cache, not which positions, and still read everything or a recent window. Neither rule is made for the query at hand, and computing a selection per query in the drafter would cost more as the context grows. Yet a natively sparse target already picks positions for each query, over a cache it keeps anyway. Both of the drafter's choices are therefore already made, and paid for, by the target: its cache and its selection. We measure how far one selection carries: made a step early, it still covers close to nine tenths of what each later token selects on DS-V4.1-Flash. We present DFly2, a block-parallel drafter that shares the target's sparsity. Each draft layer reads the KV its paired target layer cached (KV sharing), at the positions that layer's indexer selected, a fixed number anywhere in the context (Index sharing). DFly2 thus runs no scoring pass and keeps no cache of its own. On DS-V4.1-Flash, GLM-5.3-Flash and Hy4~flash, whose sparse attention and architecture differ, it accepts more tokens per step than DFlash and DSpark trained on the same recipe, over general, long-context and agentic benchmarks. Its margin over the stronger baseline widens from 3.9%-10.5% on general workloads to 10.0%-31.5% on long-context and agentic ones. At high concurrency on DS-V4.1-Flash, at matched per-user decode speed, its throughput is 62% and 81% higher on two 64K sets.
papers.summary: Speculative decoding on natively sparse-attention models still relies on draft models that keep their own context cache, which costs memory, prefill time, prefix-cache hits, and decode concurrency. `DFly2` is a block-parallel drafter in which each draft layer reads the keys and values its paired target layer already cached, at the positions that layer's indexer already selected, so it runs no scoring pass and keeps no cache of its own. The authors measure that a selection made one step early still covers close to nine tenths of what each later token selects on `DS-V4.1-Flash`. Across `DS-V4.1-Flash`, `GLM-5.3-Flash`, and `Hy4 flash` it accepts more tokens per step than `DFlash` and `DSpark`, with its **margin over the stronger baseline widening to 10.0%-31.5% on long-context and agentic workloads**, and throughput at high concurrency is 62% and 81% higher on two 64K sets.

papers.title: When Every Rollout Fails: Splicing Learner-Conditioned Options into Long-Horizon Agent RL
papers.abstract: Group-based reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards often yields all-fail groups on long-horizon agent tasks: every sampled trajectory receives zero reward, leaving group-relative methods without a reward-based policy gradient. A common remedy supplies complete solutions from a stronger model, but full trajectories are expensive and expose the learner to long off-policy histories. We introduce SPLICE, which constructs local training targets from failed current-policy trajectories online. For each all-fail group, a proposal model selects a splice point in a current-policy trajectory and generates several bounded options from that point. We estimate each option's value using repeated current-policy continuations, convert positive estimates into a return-weighted local target, and fit the current policy on the options. We evaluate SPLICE across two policy families on two long-horizon agent tasks, Software Engineering with SWE-bench Verified and Deep Research with BrowseComp-Plus. SPLICE outperforms GRPO and full-trajectory guidance baselines in all four settings, improving over GRPO by 2.8--9.8 percentage points. On initially failed SWE tasks, it raises GRPO's graduation rate by 10.8 percentage points. Further experiments show that SPLICE improves performance while reducing costly proposal-model computation.
papers.summary: Group-based reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards stalls on long-horizon agent tasks when every sampled trajectory in a group fails, because group-relative methods then have no reward signal, and supplying full solutions from a stronger model is costly and far off-policy. `SPLICE` instead has a proposal model pick a splice point in a failed current-policy trajectory and generate several bounded options from there, estimates each option's value with repeated current-policy continuations, and fits the policy to a return-weighted local target. Tested on two policy families with `SWE-bench Verified` and `BrowseComp-Plus`, it beats `GRPO` and full-trajectory guidance in all four settings, improving over `GRPO` by **2.8 to 9.8 percentage points**. On software engineering tasks that initially failed, it raises the graduation rate of `GRPO` by 10.8 percentage points while reducing proposal-model computation.

papers.title: PersonaFactory: Stylistic User Prompt Augmentation with Synthetic Persona Bank
papers.abstract: Large language models increasingly replace real people in the AI development pipeline, as they are used to generate training dialogues at scale and to drive alignment and evaluation. However, out-of-the-box models produce monolingual and stylistically flat texts as synthetic user prompts, failing to replicate the real user-AI communication mechanics. We present PersonaFactory, an end-to-end pipeline that generates detailed user personas and uses them to augment existing user prompts from their point of view, producing a bank of over 740000 structured synthetic personas detailing their background and communication behaviors, and a corpus of roughly 1.24 million persona-styled synthetic conversations spanning 85 languages. We evaluate the effect of personal features on style adoption and intent preservation, using an LLM-judge and heuristic metrics to assess augmentation fidelity together with the downstream impact on assistant persona control through training data. Results show that our structured, attribute-based style representation enables per-axis control and better intent preservation at comparable style fidelity than free-text persona descriptions used in existing methods. A human expert evaluation found the augmented conversations plausible, with favorable ratings for intent preservation, style naturalness, and multilingual authenticity. Finally, PersonaFactory conversations achieve comparable performance to original training data on capability benchmarks, are preferred on real user prompts at equal reply length, and adapt their reply style more closely to users without explicit steering.
papers.summary: Language models used to generate synthetic user prompts for training and evaluation tend to produce monolingual, stylistically flat text that does not resemble how real users write. `PersonaFactory` generates detailed structured personas and rewrites existing user prompts from each persona's point of view, yielding **a bank of over 740,000 personas and roughly 1.24 million persona-styled conversations in 85 languages**. Its attribute-based style representation gives per-axis control and better intent preservation at comparable style fidelity than free-text persona descriptions, and human experts rated the conversations plausible. Models trained on the data match the original training data on capability benchmarks, are preferred on real user prompts at equal reply length, and adapt their reply style more closely to users.

papers.title: HOG-WAM: Improving Visual Robustness through Future Gradient Prediction
papers.abstract: World-action models jointly predict future observations and actions, yet visual corruption can disrupt the resulting policies. We introduce HOG-WAM, which adds future Histograms of Oriented Gradients (HOG) as structural supervision derived directly from demonstration images. An auxiliary HOG diffusion transformer (DiT) module reads RGB features through asymmetric attention, allowing its objective to shape the visual representation used for control. The module is used only during training and removed at inference, preserving FastWAM's RGB-to-action architecture. We evaluate four controlled observation corruptions through a visual-corruption extension of RoboTwin, termed RoboTwin-Plus; HOG-WAM achieves the highest success among the compared policies under all four. Mixed-noise success increases from 78.86% to 82.86% relative to FastWAM, with comparable performance on clean scenes. On LIBERO Plus, overall success increases from 74.49% to 75.26%, with the largest gain under sensor noise, from 74.14% to 78.89%. Across four Franka tasks, average success increases from 40% to 59% under clean observations and from 17% to 24% under noisy observations. A representation ablation favors combining RGB observations with auxiliary HOG prediction over replacing RGB with HOG. These findings support future-gradient prediction as complementary supervision for visually robust control, with larger absolute gains on physical tasks than in simulation. Code is available at https://github.com/iPPLab/HOG-WAM.
papers.summary: World-action models jointly predict future observations and actions for robot control, but visual corruption can disrupt the resulting policies. `HOG-WAM` adds prediction of future Histograms of Oriented Gradients (HOG) as structural supervision, using an auxiliary diffusion transformer (DiT) module that reads RGB features during training and is removed at inference, leaving the `FastWAM` architecture unchanged. On `RoboTwin-Plus`, a visual-corruption extension of `RoboTwin`, it has the highest success of the compared policies under all four corruptions, with mixed-noise success rising from 78.86% to 82.86%. Across four real Franka tasks, average success rises **from 40% to 59% under clean observations** and from 17% to 24% under noisy ones.

papers.title: Solve Vision with Code: Coding Agents Are Stronger Visual Reasoners Than Video Models
papers.abstract: Video generation models are increasingly evaluated as visual reasoners: given a first frame and a natural-language prompt, can the model produce the video in which the specified task is carried out? The paradigm is considered advantageous because the reasoning is native to the visual medium, unfolding directly in the frames rather than through language or code. Whether this native route is in fact the more reliable path to visual reasoning has not been tested against a symbolic alternative under the same conditions. We therefore pose the same tasks, with identical inputs, output specification and evaluator, to both media: rather than denoising pixels, a coding agent writes a program that renders the answer video, which an unmodified rule-based evaluator scores. On VBVR-Pro-Bench (Xu et al., 2026), a 500-instance suite spanning five cognitive categories with symbolic ground truth, the agent receives the same first frame and prompt as the video model, with no access to ground truth, metadata or generation models, and one attempt per instance. Three closed-model agents (Codex with gpt-6-astra, Claude Code with Fable 5.1 and Gemini CLI with Gemini 3.1 Pro) score 0.923, 0.894 and 0.893, each more than 0.22 above the strongest video model. Among 23 runnable open-weight models, the best, GLM-5, reaches 0.572, above all video models except the RL-trained one. Together, we show that for tasks whose solutions can be computed from a first frame and a prompt, program synthesis is currently a substantially more reliable route to visual reasoning than video generation. We further distinguish depictive programs, which navigate the image to recover a transferable scheme, from propositional programs, which operate on hard-coded values, revealing how visual reasoning unfolds in agent-written programs and what it implies for its nature of reasoning in general.
papers.summary: Video generation models are increasingly evaluated as visual reasoners that must render a video carrying out a task from a first frame and a prompt, and this study pits them against coding agents that write a program to render the answer video under identical inputs and the same rule-based evaluator. On `VBVR-Pro-Bench`, a 500-instance suite across five cognitive categories, three closed-model agents (`Codex` with `gpt-6-astra`, `Claude Code` with `Fable 5.1`, and `Gemini CLI` with `Gemini 3.1 Pro`) **score 0.923, 0.894, and 0.893, each more than 0.22 above the strongest video model**. Among 23 runnable open-weight models the best, `GLM-5`, reaches 0.572, above every video model except one trained with reinforcement learning. The authors also distinguish depictive programs, which navigate the image to recover a transferable scheme, from propositional programs, which operate on hard-coded values.
papers.highlight_summary:
Video generation models are increasingly benchmarked as visual reasoners, but nobody had tested them against a symbolic route under identical conditions. Here a coding agent gets the same first frame and prompt and writes a program that renders the answer video, and for tasks whose answer is computable from those inputs, that route wins by a wide margin.

- On the 500-instance `VBVR-Pro-Bench`, each agent gets one attempt in a CPU-only sandbox with a 30-minute budget, no ground truth or metadata, and no generative image or video models, and its output is scored by the unmodified official rule-based evaluator.
- `Codex` (`gpt-6-astra`), `Claude Code` (`Fable 5.1`) and `Gemini CLI` (`Gemini 3.1 Pro`) score **0.923**, **0.894** and **0.893**, leading in all five task categories against **0.670** for the strongest video model, which was RL-trained on the benchmark's own task families with the evaluator as reward.
- Among 23 open-weight models run through `OpenCode`, the best, `GLM-5`, reaches **0.572** and beats every video model except the RL-trained one, while the low scorers mostly fail to deliver a video at all, and the three closed agents sit within 0.030 of each other despite spanning nearly **an order of magnitude** in cost.
- Re-running 1,385 successful programs on sibling instances separates *depictive* programs, which measure the frame at runtime and transfer, from *propositional* ones, which only render hard-coded answers, with the depictive share at **67%** on Perception against **27%** on Knowledge and neither mode predicting score.
- The authors caution that the benchmark is itself code-rendered with flat colours and exact geometry, which favours programmatic solutions and may not transfer to real footage, and that the comparison is asymmetric because agents iterate with tools while video models produce one sample and their scores come from the published leaderboard, not reruns.

papers.title: Transferring Architecture as an Optimization Prior
papers.abstract: Initialization determines the optimization "fate" of a model, going far beyond just setting the scale of its weights. It establishes a fundamental initial geometry over the input data, dictating certain aspects such as which examples are considered close and which representations gradient descent will naturally refine first. In this paper, we view the initial geometry of a network as an optimization prior and ask whether a network can change its optimization prior by referencing a completely different architecture. To investigate this question, we use an initialization procedure where a target network is aligned to the representational geometry of a randomly initialized guide network before any downstream training occurs. Crucially, alignment to the guide network cannot transfer learned features, never receives gradients, and does not use labels. We demonstrate that this cross-architecture transfer of "fate" benefits the target network in two key domains: (1) instilling the optimization benefits of depth into shallow networks by aligning them to deeper networks, and (2) transferring representational granularity by using fine-resolution networks to shape the geometry of networks with coarser representations. In both cases, the alignment results in improved downstream performance of the target network. Ultimately, this demonstrates that a model's architectural destiny can be decoupled from its physical structure and explicitly modified at initialization.
papers.summary: A network's initialization sets an initial geometry over the input data that shapes which examples are treated as close and which representations gradient descent refines first. The authors treat this geometry as an optimization prior and test whether it can be borrowed from a different architecture, by aligning a target network to the representational geometry of a randomly initialized guide network before any training, with no labels, no learned features, and no gradients to the guide. Aligning shallow networks to deeper ones transfers optimization benefits of depth, and aligning coarse-resolution networks to fine-resolution ones transfers representational granularity. In both cases **the aligned target network reaches better downstream performance**.

papers.title: VulnSafe: Measuring Vulnerability-Aware Relational Safety in Large Language Models
